short_term_effects: A lacrimator. Chlorine is corrosive to the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract. Eye contact can cause permanent damage. Inhalation of the gas can cause pulmonary edema, a medical emergency that can be delayed for several hours. This can cause death. Rapid evaporation of the liquid may cause frostbite. Chlorine reacts with body moisture to form acids. Extremely irritating to skin, eyes, and mucous membranes; may cause corrosion of teeth. High concentrations act as an asphyxiant by causing cramps in the muscles of the larynx (choking), swelling of the mucous membranes, nausea, vomiting, anxiety, and syncope. Acute respiratory distress including cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, dyspnea, and cyanosis develop; later tracheobronchitis, pulmonary edema, and pneumonia may supervene. Death may occur after a few breaths at 1000 ppm.
long_term_effects: Repeated exposure may permanently damage the lungs, or cause chronic bronchitis. Chlorine may affect the teeth, resulting in erosion, and cause skin rash. A single high exposure may cause similar health effects. Chronic exposure to chlorine causes olfactory fatigue and tolerance to its irritant effects. Those with a history of prolonged exposure to chlorine may eventually lose their ability to identify incidents of exposure.
mutagenicity: NCI: equivocal evidence (rat); no evidence (mouse). Compound Description: Tumorigen, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data.
medical_surveillance: Special emphasis should be given to the skin, eyes, teeth, and cardiovascular status in placement and periodic examinations. Chest X-rays should be taken and pulmonary function followed.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 30 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Medical observation is recommended for 24-48 h after breathing overexposure, as pulmonary edema may be delayed. As first aid for pulmonary edema, a doctor or authorized paramedic may consider administering a corticosteroid spray. If frostbite has occurred, seek medical attention immediately; do NOT rub the affected areas or flush them with water. In order to prevent further tissue damage, do NOT attempt to remove frozen clothing from frostbitten areas. If frostbite has NOT occurred, immediately and thoroughly wash contaminated skin with soap and water.
Decontamination: Bubble chlorine through sodium sulfide and excess sodium bicarbonate solution with trap in line. For liquid spills: ventilate area and wash down spill with water.
personal_protective_methods: Wear appropriate personal protective clothing to prevent the skin from becoming frozen from contact with the evaporating liquid or from contact with vessels containing the liquid. Full-face gas masks with proper canisters or supplied-air respirators for excessive gas levels. Where very high gas concentrations or liquid chlorine may be present: full protective clothing, gloves, and eye protection. Saranex, Butyl rubber/Neoprene, Viton, Neoprene, butyl rubber, and Viton/Neoprene are among the recommended protective materials. Changing work clothes daily and showering following each shift.

potential_exposure: Highly toxic by inhalation. Chloroacetyl chloride is used in the manufacture of acetophenone. It is also used in the manufacture of pharmaceuticals, such as chlordiazepoxide hydrochloride, diazepam, lidocaine, mianserin.

routes_of_entry: Skin absorption, skin and eye contact, inhalation, ingestion.
short_term_effects: A tissue corrosive and a lacrimator. Chloroacetyl chloride can severely irritate the eyes and cause permanent damage. It is corrosive to the skin and respiratory tract. Corrosive on ingestion. Inhalation of vapor or aerosol can cause pulmonary edema, a medical emergency that can be delayed for several hours. This can cause death. The substance may affect the cardiovascular system. Exposure far above the PEL may cause death.
long_term_effects: Repeated or prolonged contact with skin may cause dermatitis. Lungs may be affected by repeated or prolonged exposure.
medical_surveillance: Attention to skin, eyes, and respiratory system in preplacement and regular physical examinations. Lung function tests. Consider chest X-ray following acute overexposure.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. If victim is conscious, administer water or milk. Do not induce vomiting. Medical observation is recommended for 24-48 h after breathing overexposure, as pulmonary edema may be delayed. As first aid for pulmonary edema, a doctor or authorized paramedic may consider administering a corticosteroid spray.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing to prevent any reasonable probability of skin contact. 4h (at least 4 h but <8 h resistance): Teflon gloves, suits, boots. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof chemical goggles and face shield unless full face-piece respiratory protection is worn. Employees should wash immediately with soap when skin is wet or contaminated. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.
respirator_selection: At any concentrations above the NIOSH REL, or where there is no REL, at any detectable concentration: SCBAF:Pd,Pp (APF=10,000) or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA (APF=10,000).
storage: Color Code White: Corrosive or Contact Hazard; Store separately in a corrosion-resistant location. Store in tightly closed containers in a cool, well-ventilated area away from water, steam, heat, and combustibles. Sources of ignition prohibited.
shipping: Chloroacetyl chloride must carry a CORROSIVE label. Hazard Class 8, Packing Group I.
spill_handling: Evacuate and restrict persons not wearing protective equipment. Remove all ignition sources. Ventilate area. Soak up spill with quicklime, sodium/potassium chloride, or absorb in vermiculite, dry sand, earth, peat, carbon, or similar material and deposit in sealed containers. fire_extinguishing: This chemical is a nonflammable liquid. Do not use water or water-based extinguishers. Use extinguishing agent suitable for surrounding fire. This chemical decomposes in heat, producing phosgene, chlorine, and hydrogen chloride. From a secure, explosion-proof location, use water spray to cool exposed containers.
disposal_method: It may be discharged into sodium bicarbonate solution, then flushed to the sewer with water.

short_term_effects: The liquid can irritate and burn the skin. The vapor can irritate the eyes, nose, and throat. long_term_effects: May cause damage to the lungs, blood, nervous system, liver, and kidneys. Repeated exposure to the liquid may cause skin burns. points_of_attack: Respiratory system, eyes, skin, central nervous system, liver.

medical_surveillance: For those with frequent or potentially high exposure (half the TLV or greater, or significant skin contact): liver function tests before beginning work and at regular times after. If symptoms develop: lung and kidney function tests. Interview for brain effects.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit.
personal_protective_methods: Wear solvent-resistant gloves and clothing. 8h: Viton gloves, suits, Barricade coated suits; Responder suits, Trellchem HPS suits; Trychem 1000 suits. 4h: polyvinyl alcohol gloves; Teflon gloves, suits, boots. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof chemical goggles and face shield unless full face-piece respiratory protection is worn. Remove nonimpervious clothing immediately if wet or contaminated. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.

spill_handling: Evacuate and restrict persons not wearing protective equipment. Remove all ignition sources. Establish forced ventilation to keep levels below explosive limit. ld50: Can lower ability of blood to carry oxygen (methemoglobinemia) causing blue skin, headaches, dizziness, nausea, and death. Can damage kidneys and bladder causing painful, bloody urine.
routes_of_entry: Inhalation, skin contact, ingestion. These chemicals can be absorbed through the skin, thereby increasing exposure.
short_term_effects: Chloromethyl anilines can affect you when breathed in and by passing through your skin. Eye contact causes irritation and can lead to permanent damage. Skin contact can cause a rash and produce a burning feeling. Exposure can lower the ability of the blood to carry oxygen (methemoglobinemia) causing a bluish color of the skin, headaches, dizziness, nausea, and even death. They can damage the kidneys and bladder, causing painful, bloody urine.
long_term_effects: The methemoglobinemia condition may occur gradually from repeated exposure or all at once. Some of these chemicals like 4-chloro-2-methyl aniline and 5-chloro-2-methyl aniline are probable carcinogens in humans; they cause bladder and liver cancer in animals.

medical_surveillance: If symptoms develop or overexposure has occurred: blood tests for methemoglobin levels. Kidney function tests. Urine tests for blood and for n-acetyl p-aminophenol.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Note to physician: Treat for methemoglobinemia. Spectrophotometry may be required for precise determination of levels of methemoglobinemia in urine.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing. Contact lenses should not be worn. When working with liquids or solids wear indirect-vent, impact-resistant chemical goggles and face shield unless full face-piece respiratory protection is worn. Employees should wash immediately with soap when skin is wet or contaminated. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.

first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. If frostbite has occurred, seek medical attention immediately; do NOT rub the affected areas or flush them with water. In order to prevent further tissue damage, do NOT attempt to remove frozen clothing from frostbitten areas. If frostbite has NOT occurred, immediately and thoroughly wash contaminated skin with soap and water.

potential_exposure: Compound Description: Agricultural Chemical; Tumorigen, Mutagen; Human Data. Chloropicrin is an important insecticide and is used in the manufacture of the dyestuff methyl violet and in other organic syntheses. It is used as a fumigant insecticide. It is a riot control and tear agent and has been used as a military poison gas. Some forms of tear gas also contain chloropicrin. Since tank trucks, tank cars, and tank vessels carry this throughout the world in large quantities, it is a potential problem.
incompatibilities: Chloropicrin decomposes explosively when heated above 112 deg C. It can be dangerously self-reactive; and may explode when heated under confinement or if shocked. Explosively breaks down releasing nitrogen oxides, nitrosyl chloride, chlorine, phosgene, and carbon monoxide. Liquid chloropicrin is unstable with high temperatures or severe shock, particularly when involving containers of greater than 30 gallons capacity. Reacts violently with aniline, sodium methoxide, and propargyl bromide; 2-bromopropyne and strong oxidizers. Violent reaction with reducing agents; aniline (especially in presence of heat); alcoholic sodium hydroxide. Quickly elevated temperatures, shock, contact with alkali metals or alkaline earth may cause explosions. Strong acid; reacts violently with bases and alkali materials. Liquid attacks some plastics, rubber, and coatings. Reacts with iron, zinc, light metals (Al, Mg and alloys). Reacts, sometimes violently, with some types of rubbers, plastics, sulfuric acid, and bases. Contact with metals may evolve explosive hydrogen gas.

short_term_effects: Chloropicrin was used as poison gas in WW1. Exposure causes intense tearing of the eyes, headache, nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, and cough. Contact can severely irritate the skin causing rash or burning sensation. Higher exposures can irritate and burn the lungs, causing a buildup of fluid (pulmonary edema), a medical emergency that can be delayed for several hours. This can cause death. LD50 (rat): 250 mg/kg.
long_term_effects: Repeated exposure can damage the lungs, causing bronchitis. It may also damage the liver and kidneys.

medical_surveillance: Before beginning employment and at regular times after: lung function tests. If symptoms develop or overexposure has occurred: liver and kidney function tests. Consider chest X-ray following acute overexposure. NIOSH suggests the following tests: electrocardiogram, expired air, pulmonary function tests (FVC and FEV1), sputum cytology, and white blood cell count/differential.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Medical observation is recommended for 24-48 h after breathing overexposure, as pulmonary edema may be delayed. As first aid for pulmonary edema, a doctor or authorized paramedic may consider administering a corticosteroid spray.
Decontamination: Decontaminate as soon as possible. This is extremely important. Use clean water from any source. Wash-strip-wash-evacuate upwind and uphill (WSWU protocol). Flush eyes with water for at least 15 min. Wash victim with warm water and soap. Decontaminate with diluted household bleach (10%, one part bleach to nine parts water); do not let bleach get in eyes, open wounds, or mouth. Rinse off bleach solution after 15 min. Be certain victims are decontaminated before leaving decontamination area.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing. The International Technical Information Institute recommends wearing Neoprene gloves. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof chemical goggles and face shield unless full face-piece respiratory protection is worn. Employees should wash immediately with soap when skin is wet. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.

Must be stored to avoid contact with strong oxidizers (chlorine, chlorine dioxide) since violent reactions occur. Store in tightly closed containers in cool, well-ventilated area away from heat. High temperatures or severe shock may cause an explosion, particularly with containers >30 gallons. Where possible automatically pump from storage to process. Sources of ignition prohibited.

spill_handling: Evacuate and restrict persons not wearing protective equipment. Remove all ignition sources. Ventilate area. Absorb in vermiculite, dry sand, earth, peat, carbon, or similar material and deposit in sealed containers. fire_extinguishing: Chloropicrin is a noncombustible liquid. However, if a chloropicrin tank is adjacent to a fire, the tank will heat causing extremely high pressurization and explosion. Evacuate area. Even if tank does not fail, safety valve may open releasing chloropicrin. If necessary fight fire from explosion-resistant location. When heated, chloropicrin breaks down to phosgene. At high temperature violently breaks down to several poisonous gases including HCl and nitrous vapors. Danger from heated chloropicrin tank is too great to risk a manned firefighting effort; if possible, an unattended fire monitor aimed at the upper part of the tank will cool the tank and may prevent failure. If there is a reason to extinguish a nearby fire, use agent appropriate for that fuel (water, ordinary foam, alcohol foam, or dry chemical).
disposal_method: (1) Incineration (816 deg C, 0.5 s minimum primary combustion; 1204 deg C, 1.0 s secondary combustion) after mixing with other fuel. Formation of elemental chlorine may be prevented by injection of steam or using methane as fuel. (2) Chloropicrin reacts readily with alcoholic sodium sulfite solutions to produce methanetrisulfonic acid (relatively nonvolatile and less harmful) - recommended for treating spills and cleaning equipment. (3) Rapid reaction with ammonia to produce guanidine (LD50=500 mg/kg) could be used for detoxification. (4) Pour or sift over soda ash, mix and wash slowly into large tank, neutralize and pass to sewer with excess water. (5) Absorb on vermiculite, mix and shovel into paper boxes, drop into incinerator with afterburner and scrubber.

first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. long_term_effects: May cause skin allergy with itching and rash. Some related chromium compounds are known carcinogens; although this chemical has not been identified as a carcinogen, it should be handled with extreme caution.
mutagenicity: IARC Group 3, 1997 (not classifiable).
medical_surveillance: Lung function tests. Consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure. Evaluation by a qualified allergist. NIOSH lists [chromium(III) compounds]: whole blood (chemical/metabolite); biologic tissue/biopsy; chest X-ray; pulmonary function tests; red blood cells/count; urine (chemical/metabolite) [end-of-shift] [end-of-shift at end-of-work-week] [end-of-work-week] [pre- & postshift].
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. If victim is conscious, administer water or milk. Do not induce vomiting.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing to prevent any reasonable probability of skin contact. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear dust-proof chemical goggles and face shield unless full face-piece respiratory protection is worn. Employees should wash immediately with soap when skin is wet or contaminated. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.
respirator_selection: Up to 2.5 mg/m3: Qm* (APF=25). Up to 5 mg/m3: 95XQ* (APF=10) or Sa* (APF=10). Up to 12.5 mg/m3: Sa:Cf* or PaprHie*. storage: Color Code White: Corrosive or Contact Hazard; Store separately in a corrosion-resistant location. Must be stored to avoid contact with water and other incompatible materials since violent reactions occur. Store in tightly closed containers in a cool, well-ventilated area away from flammable and combustible materials.
shipping: Chromosulfuric acid requires a CORROSIVE label. Hazard Class 8, Packing Group I.
spill_handling: Evacuate persons not wearing protective equipment. Remove all ignition sources. Collect powdered material in the most convenient and safe manner and deposit in sealed containers. Ventilate area after cleanup. Keep out of confined spaces (sewer) because of possibility of explosion. OSHA 1910.120(q) may be applicable.
fire_extinguishing: Chromosulfuric acid may burn but does not readily ignite. It will increase the intensity of a fire since it is an oxidizer. Use dry chemical or CO2 extinguishers. Use water spray to keep fire-exposed containers cool, but do not get water inside containers. Poisonous gases produced in fire including sulfur oxides and chromium.

Higher exposures can cause pulmonary edema (delayed several hours; can cause death). Ingestion: vomiting, diarrhea, sensation of hotness.
long_term_effects: Repeated or prolonged inhalation may cause asthma-like disease with cough and dyspnea; may progress to interstitial pneumonia with marked fibrosis. Gloves and barrier creams may help prevent dermatitis. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.

first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. If victim is conscious, administer water or milk. Do not induce vomiting.

short_term_effects: Irritates eyes, skin, and respiratory tract. Skin contact may cause burning sensation and/or rash. long_term_effects: Drying and cracking of the skin. May cause lung, liver, and kidney damage. medical_surveillance: Points of attack in preplacement and periodic physical examinations. Interview for brain effects including recent memory, mood, concentration, altered sleep patterns; nervous system evaluation. NIOSH tests: whole blood (chemical/metabolite); expired air; urine (chemical/metabolite): last 2 h of 8-h exposure; urine (chemical/metabolite).
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Do not induce vomiting when this chemical has been swallowed (aspiration hazard for hydrocarbons). Note: promptly remove nonimpervious clothing when wet or contaminated.
personal_protective_methods: Wear appropriate clothing to prevent repeated or prolonged skin contact. Remove nonimpervious clothing promptly if contaminated or wet. 8h (>8h resistance): Tychem 1000 suits. 4h (at least 4 but <8h resistance): Teflon gloves/suits/boots. Chlorinated polyethylene (CPE) also recommended. Wear eye protection to prevent any reasonable probability of eye contact. Employees should wash promptly when skin is wet or contaminated. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.
respirator_selection: 500 ppm: CcrOv (APF=10) or Sa (APF=10). 1000 ppm: Sa:Cf (APF=25) or PaprOv (APF=25) or CcrFOv (APF=50) or GmFOv (APF=50) or SCBAF (APF=50) or SaF (APF=50). Emergency/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp (APF=10,000) or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA (APF=10,000). Escape: GmFOv (APF=50) or SCBAE. Note: substance reported to cause eye irritation or damage; may require eye protection.
storage: Color Code Red: Flammability Hazard: Store in a flammable liquid storage area or approved cabinet away from ignition sources and corrosive and reactive materials. May form peroxides in storage. Store to avoid contact with oxidizers (permanganates, nitrites, peroxides, chlorates, perchlorates) since violent reactions occur. Store in tightly closed containers in a cool, well-ventilated area away from heat. Sources of ignition prohibited. Metal containers involving the transfer of 5 gallons or more should be grounded and bonded. Drums equipped with self-closing valves, pressure vacuum bungs, and flame arresters. Only nonsparking tools.
shipping: Cumene requires a FLAMMABLE LIQUID label. Hazard Class 3 and Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate and restrict persons not wearing protective equipment. Remove all ignition sources. Establish forced ventilation to keep levels below explosive limit. Absorb liquids in vermiculite, dry sand, earth, peat, carbon, or a similar material and deposit in sealed containers. OSHA 1910.120(q) may be applicable.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible liquid. Poisonous gases produced in fire. Use dry chemical, CO2, or alcohol foam extinguishers. Vapors heavier than air; collect in low areas. Vapors may travel long distances to ignition and flashback. Containers may explode in fire; may rocket.
disposal_method: Dissolve or mix the material with a combustible solvent and burn in a chemical incinerator equipped with an afterburner and scrubber. All federal, state, and local environmental regulations must be observed.

short_term_effects: Skin and eye contact can cause irritation and burns. Inhalation can irritate the nose and throat, causing coughing and wheezing. Cupric nitrate may produce fumes that can cause metal fume fever. Ingestion causes salivation, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain. May cause blood effects if swallowed. High exposure can cause unconsciousness. LD50(oral-rat)=940 mg/kg (slightly toxic).
long_term_effects: Repeated exposure can cause copper to deposit in various parts of the body. Large deposits can make the skin and hair a green color. Repeated exposure can cause shrinking of the inner lining of the nose, and may cause runny nose and sores. Excess deposits in the liver can cause liver damage. Metallic taste may also occur. Skin allergy with rash sometimes occurs. If allergy develops, even small future exposures can trigger rash. Repeated exposures can also cause thickening of the skin.
mutagenicity: Not listed as carcinogen. Strong oxidizer.
medical_surveillance: Lung function tests. Urine test for copper. Evaluation by qualified allergist. Liver function tests.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Note to physician: In case of fume inhalation, treat for pulmonary edema. Give prednisone or other corticosteroid orally to reduce tissue response to fume. Positive pressure ventilation may be necessary. Treat metal fume fever with bed rest, analgesics, and antipyretics. Symptoms of metal fume fever may be delayed for 4-12 h following exposure; may last less than 36 h.

Use dry chemical, CO2, water spray, or alcohol foam extinguishers. Decomposes below 170 deg C forming nitrogen oxides. Containers may explode in fire.
disposal_method: Add slowly to water; stir in excess soda ash. Let stand, then neutralize. Decant solution and flush to sewer; landfill sludge.

short_term_effects: Cyanamide is caustic and severely irritates the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract; and may affect the liver. Ingestion or inhalation may cause transitory intense redness of the face, headache, vertigo, increased respiration, tachycardia, and hypotension. The adverse effects of cyanamide are POTENTIATED BY THE INGESTION OF ALCOHOL (beer, wine, or liquor) within 1-2 days before or after exposure. Cyanamide is a highly reactive chemical and is a DANGEROUS EXPLOSION HAZARD.
long_term_effects: Repeated or prolonged contact may cause skin sensitization and allergy. Exposure may cause liver and nervous system damage.
mutagenicity: Not listed as carcinogen. EU R43 (may cause sensitization by skin contact). DFG: Danger of sensitization of skin and airways. Compound Description: Reproductive Effector.
medical_surveillance: Liver function tests. Examination of nervous system. Examination by qualified allergist.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing. Contact lenses should not be worn. When working with liquids: splash-proof chemical goggles and face shield. When working with powders/dusts: dust-proof chemical goggles and face shield. Provide emergency showers and eyewash. See NIOSH Criteria Document 212 Nitriles.
respirator_selection: Where there is potential for exposures over 2 mg/m3, use a NIOSH/MSHA- or EN 149-approved supplied-air respirator with full face-piece in positive-pressure mode, or with full face-piece/hood/helmet in continuous-flow mode; or NIOSH/MSHA- or EN 149-approved SCBA with full face-piece in pressure-demand or other positive-pressure mode.
storage: Two storage codes: (1) Color Code Yellow: Reactive Hazard; Store in location separate from other materials, especially flammables and combustibles. (2) Color Code Blue: Health Hazard/Poison: Store in a secure poison location. Store in tightly closed containers in cool well-ventilated area away from acids or acid fumes. Cyanamide can be stored in glass containers if stabilized with phosphoric, acetic, sulfuric, or boric acid; it attacks iron and steel, copper, and brass. Sources of ignition prohibited. Use explosion-proof electrical equipment and fittings.
shipping: Nitriles, toxic, n.o.s. require a POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS label. Hazard Class 6.1 and Packing Group III.
spill_handling: Evacuate persons not wearing protective equipment. Remove all ignition sources. Ventilate area. Collect powdered material in sealed containers. Absorb liquids in vermiculite, dry sand, earth, peat, carbon, or similar material. Keep out of confined spaces (sewer) because of explosion risk. fire_extinguishing: Cyanamide may burn but does not readily ignite. Poisonous gas is produced in fire, including nitrogen oxides and cyanides. Use dry chemical or CO2 extinguishers. Containers may explode in fire.
disposal_method: Add excess alkaline calcium hypochlorite with agitation. Flush to sewer after 24 h. Cyanamide can also be destroyed in an incinerator equipped with afterburner and scrubber.

iarc_classification: EPA (cyanide, free): Not Classifiable as to human carcinogenicity. Banned/Severely Restricted: agriculture (Germany); consumer products (US). routes_of_entry: Potassium cyanide can be absorbed through the skin, inhalation, ingestion.
target_organs: Liver, kidneys, skin, cardiovascular system, central nervous system, thyroid.
short_term_effects: KCN and NaCN are corrosive to eyes, skin, and respiratory tract. Contact can cause eye and skin burns; may cause permanent eye damage. Corrosive if swallowed. May affect CNS. Symptoms: headaches, confusion, nausea, pounding heart, weakness, unconsciousness, and death. Cherry-red lips, tachypnea, hypernea, bradycardia, headache, vertigo, convulsions, dizziness. The cyanide ion inhibits cytochrome oxidase enzymes concerned with cellular respiration; although blood is saturated with oxygen, tissues cannot use it (cellular asphyxia). Symptoms appear within seconds or minutes. Death within minutes after a large dose.
long_term_effects: Repeated or prolonged contact with KCN or NaCN may cause thyroid gland enlargement. May cause nosebleed and sores in the nose; changes in blood cell count. May cause CNS damage with headache, dizziness, confusion, nausea, vomiting, pounding heart, weakness, unconsciousness, and death. May affect liver and kidney function.
points_of_attack: Liver, kidneys, skin, cardiovascular system, central nervous system, thyroid.
mutagenicity: EPA (cyanide, free): Not Classifiable. Banned/Severely Restricted.
medical_surveillance: Consider the points of attack in preplacement and periodic physical examinations. Urine thiocyanate levels. Blood cyanide levels. CBC. Evaluation of thyroid function. Liver function tests. Kidney function tests. CNS tests. EKG.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Speed in removing material from skin is of extreme importance. Shampoo hair promptly if contaminated. Keep under observation for 24-48 h as symptoms may return. Use amyl nitrate capsules if symptoms develop. All area employees should be trained regularly in emergency measures for cyanide poisoning and in CPR. A cyanide antidote kit should be kept in the immediate work area and MUST be rapidly available. Kit ingredients should be replaced every 1-2 years to ensure freshness. Persons trained in the use of this kit, oxygen use, and CPR must be quickly available. Note to physician: Consider the administration of Ketocyanor (cobalt edetate) in dose of 300-600 mg i.v. initially. If recovery does not occur quickly (in 1-2 min), give a second dose of 300 mg, followed by i.v. glucose 5%. Alternatively, administer sodium nitrite (3%) in an i.v. dose of 10 mL over 3 min.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof goggles and face shield when working with liquid. Wear dust-proof goggles and face shield when working with powders or dust. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.

spill_handling: Avoid contact with solids, dusts, or solutions. Wear chemical protective suit with self-contained breathing apparatus. Evacuate persons not wearing protective equipment. short_term_effects: A lacrimator. This chemical can be absorbed through the skin. Irritates eyes, nose, upper respiratory system. Skin contact with the liquid causes frostbite. Vision loss can occur following high exposure. Cyanogen hydrolyzes to yield one molecule of HCN and one of cyanate; toxic effects are thought to be comparable to HCN. The cyanide ion inhibits enzymes concerned with cellular respiration; blood is saturated with oxygen but tissues cannot use it. Symptoms appear within seconds or minutes: cherry-red lips, tachypnea, hypernea, bradycardia, headache, vertigo (illusion of movement), convulsions, dizziness. Constriction of the chest, giddiness, confusion, headache, hyperpnea, palpitation, unconsciousness, convulsions, feeble and rapid respiration, extremely weak pulse. Death occurs within a few minutes after a large dose. NOTE: Distinctive bitter almond smell of cyanogen could not be detected at concentrations of 50, 100, and 250 ppm (human subject testing; irritant properties tested in humans aged 21-65 years).
long_term_effects: Enlargement of the thyroid gland. Some evidence that long-term exposure can damage the nervous system. Victims experience loss of appetite and weight loss.
points_of_attack: Eyes, respiratory system, central nervous system, cardiovascular system.
mutagenicity: Not listed as carcinogen. Former chemical warfare agent. DFG Pregnancy Group D (teratogenicity suspect; specific reproductive concern).
medical_surveillance: Serum and urine thiocyanate levels. If symptoms develop or overexposure is suspected: examination of the thyroid.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Medical observation advised for 24-48 h. If frostbite has occurred, seek medical attention immediately; do NOT rub the affected areas or flush them with water. In order to prevent further tissue damage, do NOT attempt to remove frozen clothing from frostbitten areas. If frostbite has NOT occurred, immediately and thoroughly wash contaminated skin with soap and water. If cyanide poisoning is suspected: Use amyl nitrate capsules if symptoms develop. All area employees should be trained regularly in emergency measures for cyanide poisoning and in CPR. A cyanide antidote kit should be kept in the immediate work area and must be rapidly available. Kit ingredients should be replaced every 1-2 years to ensure freshness. Persons trained in the use of this kit, oxygen use, and CPR must be quickly available.
personal_protective_methods: Lower exposure can cause irritation of eyes, nose, and throat; immediately leave work area if these symptoms are noticed. Wear appropriate personal protective clothing to prevent skin from becoming frozen from contact with the evaporating liquid or from contact with vessels containing the liquid. Avoid skin contact with cyanogen. Wear protective gloves and clothing. Wear air-tight gas-proof goggles unless full face-piece respiratory protection is worn. See NIOSH Criteria Document 212 Nitriles.
respirator_selection: Where there is potential for exposures over 10 ppm, use an NIOSH/MSHA- or EN 149-approved supplied-air respirator with full face-piece in positive-pressure mode, or with full face-piece/hood/helmet in continuous-flow mode; or NIOSH/MSHA- or EN 149-approved SCBA with full face-piece in pressure-demand or other positive-pressure mode.
storage: Two storage codes: (1) Color Code Red Stripe: Flammability Hazard: Store separately from all other flammable materials. (2) Color Code Blue: Health Hazard/Poison: Store in a secure poison location. Before entering confined space, check for explosive concentration. Store in tightly closed containers in a cool well-ventilated area away from heat and light. Must be stored to avoid contact with fluorine and oxygen, water or steam, acid or acid fumes, since violent reactions occur. Sources of ignition prohibited. Outside storage or storage in area of noncombustible construction is preferable. Only nonsparking tools. Use explosion-proof electrical equipment and fittings. Cylinder handling per OSHA 1910.101 and 1910.169.
shipping: Cyanogen must be labeled: POISON GAS, FLAMMABLE GAS. Hazard Class 2.3. No Packing Group. It is a violation of transportation regulations to refill compressed gas cylinders without the express written permission of the owner.
spill_handling: Evacuate and restrict persons not wearing protective equipment. Remove all ignition sources. Establish forced ventilation to keep levels below explosive limit. Stop the flow of gas if it can be done safely. If source is a cylinder and leak cannot be stopped in place, remove to a safe place in the open air; repair leak or allow cylinder to empty. Keep out of confined spaces because of explosion risk. Initial isolation distances: small spill: isolate 100 ft all directions; protect 0.1/0.2 miles Day/Night. Large spill: isolate 500 ft all directions; protect 0.7/1.1 miles Day, 2.2/3.5 km Night. OSHA 1910.120(q) may be applicable.
fire_extinguishing: Highly flammable gas; burns with a PURPLE-TINGED FLAME. Poisonous gases, including HCN, are produced in fire. Stop the flow of gas if it can be done safely. DO NOT USE WATER. disposal_method: Incineration; oxides of nitrogen are removed from the effluent gas by scrubbers and/or thermal devices.

Subsequently move away from the hot zone in an upwind and uphill direction. Do NOT use household or other bleach products to decontaminate the victim. Wash victim with warm water and soap. FDA banned cyclamates in 1969 due to conversion to CHA; however, there is now no evidence that CHA is a carcinogen.
ld50: LD50=(oral-rat) 156 mg/kg (moderately toxic). Probable oral lethal dose: 50-500 mg/kg or between 1 teaspoon and 1 oz for a 70-kg (150-lb) person.
routes_of_entry: Inhalation, ingestion, skin absorption, eye and skin contact.
target_organs: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, central nervous system.
short_term_effects: This chemical can be absorbed through the skin. Cyclohexylamine is caustic to the skin, eyes, and respiratory tract. Systemic effects: nausea, vomiting, anxiety, restlessness, drowsiness, lightheadedness, anxiety, apprehension, slurred speech, papillary dilation, severe skin irritation. May be a skin sensitizer. Inhalation can cause pulmonary edema (delayed; can cause death). Moderately toxic: LD50(oral-rat)=156 mg/kg. Considered a nerve poison; and is a weak methemoglobin-forming substance.
long_term_effects: Cyclohexylamine causes mutations (genetic changes). Such chemicals may have a cancer risk. It may damage the developing fetus. It may damage the testes (male reproductive gland) and reduce the fertility of females. Exposure may increase blood pressure. Repeated or severe exposures may damage vision and possibly kidneys and liver. May cause skin allergy. The Food and Drug Administration banned the use of cyclamates as artificial sweeteners in 1969 because of their metabolic conversion to cyclohexylamine, which was thought to be carcinogenic in rats. There is now no evidence that CHA is a carcinogen.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, central nervous system.
mutagenicity: IARC Group 3, 1987 (not classifiable). EPA Gene-Tox: Positive (cell transformation; cytogenetics—male germ cell). Compound Description: Tumorigen, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector. EU R62 (possible risk of impaired fertility). Causes mutations. Damages developing fetus. Damages testes.
medical_surveillance: Blood pressure check before beginning employment and regularly. If symptoms develop or overexposure is suspected: eye and vision examination. Kidney and liver function tests. Skin testing with dilute cyclohexylamine for allergy diagnosis by qualified allergist.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. If victim is conscious, administer water or milk. Do not induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Medical observation recommended for 24-48 h after breathing overexposure, as pulmonary edema may be delayed. A doctor or authorized paramedic may consider administering a corticosteroid spray. Note to physician: Treat for methemoglobinemia. Spectrophotometry may be required for precise determination of levels of methemoglobinemia in urine.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing. 8h: Responder suits. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof chemical goggles and face shield. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.
respirator_selection: Where there is potential for exposures over 10 ppm: NIOSH/MSHA- or EN 149-approved full face-piece respirator with organic vapor cartridge/canister, or full face-piece powered air-purifying respirator, or supplied-air respirator with full face-piece in positive-pressure mode, or SCBA with full face-piece in pressure-demand mode.

spill_handling: Stay upwind; keep out of low areas. Wear SCBA with full protective clothing. Establish forced ventilation. Shut off ignition sources. Do not touch spilled material; stop leak if without risk. Use water spray to reduce vapors. Small spills: vermiculite, dry sand, or other noncombustible absorbent into containers. Large spills: dike far ahead. Evacuate and restrict persons. OSHA 1910.120(q) may be applicable.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible liquid. Poisonous gases, including nitrogen oxides, produced in fire. Use dry chemical, CO2, or foam extinguishers. Vapors heavier than air; collect in low areas. Containers may explode in fire; may rocket.
disposal_method: Incineration; incinerator equipped with a scrubber or thermal unit to reduce nitrogen oxides emissions.

The immediate treatment for nerve agent intoxication is intravenous injection of 2 mg atropine sulfate (intramuscular if patient is hypoxic and ventilation cannot be initiated). If breathing has stopped, a mechanical respirator should be used; do not attempt mouth-to-mouth resuscitation. If possible, use oxygen or oxygen-enriched air for ventilation. Obidoxime may be used for GF intoxication but may cause liver damage. Animal studies indicate oxime Hi-6 may be significantly superior for GF but is not widely available; therefore use pralidoxime salts (500 mg to 1 g slow IV infusion initially). Diazepam 5 mg initial dose may be followed by additional doses at 15-min intervals up to 15 mg to control convulsions. Immediately flush eyes with water for at least 15 min. Liquid patients: Blot (not wipe) visible droplets with absorbent material (paper towels, facial tissues). Towelettes moistened with neutralizing solution or absorbent powders may be used. GF should be decontaminated by washing with available clean water at least 3 times. Skin decontamination may be unnecessary if exposure was to GF vapor only. Use liquid soap, large amounts of water, and mild to moderate friction with single-use sponge or washcloth in first and second washes. Scrubbing with a brush is discouraged (skin damage may increase absorption). Third wash: rinse with large amounts of warm or hot water. Wash off diluted bleach solution after 15 min. Decontaminants (in order of preference): 10 wt. % sodium hydroxide solution; DS2 (2% NaOH; 70% diethylene triamine; 28% ethylene glycol monomethyl ether); sodium carbonate; Supertropical Bleach Slurry (STB). Scoop all material into fully removable head drum with high-density polyethylene liner. Decontamination solution must be treated with excess bleach to destroy CN formed during hydrolysis. All leaking containers shall be overpacked with vermiculite between interior and exterior containers. Vapors heavier than air; collect in low areas. Vapors may travel to ignition and flashback. Containers may explode in fire; may rocket.

USACE and DOD use safety procedures including head space (off gas) monitoring around containers prior to shipment. Waste will be transported per state requirements to a designated disposal facility (typically RCRA-permitted hazardous waste incinerator). Wastewater solution from decontamination process will be analyzed; if no residual agents, may not need to be classified as hazardous waste (sampling must verify). Chlorinated wastewater may need treatment/neutralization prior to disposal. US munitions stockpiles of G-agent have undergone destruction/disposal in Utah, Oregon, Arkansas, Alabama, and Kentucky. ld50: Highly toxic organophosphate. See also 'Demeton' entry. May be fatal by skin contact.
target_organs: Respiratory system, lungs, central nervous system, cardiovascular system, skin, eyes, plasma and red blood cell cholinesterase.
short_term_effects: Methyl demeton can be fatal by skin contact even if there is no feeling of irritation. Exposure can cause rapid, fatal organophosphate poisoning. Acute signs and symptoms: pinpoint pupils, blurred vision, headache, dizziness, muscle spasms, profound weakness, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, loss of coordination, seizures, coma, and death. Heart rate may decrease (oral) or increase (dermal). Hypotension not uncommon. Respiratory symptoms include dyspnea, respiratory depression, and respiratory paralysis. Psychosis may occur. Eye contact may cause irritation.
long_term_effects: May cause mutations. In animal studies: decrease in fertility; toxic to animal fetus. See also Demeton entry.
points_of_attack: Respiratory system, lungs, central nervous system, cardiovascular system, skin, eyes, plasma and red blood cell cholinesterase.
mutagenicity: Not listed as carcinogen. May cause mutations. Animal fetal toxicity. Banned/Severely Restricted. EU R27/28+R50/53.
medical_surveillance: Plasma and red blood cell cholinesterase levels before employment and at regular times. If exposure stops, plasma returns to normal in 1-2 weeks; RBC levels may be reduced for 1-3 months. When levels reduced 25%+ below preemployment: increased risk of poisoning. Reassignment recommended until enzyme levels recover. Consider CBC. Consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure. Do not drink alcoholic beverages before or during use. Alcohol promotes absorption.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 30 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Speed in removing material from skin is of extreme importance. Shampoo hair promptly if contaminated. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Effects may be delayed; medical observation is recommended. Note to physician: 1,1'-trimethylenebis(4-formylpyridinium bromide)dioxime (a.k.a TMB-4 dibromide and TMV-4) has been used as an antidote for organophosphate poisoning. Contact local poison control center for additional guidance.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof chemical goggles and face shield unless full face-piece respiratory protection is worn. Employees should wash immediately with soap. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.

first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit.

short_term_effects: Diborane is the least toxic of the boron hydrides. Acute poisoning: symptoms similar to metal fume fever: tightness, heaviness and burning in chest, coughing, shortness of breath, chills, fever, pericardial pain, nausea, shivering, and drowsiness. Signs appear soon after exposure or after a latent period of up to 24 h and persist for 1-3 days or more. Pneumonia may develop later. Subacute poisoning: pulmonary irritation symptoms; if prolonged, CNS symptoms (headaches, dizziness, vertigo, chills, fatigue, muscular weakness, and only infrequent transient tremors). Convulsions do not occur. In animals: liver, kidney damage, pulmonary edema, hemorrhage.
long_term_effects: Prolonged exposure may cause lung damage. Chronic exposure leads to wheezing, dyspnea, tightness, dry cough, rales, and hyperventilation which persist for several years.
points_of_attack: Respiratory system, central nervous system, liver, kidneys.
mutagenicity: Not listed as carcinogen. Compound Description: Mutagen.
medical_surveillance: Lung function tests before beginning employment and at regular times. If symptoms develop or overexposure: liver and kidney function tests. Examination of the nervous system. NIOSH tests: chest X-ray; pulmonary function tests (FVC, FEV1).
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Medical observation recommended for 24-48 h after breathing overexposure, as pulmonary edema may be delayed. A doctor or authorized paramedic may consider administering a corticosteroid spray.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing. For emergency situations, wear positive-pressure, pressure-demand, full face-piece SCBA or pressure-demand supplied-air respirator with escape SCBA and a fully encapsulating, chemical-resistant suit. Wear gas-proof chemical goggles and face shield unless full face-piece respiratory protection is worn. Employees should wash immediately with soap. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.
respirator_selection: Up to 1 ppm: Sa (APF=10). Up to 2.5 ppm: Sa:Cf (APF=25). Up to 5 ppm: SCBAF (APF=50) or SaF (APF=50) or SaT:Cf (APF=50). Up to 15 ppm: SaF:Pd,Pp (APF=2000). Emergency/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp (APF=10,000) or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA (APF=10,000). Escape: GmFS (APF=50) or SCBAE.
storage: Three storage codes: (1) Color Code Red Stripe: Flammability Hazard: Store separately from all other flammable materials. (2) Color Code Blue: Health Hazard/Poison. (3) Color Code Yellow Stripe (strong reducing agent): Reactivity Hazard; Store separately in area isolated from flammables, combustibles, or other yellow-coded materials. Must be stored to avoid contact with air, active metals (aluminum, lithium), halogenated compounds (chlorine), and oxidizing agents (permanganates, nitrates, peroxides, chlorates, perchlorates). Containers should be dry, clean, and free of oxygen. Store in cool, well-ventilated area away from heat and moisture. Containers usually stored in dry ice or refrigerated. Diborane can ignite spontaneously in moist air at room temperature. Use dry nitrogen purge in any transfer. Sources of ignition prohibited. Use only nonsparking tools. Comply with OSHA 1910.101 and 1910.169 and Compressed Gas Association recommendations.
shipping: Diborane must be labeled POISON GAS, FLAMMABLE GAS. Hazard Class 2.3 and Packing Group I. Violation of transportation regulations to refill compressed gas cylinders without express written permission of the owner.
spill_handling: If in a building, evacuate building and confine vapors by closing doors and shutting down HVAC systems. Restrict persons not wearing protective equipment. Remove all ignition sources. Establish forced ventilation. Wear chemical protective suit with SCBA. Stay upwind; use water spray to knock down vapor; contain runoff. Stop the flow of gas if safely done from a distance. Dilute leak with inert gas and exhaust through fume hood if possible. If cylinder leak cannot be stopped in place, trained personnel may remove to safe place in open air. Keep out of confined spaces. Initial isolation distances (Diborane and diborane, compressed): Small spill: 200 ft/60 m; protect 0.2/0.3 miles Day, 0.8/1.3 miles Night. Large spill: 1000 ft/300 m; protect 1.1/1.8 miles Day, 2.7/4.3 miles Night. OSHA 1910.120(q) may be applicable.
fire_extinguishing: FIREFIGHTING GEAR (INCLUDING SCBA) DOES NOT PROVIDE ADEQUATE PROTECTION. Remove and isolate gear immediately; thoroughly decontaminate personnel if exposed. Highly flammable and reactive gas; ignites without warning in moist air at room temperature. Poisonous gases produced in fire, including boron and hydrogen at higher temperatures and hydrogen and boron hydrides at lower temperatures. Approach fire with extreme caution; consider letting it burn. DO NOT EXTINGUISH unless gas flow can be stopped and remaining gas is out of line. Fog lines to cool exposures and let fire burn itself out. Stop gas flow and use water spray to protect personnel during shut-off. Use water from unmanned source to keep fire-exposed containers cool. DIBORANE MAY REACT VIOLENTLY WITH HALOGENATED EXTINGUISHING AGENTS. Vapors heavier than air; collect in low areas. Containers may explode in fire; may rocket.
disposal_method: Incineration with aqueous scrubbing of exhaust gases to remove B2O3 particulates.

VP=39.5 atm at 17 deg C (HIGH PRESSURE AT NEAR ROOM TEMPERATURE). Flash point=-90 deg C (extremely flammable; compressed gas). AUTOIGNITION=40-50 DEG C (slightly above room temperature — extremely low; ignites almost spontaneously). LEL=0.8%; UEL=88% (EXTREMELY WIDE EXPLOSIVE RANGE — second widest after hydrogen). NFPA H4/F4/R3 (SIMULTANEOUSLY THE MOST HAZARDOUS IN ALL THREE NFPA CATEGORIES). NAUSEATING SICKLY-SWEET ODOR. Odor threshold=2.5 ppm (above NIOSH IDLH implies poor warning properties). UNSTABLE ABOVE 8 DEG C (unstable even at cold temperatures). IGNITES SPONTANEOUSLY IN MOIST AIR AT ROOM TEMPERATURE. Hydrolyzes exothermically with water forming HYDROGEN AND BORIC ACID (pyrophoric + exothermic + H2 generation = compounding hazards). CAN POLYMERIZE FORMING LIQUID PENTABORANE (also hazardous). CONTACT WITH HALOGENATED COMPOUNDS (including fire extinguishers) causes FIRE AND EXPLOSION (cannot use standard extinguishing methods). Contact with aluminum/lithium/active metals forms HYDRIDES THAT MAY IGNITE SPONTANEOUSLY. OSHA PEL=NIOSH REL=ACGIH TLV=0.1 ppm (unusual consensus across all three regulators; equal values). THREE STORAGE CODES: RED STRIPE (flammability) + BLUE (health/poison) + YELLOW STRIPE (strong reducing agent) — one of the most codes seen in this project. CONTAINERS STORED IN DRY ICE OR REFRIGERATED (unusual cryogenic storage requirement). DRY NITROGEN PURGE in any transfer. FIREFIGHTING GEAR (INCLUDING SCBA) DOES NOT PROVIDE ADEQUATE PROTECTION (cannot fight fires of diborane with standard firefighting equipment). Approach fire: CONSIDER LETTING IT BURN. DO NOT EXTINGUISH unless gas flow can be stopped. HALOGENATED EXTINGUISHING AGENTS: REACT VIOLENTLY WITH DIBORANE. Initial isolation distances: Small: 200 ft/0.2/0.8 mi Day/Night; Large: 1000 ft/1.1/2.7 mi Day/Night. POISON GAS + FLAMMABLE GAS (dual hazard label). Class 2.3, PG I (most hazardous classifications). DISPOSAL: incineration with aqueous scrubbing for B2O3. APPLICATIONS: semiconductor industry (boron doping) + olefin polymerization + rubber vulcanizer + flame-speed accelerator + rocket propellants + trialkyl borane production + primary alcohol production (8 uses). References: Sax 1982; US EPA November 1987; NJ DHSS December 1999.

medical_surveillance: Medical surveillance to be made available to employees as outlined: Comprehensive preplacement/initial medical and work histories with emphasis on reproductive experience and menstrual history. Comprehensive physical examination with emphasis on genito-urinary tract including testicle size and consistency in males. Semen analysis including sperm count, motility, and morphology. Other tests (serum testosterone, FSH, LH) if indicated by responsible physician. Screening tests of renal and hepatic systems. Judgment of worker's ability to use positive-pressure respirators. Employees shall be counseled that DBCP has been implicated in reproductive effects including sterility in male workers, and that cancer was produced in some animals. Periodic examinations (at least annual) containing elements of preplacement examination. Examinations made available to current employees as soon as practicable after promulgation. Medical surveillance available to any worker suspected of having been exposed. PERTINENT MEDICAL RECORDS SHALL BE MAINTAINED FOR 30 YEARS. Available to medical representatives of US Government, employer, and employee. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Contact local poison control center for advice about inducing vomiting. Medical observation is recommended for 24-48 h after breathing overexposure, as pulmonary edema may be delayed. A doctor or authorized paramedic may consider administering a corticosteroid spray.

Additional protection (gloves, bib-type aprons, boots, overshoes) for any operation that may cause direct contact with liquid DBCP. Supplied-air hoods or suits resistant to DBCP penetration shall be worn when entering confined spaces (pits or storage tanks). In situations where heat stress is likely to occur, supplied-air suits (preferably cooled) are recommended. The employer shall ensure that all personal protective clothing is inspected regularly for defects and is maintained in clean and satisfactory condition by the employee.

routes_of_entry: Inhalation, skin and eye contact, ingestion.
short_term_effects: Eye contact can cause vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Ingestion causes burning pain in the mouth, throat, and abdomen with spitting of blood; drooling, vomiting; burns and ulcers in the mouth, throat, pharynx, and esophagus; shock, restlessness, confusion, weakness, apprehension; muscle weakness; difficulty in breathing; depression; bluing of the skin; and death from shock or asphyxiation. 10% concentrated aqueous solutions are irritating to the skin; concentrations as low as 0.1-0.5% are irritating to the eyes and mucous membranes. Concentrations ranging from 2% to 17.5% have caused dermal necrosis. Ingestion can cause corrosion of upper intestinal tract. Swelling of throat and lungs with fluid (edema). Death can occur due to paralysis of respiratory muscles or circulatory collapse. LD50(oral-rat)=730 mg/kg (slightly toxic).
long_term_effects: May cause liver and kidney damage. Repeated contact may cause allergic contact dermatitis and allergic reaction in the lungs.
mutagenicity: Not listed as carcinogen.
medical_surveillance: Liver and kidney function tests. Lung function tests. Examination by a qualified allergist.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. If concentrated (10% or greater) solution is ingested, patient should swallow a large quantity of milk, egg whites, or gelatin solution. If breathing is difficult, give oxygen.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear dust-proof chemical goggles and face shield. Employees should wash immediately with soap. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.

storage: Color Code Green: General storage may be used. Store in tightly closed containers in a cool, well-ventilated area away from acids, acid fumes, moisture, and nitrates.
spill_handling: Evacuate persons not wearing protective equipment. Remove all ignition sources. Collect powdered material in sealed containers. Ventilate area. OSHA 1910.120(q) may be applicable.
fire_extinguishing: Use dry chemical, CO2, or foam extinguishers. Poisonous gases produced in fire, including nitrogen oxides, ammonia, and hydrogen chloride. Containers may explode in fire.

short_term_effects: This chemical may affect the central nervous system. Exposure can cause drowsiness, unconsciousness, and death. High exposures may damage the liver or kidneys. Contact can cause eye and skin irritation with eye burns. Long-term exposure can cause thickening and cracking of skin. Highly flammable liquid and dangerous fire hazard. Never use near combustion sources. Do not use where welding is being done because deadly phosgene gas can be formed.
long_term_effects: May damage the developing fetus. The liquid destroys the skin's natural oils. May affect the kidneys and liver. A chloroethane; may be a potential occupational carcinogen. medical_surveillance: If overexposure or illness suspected: liver and kidney function tests. Interview for brain effects (recent memory, mood, concentration, headaches, malaise, altered sleep patterns). Consider autonomic and peripheral nervous system evaluation. Positive and borderline cases should be referred for neuropsychological testing.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. If victim is conscious, administer water or milk. Do not induce vomiting.
personal_protective_methods: Wear solvent-resistant protective gloves and clothing. NIOSH recommends: 8h: Tychem 10000 suits. Teflon is among the recommended protective materials. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof chemical goggles and face shield. Employees should wash immediately with soap. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.

If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Speed in removing material from skin is of extreme importance. Shampoo hair promptly if contaminated.

Soluble. 2,3-Dichloro-1-propanol: BP=182 deg C. IARC (chlorophenols): Group 2B, 1973. DFG (96-23-1): Category 2. California Prop 65 (96-23-1): Cancer 10/8/10. Canada WHMIS 1.0%. WGK: No value assigned. No OEL. TEEL-0: 6 ppm; PAC-1: 0.2 ppm (ANOMALY: PAC-1 < TEEL-0); PAC-2=PAC-3=50 ppm (anomaly). DFG MAK [skin]: Carcinogen Category 2 (96-23-1). Very severe acute toxicity from 2,3-dichloro-1-propanol: GI hemorrhage, toxic hepatitis, hemolytic anemia, nephritis, renal failure, cerebral hemorrhage, coma. Pulmonary edema (delayed). Used as solvent for hard resins and nitrocellulose; manufacturing photographic chemicals and lacquer; also occurs in effluents from glycerol and halohydrin production plants. Store in refrigerator under inert atmosphere. OSHA 1910.1045. Class 6.1, PG II. Blue storage. Fire: chlorine + phosgene; alcohol foam only.

short_term_effects: 2,3-dichloro-1-propanol: Irritation of the eyes, skin, and mucous membranes; dyspnea, coughing, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain; gastrointestinal hemorrhage; toxic hepatitis; jaundice, hemolytic anemia; decreased urinary output from nephritis and renal failure; somnolence, cerebral hemorrhage; central nervous system depression, and coma. High exposures can cause pulmonary edema (delayed; can cause death). 1,3-dichloro-2-propanol: Irritation of skin, eyes, and respiratory system; inhalation may cause headache, vertigo, nausea, vomiting; may also cause coma and liver damage.
long_term_effects: Causes cancer in animals; may be a potential human carcinogen. May cause liver, kidney, and/or lung damage.
points_of_attack: Central nervous system, liver, kidneys, lungs.
mutagenicity: IARC (chlorophenols): Group 2B, 1973. DFG (96-23-1): Category 2. California Prop 65 (96-23-1): Cancer 10/8/10. Causes cancer in animals; may be a potential human carcinogen.
medical_surveillance: Kidney function tests. Liver function tests. Lung function tests. Consider chest X-ray following acute overexposure.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Medical observation is recommended for 24-48 h after breathing overexposure, as pulmonary edema may be delayed. A doctor or authorized paramedic may consider administering a corticosteroid spray.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof chemical goggles and face shield. Employees should wash immediately with soap. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.
respirator_selection: At any detectable concentration: SCBAF:Pd,Pp (APF=10,000) or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA (APF=10,000). Escape: 100F (APF=50) or SCBAE.

MULTIPLE ISOMERS: 26545-73-3 (dichloropropanol/1,3-dichloro-2-propanol); 96-23-1 (alpha-dichlorohydrin/1,3-dichloro-2-propanol; California Prop 65 chemical); 616-23-9 (2,3-dichloropropanol). FOUR ISOMERS TOTAL: 1,3-Dichloro-2-propanol (BP=174 deg C; Flash point=74 deg C; MP=-4 deg C; NFPA H2/F2/R0; SOLUBLE); 2,3-Dichloro-1-propanol (BP=182 deg C); 3,3-Dichloro-1-propanol (BP=82-83 deg C); 1,1-Dichloro-2-propanol (BP=146-148 deg C). VERY SEVERE ACUTE TOXICITY FROM 2,3-DICHLORO-1-PROPANOL: GI HEMORRHAGE + TOXIC HEPATITIS + JAUNDICE + HEMOLYTIC ANEMIA + NEPHRITIS + RENAL FAILURE + SOMNOLENCE + CEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE + CNS DEPRESSION + COMA (9 distinct severe effects from a single compound). Pulmonary edema (delayed). REFRIGERATOR + INERT ATMOSPHERE STORAGE REQUIRED. OSHA 1910.1045. Class 6.1, PG II. Blue storage. Fire: CHLORINE + PHOSGENE; ALCOHOL FOAM ONLY (strict fire extinguisher restriction). USED IN GLYCEROL AND HALOHYDRIN PRODUCTION PLANT EFFLUENTS (environmental release source; not just industrial use). References: US EPA April 1980 Profile No. 80; NJ DHSS January 2001.

target_organs: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, gastrointestinal tract, central nervous system.
short_term_effects: 2,2-Dichloropropionic acid is a corrosive chemical; can cause irritation and burns to skin and eyes, causing permanent damage. Exposure may cause throat pain, loss of appetite, nausea and sweating, lassitude (weakness, exhaustion), diarrhea, vomiting, slowing of pulse, CNS depression. Can irritate the upper respiratory tract. May cause a skin allergy; very low future exposures can cause itching and a skin rash.
long_term_effects: May cause liver and kidney damage. May cause skin allergy.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, gastrointestinal tract, central nervous system.
mutagenicity: Not listed as carcinogen. Compound Description: Agricultural Chemical; Mutagen. ACGIH: Not classifiable.
medical_surveillance: If overexposure or illness is suspected, consider lung function tests. Kidney and liver function tests.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. If victim is conscious, administer water or milk. Do not induce vomiting.
personal_protective_methods: Wear ACID-RESISTANT protective gloves and clothing. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof chemical goggles and face shield when working with liquids or dust-proof goggles and face shield when working with powders or dusts. Employees should wash immediately with soap. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.
respirator_selection: Where there is potential for exposures over 1 ppm: NIOSH/MSHA- or EN149-approved supplied-air respirator with full face-piece in positive-pressure mode, or SCBA with full face-piece in pressure-demand mode.

Absorb liquids in vermiculite, dry sand, earth, peat, carbon, or similar material in sealed containers. Keep out of confined spaces. OSHA 1910.120(q) may be applicable. Powder: Evacuate persons. Remove all ignition sources. Collect powdered material in sealed containers. Ventilate area.
fire_extinguishing: May burn but does not easily ignite. Poisonous gases, including chlorine, produced in fire. Use dry chemical, CO2, or foam extinguishers. Vapors heavier than air. Containers may explode in fire; may rocket.
disposal_method: Incineration in a unit with efficient gas scrubbing. In accordance with 40CFR165. Follow recommendations for disposal of pesticides and pesticide containers.
