short_term_effects: Dichlorotetrafluoroethane can affect you when breathed in. Irritates the eyes and upper respiratory tract. Inhalation of vapors can cause you to become dizzy and lightheaded, drowsy, and pass out. It can cause the heart to beat irregularly or stop, which can cause death. Contact with the liquid can cause frostbite, burning of eyes and skin.
long_term_effects: Can irritate the lungs and cause bronchitis with coughing, phlegm, and/or shortness of breath.
mutagenicity: Not listed as carcinogen. ACGIH: not classifiable as human carcinogen.
medical_surveillance: Lung function tests for those with frequent or potentially high exposure. If symptoms develop: Holter monitor (a special 24-h EKG to look for irregular heart rhythms).
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. If frostbite has occurred, seek medical attention immediately; do NOT rub the affected areas or flush them with water. Do NOT attempt to remove frozen clothing from frostbitten areas. If frostbite has NOT occurred, immediately and thoroughly wash contaminated skin with soap and water.
personal_protective_methods: Wear appropriate personal protective clothing to prevent the skin from becoming frozen from contact with the evaporating liquid or from contact with vessels containing the liquid. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof chemical goggles and face shield when working with the liquid, wear gas-proof goggles and face shield when working with the gas unless full face-piece respiratory protection is worn. Employees should wash immediately with soap. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.
respirator_selection: 10,000 ppm: Sa (APF=10) (any supplied-air respirator). 15,000 ppm: Sa:Cf (APF=25) or SCBAF (APF=50) or SaF (APF=50). Emergency/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp (APF=10,000) or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA (APF=10,000). Escape: GmFOv (APF=50) or SCBAE.
storage: Color Code Green: General storage may be used. Store to avoid contact with acids, acid fumes, chemically active metals (sodium, potassium, calcium, powdered aluminum, zinc, and magnesium) since violent reactions occur. Store in tightly closed containers in a cool, well-ventilated area away from heat. Comply with OSHA 1910.101 and 1910.169.
shipping: Dichlorotetrafluoroethane requires a shipping label of NONFLAMMABLE GAS. Hazard Class 2.2; there is no Packing Group.
spill_handling: Evacuate and restrict persons not wearing protective equipment. Remove all ignition sources. Ventilate area to disperse the gas. Stop flow of gas. If cylinder leak cannot be stopped in place, remove to safe place in open air. If liquid spilled or leaked, allow it to vaporize. OSHA 1910.120(q) may be applicable.
fire_extinguishing: Dichlorotetrafluoroethane is a nonflammable liquid or gas. Extinguish fire using an agent suitable for type of surrounding fire. Poisonous gases are produced in fire, including hydrogen chloride, phosgene, and hydrogen fluoride. Vapors are heavier than air and will collect in low areas. Containers may explode in fire. From a secure, explosion-proof location, use water spray to cool exposed containers.
disposal_method: Incineration after mixing with combustible fuel. Use flue gas scrubber.

short_term_effects: Dichlorvos irritates the eyes and skin. Symptoms include miosis, aching eyes, rhinorrhea, headache, chest tightness, wheezing, laryngeal spasm, salivation, cyanosis, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, muscle fasiculation, paralysis, giddiness, ataxia, convulsions, low blood pressure, cardiac irregularities. The substance may cause effects on the central nervous system. Cholinesterase inhibitor. High levels of exposure may result in death.
long_term_effects: Repeated or prolonged contact with skin may cause skin sensitization and dermatitis. Cholinesterase inhibitor; cumulative effect is possible. This substance may be carcinogenic to humans; it has been shown to cause cancer of the pancreas in animals. There is limited evidence that Dichlorvos is a teratogen in animals, and may cause birth defects or damage the fetus in humans.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, cardiovascular system, central nervous system, blood cholinesterase.
mutagenicity: IARC Group 2B, 1991. NCI: Clear evidence (mouse). EPA Gene-Tox: Positive (Ames; S. cerevisiae gene conversion; etc.). California Prop 65: Cancer 1/1/89. Compound Description: Agricultural Chemical; Tumorigen, Drug, Organometallic, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector.
medical_surveillance: Plasma and red blood cell cholinesterase levels before employment and at regular times. If exposure stops, plasma levels return to normal in 1-2 weeks while red blood cell levels may be reduced for 1-3 months. When cholinesterase enzyme levels are reduced by 25% or more below preemployment levels, risk of poisoning is increased. Reassignment recommended until enzyme levels recover. If symptoms develop or overexposure occurs: repeat cholinesterase tests plus examination of nervous system. Complete blood count. Consider chest X-ray following acute overexposure. Do not drink alcoholic beverages before or during use. NIOSH lists: blood serum; cholinesterase: whole blood; blood plasma, RBC/count; blood serum, RBC/count; urine (chemical/metabolite).
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Speed in removing material from skin is of extreme importance. Shampoo hair promptly if contaminated. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Medical observation is recommended for 24-48 h following overexposure.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof chemical goggles and face shield. Employees should wash immediately with soap. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.
respirator_selection: 10 mg/m3: Sa (APF=10). 25 mg/m3: Sa:Cf (APF=25). 50 mg/m3: SaT:Cf (APF=50) or SCBAF (APF=50) or SaF (APF=50). 100 mg/m3: Sa:Pd,Pp (APF=1000). Emergency/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp (APF=10,000) or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA (APF=10,000). Escape: GmFOv100 (APF=50) or SCBAE.
storage: Color Code Blue: Health Hazard/Poison: Store in a secure poison location. Store in tightly closed containers in a cool, well-ventilated area away from strong acids and strong alkalis. Dichlorvos will attack some forms of mild iron, plastics, rubber, and coatings.
shipping: Organophosphorus pesticides, liquid, toxic, n.o.s. require a POISON, FLAMMABLE LIQUID label. Dichlorvos falls in Hazard Class 6.1 and Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate and restrict persons not wearing protective equipment. Remove all ignition sources. Ventilate area. Do not touch spilled material; stop leaks if you can do it without risk. Reduce vapors with water spray. Take up small spills with sand or other noncombustible absorbent material. Dike large spills far ahead of spill for later disposal. OSHA 1910.120(q) may be applicable.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible liquid. Poisonous gases, including hydrogen chloride and phosphoric acid, are produced in fire. Use dry chemical, carbon dioxide, or foam extinguishers. disposal_method: 50% hydrolysis in pure water: 25 min at 70 deg C; 61.5 days at 20 deg C. Buffered solution yields 50% hydrolysis at 37.5 deg C: 301 min at pH 8, 462 min at pH 7, 620 min at pH 5.4. Hydrolysis yields no toxic residues. Incineration in furnace equipped with afterburner and alkaline scrubber is recommended, as is alkaline hydrolysis followed by soil burial. In accordance with 40CFR165.

first_aid: Eyes: Check victim for contact lenses and remove. Flush victim's eyes with water or normal saline for 20-30 min, lifting lower and upper eyelids occasionally. Remove contaminated clothing and shoes. Get medical attention immediately. Do not put any ointments, oils, or medication in the victim's eyes without specific instructions from a physician. Immediately transport the victim after flushing eyes to a hospital even if no symptoms develop. Skin: Immediately flood affected skin with water and wash for at least 15 min. Remove and isolate all contaminated clothing. Gently wash all affected skin areas thoroughly with soap and water. If symptoms such as redness or irritation develop, immediately call a physician. Transport the victim to a hospital for treatment. Inhalation: Remove victim to fresh air. If not breathing, give artificial respiration. If breathing is difficult, give oxygen. Get medical attention immediately. Ingestion: Do not induce vomiting. If the victim is conscious and not convulsing, give large amount of water to dilute the chemical. Never give anything by mouth to an unconscious person. If symptoms develop, call a physician. If the victim is convulsing or unconscious, ensure that the victim's airway is open and lay the victim on his/her side with the head lower than the body.

Employees should wash immediately with soap. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.

Higher exposures can cause pulmonary edema (delayed; can cause death). Bleeding of nose and gums, ulceration of the nasal and oral mucosa, pulmonary edema, chronic bronchitis, and pneumonia may also occur. Eye contact: irritation, pain, swelling, corneal erosion, and blindness. Dermatitis, severe burns, pain, and shock follow dermal exposure. Upon short contact, second- and third-degree burns may occur. Signs and symptoms of acute ingestion include increased salivation, intense thirst, difficulty swallowing, chills, pain, and shock. Oral, esophageal, and stomach burns are common. Vomitus generally has a coffee-ground appearance. High potential for circulatory collapse following ingestion.
long_term_effects: Very irritating substances may affect the lungs.
mutagenicity: Not listed as carcinogen.
medical_surveillance: Lung function tests before beginning employment and at regular times for frequent or potentially high exposures. Consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. If victim is conscious, administer water or milk. Do not induce vomiting. Medical observation is recommended for 24-48 h after breathing overexposure, as pulmonary edema may be delayed. As first aid for pulmonary edema, a doctor or authorized paramedic may consider administering a corticosteroid spray.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof chemical goggles and face shield. Employees should wash immediately with soap. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.
respirator_selection: Where there is potential for exposure: NIOSH/MSHA- or EN149-approved supplied-air respirator with full face-piece in positive-pressure mode; or NIOSH/MSHA- or EN149-approved SCBA with full face-piece in pressure-demand mode.
storage: Dual storage: (1) Color Code Red: Flammability Hazard: Store in a flammable liquid storage area away from ignition sources. Store to avoid contact with oxidizers (perchlorates, peroxides, permanganates, chlorates, and nitrates) since violent reactions occur. Store in tightly closed containers away from water, steam, or moisture (toxic HCl produced). Do not store at temperatures above 50 deg C/122 deg F. Metal containers (5+ gallons): grounded and bonded. Drums: self-closing valves, pressure vacuum bungs, flame arresters. Only nonsparking tools. Sources of ignition prohibited.

short_term_effects: DMF irritates the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract. Thirteen workers exposed to concentrations below 20 ppm and occasionally to higher levels for up to 32 weeks complained of nausea, vomiting, and colicky abdominal pain; some cases of liver enlargement were detected. A worker splashed over 20% of his body surface: abdominal pain began 62 h after exposure and became progressively more severe, with vomiting and high blood pressure. Rapidly penetrates the skin. Some workers have noted facial flushing (especially after alcohol ingestion). Highly irritating to eyes and mucous membranes. Fatal dose for humans has been estimated at 10 g (about 1/3 oz).

first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit.

short_term_effects: Dinitrobenzene irritates the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract. May affect the lungs and the ability of the blood to carry oxygen, resulting in methemoglobin formation. Symptoms: headache, weakness, fatigue, dizziness, and blue color to the skin and lips. Higher levels may cause difficulty in breathing, collapse, unconsciousness, and death. Effects may be delayed. Consuming alcohol, exposure to sunlight, or hot baths may worsen symptoms. Exposure may produce yellowish coloration of the skin, eyes, and hair. Any isomer may produce methemoglobinemia with symptoms of headaches, irritability, dizziness, weakness, nausea, vomiting, dyspnea, drowsiness, and unconsciousness. If treatment not given promptly, death may occur. May also cause bitter almond taste, dry throat, thirst, reduced vision, liver damage, hearing loss, and ringing of the ears. Repeated or prolonged exposure may cause anemia.
long_term_effects: Repeated exposure may cause hearing loss and changes to vision. Prolonged exposure may lead to liver damage and anemia. Can cause serious reproductive toxicity in humans. May affect the respiratory tract and methemoglobin formation.
points_of_attack: Blood, liver, cardiovascular system, eyes, central nervous system.

medical_surveillance: Preemployment and periodic examinations: history of blood dyscrasias, reactions to medications, alcohol intake, eye disease, skin, cardiovascular status. Liver and renal functions; blood. Blood methemoglobin levels should be followed. DNB can be determined in urine; levels >25 mg/L may indicate significant absorption. CBC. Eye examination and color vision. G-6-P-D deficiency increases risk. NIOSH lists: whole blood (chemical/metabolite), methemoglobin; CBC; liver function tests.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Effects may be delayed; medical observation is recommended. Note to physician: Treat for methemoglobinemia. Spectrophotometry may be required for precise determination of levels of methemoglobinemia in urine.
personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear dust-proof chemical goggles and face shield. Employees should wash immediately with soap. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.

storage: Dual storage: (1) Color Code Yellow Stripe: Reactivity Hazard; Store separately from flammables, combustibles, other yellow-coded materials. (2) Color Code Blue: Health Hazard/Poison: Store in a secure poison location. Store to avoid contact with strong oxidizers (chloride, bromine, chlorine dioxide, nitrates, permanganates) since violent reactions occur. Contact with caustics and chemically active metals (tin, zinc) may evolve heat and build pressure. Store in tightly closed containers in a cool, well-ventilated area away from shock or heat. Outdoor or explosion-proof storage preferred. Sources of ignition prohibited. Metal containers (5+ gallons): grounded and bonded. Drums: self-closing valves, pressure vacuum bungs, flame arresters. Only nonsparking tools. Use explosion-proof electrical equipment.

spill_handling: Evacuate persons not wearing protective equipment. Remove all ignition sources. Collect powdered material in sealed containers. Ventilate area after cleanup. OSHA 1910.120(q) may be applicable.
fire_extinguishing: Extremely explosive solid. Prolonged exposure to fire and heat may result in an explosion due to spontaneous decomposition. May explode on heating under confinement. Fight fires from an explosion-resistant location. Cool fire-exposed containers with water. In advanced or massive fires, evacuate the area. Use dry chemical, carbon dioxide, water spray, or alcohol foam extinguishers. Poisonous gases produced in fire including nitrogen oxides.
disposal_method: Incineration (982 deg C, 2.0 s minimum) followed by removal of the oxides of nitrogen using scrubbers and/or catalytic or thermal devices. The dilute wastes should be concentrated before incineration.

short_term_effects: Early manifestations include fever, sweating, headache, and confusion. Blood pressure, pulse, and respiratory rate are often elevated. Severe exposure may result in restlessness, seizures, and coma. Other signs and symptoms include dyspnea, cyanosis, pulmonary edema, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Liver injury with jaundice, kidney failure, and cardiac arrhythmias are commonly noted. Dermal exposure results in yellow staining of the skin and may produce burns. Dinitrocresol may irritate and burn the eyes and mucous membranes. Extremely toxic; probable oral lethal dose 5-50 mg/kg (7 drops to 1 teaspoon for 70-kg person). If high fever is present, drench victim's clothes in cool water or immerse person in cool bath before transfer.
long_term_effects: May damage the liver, kidneys, and blood cells. May stain yellow the skin, eyes, and fingernails. Repeated exposure can cause anxiety, fatigue, insomnia, excessive perspiration, unusual thirst, weight loss, and cataracts in the eyes.

If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. If high fever is present, drench victim's clothes in cool water, or immerse person in cool bath before transfer.

first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. The formation of methemoglobin may be delayed; medical observation is recommended. Note to physician: Treat for methemoglobinemia. Spectrophotometry may be required for precise determination of levels of methemoglobinemia in urine.

first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. personal_protective_methods: Wear protective gloves and clothing. Prevent skin contact. Consider chest X-ray. Examination of nervous system. CBC. Do not drink alcoholic beverages. Alcohol promotes absorption of organic phosphates.

short_term_effects: Endosulfan may affect the central nervous system, blood, resulting in irritability, convulsions, and renal failure. High-level exposure may result in death. long_term_effects: Repeated exposure may cause brain damage, causing convulsions, loss of coordination, and memory loss. May cause liver and kidney damage. May damage the testes.

first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit.
Decontamination: Workers leaving polluted area should undress, take a shower, wash hair, clean nails, and put on own clothes. Contaminated work clothing should be thoroughly cleaned. Disposable paper garments can be burned. Gloves rinsed with acetone or methanol, then washed and dried. Respiratory protection equipment cleaned before reuse.
personal_protective_methods: Adequate preventive measures have succeeded in eliminating intoxications almost completely in pharmaceutical industry. Air polluting processes isolated in areas with adequate exhaust facilities and hermetically sealed machines. Workers entering isolated areas must wear: special clothing including underwear, stockings, long-sleeved overalls (no pockets) buttoned to neck with ties at bottom of trousers for tying over boots, rubber gloves, head cover, and dust respirators. Air-supplied vinyl suits for groups at highest risk. Workers must not: put on rubber gloves after working barehanded; rub face or nose with contaminated gloves; contaminate inside of respirators; use outside-work-area items inside it (cigarettes, pipes, handkerchiefs). Alkaline detergent found most suitable for washing clothes and wiping surfaces. Gloves rinsed with acetone or methanol in a hood or near a vacuum then washed conventionally. Methanol for plastic items. Workrooms must be kept very clean. Some companies: alternate 1 week in polluted areas with 2 weeks elsewhere. Women's alternating work should respect cyclic hormonal pattern. Workers who develop symptoms of chronic intoxication in presence of low hormone concentrations in air MUST BE FORBIDDEN TO RETURN to polluted area.

long_term_effects: Chronic health effects are unknown at this time.
mutagenicity: Not listed as carcinogen.
first_aid: Remove the person from exposure. Begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. If frostbite has occurred, seek medical attention immediately; do NOT rub the affected areas or flush them with water. In order to prevent further tissue damage, do NOT attempt to remove frozen clothing from frostbitten areas. If frostbite has NOT occurred, immediately and thoroughly wash contaminated skin with soap and water.
personal_protective_methods: Wear appropriate personal protective clothing to prevent the skin from becoming frozen from contact with the evaporating liquid or from contact with vessels containing the liquid. Polyethylene is among the recommended protective materials. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof chemical goggles and face shield unless full face-piece respiratory protection is worn. Wear gas-proof goggles. Employees should wash immediately with soap. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.
respirator_selection: Chemical cartridge respirators should NOT be used where ethane exposure occurs. For high exposures use air-supplied respirators. Only NIOSH/MSHA- or EN149-approved SCBA with full face-piece operated in positive-pressure mode should be used in oxygen-deficient environments.
storage: Color Code Red Stripe: Flammability Hazard: Store separately from all other flammable materials. Store to avoid contact with oxidizers since violent reactions occur. Sources of ignition prohibited. Use only nonsparking tools. Use explosion-proof electrical equipment. Piping should be electrically bonded and grounded. Cylinders: compliance with OSHA 1910.101 and 1910.169 and Compressed Gas Association recommendations.
shipping: Ethane requires a shipping label of FLAMMABLE GAS. Hazard Class 2.1; no Packing Group.
spill_handling: Evacuate building; confine vapors by closing doors and shutting down HVAC. Remove all ignition sources. Establish forced ventilation to keep levels below explosive limit. Wear chemical protective suit with SCBA. Stop gas flow if safely possible. Keep out of confined spaces.
fire_extinguishing: Flammable gas. Use dry chemical, carbon dioxide, water spray, or foam. Ventilate area. Stop flow of gas if safely possible. If source is cylinder and leak cannot be stopped in place, remove to safe place in open air.
disposal_method: Dissolve or mix the material with a combustible solvent and burn in a chemical incinerator with afterburner and scrubber.

first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. short_term_effects: Ethylbenzene irritates the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract. Exposure to high concentrations can cause dizziness, lightheadedness, and unconsciousness. first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit.

short_term_effects: Irritates the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract. Can cause pulmonary edema (delayed; can cause death). Exposure to 18 ppm: vomiting and shock. Death from inhalation of 300 ppm for 2.5 h. Readily absorbed through the skin without causing irritation. Death from skin absorption of 1 teaspoon.
long_term_effects: Damage to the kidneys, liver, cardiovascular system, and nervous system. May cause reproductive damage. Repeated exposure may cause bronchitis.
points_of_attack: Respiratory system, liver, kidneys, central nervous system, cardiovascular system, eyes.
mutagenicity: NCI: No evidence (dermal). EPA Gene-Tox: Positive (E. coli polA; Ames EPA); Negative (multiple). Compound Description: Agricultural Chemical; Tumorigen, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data; Primary Irritant.
medical_surveillance: Respiratory system, liver, kidneys, CNS. Chest X-ray and pulmonary function tests. NIOSH: expired air; liver function tests; urinalysis.
first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 15 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing (using universal precautions, including resuscitation mask) if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Medical observation 24-48 h (pulmonary edema may be delayed). Corticosteroid spray for pulmonary edema. Note: Substance causes eye irritation; eye protection needed.
personal_protective_methods: Beware: liquid penetrates rubber. 8h: Viton+PVA+Barricade. 4h: 4H+Silver Shield. Contact lenses should not be worn. Wear splash-proof goggles and face shield. Provide emergency showers and eyewash.

disposal_method: Incineration with acid scrubber; prevent phosgene formation.

first_aid: If this chemical gets into the eyes, remove any contact lenses at once and irrigate immediately for at least 45 min, occasionally lifting upper and lower lids. Seek medical attention immediately since eye splashes can cause severe illness or death. If this chemical contacts the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash immediately with soap and water. Seek medical attention immediately. If this chemical has been inhaled, remove from exposure, begin rescue breathing if breathing has stopped and CPR if heart action has stopped. Transfer promptly to a medical facility. When this chemical has been swallowed, get medical attention. Give large quantities of water and induce vomiting. Do not make an unconscious person vomit. Inhalation: bronchial irritation, dizziness, rapid and shallow breathing, pulmonary edema (delayed). Skin: inflammation, sensitization, allergic dermatitis. Eyes: burns. Severe symptoms of exposure include: severe irritation of all tissues, dysuria, hematuria, tachycardia, pulmonary edema, potential circulatory collapse, bronchial pneumonia, abortion, unconsciousness.

first_aid: Eyes: Remove contact lenses. Flush victim's eyes with water or normal saline solution for 20-30 min, lifting lower and upper eyelids occasionally. Remove contaminated clothing. Get medical attention immediately. Do not put any ointments, oils, or medication in the victim's eyes without specific instructions from a physician. Skin: Immediately flood affected skin with water and wash for at least 15 min. Remove and isolate all contaminated clothing. Gently wash all affected skin areas with soap and water. If symptoms develop, call a physician. Inhalation: Remove victim to fresh air. If not breathing, give artificial respiration. If breathing is difficult, give oxygen. Get medical attention immediately. Ingestion: Do not induce vomiting. If victim is conscious and not convulsing, give large amount of water to dilute the chemical. Never give anything by mouth to an unconscious person. Get medical attention immediately.

Reassignment to work not involving organophosphate or carbamate pesticides until enzyme levels recover. Complete blood count. Consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure. Do not drink alcoholic beverages before or during use.

description: Fibrous glass is the name for a manufactured fiber in which the fiber-forming substance is glass. description: Colorless, oily liquid, ammoniacal odor (threshold 3.7ppm). Relative vapor density (air=1)=1.1. Autoignition 24°C (rusty iron) to 270°C (glass). LEL 2.9%/UEL 98%.
potential_exposure: Strong reducing capabilities → chemical synthesis intermediate, photography, metallurgy. Rocket fuel; anticorrosive/textile agent preparation; pesticides; boiler-water oxygen scavenger. Widely used in pharmaceutical synthesis.
incompatibilities: Forms explosive mixture w/ air. Highly reactive reducing agent, medium-strong base. niosh_rel: 0.03 ppm/0.04 mg/m3 Ceiling (120 min); potential occup. carcinogen, limit to lowest feasible.
acgih_tlv: 0.01 ppm/0.013 mg/m3 [skin]; confirmed animal carcinogen, human relevance unknown.
dfg_mak: [skin] skin sensitization danger; Carcinogen Cat 2; TRK sampling end-of-shift: 380μg[creatinine]/L urine hydrazine; 340μg/L plasma hydrazine.
other_national_oels: Australia 0.1ppm[skin] carcinogen; Austria [skin] carcinogen; Denmark 0.1ppm[skin]; Finland TWA0.1/STEL0.3[skin] carcinogen; Japan 0.01ppm[skin]; Norway 0.1ppm; Philippines/Turkey 1ppm[skin]; Poland TWA0.05/STEL0.1; Russia STEL0.1[skin]; Sweden NGV0.1/KTV0.3[skin] carcinogen; Switzerland MAK-W0.1[skin] carcinogen; UK TWA0.03/STEL0.13[skin] carcinogen (2000). routes_of_entry: Inhalation, skin absorption, ingestion, eye/skin contact.
target_organs: Central nervous system, respiratory system, skin, eyes (chronic: also liver, kidneys). Cancer site in animals: lungs, liver, blood vessels, intestine.
short_term_effects: Corrosive to eyes/skin/resp tract. Vapor inhalation: pulmonary edema (delayed, can be fatal). Liver/kidney/CNS effects possible; death possible, effects may be delayed. Acute signs: severe eye irritation, facial numbness/swelling, salivation, nose/throat irritation, headache, twitching, seizures, convulsions, coma. GI: anorexia, nausea, vomiting. Pulmonary edema + hypotension common. Toxic to liver, ruptures RBCs, kidney damage possible. Dermal: irritation or severe burns.
long_term_effects: Sensitization/skin allergy w/ repeated contact. Liver/kidney/CNS effects. Probable human carcinogen. Lung irritation/bronchitis. Nervous system damage (weakness, shaking, coordination loss). Blood damage/anemia possible. Chronic human exposure: pneumonia, liver/kidney damage (liver often worse); suspected human carcinogen.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, CNS, liver, kidneys. Cancer site in animals: lungs, liver, blood vessels, intestine.
mutagenicity: EPA Gene-Tox: positive mouse/rat carcinogenicity, inconclusive D.melanogaster sex-linked lethal.

first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered. Note to physician: consider pyridoxine (25 mg/kg) — effective anticonvulsant for hydrazine poisoning.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing (nitrile, Silvershield, PVC, Neoprene, butyl rubber recommended) to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: At any detectable conc. above NIOSH REL: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: SCBAE.

spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; stay upwind, avoid low areas; flush skin/eyes ≥15 min on contact; forced ventilation below explosive limit; absorb in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid sewers; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.

Vapors heavier than air, flashback risk; containers may explode/rocket; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Controlled incineration w/ effluent scrubbing (abate nitrogen compounds). Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators).

extraction_notes: Reference: NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet (Aug 2002).

Acute inhalation: sneezing, hoarseness, choking, laryngitis, resp tract irritation, nose/gum bleeding, mucosal ulceration, bronchitis, pneumonia, dyspnea, chest pain, pulmonary edema. Liquid: evacuate/restrict; remove ignition sources; ventilate; absorb in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid sewers; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Refrigerated liquid large spills: 1500ft/500m, downwind 1.7-2.8mi day/6.3-10.2mi night.
fire_extinguishing: Itself doesn't burn; metal contact produces H2 gas (explosion risk); poisonous Cl2/HCl gases; extinguishers other than water preferred (water contact→heat+HCl); if water used, flooding quantities only; vapors heavier than air; containers may explode/rocket; do not apply water to cryogenic liquid containers; cool from secure location (non-cryogenic); SCBA for firefighters.

description: Volatile, colorless-or-pale-blue liquid or colorless gas. Bitter almond odor (some describe musty 'old sneakers' smell) — many can't detect it, odor unreliable as warning. Bitter burning taste; often used as aqueous solution (typically 96%). Intensely poisonous, highly flammable, explosive. Odor threshold 0.58ppm. Autoignition 537.8°C (96%). LEL 5.6%/UEL 40.0%.
potential_exposure: Chemical synthesis of sequestrants, polymers, weed killers, pharmaceuticals; fumigant; electroplating, mining, synthetic fiber/plastic/dye/pesticide production; acrylate/nitrile (esp. acrylonitrile) synthesis. May be generated in blast furnaces, gas works, coke ovens. Cyanide salts: steel hardening, gold/silver ore extraction. AC used as chemical warfare agent (blood/systemic agent) — forms cyanide in body.
incompatibilities: Unless stabilized/maintained, samples stored >90 days are hazardous. Gas forms explosive air mixture. Material w/ >2-5% water less stable, can self-react/form explosive mixture. Heat >50-60°C or contact w/ heat/water/alkaline material/amines/strong bases → polymerization. Aqueous solution = weak acid. Violent w/ oxidizers, acetaldehyde, acids, HCl in alcoholic mixtures, sodium carbonate, caustics. Incompatible w/ amines, strong acids, sodium/calcium hydroxide, sodium carbonate, ammonia. Attacks plastics/rubber/coatings.

routes_of_entry: Vapor inhalation; percutaneous absorption of liquid/concentrated vapor; ingestion; eye/skin contact.
short_term_effects: Skin/eye irritation/burns. Resp tract irritation. Tearing, mouth/throat burning. Dizziness, headache, weakness, anxiety, confusion, pounding heart, difficult breathing, nausea — can rapidly progress to convulsions/death without immediate treatment. High exposure: sudden death. Acute signs: hypertension/tachycardia then hypotension/bradycardia; cherry-red mucous membranes/blood; cardiac arrhythmias; cyanosis; weakness, headache, vertigo, agitation, giddiness, salivation, nausea/vomiting → combative behavior, convulsions, paralysis, protruding eyeballs, dilated/unreactive pupils, coma; tachypnea/hyperpnea → respiratory depression; lung hemorrhage/pulmonary edema. Inhalation tiers: <20ppm headache/dizziness/nausea/vomiting; >50ppm difficulty breathing/rapid heartbeat/paralysis/unconsciousness/respiratory arrest/death; 135ppm/30min may cause death, 270ppm immediate death. Skin: readily absorbed, similar symptoms. Ingestion: 570mg/kg (1.4oz/150lb person) has caused death.
long_term_effects: Thyroid function interference/goiter. Itching, scarlet rash, red bumps, nose itch/bleeding, possible nasal perforation. Headache, nausea, vomiting, weakness, enlarged thyroid at 4-12ppm exposure. Nervous system damage possible.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: whole blood chemical/metabolite, lactic acid, blood pH, carboxyhemoglobin, blood plasma bicarbonate, EKG (workers >40yo), expired air. Preplacement/periodic: cardiovascular/CNS exam, liver/kidney function, blood, fainting/dizziness history, blood cyanide test, thyroid function, nervous system exam. Urinary thiocyanate nonspecific (elevated in smokers).
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Use amyl nitrite capsules if symptoms develop. All area employees trained in cyanide-poisoning emergency measures + CPR. Cyanide antidote kit kept in work area, ingredients replaced every 1-2 years. DECONTAMINATION IMPORTANT: wash-strip-wash-evacuate upwind/uphill protocol; diluted household bleach (10%, 1:9 bleach:water) for skin decon, avoid eyes/wounds/mouth, wash off after 15 min; 5% bleach or calcium hypochlorite solution for tool decontamination.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; eye protection to prevent eye contact; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash. See NIOSH Criteria Doc 212, Nitriles.
respirator_selection: When used as a weapon: SCBA certified by NIOSH for CBRN environments. 47ppm: Sa. 50ppm: Sa:Cf/SCBAF/SaF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFS/SCBAE.
storage: (1) Red stripe: separate from all other flammables. (2) Blue: poison, secure location. Check explosive conc. before confined entry; away from incompatibles; outdoors preferred, or standard combustible-liquid room/cabinet away from ignition; protect from damage; grounded/bonded metal containers; self-closing valves/flame arresters on drums; nonsparking tools; no smoking/open flames; explosion-proof electrical.
shipping: Aqueous solutions <20% HCN: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label, Class 6.1, Packing Group I. Stabilized <3% water: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS, FLAMMABLE LIQUID' label, Class 6.1, Packing Group I. Stabilized <3% water absorbed in porous material: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label, Class 6.1, Packing Group I.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; forced ventilation below explosive limit; stay upwind, avoid low areas; ventilate closed spaces before entry; water spray to reduce vapors; don't touch spilled material; stop leak if safe; shut off ignition sources; isolate until gas disperses; absorb liquid in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid sewers; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Isolation — 'AC when used as weapon' small: 300ft/100m, downwind 0.2-0.3mi day/0.7-1.2mi night; large: 3000ft/1000m, downwind 2.4-3.8mi day/4.5-7.2mi night. Standard 'Hydrogen cyanide/Hydrocyanic acid' small: 200ft/60m, downwind 0.1-0.2mi day/0.4-0.6mi night; large: 1250ft/400m, downwind 1.0-1.5mi day/2.5-4.1mi night.
fire_extinguishing: Poisonous cyanide gases; if fire conditions permit, don't extinguish (combustion products less toxic than material itself); cool exposures w/ unattended monitors; don't use water directly on fire (cyanide gas may form) — use water for vapor control only; may self-react explosively without warning. Gas: keep people away, isolate, deny entry; stay upwind; ventilate closed spaces; positive-pressure gear + special protective clothing; use dry chemicals/AFFF foam/CO2; small fires — let burn unless leak stoppable; large fires — water spray/fog/foam; move container if safe; withdraw if venting/discoloration observed; firefighting from safe distance (a few whiffs or liquid penetrating gear could be fatal). Liquid: dry chemical/CO2/AFFF foam extinguishers; vapors heavier than air, flashback risk; containers may explode/rocket; cool from secure location, coordinated fog streams may sweep flames (experienced crews); SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Chemical conversion to ammonia + CO2 using chlorine/hypochlorite in basic media; controlled incineration also adequate. HCN may alternatively be recovered from ammonoxidation process waste streams. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators).

OSHA 29CFR1910.119 App A, TQ 2500 lb (1135 kg). Canada WHMIS 1.0%. Hazard Symbol E,Xn,N; R2;R21/22;R37/38;R40;R41;R43;R48/22; S2;S26;S36/37/39;S61. WGK: none assigned.
description: White crystalline substance, very hygroscopic and unstable. Autoignition 265°C.
potential_exposure: Chemical synthesis/use as reducing agent.
incompatibilities: Self-reactive. Contaminants, temps >129.4°C, or open flame → explosive decomposition (esp. w/ moisture/CO2). Incompatible w/ strong acids, organic anhydrides, isocyanates, aldehydes, sodium, finely divided zinc, some metal oxides. Aqueous solution = weak base. Strong oxidizer contact → fire/explosion. Attacks some metals. Calcium/zinc contact forms heat-sensitive explosive bis(hydroxylamide).
dfg_mak: Danger of skin sensitization.
short_term_effects: Corrosive to skin/eyes/mucous membranes. Methemoglobinemia possible; effects may be delayed. Headache, vertigo, tinnitus, dyspnea, nausea/vomiting, cyanosis, proteinuria/hematuria, jaundice, restlessness, convulsion; yellowish-brown conjunctiva/cornea deposit; astigmatism; hair/exposed skin reddening.
long_term_effects: Skin sensitization/eczema w/ repeated contact. Nervous system effects possible. Anemia and liver damage possible.
mutagenicity: See regulatory_authority — EPA Gene-Tox mixed results.
medical_surveillance: Annual physical exams incl. renal/hepatic. Allergist examination. CBC. Nervous system exam.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: if conscious, water/milk (no induced vomiting). Note to physician: treat for methemoglobinemia; test urine; spectrophotometry may be required for precise urine methemoglobin determination.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Per OSHA 29CFR1910.134/EN149: NIOSH/MSHA-approved respirator, or supplied-air (positive-pressure/continuous-flow), or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure.
storage: (1) Yellow stripe: strong reducing agent, isolated from flammables/combustibles/other yellow materials. (2) Blue: poison, secure location. Protect against physical damage; cool, noncombustible buildings, separate from oxidizers; open airtight containers occasionally to relieve decomposition pressure.
shipping: Toxic solid, corrosive, inorganic, n.o.s.: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS, CORROSIVE' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; cover spill w/ sodium bisulfite + sprinkle water; collect, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Extreme caution — material may explode when exposed to heat/flame. No fire-fighting attempt except remotely activated equipment. Evacuate surrounding area. Water/foam may cause frothing. Use dry chemical/CO2/alcohol foam. Poisonous NOx/SOx gases produced. Cool exposed containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Add sodium bisulfite solution and flush to sewer, or incinerate.
extraction_notes: Reference: Sax DPIM Vol2No.2 pp.37-39(1982) & Vol8No.4 pp.34-39(1988).

regulatory_authority: Air Pollutant Standard Set (see PEL). Hazard Symbol T; R23/24/25;R34;R43; S1/2;S26;S36/37/39;S45. WGK: none assigned.
description: Clear-to-light-yellow liquid, sweetish solvent odor. Relative vapor density (air=1)=4.5. LEL 1.8%/UEL unknown.
potential_exposure: Bifunctional monomer for acrylic resins; nonwoven-fabric binder; detergent lube-oil additive production.
incompatibilities: Can polymerize (heating, initiators, UV light). Unstable at high temp/pressure; may react w/ water releasing energy (not violent). Reacts w/ oxidizers, strong acids, nitrates.
acgih_tlv: 0.5 ppm/2.8 mg/m3 TWA [skin]; skin sensitization danger.
dfg_mak: Skin sensitization danger.
other_national_oels: Australia/Denmark/France 0.5ppm[skin]; Belgium 0.5[skin]; Norway 0.5; Russia STEL1[skin]; Switzerland MAK-W0.5[skin]; Netherlands MAC-TGG 3. US states 30-71 μg/m3.
ld50: (oral-rat) 250 mg/kg (moderately toxic).
short_term_effects: Corrosive to eyes/skin/resp tract. Eye contact: burns, permanent damage possible. Vapor inhalation: pulmonary edema (delayed, can be fatal).
long_term_effects: Repeated/prolonged skin contact: dermatitis, eczema, sensitization.
medical_surveillance: Lung function tests. Allergist evaluation.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water, do NOT induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Per OSHA 29CFR1910.134/EN149: NIOSH/MSHA-approved respirator, or supplied-air (positive-pressure/continuous-flow), or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure.
storage: White: corrosive/contact hazard, corrosion-resistant location. Check explosive conc. before confined entry; tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from oxidizers/reducing agents.
shipping: Corrosive liquids, n.o.s.: 'CORROSIVE' label; Class 8, Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; forced ventilation below explosive limit; absorb in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid sewers; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible liquid; poisonous/acid fumes (acrylic acid, acrolein); water may be ineffective — use dry chemical/alcohol foam/CO2; vapors heavier than air, flashback risk; containers may explode/rocket; cool from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
extraction_notes: No dedicated Disposal Method or References section visible in source (entry transitions into I section: 'Incapacitating agents' header, then Indene).

Synonyms: 1H-Indene; Indonaphthene
un_na_number: UN1993 (Combustible liquid, n.o.s.)/128 — only regulated in bulk
regulatory_authority: Air Pollutant Standard Set (see PEL). Canada WHMIS 1.0%. Not listed Annex 1. WGK: 1.
international_regulations: Not listed in Annex 1.
description: Colorless liquid from coal tars. Odor threshold 0.015 ppm.
potential_exposure: Synthetic resin preparation (coumarone indene resins); organic intermediate. Asphalt/naphtha constituent — petroleum refining and coke processing.
incompatibilities: Strong oxidizers/acids → fire/explosion. Polymerizes/oxidizes on standing. Sunlight can cause polymerization. Has exploded during nitration w/ sulfuric+nitric acid.
acgih_tlv: 5 ppm/24 mg/m3 TWA.
other_national_oels: Australia/Belgium/Denmark/France/Norway/Switzerland 10ppm; Finland TWA10/STEL20. US states 450-1071 μg/m3.
determination_in_air: Coal tar products methods: OSHA Method 58; NIOSH #5506 (HPLC), #5515 (GC).
human_health_water: No criteria set, but EPA suggests permissible ambient goal of 621 μg/L based on health effects.
target_organs: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, liver, kidneys, spleen.
short_term_effects: Eye/skin/resp irritation. Animal studies: liver damage, occasional spleen/kidney injury at high (800-900ppm) vapor conc. Liquid defats skin but no dermatitis observed. Lung aspiration caused pneumonitis, pulmonary edema, hemorrhage in animals.
long_term_effects: Skin sensitization/allergy possible. Liver, kidney, spleen injury observed in laboratory animals.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, liver, kidneys, spleen.
medical_surveillance: If overexposed: liver/kidney function tests; allergist evaluation. Full coal tar products medical surveillance program: comprehensive initial medical/work history (skin, resp tract, liver, kidney disorders); physical exam (oral cavity, skin, resp system); posteroanterior+lateral chest X-rays; pulmonary function (FVC, FEV1); sputum cytology offered; liver function/urinalysis as appropriate; oral mucous membrane exam; positive-pressure respirator fitness judgment. Periodic exams ≥annually (interim history + physical). Records retained ≥30 years post-employment, available to medical reps of government/employer/employee.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Above 10ppm: organic vapor cartridge/canister respirator (full face-piece better than half-mask; PAPR even greater protection). High exposures: supplied-air respirator (positive-pressure/continuous-flow) or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure.
storage: Green (small quantities, general storage); tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from sunlight/air/strong acids/oxidizers; no smoking/open flames.
shipping: Only regulated when shipped in bulk: Class 3 combustible liquid, Packing Group III.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate; absorb in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid sewers; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible liquid, burns but doesn't readily ignite; extinguish per surrounding fire; poisonous gases produced; vapors heavier than air, may explode in confined spaces; containers may explode/rocket; cool from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
extraction_notes: Reference: NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet (Nov 1999). No Disposal Method Suggested section visible in source. NOTE: immediately preceding this entry, source includes a short 'I' section header on 'Incapacitating agents' — a category note describing chemical warfare agents causing temporary disability, cross-referencing Quinuclidinyl benzilate/Agent BZ at record Q:0120 elsewhere in the book. It's not a chemical data entry itself (no extractable field data), so no separate JSON record was created for it.

Synonyms: Indenopyrene; IP; o-Phenylenepyrene; 1,10-(o-Phenylene)pyrene; 2,3-Phenylenepyrene
regulatory_authority: Carcinogenicity: IARC 2B (1997); NTP reasonably anticipated (2004); EPA sufficient animal/inadequate human. EPA Gene-Tox: positive mouse/rat carcinogenicity. Air Pollutant Standard Set. CWA §423 App A/§401.15 (PAHs). RCRA #U139; App 8; UTS wastewater 0.0055/nonwastewater 3.4 mg/kg. EPCRA 313 de minimis 0.1%. CA Prop 65 (cancer 1/1/88). Canada WHMIS 0.1%. Not listed Annex 1. WGK: none assigned.
carcinogenicity_status: IARC 2B (1997). NTP reasonably anticipated (2004). EPA: sufficient animal/inadequate human. EPA Gene-Tox: positive mouse/rat carcinogenicity.
rcra_waste_numbers: U139. App 8 Hazardous Constituents. UTS: wastewater 0.0055 mg/L, nonwastewater 3.4 mg/kg. GW monitoring PQL: 8100(200), 8270(10).
epcra_status: Section 313 de minimis 0.1%.
clean_ water_act: 40CFR423 App A; §401.15 (PAHs).
international_regulations: Not listed in Annex 1.
description: Yellow crystalline solid. PAH class (multiple benzene rings).
potential_exposure: Found in internal combustion engine exhaust, cigarette smoke condensate, soot, coal tar pitch.
incompatibilities: Strong oxidizers.
osha_pel: 0.2 mg/m3 TWA [1910.1002] (benzene-soluble fraction). OSHA defines 'coal tar pitch volatiles' as fused polycyclic hydrocarbons volatilizing from distillation residues of coal, petroleum (excl. asphalt), wood, other organic matter.
niosh_rel: 0.1 mg/m3 (cyclohexane-extractable fraction). NIOSH considers coal tar products (coal tar, coal tar pitch, creosote) potential occup. carcinogens.
acgih_tlv: 0.2 mg/m3 TWA (benzene-soluble aerosol); Confirmed Human Carcinogen.
dfg_mak: [skin] skin sensitization danger; Carcinogen Cat 2.
other_national_oels: Austria/France: carcinogen (1999/1993).
determination_in_air: NIOSH #5506 (PAHs by HPLC), #5515 (PAHs by GC); OSHA Method ID-58.
freshwater_aquatic_life_acute: Insufficient data to propose freshwater/saltwater aquatic life criterion (US EPA, one of 65 priority toxic pollutants).
human_health_water: Preferably zero; 1:100,000 cancer risk at 0.028 μg/L. 1970 WHO European Drinking Water Standards: PAH ≤0.2 μg/L (composite of 6 PAHs incl. this compound). Kansas guideline 0.029 μg/L.
determination_in_water: Methylene chloride extraction + HPLC (fluorescence/UV) or GC (EPA 610) or GC-MS (EPA 625). Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow=6.6.
iarc_classification: Group 2B (1997).
target_organs: Respiratory system, skin, bladder, kidneys. Cancer site (coal tar pitch volatiles): lung, kidney, skin.
long_term_effects: May be carcinogenic in humans. Dermatitis, bronchitis w/ repeated exposure. Complete carcinogen and skin-carcinogenesis initiator in mouse. Subcutaneous injection produces local sarcomas in mice.
points_of_attack: Respiratory system, skin, bladder, kidneys. Cancer site (coal tar pitch volatiles): lung, kidney, skin.
mutagenicity: EPA Gene-Tox: positive mouse/rat carcinogenicity.
medical_surveillance: Full coal tar products medical surveillance program (identical to Indene entry): comprehensive initial medical/work history (skin, resp tract, liver, kidney disorders); physical exam w/ chest X-rays, pulmonary function, sputum cytology; liver function/urinalysis as appropriate; positive-pressure respirator fitness judgment; periodic exams ≥annually; records retained ≥30 years.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: At any detectable conc. above NIOSH REL: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFOv/SCBAE.
storage: Green (general storage); tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from strong oxidizers; regulated area per OSHA 1910.1045.
shipping: Not on DOT materials list; bulk quantities may be classified as Environmentally hazardous substances, solid, n.o.s.; 'CLASS 9' label; Class 9, Packing Group III.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Burns only w/ difficulty; extinguish per surrounding fire; poisonous gases produced; cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: May be destroyed by permanganate oxidation, high-temp incineration w/ scrubbing equipment, or microwave plasma treatment. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators).
extraction_notes: References: Eller & Cassinelli (Eds.) NIOSH Manual of Analytical Methods 4th ed. 2nd Supp. #98-119 (1998); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet (Mar 2007).

Synonyms: Elemental indium; Indium metal
regulatory_authority: Air Pollutant Standard Set (see PEL). Canada WHMIS 1.0% (all indium compounds). Not listed Annex 1. WGK: none assigned (all CAS numbers).
international_regulations: Not listed in Annex 1.
water_solubility: Insoluble (elemental; finely divided forms hydroxide on water contact). Sulfate: soluble.
description: Malleable, ductile, shiny metal, softer than lead; may be found as white/gray powder. Two most important compounds: oxide and sulfate. Sulfate is grayish-white hygroscopic powder.
potential_exposure: Dental alloy; high-quality solders/braze-bonded connectors; automotive bearings (Europe); low-pressure sodium lamps (Europe); nuclear reactor control rod alloys; catalysts; indium oxide fuel cells; cryogenic gasket material. Oxide: glass coloring (light-to-dark brown). Sulfate: electroplating (sulfate electrolytes). Radioisotopes: cancer treatment, diagnostic organ scanning.
incompatibilities: Not flammable in bulk; dust/powder may ignite when dispersed in air. Violent reaction w/ acetonitrile, dinitrogen tetroxide, mercury(II) bromide (350°C), sulfur (ignites when heated). Oxidizes readily at higher temps. Keep away from oxidizers.
niosh_rel: 0.1 mg/m3 TWA; also applies to other indium compounds [as In].
acgih_tlv: 0.1 mg/m3 TWA.
teel: Elemental TEEL-0: 0.1 mg/m3; Sulfate TEEL-0: 0.225; Trichloride TEEL-0: 0.193; Oxide TEEL-0: 0.121; Oxide vapor TEEL-0: 0.107
pac1: Elemental 0.1; Sulfate 0.676; Trichloride 0.578; Oxide 0.363; Oxide vapor 0.321 mg/m3
pac2: Elemental 0.6; Sulfate 1.13; Trichloride 1; Oxide 0.605; Oxide vapor 100 mg/m3
pac3: Elemental 3.5; Sulfate 4; Trichloride 1; Oxide 500; Oxide vapor 500 mg/m3
other_national_oels: Australia/Belgium/Finland/Norway 0.1mg/m3; Denmark TWA0.1mg[In]; Netherlands MAC-TGG 0.1; Switzerland MAK-W0.1; UK TWA0.1[In]/STEL0.3[In] (2000). Indium chloride: UK TWA0.1[In]/STEL0.3[In]; Netherlands MAC-TGG 0.1[In]. US states zero-2.0 μg/m3.
determination_in_water: Neutron activation used to analyze indium in seawater (detection limit 0.006 ng/L). Polarography also used (detection limit 1.0 μg/L).
target_organs: Eyes, skin, respiratory system; possible liver/kidney/heart/blood effects.
short_term_effects: Eye/skin irritation. High-level exposure may damage kidneys/liver. Lung irritation, possible permanent damage. Higher exposures: pulmonary edema (delayed, can be fatal).
long_term_effects: Possible liver/kidney/heart/blood effects (NIOSH). May damage developing fetus. Lung damage possible.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory system; possible liver, kidney, heart, blood effects.
medical_surveillance: For ≥half-TLV exposure: lung function tests before work + periodically. If overexposed: liver/kidney function tests, CBC, chest X-ray after acute overexposure.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Above 0.1mg/m3: particulate (dust/fume/mist) filter respirator (check daily for damage). High exposures: supplied-air respirator (positive-pressure/continuous-flow) or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure.
storage: Green (metal, general storage); bulk indium powder is pyrophoric and requires Red Code. Check explosive conc. before confined entry w/ powder/dust present; tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from mineral acids/sulfur.
shipping: Not regulated.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources + nonsparking tools when cleaning powder/dust; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Indium itself doesn't burn, but powder/dust flammable, may ignite w/ heat/flame; extinguish per surrounding fire; poisonous gases produced; cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Moderately toxic rating. Recovered indium has recycle value, minimal quantity discarded. Closed containers required for disposal. Environmental hazard appears to stem from radioactive isotope use/disposal, not chemical toxicity.
extraction_notes: References: EPA Report EPA-460/2-75-005b (Aug 1975); EPA Toxicology of Metals Vol II pp.234-241 (May 1977); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet (Aug 1999).

Synonyms: Amuno; Artracin; Confortid; Dolovin; Indocid; Indomed; Metacen; Mobilan; NCI-C56144; Reumacide; Tannex — and numerous other trade names
regulatory_authority: WGK: 3 (severe hazard to waters).
description: Pale yellow to tan crystalline powder.
potential_exposure: Anti-inflammatory, antipyretic, analgesic medication.
incompatibilities: Strong alkalis.
teel: No standards or TEEL available. Material is poisonous.
short_term_effects: Classified very toxic. Probable oral lethal dose in humans 50-500 mg/kg (1tsp-1oz/150lb person). Symptoms: GI complaints (appetite loss, nausea, abdominal pain, ulcers, diarrhea); dizziness, lightheadedness, mental confusion; severe depression, psychosis; hypersensitivity reactions (rashes, asthma, urticaria); tinnitus; coma, convulsions. Acute pancreatitis, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia also reported. Persons with renal disease or GI ulcerative lesions at risk. Pregnant/nursing women should avoid exposure. Use cautiously in elderly.
long_term_effects: Liver and kidney effects possible.
medical_surveillance: Liver function tests. Kidney function tests.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Where exposure potential exists: supplied-air respirator (positive-pressure/continuous-flow) or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure.
storage: Blue (poison, secure location); tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from strong alkalis.
shipping: May be classified as medicine, poisons, solid n.o.s.: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group I.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Material itself burns w/ difficulty; extinguish per surrounding fire; water flooding as fog, alcohol foam, CO2, or dry chemical; poisonous gases produced; cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
extraction_notes: Reference: EPA CHIP: Indomethacin (Oct 1985). No Disposal Method Suggested section visible in source.

Synonyms: Iodine crystals; Molecular iodine
regulatory_authority: FIFRA status: supported. Air Pollutant Standard Set (see PEL). FDA OTC drug. Canada WHMIS 1.0%, Class E. Hazard Symbol Xn,N; R20/21;R50; S2;S23;S25;S61. WGK: 2.
international_regulations: Hazard Symbol Xn,N; R20/21;R50; S2;S23;S25;S61.
description: Blue-black or violet solid, sharp characteristic odor.
potential_exposure: Drinking-water disinfectant; organic chemical (esp. pharmaceutical) manufacture; catalyst in organic reactions; silver iodide manufacture for photography.
incompatibilities: Ammonia contact forms shock-sensitive explosive compound (fire risk). Powerful oxidizer. Violent reaction w/ reducing agents, combustibles, acetylene, acetaldehyde, antimony, cesium, francium, lithium, potassium, powdered metals, rubidium, phosphorus, sodium, sulfur.
acgih_tlv: 0.01 ppm/0.1 mg/m3, inhalable fraction and vapor, TWA; 0.1 ppm/1 mg/m3 STEL.
other_national_oels: Egypt/Australia/Denmark/Japan/Norway/Philippines/Thailand/Turkey 0.1ppm; Austria MAK0.1; Belgium STEL0.1; Finland STEL0.1[skin]; France VLE0.1; Netherlands MAC1mg/m3; Poland MAC1; Russia TWA0.1/STEL1[skin]; Sweden ceiling0.1; Switzerland MAK0.1/KZG0.2; UK STEL0.1 (2000). US states 8-24 μg/m3.
determination_in_air: NIOSH #6005; OSHA Method ID-212, see also ID-177.
human_health_water: Maine guideline 340 μg/L drinking water.
determination_in_water: Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow=2.5.
target_organs: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, CNS, cardiovascular system.
short_term_effects: Eye/skin/resp tract irritation. Note: thyroid/lung/kidney disease individuals should consult physician before iodine work. Inhalation dose tiers: irritation at 0.1ppm; work difficult 0.15-0.2ppm, impossible at 0.3ppm; ≥1ppm highly irritating (similar to chlorine, more lung-irritating); tearing, chest tightness, sore throat, headache; painful cough/breathing difficulty may persist weeks after severe exposure. Higher exposures: pulmonary edema (delayed, can be fatal). Skin: solid/vapor/solution stains/irritates/damages/penetrates skin. Eyes: 0.57ppm/5min causes irritation; 1.63ppm irritation within 2min; saturated vapor 3-4min causes brown staining + cornea outer-layer loss (heals 2-3 days). Ingestion: small doses → salivation, tearing, eyelid swelling, salivary gland soreness, metallic taste, skin rash, fever, lymph gland enlargement; larger doses → severe vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, thirst, shock, fever, urine suppression, delirium, stupor, death. 1mL tincture or 1g crystals → giddiness, faintness, pallor, weak rapid pulse, excitement, convulsions, collapse, unconsciousness. Fatal adult dose ~1/15 oz.
long_term_effects: Prolonged exposure → iodism, thyroid hormone deficiency. Potent sensitizer — repeated contact may cause rash, vocal cord swelling, severe generalized allergic reaction, joint pain/swelling.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, CNS, cardiovascular system.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: chest X-ray, pulmonary function (FVC, FEV1). If overexposed: thyroid function tests, liver function tests.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered.
personal_protective_methods: Solid: gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact (8h: Saranex-coated suits; 4h: polyethylene gloves/suits/boots); no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash. Liquid: avoid skin contact w/ ≥7% content; eye protection for ≥7% content; wash immediately if contaminated w/ ≥7% content; remove nonimpervious clothing immediately if wet w/ ≥7% or promptly if <7%.
respirator_selection: Up to 1ppm: Sa*. Up to 2ppm: Sa:Cf*/SCBAF/SaF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFAg100/SCBAE. *Eye irritant — may need eye protection.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Avoid aqueous ammonia, acetylene, acetaldehyde, powdered aluminum, active metals (potassium, sodium, magnesium, zinc); tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from incompatibles.
shipping: 'CORROSIVE' label; Class 8, Packing Group III.
spill_handling: Solid: evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Liquid: evacuate/restrict; remove ignition sources; ventilate; absorb in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid sewers.
fire_extinguishing: Noncombustible solid; itself doesn't burn; extinguish per surrounding fire; poisonous gases produced; cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: React w/ large volumes of reducing agent (hypo-/bisulfites or ferrous salts) solution, neutralize, flush to sewer w/ water. Alternatively iodine may be recovered from process waste streams.
extraction_notes: References: Sax DPIM Vol1No.5 pp.65-68 (1981); NY DOH Fact Sheet (May 1986); EPA Rainbow Report (1998); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet (May 2001).

Synonyms: Iodine chloride; Iodochlorine; Protochlorure d'iode (French); Wijs' chloride
regulatory_authority: Canada WHMIS 1.0%. Not listed Annex 1. WGK: none assigned.
international_regulations: Not listed in Annex 1.
description: Black crystalline solid or reddish-brown liquid.
potential_exposure: Used as a chemical reagent.
incompatibilities: Strong oxidizer. Reacts w/ air forming iodine pentoxide; heat may cause explosions. Violent reaction w/ water/steam/moisture (toxic/corrosive fumes); organic matter; aluminum foil; cadmium sulfide, hydrides, lead sulfide; metal powders, phosphorus, phosphorus trichloride; potassium, reducing agents, rubber, silver sulfide; sodium, zinc sulfide, other metals. regulatory_authority: DHS Screening Threshold: release hazard 20,000 lb (≥1.00%). Air Pollutant Standard Set. CAA Accidental Release Prevention TQ 20,000 lb (9080 kg). TPQ 1000 lb. RQ 1000 lb. Not listed Annex 1. WGK: 2.

first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: immediately administer 100% oxygen to all victims; monitor for respiratory distress; rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: evaluate vital signs, rush to healthcare facility, do NOT induce vomiting or attempt to neutralize. Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered.

Toxic nitrogen oxides produced. Vapor explosion + poison hazard indoors/outdoors/sewers; runoff to sewer may create fire/explosion hazard. description: Oily, colorless to faintly yellow liquid.
potential_exposure: Insecticide. Neuroscience research tool — inhibits cholinesterase (via phosphorylation) acutely/subacutely, produces delayed neuropathy. Used as basis for 'nerve gases.'
incompatibilities: Forms hydrofluoric acid w/ water. Moisture attacks metals, rubbers, plastics, coatings, silica-containing materials (glass). Strong oxidizers may release toxic phosphorus oxides. Strong reducing agents (hydrides) may form highly toxic/flammable phosphine gas.
determination_in_air: OSHA versatile sampler-2, toluene/acetone, GC-flame photometric detection for S/N/P; NIOSH #5600 (Organophosphorus Pesticides).
target_organs: Respiratory system, lungs, CNS, cardiovascular system, skin, eyes, plasma/RBC cholinesterase.
short_term_effects: Organic phosphorus insecticides absorbed by skin/resp/GI tracts, cholinesterase inhibitors. Headache, giddiness, blurred vision, nervousness, weakness, nausea, cramps, diarrhea, chest discomfort. Signs: sweating, tearing, salivation, vomiting, cyanosis, convulsions, coma, reflex/sphincter control loss. Extremely toxic — probable oral lethal dose 5-50 mg/kg (7 drops-1tsp/70kg person). Even trace vapor causes pinpoint pupils. High exposures may cause pulmonary edema.
long_term_effects: Cholinesterase inhibitor — cumulative effect possible. Repeated exposure may damage nervous system (convulsions, respiratory failure). Liver damage possible.
points_of_attack: Respiratory system, lungs, CNS, cardiovascular system, skin, eyes, plasma/RBC cholinesterase.
medical_surveillance: Plasma/RBC cholinesterase levels before employment + regularly (plasma normalizes in 1-2wk after exposure stops, RBC may stay reduced 1-3mo). ≥25% reduction below preemployment level increases poisoning risk even in 'normal' range — reassignment away from organophosphate/carbamate work recommended until recovery. If overexposed: repeat tests ASAP, nervous system exam, CBC, chest X-ray after acute overexposure. Avoid alcohol before/during use (promotes organic phosphate absorption).
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash immediately (speed critical), shampoo hair if contaminated, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious); keep victim quiet, maintain normal body temp. Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered.

Use positive pressure, pressure-demand, full face-piece SCBA or pressure-demand supplied-air respirator with escape SCBA and fully encapsulating chemical-resistant suit.

storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from water and steam.
shipping: Organophosphorus pesticides, liquid, toxic, n.o.s.: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group I.

Containers may explode/rocket; cool from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
