short_term_effects: Effects of fume/dust exposure may be slow to develop. Extremely high exposures can cause seizures, coma, death — but symptoms occur weeks-to-months after exposure begins. Earliest symptoms: tiredness, decreased fitness, fatigue, sleep disturbance, headache, aching bones/muscles, constipation, abdominal pain, decreased appetite, moodiness. Skin/eye contact may cause irritation. Large-amount ingestion may lead to seizures, coma, death.
long_term_effects: Lead accumulates over time — long-term lower-level exposure builds up, causing more severe symptoms: high BP, anemia, pale skin, blue gum-margin line, forearm/wrist/finger paralysis, abdominal pain, severe constipation, nausea, vomiting. Prolonged high exposure: serious permanent kidney/brain damage. Nervous system effects (very high exposures): severe headache, mood/personality changes, retarded mental development, convulsions, coma, delirium, death; nonfatal recovery slow/incomplete. Alcohol/exertion may bring on symptoms. Probable human teratogen. Continuous exposure → decreased male/female fertility. Elevated parental exposure before pregnancy increases miscarriage/birth-defect risk. Cumulative poison — builds up until symptoms/disability occur. Contaminated clothing can expose family members. Standards protect inhalation exposure only. Biological half-life in human bone ~10 years.
points_of_attack: Eyes, GI tract, CNS, kidneys, blood, gingival tissue.
mutagenicity: See regulatory_authority — EPA Gene-Tox mixed results (positive sperm morphology-human).
medical_surveillance: OSHA-mandated: whole blood chemical/metabolite, blood lead level, hemoglobin, hematocrit, zinc protoporphyrin, BUN, serum creatinine, urinalysis, microscopic exam. Prior to initial exposure + annually for blood lead >40μg/100g: complete medical history, CBC, kidney function tests. OSHA 'exposure' = air levels averaging ≥30μg lead/m3. Blood-lead ≥0.050mg/100mL → removal from exposure until falls to ≤0.040mg/100mL. Tolerance levels: ACGIH BEI ≤50mg/L blood, 150mg/g creatinine urine; DFG BAT ≤70mg/L blood, 30mg/L women <45. NIOSH tests: whole blood chemical/metabolite, blood lead level, tissue biopsy, CBC, nerve conduction studies, neurologic exam/EMG, RBC count, zinc protoporphyrin (incl. after 1mo exposure), urine chemical/metabolite (end-of-shift, 24h collection).
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Swallowed: get medical attention. Antidotes/special procedures: significant poisoning sometimes treated with Ca EDTA while hospitalized — chelating drug causes lead rush from organs into blood/kidneys, own hazards, must be administered only by experienced medical personnel under controlled conditions. Never used to prevent poisoning during continued exposure without strict control — severe kidney damage can result. Note to physician: BAL [British Anti-Lewisite, dimercaprol, dithiopropanol] used for heavy-metal poisoning, may have SOME value for lead; large margin of safety reported but caution needed re: excessive dosage; most preventable by premedication with l-ephedrine sulfate (CAS 134-72-5).
personal_protective_methods: Prevent skin contact with any dust-blocking barrier. All protective clothing (suits, gloves, footwear, headgear) clean, available daily, put on before work. Vacuum clothing with HEPA. Dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator worn. Wash immediately with soap if skin wet/contaminated. Emergency showers/eyewash. See also NIOSH #78-158, Lead: inorganic dusts and fumes.

shipping: Metal powder, flammable, n.o.s.: 'SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE' label; Class 4.2, Packing Group I.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; get all workers out of spill area; put on protective equipment incl. respirators. Cool exposed containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Recycle wherever possible. May be treated with HNO3 to give lead nitrate; lead may be precipitated as sulfide, sent to lead recovery plant. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators).

description: Colorless, odorless liquid when pure. Industrially produced: amber-to-dark-brown oily liquid, geranium odor, turns violet/black/green with age. Odor not a reliable toxic-vapor indicator. Complex mixture of cis-/trans-isomers: L-1 [2-chlorovinylarsonous dichloride, the vesicant agent, generally predominates in chemical-agent-grade material], L-2 [bis(2-chlorovinyl)arsinous chloride], L-3 [tris(2-chlorovinyl)arsine] — all form via catalyzed arsenic trichloride + acetylene reaction; L-2/L-3 are toxic but considerably less than L-1. Mustard-lewisite (military designation HL) = liquid mixture of distilled mustard (HD) + lewisite (L), both a blister agent and DNA-alkylating agent; lower freezing point (lowest at 63% lewisite/37% mustard) allows ground dispersal/aerial spraying in cold weather/high altitude; may have garlic odor (also unreliable for detection). potential_exposure: Manufacture or use of this chemical warfare agent (vesicant). L-1/L-2/L-3 used as blister-agent-type war gas. Mustard-lewisite mixture developed to achieve lower freezing point for ground/aerial deployment.

Mustard-lewisite mixture rapidly corrosive to brass at 65°C, corrodes steel at 0.0001in/month at 65°C; hydrolyzes into HCl, thiodiglycol, nonvesicant arsenic compounds.

Pulmonary edema, diarrhea, restlessness, weakness, subnormal temperature, low BP. High-conc. inhalation may be fatal within 10 min. Lethal dose in humans: 6ppm inhalation, 20mg/kg skin. Eye injury below 300 mg-min/m3. Pulmonary edema (delayed medical emergency, can cause death).
long_term_effects: May cause sensitization and chronic lung impairment. Suspected carcinogen.

personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; full face-piece respiratory protection; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: When used as a weapon: SCBA certified by NIOSH for CBRN environments. Otherwise per OSHA 29CFR1910.134/EN149: NIOSH/MSHA-approved respirator, or supplied-air (positive-pressure/continuous-flow), or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure.

shipping: Toxic liquids, organic, n.o.s. [Inhalation hazard, Packing Group I, Zone A]: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label, inhalation hazard, technical name required.
spill_handling: BACK OFF — isolate wide area, call for expert help. If in building: evacuate, close doors, shut down HVAC. description: Light, silvery-white metal in various forms; fire hazard. Autoignition (powder) 473°C. LEL 0.03 kg/m3. Dust cloud ignition temp 520°C; minimum explosive conc. 0.020 oz/ft3. Relative explosion hazard of dust: severe.
potential_exposure: Alloyed w/ manganese/aluminum/thorium/zinc/cerium/zirconium for aircraft, ships, automobiles, hand tools (lightness). Dow metal = general name for alloys >85% magnesium. Wire/ribbon: radio-industry degassing valves, heating appliances; deoxidizer/desulfurizer in copper/brass/nickel alloys; chemical reagents; powder for flares, incendiary bombs, tracer bullets, flashlight powders; nuclear energy process; magnesium oxide/chloride floor cement. Essential nutrient element (humans/animals/plants) — chlorophyll component, most abundant intracellular divalent cation, activates many mammalian enzymes.
incompatibilities: Strong reducing agent. Reacts violently w/ oxidizers, strong acids, acetylene, ammonium salts, arsenic, beryllium fluoride, carbon tetrachloride, carbonates, chloroform, cyanides, chlorinated hydrocarbons, ethylene oxide, hydrocarbons, metal oxides, methanol, phosphates, silver nitrate, sodium peroxide, sulfates, trichloroethylene, many others → fire/explosion. Finely powdered/chip/sheet form reacts w/ moisture/acids, evolving flammable hydrogen → fire/explosion. Finely divided form readily ignites via spark/flame, splatters/burns above 1260°C.
osha_pel: No standards set for elemental magnesium.
human_health_water: WHO desirable limits 30-125 mg/L (sulfate-dependent); if sulfate >250mg/L, Mg limited to 30mg/L; WHO absolute max 150mg/L. Concentrations below astringent-taste threshold pose no health problem, may be beneficial — no health-based limitation needed.
mexico_drinking_water: USSR-UNEP/IRPTC MAC 50 mg/L for fishery-purpose water bodies.
determination_in_water: Atomic-absorption spectrophotometry (sensitivity 15mg/L) or photometry (sensitivity 100μg/L).
short_term_effects: Eye/skin irritation. Dust inhalation: resp tract irritation (coughing, wheezing, SOB). Mild conjunctiva/nasal mucosa irritant, not specifically toxic. Inhalation may cause metal fume fever (symptoms delayed 4-12h). Hot particles on skin: second/third-degree burns (respond to standard thermal-burn treatment). Metallic Mg foreign bodies in skin cause no unusual human problems, but animal experiments show 'gas gangrene' (massive localized gaseous tumors w/ extensive necrosis). Magnesium salts >700g/L (esp. magnesium sulfate) have laxative effect, especially in new users (body adapts over time).
long_term_effects: Repeated exposure can cause body accumulation, upset stomach.
medical_surveillance: No special test.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care; if fragments embedded and removal by scrubbing not ensured, seek medical removal. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Metal fume fever symptoms may be delayed 4-12h, may last <36h. Note to physician: treat pulmonary edema for fume inhalation; oral prednisone/corticosteroid to reduce tissue response; positive-pressure ventilation may be necessary; treat metal fume fever w/ bed rest, analgesics, antipyretics.
personal_protective_methods: Burns with intense flame — don't look directly at fire, wear adequate eye protection. Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Particulate (dust/fume/mist) filter respirator (checked daily). High exposures: supplied-air respirator (positive-pressure/continuous-flow) or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure.
storage: (1) Red stripe (powder/turnings/ribbon): flammability hazard, don't store w/ other flammables. (2) Yellow stripe: strong reducing agent, isolated from flammables/combustibles/other yellow materials. Avoid strong oxidizers (chlorine, bromine, fluorine), strong acids (HCl, sulfuric, nitric), chlorine trifluoride. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from water. Nonsparking tools; protect from physical damage.
shipping: Pellets/turnings/ribbons (UN1869): 'FLAMMABLE SOLID' label; Class 4.1, Packing Group III. Powder: 'DANGEROUS WHEN WET, SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE' label; Class 4.3, Packing Group III. Coated granules (particle size ≥149μm): 'DANGEROUS WHEN WET' label; Class 4.3, Packing Group III.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; use vacuum to reduce dust — no dry sweeping; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; keep out of confined spaces (sewers) due to explosion risk; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible solid/flammable powder; burns w/ intense flame. Reacts violently w/ water/CO2/powder extinguishing agents — dangerous when wet, burns in steam current. Powders form explosive air mixtures. Poisonous magnesium oxide gas produced; fire may restart after extinguished. Use dry sand, MetL-X powder, G-1 graphite powder, soda ash, Class D extinguishers, or talc — do NOT use water or hydrous agents. Cool exposed containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
extraction_notes: References: Sax DPIM Vol4No.2 pp.79-81 (1984); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet (Sep 1999). No Disposal Method Suggested section visible in source.

Inhalation: airway injury within 2-6h (severe) or 12-24h (mild). Skin: latent period 6-12h in temperate conditions (hot/humid weather strikingly increases action); some injury may appear as late as 48h. Extremely toxic. Eye/skin burns w/ possible permanent damage; irritation, itching, blisters. Resp tract irritation (wheezing, coughing). Higher exposure: headache, nausea, vomiting, dizziness. Nausea/vomiting, bleeding, skin lesions, menstrual irregularities. Toxic doses as low as 400mg/kg reported in humans. Blood clots at IV injection site, tissue damage if outside vein. Powerful vesicant on skin/mucous membranes/eyes. Delayed toxicity: missed menstrual periods, alopecia, hearing loss, tinnitus, jaundice, impaired spermatogenesis/germinal aplasia, swelling, hypersensitivity.
long_term_effects: Bone marrow suppression → hematopoietic system damage. Early signs: low WBC count, increased infection risk, easy bruising/bleeding. Lymph node damage, weakened immune system. Liver/kidney damage. Reproductive system damage (both sexes) → decreased fertility. Mutagenic, embryo-toxic, carcinogenic. Significant systemic absorption: bone marrow/lymph node/spleen injury → WBC count drop beginning days 3-5 (infection risk); RBC/platelet counts may also fall.
mutagenicity: Mutagenic (per Long Term Exposure). DFG: Germ Cell Mutation Cat 2.
medical_surveillance: CBC. Audiogram.
first_aid: No antidote exists. Decontamination of all potentially exposed areas within minutes is the only effective means of decreasing tissue damage. Health effects may not occur until hours after exposure — observe in hospital ≥24h. Gastric lavage contraindicated after ingestion (esophageal/airway perforation risk). Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash immediately (speed critical), seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Keep victim quiet, maintain normal body temp; effects may be delayed, keep under observation. Decontamination: within minutes is the only effective means; remove clothes into sealed double bag; vapor/liquid exposure decontamination within first 2min ideally to prevent tissue damage — still perform even if delayed (removes residual liquid/trapped vapor, prevents off-gassing/cross-contamination); physical removal (not detoxification/neutralization) is the key principle — mustard isn't detoxified by water alone and persists in dilute effluent absent hydrolysis. Vapor-exposed patients: remove all clothing in clean air, shampoo/rinse hair. Liquid-exposed patients: wash in warm/hot water ≥3 times with liquid soap (dispose/replace container), large water volumes, mild-moderate friction w/ single-use sponge/washcloth (avoid brush scrubbing — may enhance absorption via skin damage); third wash rinses with large warm/hot water; shampoo hair; use cold water if warm unavailable rather than delaying; rinse eyes/mucous membranes/wounds w/ sterile saline/water. Health-care provider verifies adequate decontamination before medical-facility entry (repeat if inadequate); be prepared to stabilize conventional injuries during the (time-consuming) decontamination process; wear proper PPE.
personal_protective_methods: Totally Encapsulating Chemical Protective (TECP) suit providing CBRN protection; chemical-resistant inner/outer gloves; chemical-resistant steel-toe/shank boots; coveralls, long underwear, hard hat under TECP suit optional. All necessary precautions to prevent skin contact. No contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.

short_term_effects: Absorbed through skin — gives no warning on skin contact; if maintained, can cause second-degree burns. Sensitization possible. Very high toxicity. CNS (incl. brain) is principal target tissue. Severe poisoning may cause irreversible brain damage w/ loss of higher functions. Chronic poisoning effects are progressive — early stages: fine hand tremors, sometimes face/arms.
long_term_effects: Repeated/prolonged skin contact: dermatitis. Repeated/prolonged exposure may cause death via hypovolemic shock, nephrotic syndrome, kidney failure. Repeated/continued exposure: tremors become coarse/convulsive, scanning speech w/ slurring/pronunciation difficulty. Unsteady spastic gait progressing to severe arm/leg ataxia. Sensory disturbances incl. tunnel vision, blindness, deafness. Late symptom: visual field constriction, rarely reversible, may be associated w/ loss of understanding/reason. Severe cerebral effects seen in infants born to mothers who ate large amounts of methylmercury-contaminated fish.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, CNS, peripheral nervous system, kidneys.
medical_surveillance: Preplacement/periodic exams should focus on skin, vision, CNS, kidneys. Consider possible fetal effects of maternal alkyl mercury exposure. Blood/urine mercury levels studied especially for methylmercury — no precise exposure-concentration correlation found, but may indicate exposure occurred.

description: Colorless gas, faint sweet odor (not noticeable at dangerous conc., threshold 10ppm). Shipped as liquefied compressed gas. Autoignition 632°C. LEL 8.1%/UEL 17.4%. Relative vapor density (air=1): 1.78.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Tumorigen, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data. Methylating/chlorinating agent in organic chemistry; silicone/tetramethyl lead production; petroleum-refinery extractant for greases/oils/resins; synthetic rubber solvent; refrigerant; polystyrene foam propellant; formerly local anesthetic (freezing); drug-manufacture intermediate.
incompatibilities: Violent reaction w/ chemically active metals (potassium, powdered aluminum, zinc, magnesium). Reacts w/ aluminum trichloride, ethylene. Hydrolyzes w/ water to form HCl. Attacks many metals w/ moisture present.
osha_pel: 100 ppm TWA; 200 ppm Ceiling; 300 ppm [5min max peak/3h] [skin].
niosh_rel: Potential occupational carcinogen — limit to lowest feasible concentration.

dfg_mak: 50 ppm/100 mg/m3 TWA; Peak Cat II(2)[skin]; Pregnancy Grp B; Carcinogen Cat 3.
other_national_oels: Egypt/Denmark/Japan 50ppm(105/100); Australia TWA50(105)/STEL100; Austria MAK50(105) suspected carcinogen; Belgium TWA50(103)/STEL100(207); Finland TWA50(105)/STEL75(160); France VME50(105)/VLE100 carcinogen; Netherlands MAC-TGG 52; Norway TWA25(50); Philippines/Turkey TWA100(210); Poland MAC(TWA)20/STEL160; Russia TWA50ppm/STEL5; Sweden NGV50(100)/KTV100(200); Switzerland MAK-W50(105)/KZG-W100(210); Thailand TWA100/STEL200; UK TWA50(105)/STEL100 (2000). human_health_water: Preferably zero. 1:100,000 additional lifetime cancer risk at 1.9μg/L. States: Kansas 0.19μg/L, Arizona 0.50μg/L guidelines.
determination_in_water: GC (EPA 601) or GC-MS (EPA 624). Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow=0.9.
target_organs: CNS, liver, kidneys, brain, reproductive system.
short_term_effects: Inhalation: illness reported at 500ppm; 10,000ppm/30min caused death. Nausea, vomiting, painful neck, appetite loss. More severe: headache, diarrhea, dizziness, coordination loss, hand/lip tremors, drooping eyelids, eye twitch. Very severe: mouth/throat burning, mustard-like taste, swallowing difficulty, hallucinations, memory loss, cold/clammy skin, rapid breathing, unconsciousness, coma, death. Onset may be delayed several hours; effects may last weeks/months. Higher exposures: pulmonary edema (delayed, can be fatal). Skin: liquefied-gas contact causes freezing/burns/permanent damage; also muscular pain, anemia, muscle weakness, fever. Eyes: frostbite, severe burns, permanent damage; dimmed sight, dilated pupils. Ingestion of liquefied gas causes mouth/throat freezing.
long_term_effects: May affect testes — decreased male hormone/sperm production. Limited evidence of animal kidney cancer. May damage liver/kidneys, cause brain damage. May cause blurred/double vision, 'drunken' behavior.
points_of_attack: CNS, liver, kidneys, brain, reproductive system.
mutagenicity: EPA Gene-Tox: positive histidine reversion-Ames test.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: whole blood chemical/metabolite, expired air, urine chemical/metabolite. For ≥half-TLV exposure or significant skin contact: lung function tests, nervous system exam before work + periodically. If symptoms/overexposure: nervous system exam, kidney/liver function tests, brain-effect evaluation, consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Frostbite: seek care immediately, don't rub or flush w/ water, don't remove frozen clothing. No frostbite: wash contaminated skin thoroughly. Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered.
personal_protective_methods: Protective clothing to prevent skin freezing (8h: Viton gloves/suits, Saranex-coated suits, Barricade-coated suits, Responder suits, Trellchem HPS suits, Tychem 1000 suits; 4h: Teflon gloves/suits/boots); no contact lenses; eye protection; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: NIOSH: above REL, or where no REL at any detectable conc.: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: SCBAE.
storage: Red stripe: separate from all other flammables. Avoid oxidizers (perchlorates, peroxides, chlorates, nitrates, permanganates)/chemically active metals (sodium, potassium, powdered aluminum, zinc, magnesium). Check explosive conc. before confined entry. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from heat/direct sunlight. No smoking/open flames; explosion-proof electrical. Per OSHA 1910.101/1910.169 & CGA recommendations. Regulated area per OSHA 1910.1045.
shipping: 'FLAMMABLE GAS' label; Class 2.1.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; forced ventilation below explosive limit; stop gas flow if safe; move/repair leaking cylinder if possible; avoid sewers (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Flammable gas; poisonous HCl gases produced. Don't extinguish unless gas flow can be stopped and line emptied. Specially trained personnel may use fog lines to cool exposures and let fire burn out. Vapors heavier than air, flashback risk; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Consult environmental regulatory agencies. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators). Controlled incineration w/ adequate scrubbing and ash disposal facilities.
extraction_notes: References: EPA Halomethanes: Ambient WQ Criteria, Report PB-296-797 (1980); NIOSH Info Profiles: Methyl Chloride, Report PB-276-678 (Oct 1977); EPA HEEP #48 (Apr 1980); NY DOH Fact Sheet v2 (Mar 1986); Sax DPIM Vol2No.4 pp.76-78 (1982); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet.

No smoking/open flames; ≥5-gal metal containers grounded/bonded; self-closing valves/flame arresters on drums; nonsparking tools; explosion-proof electrical.

routes_of_entry: Inhalation, skin absorption, ingestion, skin/eye contact.

short_term_effects: Corrosive to eyes/skin/resp tract; ingestion may cause permanent damage. Inhalation: pulmonary edema (delayed, can be fatal). May affect CNS/liver/blood — excitability, vomiting, tremors, convulsions, methemoglobin formation, death (effects may be delayed). Acute exposure: facial numbness/swelling, increased salivation, headache, twitching, seizure, convulsions, coma. GI: anorexia, nausea, vomiting. long_term_effects: May damage liver, kidneys, blood (methemoglobin formation). Causes liver cancer in animals — possibly carcinogenic to humans.

Vapors heavier than air, flashback risk; containers may explode/rocket. Water spray to cool exposed containers until well after fire out. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.

potential_exposure: Compound Description: Mutagen; Reproductive Effector. Alloys (steel, stainless steel, tool steel, cast iron, mill rolls; w/ manganese, nickel, chromium, tungsten). Electronic parts (contacts, spark plugs, X-ray tubes, filaments, screens, grids), induction heating elements, glass-melting electrodes, metal spraying. Compounds used as lubricants, printing-ink pigments, lacquers/paints, rubber/animal-fiber/leather coloring/mordant, hydrogenation-cracking/alkylation/reforming catalysts, Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, ammonia production, quartz-glass coating, vitreous enamels, fertilizers (legumes), electroplating, tungsten production. Hazardous exposures possible during high-temp treatment, spraying, or catalyst loss. MoO3 sublimes above 800°C.
incompatibilities: Soluble compounds: alkali metals, sodium, potassium, molten magnesium. Insoluble compounds: violent reaction w/ oxidizers, nitric acid, sulfuric acid. Forms explosive mixture w/ potassium nitrate. Metallic Mo dust/powder is combustible, potentially explosive.

niosh_rel: See Appendix D of NIOSH Pocket Guide.

long_term_effects: Can cause headache, fatigue, appetite loss, muscle/joint pain. Elevated uric acid may lead to gout. May damage liver/kidneys. May cause anemia. Animal evidence: eye/nose/throat irritation, anorexia, diarrhea, weight loss, listlessness, liver/kidney damage. Soluble compounds (e.g. sodium molybdate) and freshly generated fumes considerably more toxic. High-conc. molybdenum trioxide dust inhalation highly irritating to animals — weight loss, diarrhea, coordination loss, high mortality; MoO3 dust more toxic than fumes. Large oral doses of ammonium molybdate caused fetal deformities in rabbits.
points_of_attack: Soluble compounds: eyes, respiratory system, kidneys, blood. Insoluble compounds: eyes, respiratory system, liver, kidneys.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: whole blood chemical/metabolite, biologic tissue/biopsy, urine chemical/metabolite. Preemployment/periodic exams: eye/resp tract irritant effects, general health. Liver/kidney function tests. CBC. Uric acid level. Essential trace element in many species incl. humans, but excessive intake may produce copper-deficiency signs; normal dietary copper intake may combat/prevent systemic toxicity from molybdenum poisoning.

personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; chemical goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated.

Escape: 100F/SCBAE.

fire_extinguishing: Dry chemicals for metal fires (dry sand, dolomite, graphite). Do NOT use water. Poisonous gases produced. Dust/powdered molybdenum may cause dust explosion. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.

Synonyms: Bis(2-chloroethyl) sulfide; Distilled mustard (HD); H and HD (military designations); Iprit; Lost (German); Senfgas; Sulfur mustard; Sulfur mustard gas; Yellow cross gas; Yperite. HT: mixture of bis(2-chloroethyl)sulfide + bis[2-(2-chloroethylthio)ethyl]ether.
regulatory_authority: DHS Screening Threshold: theft hazard CUM 100g [505-60-2; 3563-36-8 (HD)]. Carcinogenicity: NTP 11th Report (2004) known human carcinogen; IARC human sufficient/animal limited evidence, Group 1 (1998); HT treated as suspect carcinogen (similarity to HD). EPA Gene-Tox: multiple positive assays (D.melanogaster whole sex chrom. loss/reciprocal translocation/sex-linked lethal; L5178Y TK test; N.crassa reversion; positive/dose-response TRP reversion; positive/limited carcinogenicity mouse/rat). WGK: none assigned (all CAS numbers).
carcinogenicity_status: NTP 11th Report (2004): known to be a human carcinogen. IARC: human sufficient/animal limited evidence, carcinogenic to humans, Group 1 (1998). HT (Agent T) treated as suspect carcinogen. EPA Gene-Tox: multiple positive genotoxicity assays.
rcra_waste_numbers: App 8 Hazardous Constituents (waste number not listed).
epcra_status: TPQ 500 lb (227 kg). RQ 1 lb (0.454 kg). Section 313 de minimis 0.1%.
water_solubility: Slightly soluble (reaction); soluble in acetone, ether, other organics
description: Oily, yellow to black liquid (clear when pure), sweet burnt-garlic/horseradish odor (threshold HD 0.0006 mg/m3). HT: mixture of 60% HD + 40% Agent T; clear, yellowish, highly viscous, more stable than HD, lower odor, longer effectiveness duration. Vapor density (air=1): 5.5-9.08.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Tumorigen, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data; Primary Irritant. Alkylating agent. Historical chemical warfare vesicant/blister agent (WWI, military designation H/HD), causing delayed casualties. Biological model compound; minimally tested as antineoplastic agent.
incompatibilities: Stable at ambient temps; decomposes 149-177°C, emitting highly toxic HCl/sulfur oxide/chlorine fumes. Reacts vigorously w/ oxidizers, strong acids, acid fumes, strong alkalis, oxygen, water, steam. Rapidly corrosive to brass at 65°C; corrodes steel. Metal contact may evolve flammable hydrogen gas. Hydrolyzes in water forming HCl + thiodiglycol. Persistence: Summer 3 days-1 week; Winter may last weeks (up to 3 years in soil).
niosh_rel: IDLH 0.7 mg/m3; STEL 0.003 mg/m3; WPL (worker population limit) 0.0004 mg/m3; GPL (general population limit) 0.00002 mg/m3.
dfg_mak: [skin]; Carcinogen Cat 1 (as bis(β-chloroethyl)sulfide).
other_national_oels: Finland/France/Sweden/Switzerland/UK: carcinogen.
determination_in_air: M8/M9 Detector paper, blue band tube; M256/M256A1 kits; bubbler; DAMMS; ACMS; CAM-M1/HYFED; MINICAM (specialized military/HAZMAT monitoring equipment).
determination_in_water: Octanol-water coefficient (estimated): LogKow=2.41; Log Kbenzene-water=0.15. Bulk mustard can persist decades in soil/water; forms protective 'crust' in seawater. Oxidized (air, O2, hypochlorite, H2O2, nitric acid, KMnO4, chromic acid) to less-toxic sulfoxide/sulfone forms. Doesn't significantly degrade in sunlight; stable below 49°C.
ld50: LD50 (skin, human) 100 mg/kg; LD50 (oral-rat) 0.7 mg/kg. ICt50 (skin) 1000-2000 mg-min/m3; ICt50 (eyes) 200 mg-min/m3; ICt50 (inhalation) 1500 mg-min/m3.
short_term_effects: Causes severe, delayed burns to eyes/skin/resp tract. Damages cells within minutes; pain/health-effect onset delayed hours. Large exposures may be fatal. Contact w/ liquid or high-vapor-conc. exposure: severe burns, permanent eye damage; no pain on contact, redness/swelling/pain hours later; blindness possible. Inhalation: pulmonary edema (delayed, can be fatal). 1-12h: coughing, swollen eyelids, reddened skin, severe itching; tissue swelling/destruction in resp tract and exposed skin. Ingestion: nausea, tissue destruction. Median lethal dosage 1500 mg-min/m3 inhalation, 10,000 mg-min/m3 skin (masked personnel). Median incapacitating dosage 200 mg-min/m3 eye injury, 2000 mg-min/m3 skin. Wet skin absorbs more than dry. May cause death/permanent injury after very short exposure to small quantities. Blistering gas, highly irritating to eyes/skin/lungs; pulmonary lesions often fatal. Vesicant, alkylating agent — cytotoxic to hematopoietic tissues (blood-forming, especially sensitive). Slow detoxification, repeated exposures cumulative. Skin blisters/erythema after 4-24h latency. Eye damage: necrotic damage, eyesight loss. Inhalation: upper resp tract inflammation after latency (sneezing, coughing, bronchitis, appetite loss, diarrhea, fever, apathy). Near-lethal doses: bone marrow/lymph node/spleen injury (dropped WBC count, infection susceptibility). Ingestion: severe stomach pain, vomiting, bloody stools after 15-20min latency.
long_term_effects: Can cause sensitization, chronic bronchitis, lung impairment (cough, SOB, chest pain). Can cause cancer of mouth, throat, resp tract, skin, and leukemia. May cause birth defects. Recognized human carcinogen.
mutagenicity: Multiple positive genotoxicity assay results (see regulatory_authority).
medical_surveillance: Lung function tests. Eye exam incl. slit lamp. Consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure.
first_aid: No antidote exists for sulfur mustard toxicity. Eyes: instantly flush with water — seconds' delay can cause permanent damage; tilt head, pull eyelids apart, pour water slowly; do not cover with bandages (dark/opaque goggles if needed); transfer immediately. Inhalation: remove from source immediately; artificial respiration if breathing stopped, oxygen if difficult breathing; seek care immediately. Ingestion: do NOT induce vomiting; give milk; seek care immediately. Skin: don respiratory/glove protection before approaching victim; flush skin/clothes with sodium hypochlorite (bleach) solution within 1min; cut/remove contaminated clothing; re-flush with hypochlorite, then soap+water; shower if available, transfer to medical facility. Thickened agent: blot/wipe material with absorbent pad before decontaminating solution. Decontamination (general): act within minutes for best outcome; wash-strip-wash-evacuate upwind/uphill — flush w/ clean water immediately without waiting for soap/clothing removal (hose/spray to avoid touching victim if untrained); flush eyes ≥15min; have victim (not responder) remove clothing, wash again w/ soap; decontaminate w/ diluted household bleach (10%, 1:9 bleach:water) avoiding eyes/wounds/mouth, rinse after 15min.
personal_protective_methods: Mandatory butyl toxicological-agent gloves (M3/M4 glove set); chemical goggles minimum, goggles+face shield for splash hazard. Full protective clothing: M3 butyl rubber suit w/ hood, M2A1 butyl boots, M3 gloves, impregnated underwear, M9-series mask, or Demilitarization Protective Ensemble (DPE). General lab work: gloves+lab coat w/ M9/M17 mask available; daily clean smock/foot/head covers for contaminated-animal handling. Mandatory filtered/scrubbed local exhaust ventilation; specialized lab-hood face-velocity requirements; no air recirculation between agent/non-agent areas; emergency backup power required. Documented breakthrough times for various Level A suits/gloves range 110-480+ min.
respirator_selection: When used as a weapon: SCBA certified by NIOSH for CBRN environments; do NOT use chemical cartridge/canister respirators. Below 0.003mg/m3 (8h TWA) with continuous monitoring, engineering controls, and mask availability: protective mask not required. Otherwise: full face-piece chemical-canister air-purifying respirator (M9/M17/M40 series or certified equivalent) w/ M3 TAP suit. Above 0.003mg/m3: 30-mil DPE (≤2h use) w/ AMC Field Safety Activity approval, or M9/M40 mask w/ Level A ensemble + impregnated innerwear (≤1h use, cuffs/legs taped).
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Stable at ambient temps; decomposes 149-177°C. Persistent agent, up to 3yr in soil. Regulated area per OSHA Standard 1910.1045. Buddy (two-man) system during handling. Periodic container leak inspection. Stringent personnel control; chemical showers/eyewash/cleanliness facilities required; thorough hand/shower washing before meals/end of shift. No smoking/eating/drinking at work site. Glass containers (small quantities, R&D) or one-ton steel containers (large quantities); double-contained in liquid-tight containers.
shipping: Toxic liquids, organic, n.o.s. [Inhalation hazard, Packing Group I, Zone B]: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label. Bis-(2-chloroethyl)sulfide UN2810, Inhalation Hazard; Class 6.1, Packing Group III.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate. Cover w/ up to 15% calcium hypochlorite, contain, neutralize after 12h if needed. Keep out of water/sewers. Water spray to knock down vapors; stay upwind; wash body contact w/ copious soap+water. Absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid sewers (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. THD (thickened HD): dissolve in acetone before decontaminating; scrape into removable-head polyethylene-lined drum. Detailed field/laboratory decontamination procedures use 5.25% sodium hypochlorite, DS2, or Super Tropical Bleach, w/ specific chlorine-activity testing protocols. Isolation (first 30min, may increase w/ time, when used as weapon) — small: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.1-0.2mi; large: 200ft/60m, downwind 0.2-0.5mi. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: May burn but doesn't easily ignite. HD hydrolyzes forming HCl + thiodiglycol. Poisonous sulfur/chloride oxide gases produced. Water, foam, dry chemical, or CO2. Protective clothing + SCBA required. Vapors heavier than air; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Collect, contain, chemically decontaminate or thermally decompose in EPA-approved incinerator w/ effluent filtering/scrubbing. Decontaminate protective clothing w/ HTH/bleach, verify contamination-free (3X level). Sealed double-bagged contaminated items returned per procedure. HD on glassware may be oxidized w/ concentrated nitric acid. Open-pit burning/burying of HD prohibited. Several states classify decontaminated surety material as RCRA hazardous waste.

Symptoms: headache, giddiness, blurred vision, nervousness, weakness, nausea, cramps, diarrhea, chest discomfort. Signs: sweating, tearing, salivation, vomiting, cyanosis, convulsions, coma, reflex/sphincter control loss. High exposure can result in death. Highly toxic; probable human lethal dose 1tsp-1oz. Human Tox=14.00000 ppb (INTERMEDIATE).
long_term_effects: May cause skin allergy. Cholinesterase inhibitor — cumulative effect possible. May damage nervous system w/ repeated exposure (convulsions, respiratory failure). May cause liver damage.
points_of_attack: Respiratory system, CNS, cardiovascular system, skin, eyes, blood cholinesterase.
medical_surveillance: Plasma/RBC cholinesterase levels before employment + regularly (plasma normalizes 1-2wk after exposure stops, RBC may stay reduced 1-3mo). ≥25% reduction below preemployment level increases poisoning risk even in 'normal' range. Reassignment away from organophosphate/carbamate work recommended until recovery. If overexposed: repeat tests ASAP, nervous system exam, consider CBC, consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure, allergist evaluation. Avoid alcohol before/during use.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash immediately (speed critical), shampoo hair if contaminated, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Effects may be delayed; medical observation recommended. Note to physician: 1-4mg atropine; maintenance 2mg doses at 15-60min intervals.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles for liquid, dust-proof for powders, unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: NIOSH: 30mg/m3 95XQ/Sa. 75mg/m3 Sa:Cf/PaprHie. 150mg/m3 100F/SaT:Cf/PaprTHie/SCBAF. 200mg/m3 Sa:Pd,Pp. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: 100F/SCBAE.
storage: (1) Blue: poison, secure location. (2) Red: flammability hazard. Avoid strong oxidizers (chlorine, chlorine dioxide). Keep away from acids/acid fumes/sunlight/heat/water.
shipping: Organophosphorus pesticides, liquid, toxic: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group III.
spill_handling: Dry: evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; HEPA vacuum or wet method to reduce dust — no dry sweeping; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate. Liquid: evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate; absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid sewers (explosion risk). Hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Noncombustible. Use agents suitable for surrounding fire. Poisonous HCl/hydrogen bromide/phosphorus oxide gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: More stable to hydrolysis than dichlorvos (50% hydrolysis at pH9/37.5°C in 301min). Unstable in alkaline conditions/iron presence; degraded by sunlight. ~10% hydrolysis/day in ambient water. Incineration recommended for large amounts. Per 40CFR165 pesticide/container disposal recommendations.

Electroplating, aluminum anodizing/casting for machine parts, coinage, acid-resisting/magnetic alloys, magnetic tapes, surgical/dental instruments, Ni-Cd batteries, crankcase-oil nickel soaps, ground-coat enamels, colored ceramics, glass. Catalyst in acrylic-ester hydrogenation synthesis for plastics. Mining/smelting/refining exposure. General population's largest daily intake route: food (300-600μg/day per composite diet analysis; ~300μg/day per fecal analysis). Highest observed water level: 75μg/L; average drinking water ~5μg/L (2L/day yields ~10μg additional intake, ~1μg absorbed).
incompatibilities: Nickel dust is spontaneously flammable, dangerous fire hazard. Store away from acids (HCl, sulfuric, nitric), fluorine, ammonia, phosphorus, sulfur, selenium, hydrazine, performic acid — violent reactions.

medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: blood gas analysis, whole blood chemical/metabolite, blood plasma (end-of-shift), blood serum, biologic tissue/biopsy, chest X-ray, EKG, pulmonary function tests (pre/post-shift), sputum cytology, urine chemical/metabolite (end-of-shift), WBC count/differential. If symptoms/overexposure: daily urine nickel for several days (>100μg needs medical attention), consider chest X-ray, allergist evaluation for skin allergy, liver/kidney function tests.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash. Specific engineering controls per NIOSH Criteria Doc #77-164, Inorganic Nickel.
respirator_selection: Above NIOSH REL, or where no REL at any detectable conc.: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: 100F.
storage: Pyrophoric (dry nickel powder, Raney nickel, nickel catalyst) — fire hazards. Finely divided nickel must avoid strong acids. spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; dry chemicals/sand/water spray/foam; no dry sweeping; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; keep nickel catalyst spills out of confined spaces (explosion/fire risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.

long_term_effects: Lung allergy occasionally occurs w/ asthma-type effect. Skin contact can cause allergy. High/repeated lower exposures may damage lungs (scarring), heart, liver, kidneys.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: blood gas analysis, whole blood chemical/metabolite, blood plasma (end-of-shift), blood serum, biologic tissue/biopsy, chest X-ray, EKG, pulmonary function tests (pre/post-shift), sputum cytology, urine chemical/metabolite (end-of-shift), WBC count/differential. Before employment + regularly: lung function tests, urine/plasma nickel test (unexposed <10μg/L). If symptoms/overexposure: daily urine nickel for several days (>100μg needs medical attention), consider chest X-ray, allergist evaluation for skin allergy, liver/kidney function tests.

Area employees should be regularly trained in cyanide-poisoning emergency measures and CPR; cyanide antidote kit should be kept in immediate work area, rapidly available; kit ingredients replaced every 1-2yr. regulatory_authority: Air Pollutant Standard Set. Nitrate/nitrite: SDWA MCL 10mg/L as nitrogen; MCLG 10mg/L as nitrogen. WGK: none assigned (varies by compound).
epcra_status: Section 313 de minimis 1.0% (reportable only in aqueous solution).
safe_drinking_water_act: MCL 10 mg/L as nitrogen; MCLG 10 mg/L as nitrogen.
description: Salts with properties varying by specific compound. Organic nitrates termed 'nitro' compounds.
potential_exposure: Major point sources of nitrogen entry into water: municipal/industrial wastewaters, septic tanks, feedlot discharges. Diffuse sources: farm fertilizer, animal wastes, lawn fertilizer, landfill leachate, atmospheric fallout, automobile-exhaust nitric oxide/nitrite, natural soil-organic-matter mineralization.
incompatibilities: Nearly all nitrates are powerful oxidizers. Possible violent reaction w/ reducing agents, combustibles, organics, finely divided (powdered) metals — explosive mixtures or fire/explosion. Many nitrates flammable by spontaneous chemical reaction. Some may explode spontaneously w/ elevated temp and/or shock. Some nitrates are high explosives, especially confined and/or heated.
human_health_water: Nitrite <1000mg/L not of serious direct-toxicant concern but is hazardous via conversion to nitrite; nitrite directly toxic — reacts w/ hemoglobin forming methemoglobin (methemoglobinemia); also reacts w/ secondary amines/similar nitrogenous compounds forming carcinogenic N-nitroso compounds. Epidemiological evidence supports ~10mg/L nitrate-as-nitrogen as max level w/ no observed adverse effects in infants, w/ little safety margin. EPA health advisory + Maine guideline confirm 10mg/L level.
determination_in_water: No method particularly precise/accurate/sensitive at mg/L range; further standardization needed. Standard procedures mostly spectrophotometric (nitration of phenolic substance, oxidation of organic substance, or nitrate reduction to nitrite/ammonia followed by colorimetric reaction). Direct UV spectrophotometric determination at 273nm possible/becoming established. Electrochemical determination w/ nitrate electrode feasible but subject to interferences.
short_term_effects: High dosages if swallowed may cause serious/possibly fatal effects. Symptoms: headache, dizziness, abdominal cramps, vomiting, bloody diarrhea, weakness, convulsions, collapse, death.
long_term_effects: Two health hazards from consuming nitrate/nitrite-rich water: methemoglobinemia (esp. in infants) and possible carcinogenic nitrosamine formation. Acute nitrate toxicity results from nitrite reduction (in stomach/saliva under specific conditions); nitrite oxidizes hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which doesn't carry oxygen — anoxia/death may result. Small repeated doses may cause weakness, general depression, headache, mental impairment; some evidence of increased cancer incidence among exposed persons. Acute nitrate toxicity almost always in infants rather than adults, attributed to high intake per unit weight, nitrate-reducing bacteria in upper GI tract, mucosal condition, and easier fetal-hemoglobin oxidation.
first_aid: See specific compound entries. Note to physician: treat for methemoglobinemia; spectrophotometry may be required for precise urine methemoglobin determination.
personal_protective_methods: See specific compound entries.
respirator_selection: See specific compound entries.
storage: Yellow: reactive hazard, isolated from other materials, esp. flammables/combustibles. See incompatibilities and specific entries. See OSHA Standard 1910.104 and NFPA 43A Code for Liquid/Solid Oxidizer Storage.
shipping: Nitrates, inorganic, n.o.s. and Nitrates, inorganic, aqueous solution, n.o.s.: 'OXIDIZER' label; Class 5.1, Packing Group II or III.
spill_handling: Dry: evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; HEPA vacuum or wet method to reduce dust — no dry sweeping; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate. spill_handling: Isolate hazard area, deny entry; stay upwind, avoid low areas; ventilate closed spaces before entry; remove ignition sources; keep combustibles away; water spray to reduce vapors, don't get water inside container. Small spills: flood w/ water. Large spills: dike far ahead; flush w/ copious water, neutralize w/ alkaline material (soda ash, lime); absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Isolation (fuming/red fuming, first 30min, may increase w/ time) — small: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.1mi day/0.2mi night; large: 500ft/150m, downwind 0.4mi day/0.7-1.2mi night. shipping: Nitrogen dioxide, liquefied: 'POISON GAS, OXIDIZER' label; Class 2.3, Packing Group I. Violation of transport regs to refill compressed gas cylinders without owner's express written permission.
spill_handling: Isolate hazard area, deny entry; stay upwind, avoid low areas; ventilate closed spaces before entry; evacuate area endangered by gas. Water spills: neutralize w/ agricultural lime/crushed limestone/sodium bicarbonate. Air spills: water spray/mist to knock down vapors (dike containment water, corrosive/toxic). Keep combustibles away; stop leak if safe; water spray to reduce vapor, don't put water directly on leak/spill; isolate until gas disperses. Hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Isolation (first 30min, may increase w/ time) — small: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.1mi day/0.2-0.4mi night; large: 300-1250ft/100-400m, downwind 0.4-0.7mi day/1.4-1.9mi night. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: Nonflammable but supports combustion. Shut off gas flow w/ proper equipment. Water spray to keep containers cool + direct escaping gas away from personnel. Don't extinguish unless gas flow can be stopped and line emptied. Specially trained personnel may use fog lines to cool exposures and let fire burn out. Vapors heavier than air, may travel far to ignition sources, flashback risk; confined-area vapors may explode w/ fire; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; withdraw if cylinders exposed to excessive heat; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Incineration w/ added hydrocarbon fuel, controlled to produce elemental nitrogen, CO2, water. Consult environmental regulatory agencies. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators).
extraction_notes: References: NIOSH Criteria Doc #76-149 (1976); WHO: Oxides of Nitrogen, Environmental Health Criteria No.4 (1977); Sax DPIM Vol1No.5 pp.74-76 (1981) & Vol5No.6 pp.81-83 (1985); EPA CHIP (Nov 1987); NY DOH Fact Sheet v30 (Mar 1986).

extraction_notes: References: NIOSH Criteria Doc #75-103, Inorganic Fluorides (1975); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet: Nitrogen Dioxide (Apr 2000) [note: source fact-sheet citation appears mistitled as 'Nitrogen Dioxide' rather than 'Nitrogen Trifluoride' — reproduced as printed].

long_term_effects: Repeated/prolonged skin contact may cause dermatitis. May affect kidneys. Repeated exposure may cause lung irritation, bronchitis. Limited evidence osmium tetroxide may cause mutations.

mutagenicity: Limited evidence osmium tetroxide may cause mutations.

description: Liquid.
potential_exposure: Agricultural insecticide.
incompatibilities: Strong oxidizers may release toxic phosphorus oxides. Organophosphates + strong reducing agents (hydrides) may form highly toxic/flammable phosphine gas. Keep away from alkaline materials.
target_organs: Respiratory system, lungs, CNS, cardiovascular system, skin, eyes, plasma/RBC cholinesterase.
short_term_effects: Organic phosphorus insecticides absorbed by skin/resp/GI tracts, cholinesterase inhibitors. Mild: headache, appetite loss, nausea, dizziness. Moderate: abdominal cramps, diarrhea, salivation, excessive tearing, muscular cramps. Severe: fever, blue lips, sphincter-control loss, coma, heart shock, difficult breathing.
long_term_effects: Cholinesterase inhibitor — cumulative effect possible. May damage nervous system w/ repeated exposure (convulsions, respiratory failure). May cause liver damage.
points_of_attack: Respiratory system, lungs, CNS, cardiovascular system, skin, eyes, plasma/RBC cholinesterase.
medical_surveillance: Plasma/RBC cholinesterase levels before employment + regularly (plasma normalizes 1-2wk after exposure stops, RBC may stay reduced 1-3mo). ≥25% reduction below preemployment level increases poisoning risk even in 'normal' range. Reassignment away from organophosphate/carbamate work recommended until recovery. If overexposed: repeat tests ASAP, nervous system exam, consider CBC, consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure. Avoid alcohol before/during use — promotes organic phosphate absorption.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash immediately (speed critical), shampoo hair if contaminated, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Keep victim quiet, maintain normal body temp; effects may be delayed, keep under observation.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Per OSHA 29CFR1910.134/EN149: NIOSH/MSHA-approved respirator, or supplied-air (positive-pressure/continuous-flow), or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location.
shipping: Organophosphorus pesticides, liquid, toxic: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group III.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate; don't touch spilled material. Small spills: sand/noncombustible material. Small dry spill: clean shovel into clean dry container. Large spills: dike far ahead for later disposal. Keep out of confined spaces (explosion risk). Hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Dry chemical/CO2/water spray/fog/foam. Fight fire from maximum distance; dike control water, don't scatter material. Poisonous gases from fire/runoff water. Vapors heavier than air, may travel far to ignition sources, flashback risk; confined-area vapors may explode w/ fire; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Per 40CFR165 pesticide/container disposal recommendations. Follow package label directions or contact local/federal/regional EPA office.
extraction_notes: Reference: EPA CHIP: Oxydisulfoton (Nov 1987).

Synonyms: Liquid oxygen; LOX; Oxygen, liquid
regulatory_authority: EPA Gene-Tox Program: positive V79 cell culture gene mutation. Hazard Symbol O; R8; S2;S17. WGK: nonwater polluting agent.
international_regulations: Hazard Symbol O; R8; S2;S17.
water_solubility: Slightly soluble; liquid sinks and boils in water
description: Colorless odorless gas or bluish cryogenic liquid.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Mutagen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data. Compressed oxygen: oxidation processes, feedstock, enrichment, medicinal gas, chemical intermediate, oxyacetylene welding, metallurgy. Liquid oxygen: rocket fuel. Naturally present at 21% in breathing air.
incompatibilities: Strong oxidizer. Reacts violently w/ nearly every element, combustibles, organics, reducing materials.
osha_pel: No standards or TEEL available. Minimum acceptable breathing air: 19% oxygen.
short_term_effects: Increased pressure speeds up oxygen toxic effects; drugs/chemicals can affect toxicity. Air we breathe is 21% oxygen; normal activity needs ≥19%. Breathing up to 50% oxygen at normal pressure: no symptoms. Breathing 100% oxygen at normal pressure: no symptoms after 12h, but after 24h — weakness, dizziness, nose/throat burning, fatigue, joint/muscle pain, arm/leg numbness/tingling, palpitations, headache, cough, nasal congestion, ear disturbances, nausea, vomiting, appetite loss, sore throat, fever, mucous-membrane swelling. Pressure >3× normal may cause convulsions/coma. Higher exposures: pulmonary edema (delayed hours, can be fatal). Skin/eyes: liquid oxygen causes freezing burns/tissue damage. Ingestion: liquid oxygen causes mouth/throat freezing burns.
long_term_effects: Breathing 50-100% oxygen at normal pressure even intermittently over prolonged periods can cause lung damage.
medical_surveillance: Before employment + regularly for frequent/high pure-oxygen exposure: lung function tests. If symptoms/overexposure: consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure to pure oxygen.
first_aid: Eyes (liquid oxygen): irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin (liquid oxygen): if frostbite, seek care immediately, don't rub or flush w/ water, don't remove frozen clothing. No frostbite: wash contaminated skin thoroughly. Breathing pure oxygen/>40% O2: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; pulmonary edema may be delayed.
personal_protective_methods: Protective clothing to prevent skin freezing from evaporating liquid/vessel contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield for liquefied oxygen; gas-proof goggles unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash. Specific engineering controls required by OSHA — see Standard 1910.104.
respirator_selection: Entering oxygen-enriched atmospheres (>21% oxygen) is highly dangerous. Consult NFPA Code 53M.
storage: Yellow: reactive hazard, isolated from other materials, esp. flammables/combustibles. Avoid organic/combustible materials (oil, grease, coal dust) — violent reactions. Open storage preferred. Evaporating gas easily absorbed into clothing; ignition sources (static spark) can cause flash burning. Compressed cylinders stored securely, separate from fuel cylinders. Liquid oxygen tanks stored outdoors. No smoking/open flames. See OSHA Standard 1910.104 and NFPA 43A Code for Liquid/Solid Oxidizer Storage; per OSHA 1910.101/1910.169 & CGA recommendations.
shipping: Oxygen, compressed, or oxygen, refrigerated liquid (cryogenic liquid): 'NONFLAMMABLE GAS, OXIDIZER' label; Class 2.2.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources. Liquid: do NOT absorb in sawdust/combustible absorbents (oxidizer, fire/explosion risk); use only water; don't use chemical/CO2 extinguishers; NEVER direct water jet on liquid; allow spills to evaporate. Gas: ventilate to disperse; stop gas flow; move/repair leaking cylinder if possible. Keep combustibles away from liquid oxygen spills. Hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Not flammable but supports combustion, greatly increases fire intensity. Liquid oxygen/fuel mixtures highly explosive. Don't extinguish unless gas flow can be stopped and line emptied. Specially trained personnel may use fog lines to cool exposures and let fire burn out. Large fire: evacuate, consult expert. Small fire: agent suitable for surrounding fire; doesn't burn itself; don't use chemical/CO2 on liquid oxygen. Containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; withdraw if cylinders exposed to excessive heat; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Vent to atmosphere.
extraction_notes: References: NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet (Apr 2004); NY DOH Fact Sheet (Feb 1986).

Synonyms: Difluorine monoxide; Fluorine monoxide; Fluorine oxide; Oxygen fluoride
regulatory_authority: DHS Screening Threshold: theft hazard 15lb (≥0.09% conc.). Very Toxic Substance (World Bank). Air Pollutant Standard Set. OSHA 29CFR1910.119 Appendix A, TQ 100 lb. DOT inhalation hazard chemical. Canada WHMIS 1.0%. Not listed Annex 1. WGK: none assigned.
international_regulations: Not listed in Annex 1.
description: Colorless gas, foul peculiar odor. Shipped as nonliquefied compressed gas. Relative vapor density (air=1): 1.88.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Reproductive Effector; Human Data. May be used as oxidant in missile propellant systems.
incompatibilities: Strong oxidizer. Explodes on contact w/ steam. Violent reaction w/ reducing agents, combustible materials, chlorine, bromine, iodine, platinum, metal oxides, moist air, hydrogen sulfide (explosive in ambient air), hydrocarbons, water. Attacks mercury.
acgih_tlv: 0.05 ppm/0.11 mg/m3 Ceiling.
other_national_oels: Egypt/Denmark/Norway/Philippines TWA0.05(0.1); Austria MAK2.5mg[F]/m3; Finland STEL0.05(0.1); Poland MAC(TWA)1mg[HF]/m3/MAC(STEL)3mg[HF]/m3; Netherlands MAC 0.1 (2003); UK TWA2.5mg[F]/m3 (2000). ACGIH TLV countries: Ceiling 0.05ppm. US states 1.0-80,000 μg/m3.
short_term_effects: Gas under pressure is corrosive to eyes/skin/resp tract, causes burns. Higher exposures: pulmonary edema (delayed hours, can be fatal). Low-level exposure may cause severe, intractable headaches.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: chest X-ray, EKG, pulmonary function tests (FVC, FEV1), sputum cytology, WBC count/differential.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered. Frostbite: seek care immediately, don't rub or flush w/ water, don't remove frozen clothing. No frostbite: wash contaminated skin thoroughly.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; gas-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: 0.5ppm: Sa/SCBAF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFS/SCBAE. Only nonoxidizable sorbents allowed (not charcoal).
storage: Yellow stripe: reactive hazard, isolated from flammables/combustibles/other yellow materials. Protect cylinders from physical damage; no wood pallets. Handle behind body shield, outdoors or in open protective fences. Long rubber gloves, goggles, protective clothing, SCBA. See 29CFR1910.101 for compressed-gas storage regulations, OSHA Standard 1910.104, and NFPA 43A Code for Liquid/Solid Oxidizer Storage.
shipping: 'POISON GAS, OXIDIZER, CORROSIVE' label; Class 2.3. Violation of transport regs to refill compressed gas cylinders without owner's express written permission.
spill_handling: If in building: evacuate, close doors, shut down HVAC. Restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate to disperse gas; chemical protective suit + SCBA to combat spills; stay upwind, water spray to knock down vapor, contain runoff; stop gas flow if safe; move/repair leaking cylinder if possible; avoid sewers (explosion risk); OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Isolation (first 30min, may increase w/ time) — small: 2500ft/800m, downwind 3.3-7.01mi day/7.01mi night; large: 3000ft/1000m, downwind 7.01mi day/night. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: Nonflammable gas but strong oxidizer, increases fire intensity. Poisonous gases produced. Don't extinguish unless gas flow can be stopped and line emptied. Specially trained personnel may use fog lines to cool exposures and let fire burn out. Vapors heavier than air; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; withdraw if cylinders exposed to excessive heat; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Spray/sift onto thick layer of (1:1) dry soda ash/slaked lime mixture behind shield. After mixing, spray water from atomizer w/ great precaution. Transfer slowly into large water volume. Neutralize and drain into sewer w/ sufficient water.

regulatory_authority: Carcinogenicity: NCI equivocal evidence (inhalation, mouse)/no evidence (rat); NTP some evidence (inhalation, mouse). EPA Gene-Tox: mostly negative/inconclusive across various cytogenetics assays. Air Pollutant Standard Set. OSHA 29CFR1910.119 Appendix A, TQ 100 lb. TPQ 100 lb. RQ 100 lb. EPCRA 313 de minimis 1.0%. SARA Hazard Classes: sudden release of pressure, fire, acute health, chronic health. Canada WHMIS 1.0%; Category D1A, D2B. WGK: none assigned.
carcinogenicity_status: NCI: equivocal evidence (inhalation, mouse); no evidence (rat). NTP: some evidence (inhalation, mouse). EPA Gene-Tox: mostly negative/inconclusive across various cytogenetics assays.
epcra_status: TPQ 100 lb (45.4 kg). RQ 100 lb (45.4 kg). Section 313 de minimis 1.0%.
description: Colorless to blue gas, very pungent characteristic sulfur-like odor associated w/ electrical sparks (threshold 0.045ppm); condenses to blue-black liquid or crystalline solid.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Tumorigen, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data; Natural Product; Primary Irritant. Found naturally in atmosphere (solar radiation, electrical storms); formed around electrical sources (X-ray/UV generators, electric arcs, mercury vapor lamps, linear accelerators, electrical discharges). Oxidizing agent in organic chemical industry (e.g. azelaic acid production); disinfectant for air, mold/bacteria inhibitor for cold-storage food, water treatment (public supplies, pools, sewage); bleaching textiles/waxes/flour/mineral oils/paper pulp/starch/sugar; aging liquor/wood; perfume/vanillin/camphor processing; industrial waste treatment; rapid drying of varnishes/printing inks; feather deodorizing.
incompatibilities: Powerful oxidizer. Severe explosion hazard w/ shock/heat. Spontaneously decomposes to oxygen under ordinary conditions; heating increases oxygen production. Reacts w/ all reducing agents, combustibles, organic/inorganic oxidizable materials, forming highly explosive products. Incompatible w/ alkenes, aniline, benzene, bromine, ether, ethylene, hydrogen bromide, nitric oxide, stibine. Attacks metals except gold/platinum.
acgih_tlv: Heavy work 0.05ppm/0.1mg/m3 TWA; moderate work 0.08ppm/0.16mg/m3 TWA; light work 0.1ppm/0.2mg/m3 TWA; any workload ≤2h 0.2ppm/0.4mg/m3 TWA; not classifiable as human carcinogen.
dfg_mak: Carcinogen Cat 3B.
other_national_oels: Egypt/Turkey TWA0.1(0.02 or 0.2); Australia TWA0.1(0.2)/STEL0.3; Austria MAK0.1(0.2); Belgium STEL0.1(0.2); Denmark/Norway/Philippines TWA0.1(0.2); Finland TWA0.1(0.2)/STEL0.3(0.6); France VME0.1(0.2)/VLE0.2(0.4); Hungary TWA0.2/STEL0.4; Japan 0.1(0.2); Poland MAC(TWA)0.1/MAC(STEL)0.6; Russia TWA0.1/STEL0.1; Sweden NGV0.1(0.2)/TGV0.3(0.6); Switzerland MAK-W0.1(0.2)/KZG-W0.2(0.4); UK STEL0.2(0.4) (2000). ACGIH TLV countries: not classifiable as human carcinogen. US EPA NAAQS: 0.12ppm (1h avg), 0.08ppm total photochemical oxidants (1h avg). Czech Rep TWA0.1mg/m3, ceiling 0.2mg/m3. Russia residential MAC 0.16mg/m3 once-daily/0.03mg/m3 daily average. US states 0.005-0.235 mg/m3.
short_term_effects: Irritates eyes/resp tract. Eye exposure: conjunctivitis. Inhalation: pulmonary edema (delayed hours, can be fatal); asthma-like reactions. Liquid may cause frostbite. May affect CNS — headache, impaired concentration/performance. Acute exposure: skin/eye/mucous-membrane irritation/burns, increased resp rate, shallow breathing, cough, dyspnea, bronchitis, pulmonary edema/hemorrhage, tachycardia, hypotension. Neurologic: fatigue, dizziness, drowsiness, headache, exhilaration, depression. Nausea, vomiting, anorexia possible. 0.2ppm/3h: no symptoms. 0.3ppm: chest/throat tightness, dry throat, throat/lung irritation within 30min. ≥0.5ppm: sulfur-like odor, headache, drowsiness, coordination loss, lung fluid accumulation. ~10ppm: immediate severe throat/lung irritation, excessive sweating, continual coughing, decreased blood pressure, weak rapid pulse, severe chemical pneumonia. Death possible from prolonged exposure at 2ppm or short exposure at 10ppm. Breathing-difficulty onset may delay up to 6h. Highly toxic via inhalation or liquid contact; can cause acute-to-chronic lung damage, burns, death, permanent injury. Toxic at 100ppm/1min. Capable of death from pulmonary edema. Increases lung sensitivity to bronchoconstrictors/allergens; increases susceptibility/severity of lung bacterial/viral infections.
long_term_effects: Repeated/prolonged exposure may cause lung damage/chronic respiratory disease. May damage developing fetus.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: chest X-ray, EKG, pulmonary function tests (FVC, FEV1), sputum cytology, WBC count/differential. Preplacement/periodic exams: focus on significant respiratory diseases; eye irritation may also be important.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR, administer 100% O2. Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered.
personal_protective_methods: Gas masks w/ proper canister+full face-piece, or goggles, or supplied-air respirators in excessive-concentration areas. Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; gas-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: 1ppm: CcrS/Sa. 2.5ppm: Sa:Cf/PaprS. 5ppm: CcrFS/GmFS/SaT:Cf/SCBAF/SaF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFS/SCBAE.
storage: Red stripe: flammability hazard, separate from all other flammable materials. Cool, dry, well-ventilated; detached storage preferred, away from combustible material/reducing agents. See OSHA Standard 1910.104 and NFPA 43A Code for Liquid/Solid Oxidizer Storage.
shipping: Compressed gas, toxic, n.o.s. (Ozone): 'POISON GAS, OXIDIZER' label; Class 2.3. Violation of transport regs to refill compressed gas cylinders without owner's express written permission.
spill_handling: If in building: evacuate, close doors, shut down HVAC. Restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate to disperse gas; chemical protective suit + SCBA to combat spills; stay upwind, water spray to knock down vapor, contain runoff; stop gas flow if safe; move/repair leaking cylinder if possible; absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth, seal containers; avoid sewers (explosion risk); OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Not flammable, but may react w/ combustibles to cause fire/explosion. Dry chemical/CO2/water spray/alcohol foam extinguishers. Vapors heavier than air; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; withdraw if cylinders exposed to excessive heat; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Vent to atmosphere.

incompatibilities: Strong oxidizers.
acgih_tlv: 2 mg/m3 TWA (fume).
other_national_oels: Australia/Belgium/Denmark TWA2(fume); Finland TWA1(fume); France VME2(fume); Norway TWA2; Switzerland MAK-W2(fume); Netherlands MAC-TGG 2 (2003). ACGIH TLV countries: TWA2mg/m3. US states 20-48 μg/m3.

regulatory_authority: Air Pollutant Standard Set. FIFRA status: supported. CWA §311 Hazardous Substances/RQ. RQ 1000 lb. Canada WHMIS 1.0%. Hazard Symbol (110-88-3) F, Xn; R11;R37;R63; S2;S36/37;S46. WGK: 2.

medical_surveillance: Before employment + regularly for frequent/high exposure: lung function tests (may be normal absent an active attack). If symptoms/overexposure: consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure, allergist evaluation for skin allergy, kidney function tests.

storage: Red: flammability hazard, flammable-materials storage area. Check explosive conc. before confined entry. extraction_notes: Reference: EPA CHIP: Pentaborane (Nov 1987). short_term_effects: Reacts with many enzymes, damaging the body. Blinds and severely blisters skin; enough exposure is fatal. Immediate pain and violent vomiting signal exposure. long_term_effects: Animal evidence: kidney damage, muscle tremor, seizure, possible GI-tract effects, reproductive effects, possible liver damage.

Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Keep victim quiet, maintain normal body temp; effects may be delayed, keep under observation. Note to physician: severe poisoning — BAL (British Anti-Lewisite/dimercaprol) used for certain heavy-metal poisoning incl. arsenic; large margin of safety but caution needed re: excessive dosage; premedication w/ l-ephedrine sulfate (CAS 134-72-5) prevents most effects. Penicillamine (not penicillin) used for milder poisoning w/ mixed success; side effects occur, never a substitute for exposure control; only under strict medical care.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash. Decontamination: critical and time-sensitive; do not enter hot/warm zone without proper equipment/training. Immediately flush w/ water (spray/fog to avoid touching victim) without waiting for soap/clothing removal; flush eyes ≥15min. Caution re: hypothermia in children/elderly. Wash-strip-wash-evacuate protocol upwind/uphill. Warm water+soap wash. Diluted household bleach (0.5%, 1:200) decontamination — avoid eyes/wounds/mouth; wash off after 15min. Decontaminate victims fully before they leave area. Use Anti-Lewisite antidote (see First Aid). 5% bleach or calcium hypochlorite solution (48oz/5gal water) to decontaminate scissors/clothing/items.
respirator_selection: Per OSHA 29CFR1910.134/EN149: NIOSH/MSHA-approved respirator, or supplied-air (positive-pressure/continuous-flow), or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from oxidizers. Automatic pumping preferred. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.

Vapors heavier than air; confined-area vapors may explode w/ fire; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.

ld50: Probable oral lethal dose 5-50mg/kg (7 drops-1tsp/70kg 150lb person).

target_organs: Eyes, skin, CNS, peripheral nervous system, kidneys.
short_term_effects: Irritates eyes/skin/resp tract. Overexposure affects kidneys, causing renal failure. Extremely toxic. Symptoms may occur at varying intervals up to several weeks post-exposure. Mercurial-fungicide-treated grain ingestion causes GI irritation w/ nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea. Alkylmercurials produce severe neurologic toxicity: lip/tongue/extremity numbness, confusion, hallucinations, irritability, sleep disturbances, staggering walk, memory loss, slurred speech, auditory defects, emotional instability, concentration difficulty. Strong skin irritant — erythema/blistering may result 6-12h post-exposure. May injure eyes externally at sufficient concentration. Mercury poisoning: shakes, irritability, sore gums, increased saliva, personality change, brain damage. Skin contact can cause burns, allergy, gray skin color. Heating/acid contact releases toxic mercury vapors.
long_term_effects: Mercury accumulates in the body. Repeated/prolonged skin contact may cause dermatitis. May affect nervous system, cause nervous disorders. Animal-tested teratogen — handle w/ extreme caution. May cause mutations.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, CNS, peripheral nervous system, kidneys.
mutagenicity: May cause mutations.
medical_surveillance: Before first exposure + every 6-12mo: complete medical history/exam, nervous system exam (incl. handwriting), routine UA, urine mercury test (<0.02mg/L). Keep victim quiet, maintain normal body temp; effects may be delayed, keep under observation. Antidotes: N-acetyl penicillamine (NAP) used for mercury poisoning w/ mixed success. Note to physician: severe poisoning — BAL (British Anti-Lewisite/dimercaprol) used for certain heavy-metal poisoning incl. mercury; large margin of safety but caution needed re: excessive dosage; premedication w/ l-ephedrine sulfate (CAS 134-72-5) prevents most effects.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash. Specific engineering controls per NIOSH Criteria Doc #73-11024.
respirator_selection: 0.1mg/m3: Sa. 0.25mg/m3: Sa:Cf. 0.5mg/m3: SaT:Cf/SCBAF/SaF. 2mg/m3: Sa:Pd,Pp. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: SCBAE.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from strong oxidizers (chlorine, bromine, fluorine). No smoking/open flames.
shipping: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; collect w/ special mercury vapor suppressants or special vacuums; mercury-specific cleanup kits should be available; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.

Extremely hazardous to health but areas may be entered w/ extreme care — full protective clothing incl. SCBA, rubber gloves, boots, leg/arm/waist bands, no exposed skin. Poisonous mercury gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Consult environmental regulatory agencies. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators). React to produce soluble nitrate form, precipitate as mercuric sulfide. Return to supplier.

Synonyms: Carbon dichloride oxide; Carbonyl chloride; Carbonyl dichloride; CG (military designation); Chloroformyl chloride; Combat gas; Diphosgene; DP (military designation for diphosgene); Fosgeno (Spanish); Trichloroacetyl chloride (diphosgene)
regulatory_authority: DHS Screening Threshold: release hazard 500lb (≥1.00% conc.); theft hazard 15lb (≥0.17% conc.). Carcinogenicity: EPA inadequate information to assess. Hazard Symbol (75-44-5) T+; R26;R34; S1/2;S9;S26;S36/37/39;S45. WGK: 2.
carcinogenicity_status: EPA: inadequate information to assess carcinogenic potential.
rcra_waste_numbers: P095. App 8 Hazardous Constituents.
epcra_status: TPQ 10 lb (4.54 kg). RQ 10 lb (4.54 kg). Section 313 de minimis 1.0%.
clean_air_act: Hazardous Air Pollutant + high-risk pollutant list; Accidental Release Prevention/Flammable Substances (§112r Table 3), TQ 500 lb (227 kg).
clean_ water_act: §311 Hazardous Substances/RQ (40CFR117.3); §313 Water Priority Chemicals (57FR41331, 9/9/92).
description: Colorless, noncombustible gas. Shipped as liquefied compressed gas in steel cylinders. Low concentrations: sweet odor (newly mown hay/green corn/moldy hay). Higher concentrations: suffocating, irritating, pungent odor; odor only briefly detectable and unreliable overexposure indicator. Fuming liquid below 8.3°C/47°F. Odor threshold 1.5-6mg/m3. Choking agent; rapidly decomposes at relative humidity >70%. Relative vapor density (air=1): 3.48.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Human Data. Deadly at concentrations as low as 2ppm. Industrial-chemical intermediate (dyes, plastics; triphenylmethane/coal-tar/urea dyestuffs). Organic synthesis of isocyanates+derivatives, carbonic acid esters (polycarbonates), acid chlorides. Metallurgy; some insecticide/pharmaceutical manufacture. Exposure may occur during arc welding, vinyl-chloride fires, or from household paint removers/degreasers used near heat. Used as military choking/pulmonary agent since WWI; staple of many countries' chemical arsenals (standard published civilian safety/decon/PPE data only — no synthesis or weaponization information). Persistence: Summer 1-10min; Winter 10min-1h.
incompatibilities: Moisture, alkalis, ammonia, alcohols, copper. Reacts slowly in water forming hydrochloric acid/CO2. Violent reaction w/ strong oxidizers, amines, aluminum. Attacks many metals w/ water present. Attacks plastic/rubber/coatings.
niosh_rel: 0.1 ppm/0.4 mg/m3 TWA; 0.2 ppm/0.8 mg/m3 [15min] Ceiling.
acgih_tlv: 0.1 ppm/0.4 mg/m3 TWA.
dfg_mak: 0.02 ppm; 0.082 mg/m3 TWA; Peak Cat I(2); Pregnancy Grp C.
other_national_oels: AIHA ERPG-1: inappropriate; ERPG-2: 0.2ppm; ERPG-3: 1ppm. Austria MAK0.1(0.4); Denmark TWA0.05(0.2); Finland STEL0.05(0.2)[skin]; France VLE0.1(0.4); Japan 0.1(0.4); Netherlands MAC-TGG 0.08; Philippines TWA0.1(0.1); Poland MAC(TWA)0.5/MAC(STEL)1.5; Sweden TGV0.05(0.2); Switzerland MAK-W0.1(0.4)/KZG-W0.2(0.8); Thailand/Turkey TWA0.1(0.4); UK TWA0.02(0.08)/STEL0.06 (2000).
