determination_in_water: Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow=-0.71.
short_term_effects: Acute exposure: severe irritation/burns of skin/eyes/mucous membranes/resp passages. Cough, dyspnea, chest pain, severe pulmonary edema; cyanosis/anxiety possible. Odor detection at any time indicates need for immediate action/withdrawal. Inhalation: immediate + delayed symptoms. At ≥5ppm: mouth/throat/eye irritation, tearing, coughing, difficult breathing. Delayed effects: lung fluid accumulation and death without rapid treatment (delay 2-15h depending on dose). Death from short high-level exposure (30ppm/17min) or long low-level exposure (3ppm/3h). Particularly dangerous at low levels — lethal doses may be inhaled without warning. Skin: severe chemical burns; liquid causes frostbite. Eyes: irritation begins 3-5ppm, severe/permanent damage possible; liquid more hazardous than vapor, causes frostbite. Ingestion: severe irritation/chemical burns of mouth/throat/lungs/digestive tract.
long_term_effects: Even low levels can cause permanent lung damage, emphysema, bronchitis, pulmonary fibrosis.
medical_surveillance: Preemployment exams: chest X-rays, baseline pulmonary function tests. Consider chest X-ray following acute overexposure. Eye/skin exam. Smoking history. Periodic pulmonary function studies. Workers who inhaled phosgene should remain under medical observation ≥24h to catch delayed symptoms.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate immediately. Skin: flush with water immediately. Inhaled: move to fresh air, artificial respiration. Swallowed: get medical attention, do not induce vomiting. Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered. Frostbite: seek care immediately, don't rub or flush w/ water, don't remove frozen clothing. No frostbite: wash contaminated skin thoroughly. Decontamination: critical and time-sensitive; do not enter hot zone without proper equipment/training. If victim can't move, decontaminate without touching/entering hot zone. Use clean water (hose spray/fog to avoid touching victim), begin washing immediately without waiting for soap/clothing removal. Flush eyes ≥15min. Wash-strip-wash-evacuate protocol upwind/uphill. Warm water+soap wash. Diluted household bleach (10%, 1:9) decontamination — avoid eyes/wounds/mouth, rinse after 15min. Ensure victims fully decontaminated before leaving area. Self-decontaminate immediately if exposed; shower/change clothes even if thought unexposed.
personal_protective_methods: For liquid phosgene: protective clothing impervious to phosgene. For gas above safe limits: full-face gas masks w/ phosgene canisters or supplied-air respirators. Automatic continuous monitors w/ alarm systems strongly recommended (poor warning properties). Clothing to prevent skin contact; eye protection; wash immediately if wet/contaminated; remove nonimpervious clothing immediately if contaminated; emergency showers.
respirator_selection: 1ppm: Sa. 2ppm: SCBAF/SaF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFS/SCBAE. Eye irritant — may need eye protection.
storage: Yellow stripe: reactive hazard, isolated from flammables/combustibles/other yellow materials. Blue: poison, secure location. Avoid water/moisture/steam — violent reactions. Tightly closed steel containers, isolated area away from work area, sunlight. Anhydrous equipment noncorrosive to ordinary metals; use monel/tantalum/glass-lined containers where moisture present. Away from heating/cooling ducts. Frequent leak inspection. Per OSHA 1910.101/1910.169 & CGA recommendations.
shipping: 'POISON GAS, CORROSIVE' label; Class 2.3. Violation of transport regs to refill compressed gas cylinders without owner's express written permission. Special precautions: cylinders transported secure upright in well-ventilated truck.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; ventilate to disperse gas; stop gas flow; move/repair leaking cylinder if possible; absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth, seal containers. Neutralize w/ sodium bicarbonate or soda ash/slaked lime mixture; spray carefully w/ water after mixing; transfer slowly to larger water container — do NOT use water directly on spill. Hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Isolation distances (first 30min, may increase w/ time; weapon-use scenarios differ from accidental release) — CG small: 600ft/200m, downwind 0.7-2.5mi day/4.1mi night; CG large: 3000ft/1000m, downwind 4.7-7.0mi day/11.0mi night; DP small: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.2-0.5mi day/0.8mi night; DP large: 600ft/200m, downwind 0.7-1.6mi day/2.5mi night; phosgene (accidental) small: 300ft/100m, downwind 0.4-1.6mi day/2.5mi night; large: 500ft/150m, downwind 2.0-6.1mi day/9.7mi night; diphosgene small: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.1-0.2mi day/night; large: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.2-0.3mi day/0.5mi night. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: May burn but doesn't easily ignite. Small fires: dry chemical/CO2. Larger fires: water spray/fog/foam. Move container from fire area if safe; stay away from tank ends; cool exposed containers w/ water until well after fire out; isolate area until gas disperses. Poisonous hydrogen chloride/CO/chlorine gases produced. Diphosgene (DP) won't burn but adjacent-fire tank heating may cause overpressurization/explosion — evacuate; when heated, DP breaks down to toxic phosgene then chlorine/HCl gases; too dangerous for manned firefighting, use unattended fire monitor aimed at upper tank; spray/fog pattern preferred over solid stream. Cool containers from secure location — do NOT get water inside containers; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Neutralize w/ sodium bicarbonate or soda ash/slaked lime mixture; spray carefully w/ water after mixing; transfer slowly to larger water container — do NOT use water directly on spill. Pass controlled discharges through 10% NaOH scrubbing tower. Consult environmental regulatory agencies. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators).

first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Scrape/brush visible particles from skin/hair for metallic phosphide exposure. Use clean water (hose spray/fog to avoid touching victim); don't wait for soap/clothing removal; use cold water, don't delay for warm water. Flush eyes ≥15min. Caution re: hypothermia in children/elderly. Phosphine-gas-only exposure poses minimal secondary-contamination risk; vomitus containing phosphides can off-gas phosphine. fire_extinguishing: Flammable gas. Poisonous phosphorus oxide/phosphonic acid gases/mists produced. Specially trained personnel may use fog lines to cool and let fire burn out. Don't extinguish unless flow can be stopped; flooding-quantity water fog; cool containers from maximum distance; solid streams may be ineffective; alcohol foam/CO2/dry chemical alternatives. Full protective clothing incl. SCBA, rubber gloves, boots, leg/arm/waist bands, no exposed skin. Massive cargo fires: unmanned hose holders/monitor nozzles. Gas heavier than air, may travel along ground to ignition source; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; withdraw if cylinders exposed to excessive heat; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Consult environmental regulatory agencies. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators). Per 40CFR165 pesticide/container disposal recommendations. incompatibilities: Dust forms explosive air mixture. Strong acids, caustics, ammonia, amines, strong oxidizers, water. Converted to phthalic acid in hot water. Violent reaction w/ copper oxide or sodium nitrite + heat.

short_term_effects: Irritates eyes/skin/resp tract. Inhalation: nose/throat/mouth irritation w/ coughing, sneezing, SOB, excessive nasal discharge/bleeding (occurs ~4ppm). personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles for liquid work, dust-proof goggles for powder/dust work, unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.

shipping: 'CORROSIVE' label; Class 8, Packing Group III.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; forced ventilation below explosive limit; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible solid. Dry chemical/CO2/water spray/alcohol foam extinguishers. Poisonous gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.

extraction_notes: References: EPA Phthalic Anhydride Health and Environmental Effects Profile #147 (Apr 1980); NY DOH Fact Sheet v2 (Mar 1986); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet (Aug 2001). Synonym list heavily abbreviated (20+ chemical/trade names in source).

points_of_attack: Respiratory system, lungs, CNS, cardiovascular system, skin, eyes, plasma/RBC cholinesterase.
medical_surveillance: Plasma/RBC cholinesterase levels before employment + regularly (plasma normalizes 1-2wk after exposure stops, RBC may stay reduced 1-3mo). ≥25% reduction below preemployment level increases poisoning risk even in 'normal' range. shipping: Carbamate pesticides, solid, toxic: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group I.

potential_exposure: Compound Description: Mutagen. Relays, contacts, tubes in electronics; spark plug electrodes for aircraft; high-temp furnace windings. Alloys used for weight/length/temperature measurement standards. Platinum and catalysts (e.g. hexachloroplatinic acid) widely used in persulfuric/nitric/sulfuric acid production, organic compound/vitamin synthesis, higher-octane gasoline production. Used in automobile exhaust-pollutant control catalyst systems, molten-glass/fibrous-glass equipment, lab/medical/dental apparatus, electroplating, photography, jewelry, X-ray fluorescent screens. Platinum complexes used as antitumor agents — potential carcinogenic activity should be clarified via testing. Mild dermatitis: erythema/urticaria of hands/forearms. Severe cases affect face/neck. All pathology limited to allergic manifestations. EPA research indicates platinum is more biologically/toxicologically active than previously believed — methylates in aqueous media, establishing previously unrecognized biotransformation/distribution mechanism.

international_regulations: Not listed in Annex 1. Rotterdam Convention Annex III (PIC procedure, deca-/hexa-/octa- isomers). Stockholm Convention POPs Annex A.
description: Do not occur as natural products. Hexabromobiphenyl is predominant isomer; heavy, highly brominated compounds. Produced by direct bromination of biphenyl, forming complex isomer mixtures. Possible trace contamination w/ halogenated dibenzofurans (analogous to PCBs).
potential_exposure: Inert substances, primarily used as fire retardants — e.g. incorporated into thermoplastics at ~15% conc. to increase heat stability. 1973: 1-2 tons of PBB flame retardant accidentally mixed into animal feed supplement, fed to cattle in Michigan; also contaminated via manufacturing/handling-site discharge. ~250 dairy and 500 cattle farms quarantined; tens of thousands of swine/cattle and >1 million chickens destroyed; hundreds of millions of dollars in lawsuits. Contaminated animals/products (meat, eggs, milk) were consumed before contamination was recognized — large-scale human exposure resulted. Persistent in environment, concentrated in body fat. Commercial manufacture/distribution has ceased; full problem extent not yet assessed.
iarc_classification: Group 2B.
short_term_effects: 1973 Michigan animal-feed/livestock contamination (Firemaster BP-6) stimulated extensive water-contamination, transport, bioaccumulation, biological/toxicological studies. No immediate adverse health effects noted in several thousand Michigan farm families who consumed contaminated milk/dairy; chronic/delayed effects and teratogenic potential not determinable at time of writing.
long_term_effects: Confirmed carcinogen. Firemaster FF-1 (BP-6 + 2% calcium trisilicate — pentabromobiphenyl/hexabromobiphenyl/heptabromobiphenyl mixture, hexabromobiphenyl predominant) gavage-administered produced neoplastic nodules/hepatocellular carcinomas in female Sherman rats; also carcinogenic to Fisher 344 rats and B6C3F1 mice of both sexes (neoplastic nodules, hepatocellular carcinomas, cholangiocarcinomas in rats; hepatocellular carcinomas in mice). Experimental teratogenic and reproductive effects. Mutation data reported.
mutagenicity: Mutation data reported.
medical_surveillance: Consider points of attack in preplacement/periodic exams. Liver and kidney function tests.

TSCA §12(b) Export Notification §6. Rotterdam Convention Annex III (PIC procedure, as PCBs). Banned/severely restricted in many countries (UN); Persistent Organic Pollutant (UN). international_regulations: Hazard Symbol (PCB) Xn, N; R33;R50/53; S2;S35;S60;S61. Rotterdam Convention Annex III (PIC procedure, as PCBs). Stockholm Convention POPs Annex A + Annex C.
description: Aroclor 1242: colorless to light yellow viscous liquid, mild hydrocarbon odor. Aroclor 1254: colorless to pale-yellow viscous liquid (resinous) or solid (below 10°C), mild hydrocarbon odor. Diphenyl rings w/ one or more H replaced by Cl. 209 possible chlorobiphenyl compounds exist (1-10 substitution positions); commercial mixtures contain 40-70 different congeners (e.g. Aroclor 1254 contains 69). Some non-US mixtures (France, Germany, Japan) shown to contain chlorinated naphthalenes/dibenzofurans as additional contaminant classes.
potential_exposure: Compound Description (Aroclor 1242/1254): Agricultural Chemical; Tumorigen, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data (1242). No longer produced in the US but still found in environment. Used alone/combined w/ chlorinated naphthalenes — stable, thermoplastic, nonflammable. Heat-transfer/hydraulic fluids, lubricants, insecticide formulations, electric cable/wire insulation, electric condenser production, extreme-pressure lubricant additives, foundry coating. Introduced commercially >45 years ago; concern over ubiquitous dispersal, environmental persistence, food-chain bioaccumulation w/ possible adverse effects on top-of-food-web animals including humans.
incompatibilities: Strong oxidizers.
osha_pel: 1 mg/m3 TWA [skin] (42% Cl); 0.5 mg/m3 TWA [skin] (54% Cl).
niosh_rel: 0.001 mg/m3 TWA (applies to all PCBs); potential occupational carcinogen — limit to lowest feasible concentration.
acgih_tlv: 1 mg/m3 TWA [skin] (42% Cl); 0.5 mg/m3 TWA [skin] (54% Cl, confirmed animal carcinogen, unknown human relevance). PCB oxide: 0.5 mg/m3 inhalable fraction [skin].
pac1: 0.125-40 mg/m3 (varies by Aroclor, see TEEL note)
dfg_mak: 0.1 ppm/1.1 mg/m3 TWA (42% Cl); 0.05 ppm/0.70 mg/m3 TWA (54% Cl); Peak Cat II(8) [skin]; Carcinogen Cat 3B; Pregnancy Grp B.
other_national_oels: 42% Cl: Australia TWA1/STEL2[skin] carcinogen; Austria MAK0.1(1)[skin] suspected carcinogen; Belgium TWA1/STEL2[skin]; Finland TWA0.5/STEL1.5[skin]; France VME1[skin]; Japan 0.1[skin] 2A carcinogen; Netherlands MAC-TGG 1[skin]; Philippines TWA1[skin]; Poland MAC(TWA)1; Sweden NGV0.01/KTV0.3[skin] carcinogen; Switzerland MAK-W0.1(1)[skin]; UK TWA0.1[skin] (2000). 54% Cl: Egypt/Australia TWA0.5[skin]carcinogen; Austria MAK0.05(0.5)[skin]; Belgium TWA0.5/STEL1[skin]; France VME0.5[skin]; Japan 0.1[skin]2A; Norway TWA0.01; Netherlands MAC-TGG 0.5[skin]; Poland MAC(TWA)1; Sweden NGV0.1/KTV0.3[skin]carcinogen; Switzerland MAK-W0.05(0.5)[skin]; Turkey TWA1[skin]; UK TWA0.1[skin] (2000). Czech Rep TWA0.5/ceiling1.0.
determination_in_air: NIOSH #5503 (Polychlorobiphenyls); #8004 (in serum); OSHA Method PV-2089 (42% Cl); PV-2088 (54% Cl).
human_health_water: Preferably zero. Additional lifetime cancer risk 1:100,000 at 0.00079μg/L. EPA MCL 0.0005 mg/L. Spills ≥1lb must be reported to EPA.
determination_in_water: GC (EPA 608) or GC-MS (EPA 625). Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow=6.25 (54% Cl, estimated).
iarc_classification: Group 2A (1998).
ld50: No reported human deaths from single ingestion; animal experiments suggest 6-10 fl oz would cause death to a healthy 150lb adult.
routes_of_entry: Inhalation of fume/vapor, percutaneous absorption of liquid, ingestion, skin/eye contact.
target_organs: Liver, skin, nervous system. Cancer site in animals: liver.
short_term_effects: Inhalation may irritate nose/throat/lungs, cause coughing/breathing difficulty; levels >10mg/m3 unbearable; contributes significantly to long-term-exposure symptoms. Skin: moderate absorption, contributes significantly to long-term symptoms; sensitized individuals may develop rash after 2 days contact/inhalation. Eyes: irritation/burns; 10mg/m3 severely irritating. Ingestion absorption contributes significantly to long-term symptoms.
long_term_effects: Repeated/prolonged skin contact may cause chloracne. May cause liver damage. High exposure can damage nervous system. Readily absorbed by all exposure routes; may persist in tissues for years after exposure stops. High vapor levels (1-10mg/m3) may cause burning sensation in eyes/nose/face, dry throat, lung/throat irritation, nausea, dizziness, acne aggravation (immediate or delayed weeks/months). Chemical acne, blackheads, dark skin patches, unusual eye discharge reported via all exposure routes (onset 2 days to months; effects may last months). Digestive disturbance reported in some individuals. May impair immune system function. High PCB levels produce cancer and birth defects in lab animals; human relevance unknown.
points_of_attack: Liver, skin, nervous system. Cancer site in animals: liver.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: adipose tissue, whole blood chemical/metabolite, blood serum, blood plasma, liver function tests. Before employment + regularly: serum triglycerides level, skin exam, nervous system exam. Nerve conduction studies should be considered.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact. Chlorodiphenyl 42% Cl: 8h-breakthrough (>0.1μg/cm2/min): butyl rubber, Neoprene, Teflon, Viton, Saranex-coated, Barricade-coated, Responder suits; 4h-breakthrough: 4H and Silver Shield gloves. Chlorodiphenyl 54% Cl: same recommendations. No contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash. See NIOSH Criteria Doc #77-225.
respirator_selection: At any detectable concentration: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFOv100/SCBAE.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from strong oxidizers (chlorine, bromine, fluorine). Regulated, marked area per OSHA Standard 1910.1045.
shipping: 'CLASS 9' label; Class 9, Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate; absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid sewers (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Spills ≥1lb must be reported to EPA.
fire_extinguishing: May burn but doesn't easily ignite. Poisonous dioxin/chlorinated dibenzofuran gases produced. Dry chemical/CO2/alcohol foam extinguishers. Vapors heavier than air; confined-area vapors may explode w/ fire; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Incineration at 1648°C w/ scrubbing to remove chlorine-containing products. Some approved chemical waste landfills accept PCB disposal. Metallic sodium treatment (advocated recently) yields low-molecular-weight polyphenylene + sodium chloride.

description: Class of hydraulic cements containing tri-/dicalcium silicate plus varying amounts of alumina, tricalcium aluminate, iron oxide. Quartz content usually <1%. Average composition: CaO 64.0%, SiO2 21.0%, Al2O3 5.8%, Fe2O3 2.9%, MgO 2.5%, alkali oxides 1.4%, SO3 1.7%.
potential_exposure: Binding agent in mortar and concrete (cement+gravel+sand mixture). Potentially hazardous exposure during both manufacture and use.
incompatibilities: None reported.
osha_pel: 50 mppcf TWA or 15 mg/m3 total dust TWA; 5 mg/m3 TWA respirable fraction.
niosh_rel: 10 mg/m3 total dust TWA; 5 mg/m3 TWA respirable fraction.
acgih_tlv: 1 mg/m3 respirable fraction TWA (particulate matter containing no asbestos and <1% crystalline silica); not classifiable as human carcinogen.
other_national_oels: Australia/Belgium TWA10; Sweden NGV10(total)/5(respirable); Switzerland MAK-W6; UK TWA10(total inhalable); Netherlands MAC-TGG 10 (1993-2003). ACGIH TLV countries: TWA10mg/m3 (no asbestos, <1% crystalline silica).
determination_in_air: NIOSH #0500 (Particulates NOR, total dust); OSHA Method ID-207 (Portland cement, total dust).
short_term_effects: Irritates eyes/skin/nose w/ cough, expectoration, exertional dyspnea, wheezing.
long_term_effects: May cause chronic bronchitis. Cement dermatitis usually from primary irritation (alkaline, hygroscopic, abrasive properties). Chronic eye/nose irritation possible. Some cement workers develop allergic sensitivity to constituents (e.g. hexavalent chromate). Cement dermatitis can be prolonged, involve covered body areas. No documented finished-Portland-cement pneumoconiosis/systemic-manifestation cases; conflicting pneumoconiosis reports relate to mining/quarrying/crushing exposures to silica-containing raw materials.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: chest X-ray, pulmonary function tests (FVC, FEV1). Preemployment/periodic exams should stress significant respiratory problems, smoking history, allergic skin sensitivities. Eye exam. Patch test studies may be useful for dermatitis cases.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent prolonged skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: NIOSH: 50mg/m3: Qm. 100mg/m3: 95XQ/Sa. 250mg/m3: Sa:Cf/PaprHie. 500mg/m3: 100F/SaT:Cf/PaprTHie/SCBAF/SaF. 5000mg/m3: Sa:Pd,Pp. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: 100F/SCBAE.

Synonyms: Elemental potassium; Kalium
un_na_number: UN2257/130; UN1420 (metal alloys)/138; UN3089 (metal powder, flammable, n.o.s.)/170
regulatory_authority: Hazard Symbol F, C; R14;R34; S1/2;S5(if appropriate);S8;S45. WGK: none assigned.
international_regulations: Hazard Symbol F, C; R14;R34; S1/2;S5(if appropriate);S8;S45.
description: Soft silvery metal. Autoignition 441°C.
potential_exposure: Reagent; sodium-potassium alloys used as high-temperature heat transfer media.
incompatibilities: Air contact causes spontaneous ignition. Violent water reaction — heat, spattering, corrosive potassium hydroxide, explosive hydrogen; reaction heat can ignite generated hydrogen. Powerful reducing agent. Violent reaction w/ oxidizers, organic materials, carbon dioxide, heavy metal compounds, carbon tetrachloride, halogenated hydrocarbons, easily oxidized materials, many other substances. Store under nitrogen, mineral oil, or kerosene. Oxidizes, forms unstable peroxides under storage conditions. Oxide-coated potassium metal is an extremely dangerous explosion hazard and should be removed/destroyed. Must avoid contact with carbon monoxide, moisture, heavy-metal compounds (silver oxide, silver chloride), carbon tetrachloride — violent reactions occur.
human_health_water: No criteria set (reacts with water).
short_term_effects: Can affect via inhalation. Dust/mist inhalation irritates eyes/nose/throat/lungs w/ sneezing, coughing, sore throat. Higher exposures may cause pulmonary edema, can cause death. Skin/eye contact can cause severe burns, permanent damage.
long_term_effects: Prolonged fume exposure can cause inner-nose/nasal-septum sores. Fumes can irritate lungs; bronchitis may develop.
medical_surveillance: Before employment + regularly for frequent/high exposure: lung function tests. If symptoms/overexposure: consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥30 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash immediately with large water amounts, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Observe 24-48h post-inhalation, as pulmonary edema may be delayed.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: NIOSH/MSHA-/EN149-approved respirator w/ particulate (dust/fume/mist) filters (checked daily for damage, replaced as needed). High exposures: supplied-air respirator with a full face-piece operated in the positive-pressure mode, or with a full face-piece/hood/helmet in the continuous-flow mode; or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure.
storage: Red stripe (lump): flammability hazard, don't store w/ other flammable materials. Avoid carbon monoxide/moisture/heavy-metal compounds (silver oxide, silver chloride)/carbon tetrachloride — violent reactions. Store under nitrogen, mineral oil, or kerosene. No smoking/open flames.
shipping: Potassium: 'DANGEROUS WHEN WET' label; Class 4.3, Packing Group II. Potassium, metal alloys: 'DANGEROUS WHEN WET' label; Class 4.3, Packing Group II. Metal powder, flammable, n.o.s.: 'SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE' label; Class 4.2, Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; avoid confined spaces (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Spontaneously combustible. Dry chemical/dry graphite/soda ash/lime extinguishers. Do NOT use water, CO2, or foam. May ignite in moisture presence or on air exposure. Poisonous gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.

regulatory_authority: Carcinogenicity: NTP 11th Report on Carcinogens (2004): known human carcinogen. IARC: human sufficient/animal limited evidence, carcinogenic to humans, Group 1 (1987). Air Pollutant Standard Set. CWA §311 Hazardous Substances/RQ + §313 Water Priority Chemicals. RQ 1 lb. CA Prop 65 (cancer 2/27/87). Canada WHMIS 1.0%. As arsenic compounds: CAA HAP; CWA Toxic Pollutant §401.15; RCRA App 8 (waste number not listed); RQ 1 lb; EPCRA 313 (any arsenic-containing chemical, de minimis inorganics 0.1%/organics 1.0%); DOT regulated marine pollutant (as arsenates n.o.s.); CA Prop 65 (inorganic arsenic, cancer 2/27/87). Canada Priority Substance List, ocean-dumping forbidden (CEPA), NPRI. Hazard Symbol T, N; R45;R23/25;R50/53; S53;S45;S60;S61. WGK: 3.
carcinogenicity_status: NTP 11th Report on Carcinogens (2004): known to be a human carcinogen. IARC: human sufficient/animal limited evidence, carcinogenic to humans, Group 1 (1987).
rcra_waste_numbers: App 8 Hazardous Constituents (as arsenic compound, waste number not listed).
epcra_status: RQ 1 lb (0.454 kg). Section 313 (any arsenic-containing chemical substance), de minimis inorganics 0.1%/organics 1.0%.
clean_ water_act: §311 Hazardous Substances/RQ (40CFR117.3); §313 Water Priority Chemicals (57FR41331, 9/9/92); Toxic Pollutant §401.15 (as arsenic and compounds).
international_regulations: Hazard Symbol T, N; R45;R23/25;R50/53; S53;S45;S60;S61.
description: Colorless to white crystalline solid.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Tumorigen. Textile, tanning, hide-preserving industries; textile printing, paper industries; insecticide in fly baits (esp. fly paper); laboratory reagent.
incompatibilities: Weak base. Reacts w/ strong oxidizers, bromine azide, acids; decomposes on strong-acid contact producing acetic acid fumes. Arsine (very deadly gas) can be released in presence of acid, acid mists, or hydrogen gas.
osha_pel: 0.010 mg[As]/m3 TWA; cancer hazard, can be inhaled. See 1910.1018.
niosh_rel: 0.002 mg[As]/m3 [15min] Ceiling; potential occupational carcinogen — limit to lowest feasible concentration.
acgih_tlv: 0.01 mg[As]/m3 TWA; confirmed human carcinogen.
dfg_mak: TRK 0.10 mg[As]/m3; BAT 1.30μg[As]/L urine end-of-shift; Carcinogen Cat 1.
other_national_oels: Egypt/Belgium/France/India TWA0.2; Australia TWA0.05 carcinogen; Denmark TWA0.05; Finland: carcinogen; Hungary STEL0.5 carcinogen; Norway TWA0.02; Philippines/Thailand/Turkey TWA0.5; Poland MAC(TWA)0.01; Sweden NGV0.03 carcinogen; Switzerland TWA0.1 carcinogen; UK TWA0.1 carcinogen (1993-2000). ACGIH TLV countries: confirmed human carcinogen. Russia residential MAC 0.003mg/m3 daily average. US states 0.0002-5 μg/m3 (varies widely; also CA Prop 65 0.06mg/m3).
human_health_water: EPA recommends zero for health reasons; guideline 50μg/L drinking water.
determination_in_water: See OSHA Method ID-105 for arsenic.
routes_of_entry: Inhalation, ingestion, skin/eye contact. Absorbed through skin.
short_term_effects: Can affect via inhalation and skin absorption. Carcinogen — handle with extreme caution. Eye contact causes irritation, burns, red watery eyes. Skin contact causes burning, itching, rash. Breathing causes irritation w/ sneezing, coughing. High/repeated exposure can cause disturbed sleep, numbness/weakness of arms/legs, poor appetite, nausea, cramps; severe cases: vomiting, diarrhea.
long_term_effects: Can cause nasal septum ulcer/hole, hoarseness, sore eyes. Repeated exposure can cause nervous system damage. Repeated skin contact can cause thickened skin and/or patchy darkening/pigment loss.
medical_surveillance: Before employment + regularly: nose/skin/eyes/nails/nervous system exam. Urine arsenic test (not accurate within 2 days of eating shellfish/fish; most accurate end-of-workday). At NIOSH REL, urine arsenic should not exceed 50-100 μg/L. Repeat tests after suspected overexposure. Periodic skin exam for abnormal growths — arsenic skin cancer easily cured when detected early.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Note to physician: severe poisoning — BAL used; milder poisoning — penicillamine (not penicillin) used, both w/ mixed success; side effects occur, never a substitute for exposure control; only under strict medical care.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; eye protection included in recommended respiratory protection; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Above NIOSH REL, or where no REL at any detectable conc.: Sa/SCBAF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFAg100/SCBAE.

routes_of_entry: Inhalation, ingestion, skin/eye contact. Absorbed through skin.
target_organs: Liver, kidneys, skin, cardiovascular system, CNS, thyroid gland.
short_term_effects: Corrosive to eyes/skin/resp tract. Contact causes skin/eye burns, possible permanent eye damage. Inhalation causes lung irritation w/ coughing, sneezing, difficult breathing, slow gasping respiration. Corrosive if swallowed. May affect CNS — headaches, confusion, nausea, pounding heart, weakness, unconsciousness, death.
long_term_effects: Repeated/prolonged contact may cause thyroid gland enlargement, interfere w/ thyroid function. May cause nosebleed, nose sores, blood cell count changes. May cause CNS damage — headache, dizziness, confusion, nausea, vomiting, pounding heart, arm/leg weakness, unconsciousness, death. May affect liver/kidney function.
points_of_attack: Liver, kidneys, skin, cardiovascular system, CNS, thyroid gland.
medical_surveillance: Consider points of attack in preplacement/periodic exams. Urine thiocyanate levels. Blood cyanide levels. CBC. Thyroid function evaluation. Liver/kidney function tests. CNS tests. EKG.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash immediately (speed critical), shampoo hair if contaminated, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Observe 24-48h — symptoms may return. Use amyl nitrate capsules if symptoms develop. Regular staff training in cyanide-poisoning emergency measures and CPR required. Cyanide antidote kit must be kept immediately available in work area; kit ingredients replaced every 1-2 years for freshness. Trained personnel (kit use, oxygen, CPR) must be quickly available.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield for liquid work, dust-proof goggles+face shield for powder/dust work, unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: When used as a weapon: SCBA respirator certified by NIOSH for CBRN environments. 25mg/m3: Sa/SCBAF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or Sa:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFS100/SCBAE.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Check explosive conc. before confined entry. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from strong acids/acid salts/oxidizers/light/moisture. Automatic transfer preferred.
shipping: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group I.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate closed spaces before entering (lower explosive limit applies); collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. UN1680 is on DOT's dangerous water-reactive materials list (produces large toxic-vapor amounts when spilled in water) — dangerous 0.5-10km (0.3-6.0mi) downwind. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: Not combustible itself but decomposes in moisture/damp air/CO2 presence, producing highly toxic/flammable hydrogen cyanide gas and NOx. NO acidic dry chemical extinguishers. NO hydrous agents. NO water. NO CO2. Use dry chemical and foam on surrounding fires only. Vapors heavier than air, may collect in low areas. Containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location (don't let water enter open containers); SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Consult environmental regulatory agencies. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators). Per 40CFR165 pesticide/container disposal recommendations. Follow package label directions or contact local/federal/regional EPA office. Add strong alkaline hypochlorite, react 24h, then flush to sewer with large water volumes.
extraction_notes: Reference: NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet: Potassium Cyanide (Aug 2005). Note: the source's Storage section text repeats the BAL/penicillamine antidote note (normally found under Note to Physician) verbatim twice consecutively — likely a formatting/duplication artifact in the source; captured once here under First Aid.

Synonyms: Agent 15; Agent-Buzz; BUZZ; BZ; Oksilidin; QNB; 3-Quinuclidinyl benzilate. Hydrochloride: CHEKB; HNB 3; Ro 2-3308.
regulatory_authority: DHS Screening Threshold: sabotage/contamination hazard: placarded amount (commercial grade). Report any WMD release to National Response Center 1-800-424-8802. Not a mandated federally listed RCRA waste, though more toxic than most RCRA-listed chemicals; listed hazardous waste in some states where military stockpiling occurred. WGK: none assigned.
carcinogenicity_status: Information unavailable on carcinogenicity from chronic/repeated exposure.
description: White crystalline solid, odorless. Historically considered as a chemical warfare incapacitating agent (military designation BZ/QNB); mixed with pyrotechnic compositions in small aerial bombs to produce an aerosol. Produced by the US at Pine Bluff Arsenal, Arkansas in the early 1960s; production ceased in the late 1960s, all US stockpiles destroyed by 1990. Iraq's 'Agent 15' believed identical or closely related. Effectiveness as a weapon has proven highly undependable and unpredictable.
potential_exposure: Mutagen, drug; incapacitating agent. Glycolate anticholinergic compound affecting CNS/PNS, related to atropine, scopolamine, hyoscyamine. Nonirritating; symptoms delayed several hours. Historically used in pharmacologic research. Stable in most solvents, half-life 3-4 weeks in moist air.
incompatibilities: May form explosive mixture with air. Decomposes at ~170°C in air under prolonged heating; completely decomposed after 1-2h at 200°C. No effect on steel/stainless steel after 3 months at 71°C; aluminum/anodized aluminum mildly attacked after 3 months at 71°C. Metal contact may evolve flammable/potentially explosive hydrogen gas. Very persistent in soil, water, and on surfaces.
determination_in_air: No method available for detecting in environmental samples (CDC).
determination_in_water: No method available for detecting in environmental samples (CDC).
ld50: LCt50 (estimated) 200,000 mg-min/m3 (high); ICt50=112 mg-min/m3. LD50 (iv-mouse) 18-25 mg/kg (US Army). TDLo (lowest published toxic dose, subcutaneous-human) 3μg/kg (NIOSH).
routes_of_entry: Respiratory system, ingestion, skin/eye contact. Skin/eye absorption possible depending on solvent used to enhance absorption. Inhalation and ingestion are important exposure routes for the solid (CDC).
short_term_effects: Nonirritating stunning agent. Onset of incapacitation is dose-dependent; symptoms may occur as early as 1h post-exposure, continuing 48h-4 days depending on exposure level. Untreated casualty may require 3-4 days for full recovery. Affects memory, problem-solving, decision-making, attention, instruction comprehension. Very potent — can cause confusion, dream-like state, hallucinations, severe delirium; affects circulation, digestion, salivation, sweating, vision. Causes pupil dilation. Produces profound mental disturbance at 0.1-0.2mg dose. Symptoms: agitation, restlessness, dizziness, giddiness, failure to obey orders, confusion, erratic behavior, stumbling/staggering, vomiting, hallucinations, blurred vision, dry flushed skin, urinary retention, ileus, tachycardia, hypertension, elevated temperature (>101°F/38°C). May cause short-term memory loss; side-effect severity varies by individual. Impairments generally temporary and unlikely fatal, but can be severe with high exposures. Anticholinergic. Delayed effect: disseminated intravascular coagulation (blood-vessel clot formation) is a potential complication in victims with marked agitation and/or hyperthermia.
long_term_effects: Information unavailable on carcinogenicity, developmental toxicity, or reproductive toxicity from chronic/repeated exposure.
medical_surveillance: In victims with marked agitation and/or hyperthermia: clotting studies (prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, INR) recommended. Urine tests.
first_aid: Eyes: after removing from exposure source, immediately wash with large amounts of tepid water ≥15min; don't allow rubbing; monitor for systemic effects, see Inhalation section if present; seek medical attention immediately. Ingestion: ensure unobstructed airway; do NOT induce vomiting; see Inhalation section; seek medical attention immediately. Inhalation: evaluate respiratory function/pulse; ensure unobstructed airway; administer oxygen if SOB/difficult breathing; assist ventilation as needed using barrier/bag-valve-mask device; provide artificial respiration if breathing ceased; monitor body temperature — if >102°F/39°C, initiate immediate vigorous cooling (as for heatstroke) using 72-75°F/22-24°C water and air circulation, wet cloths, or maximum shaded-area air circulation (do NOT use ice for skin cooling); give fluids sparingly; manage mouth/lip dryness with moist swabs and small petroleum-jelly amounts; monitor for skin abrasions from repetitive movements; remove potentially harmful items (cigarettes, matches, medications, small ingestible items); consider loose restraint of disoriented/agitated patients; consider separating affected individuals into small groups; seek medical attention immediately. Skin: see Decontamination section, then Inhalation-section first aid; seek medical attention immediately. Note to health professionals: treatment largely supportive care — IV fluids, appropriate cooling measures for elevated core temperature, judicious benzodiazepine sedation; severe toxicity may require physostigmine in a hospital setting (CDC). Antidote: some military references suggest physostigmine to temporarily increase synaptic acetylcholine; poses its own side-effect/drug-interaction risks and should be used only by physicians/medical personnel familiar with its safe use. Published dosage guidance (for reference; administration only by qualified medical personnel): test dose 1mg if diagnosis uncertain; routine dosing ~45mcg/kg adults, titrated hourly to mental status via IM/IV/PO routes per published military medical protocols (USAMRICD).
personal_protective_methods: First responders: NIOSH/EN149-certified CBRN SCBA with Level A protective suit when entering areas with unknown contaminant/concentration, until monitoring confirms identity/concentration. Level A (Red Zone): maximum skin/respiratory/eye protection for unknown-hazard or above-IDLH exposure — Totally-Encapsulating Chemical Protective (TECP) suit rated for CBRN agents, chemical-resistant gloves (inner+outer), chemical-resistant steel-toe/shank boots; coveralls/long underwear/hard hat optional under suit. Decontamination: establish decon corridor upwind/uphill of hot zone; warm zone includes separate entry/exit decon corridors (exit corridor upwind/uphill of entry corridor); decon workers wear appropriate PPE; detergent-water solution (pH 8-10.5) and soft brushes available; labeled durable 6-mil polyethylene bags for contaminated PPE disposal. First responder decon: wash PPE with soap-water solution and soft brush, head-to-toe motion, all clothing folds; wash/rinse until contaminant removed; remove PPE by rolling downward (avoid pulling over head); remove SCBA last; bag PPE. Patient/victim decon: remove from contaminated area to decon corridor; remove clothing to undergarments, bag; wash/rinse contaminated skin with soap-water solution, avoiding skin breaks, covering open wounds; cover patient to prevent shock/heat loss; move to emergency-treatment area.
respirator_selection: NIOSH/EN149-certified CBRN full-face-piece SCBA operated in pressure-demand mode, or pressure-demand supplied-air hose respirator with auxiliary escape bottle.
storage: Stable in most solvents, half-life 3-4 weeks in moist air. Store at 2-8°C.
shipping: 'TOXIC, LIQUIDS, ORGANIC, N.O.S.' — 'POISON (TOXIC)' subsidiary label; Class 6.1, Packing Group III.
spill_handling: Aerosol heavier than air — spreads along ground, collects/persists in poorly ventilated/low-lying/confined areas (sewers, basements, tanks); keep out of these areas; stay upwind. Environmental decontamination: avoid touching/walking through spilled agent; if unavoidable, wear appropriate PPE (see PPE section). Keep combustibles away. Water spray to reduce aerosols/divert cloud drift; avoid water runoff contacting spilled agent; don't direct water at the spill/leak source. Stop leak if safe. Prevent waterway/sewer/basement/confined-area entry. Isolate area until aerosol disperses; ventilate (NIOSH). Cover spills with vermiculite/diatomaceous earth/clay/fine sand/sponges/paper-cloth towels, then treat with copious ≥10wt% aqueous sodium hydroxide solution. Scoop into fully removable-head drum with HDPE liner; treat decon solution with excess bleach to destroy cyanide formed during hydrolysis; cover contents with additional bleach before sealing; decontaminate/label drum exterior per IAW/EPA/DOT regs. Overpack leaking containers with vermiculite between interior/exterior containers. Alternative decontaminants if 10% NaOH unavailable (in order of preference): Decontaminating Solution No. 2 (DS2: 2% NaOH, 70% diethylenetriamine, 28% ethylene glycol monomethyl ether), sodium carbonate, Supertropical Bleach Slurry (STB). Keep out of confined spaces (explosion risk). Hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Isolation (weapon-use scenario, first 30min, may increase w/ time) — small/large spills: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.1-0.3mi day/0.2-0.5mi night. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible; may burn but doesn't ignite readily; may be transported molten. Decomposes on heating, producing corrosive/toxic gases. Containers may explode when heated. Evacuate area including self in case of fire; use unattended equipment only if necessary to protect adjacent property, then evacuate. Heated aerosols may form explosive air mixtures — explosion hazard indoors, outdoors, and in sewers. Small fires: dry chemical/CO2/water spray. Large fires: dry chemical/CO2/alcohol-resistant foam/water spray. Move containers from fire area if safe; dike fire-control water for later disposal, don't scatter material. Fight tank/car/trailer fires from maximum distance or use unmanned hose holders/monitor nozzles; don't get water inside containers; cool with flooding water until well after fire out; withdraw immediately if venting sound rises or tanks discolor; stay away from fire-engulfed tanks. Runoff may be corrosive/toxic and cause pollution — control and properly dispose if situation allows.
disposal_method: See Spill Handling section above.
extraction_notes: References: Ketchum & Sidell, 'Incapacitating agents,' in Textbook of Military Medicine: Medical Aspects of Chemical and Biologic Warfare (1997); Byrd et al., 'Determination of 3-Quinuclidinyl Benzilate (QNB) and its major metabolites in urine,' J. Analytical Toxicology 16(3):182-187 (1992); US Army/Navy/Air Force publications on potential military chemical/biological agents (Dec 1990); CDC/NIOSH Emergency Response Safety and Health Database. This entry describes Agent BZ/QNB, a historical chemical warfare incapacitating agent; content reproduced is limited to standard published civilian/emergency-responder safety, decontamination, and medical-treatment data (largely sourced from CDC/NIOSH public guidance) — no synthesis or weaponization information is included.

CERCLA radionuclide RQs (curies): Ra-223 RQ=1, Ra-224 RQ=10, Ra-225 RQ=1, Ra-226 RQ=0.1, Ra-227 RQ=1000, Ra-228 RQ=0.1, Rn-220 RQ=1, Rn-222 RQ=1. Listed in TSCA inventory. CAA NESHAP limits radium air release to 10 mRem. SDWA authorizes EPA MCL limits for radium/radionuclides in drinking water.
carcinogenicity_status: IARC: known carcinogen. EPA/National Academy of Sciences Committee on Biological Effects of Ionizing Radiation: radium is a known human carcinogen (Ra-224, Ra-226, Ra-228, Rn-222 and decay products, Category 1).
epcra_status: CERCLA radionuclide RQs (curies): Ra-223 RQ=1, Ra-224 RQ=10, Ra-225 RQ=1, Ra-226 RQ=0.1, Ra-227 RQ=1000, Ra-228 RQ=0.1, Rn-220 RQ=1, Rn-222 RQ=1.

safe_drinking_water_act: Authorizes EPA MCL limits for radium/radionuclides in publicly supplied drinking water; MCL 5 pCi/L for combined Ra-226/Ra-228, 15 pCi/L for Ra-224.
description: Radium: radioactive element found naturally in the environment; silvery-white metallic solid at 25°C, tarnishes black in air; alkaline earth metal with 33 isotopes, all unstable. Commonly available as radium bromide or radium chloride. Radium bromide: white to brownish crystalline solid, radioactive. Radium chloride: yellowish-white or brownish crystalline solid, radioactive.
potential_exposure: Not available as pure metal; found in very small quantities in uranium/thorium ores, formed by radioactive decay/ore refining. One ton uranium ore yields ~0.1g radium. Principal environmental isotopes: Ra-226 and Ra-228. Ra-226 half-life ~1603-1620 years, remains in body for life. Used to produce radon gas for cancer treatment, metal radiography, and (combined with beryllium) as neutron-emitting source for research/radiation-instrument calibration. Until the 1960s, used in self-luminous paints for watch/compass/aircraft-instrument dials — later replaced by Co-60. Greatest health risk is from radon (Rn), radium's radioactive decay product, common in soils and able to accumulate in buildings.
incompatibilities: Metallic radium highly chemically reactive; forms compounds similar to barium compounds, complicating separation (EPA). Water contact forms flammable hydrogen gas. Radium bromate is a strong oxidizer; avoid combustible-material (clothing, wood, paper, oil) contact.
osha_pel: OSHA 29CFR1910.1096 (Ionizing Radiation) quarterly limits: lens of eye/gonads 1.25 Rem (0.0125 Sv); feet/ankles 18.75 Rem (0.1875 Sv); skin of whole body 7.5 Rem (0.075 Sv); minors 10% of adult limits; workers >18 may be permitted 3 Rem (0.3 Sv) under specified conditions.
other_national_oels: NCRP/NRC recommended occupational annual dose limits: whole body 5 Rem (0.05 Sv)/yr; lens of eye 15 Rem (0.15 Sv); skin 50 Rem (0.5 Sv); hands/feet 50 Rem (0.5 Sv); cumulative occupational limit 1 Rem (0.01 Sv) × age. Declared pregnant radiation worker: 500 mRem (0.005 Sv) for entire gestation; fetal limit 500 mRem for gestation, ≤50 mRem/month. NRC public dose limit 100 mRem (0.01 Sv)/yr. Indoor air advisory action level: 4 pCi/L radon.
determination_in_air: Particulate sampling for RDD incidents to measure airborne radioactivity and characterize exposures; determines needed respirator protection factor.
human_health_water: EPA MCL 5 pCi/L drinking water for combined Ra-226/Ra-228; 15 pCi/L for Ra-224. Both air/water standards limit increased lifetime cancer risk to ~2 in 10,000.
determination_in_water: EPA soil concentration limit: 5 pCi/g Ra-226 in uranium/thorium mill tailings (first 15cm of soil), 15 pCi/g in deeper soil.
iarc_classification: Known carcinogen.
routes_of_entry: Inhalation, ingestion, external exposure to alpha/beta/gamma rays.
target_organs: Liver, blood (anemia), eyes (cataracts) and other organs, bones and teeth.
short_term_effects: Highly radioactive; decay product radon (Rn) gas also radioactive. Over one million times more radioactive than equal-mass uranium. Chemically similar to calcium — can replace it in bones/teeth, later causing increased cavities/broken teeth. Inhalation/injection/ingestion/body exposure can cause cancer and other disorders; high-level exposure increases bone/liver/breast cancer risk. Emits alpha particles (harmful mainly if emitted inside body) and gamma rays (harmful both internally and externally; can penetrate body, causing exposure even at a distance). Radium bromate: highly hazardous via skin contact/eye contact/ingestion/inhalation (irritant); prolonged skin contact may cause burns, inflammation (redness, itching, scaling), blistering, ulceration; inhalation overexposure may cause respiratory irritation; eye inflammation causes redness, watering, itching. Gamma-ray exposure measured in Rads (100 Rads=1 Gray=1 J/kg): radiation sickness at 100 Rads (1 Gy) total-body exposure; radiation sickness and death in half the exposed population at 400 Rads (4 Gy); without treatment, nearly everyone receiving >400 Rads dies within 30 days; 100,000 Rads causes near-immediate unconsciousness and death within an hour.
long_term_effects: Long-term exposure increases risk of several diseases. Inhaled/ingested radium increases lymphoma, bone cancer, and blood-formation disease risk (leukemia, aplastic anemia); effects usually take years to develop. External gamma exposure increases cancer risk in varying degrees across all tissues/organs. Historically, Marie Curie's death from aplastic anemia has been attributed to radium exposure/handling. German patients injected with radium (1946-1950) for disease treatment including tuberculosis were significantly shorter as adults than untreated controls (CDC).
points_of_attack: Liver, blood (anemia), eyes (cataracts) and other organs, bones and teeth.
medical_surveillance: Whole body count measures total body radioactivity; urine/feces tested for radionuclide presence. No test can detect external gamma exposure unless doses were very high with detectable cellular damage. Exhaled-air radon (Rn) test available (radon is a radium breakdown product). None of these tests are routine in a doctor's office (require specialized lab equipment) and none can quantify exposure or predict long-term health effects.
first_aid: Unless dressed in appropriate protective gear to prevent self-contamination, do not provide medical attention. Evacuate victim from exposure area to safety ASAP. To stop ongoing contamination, have victim remove clothing if possible, seal in garbage bag/container. Check breathing/pulse; start CPR if necessary. Skin: if contaminated, measure levels with survey meter, record results, decontaminate by gentle washing with plenty of (warm if possible) water and nonabrasive disinfecting soap, washing downward toward extremities (not upward); dry body, cover irritated skin with emollient (no ointments if burns present); wrap in clean soft blanket; seek immediate medical attention, evacuate to nearest emergency facility. Eyes: check for/remove contact lenses; flush immediately with cold water (avoid eye ointment); seek immediate medical attention, evacuate to nearest emergency facility. Inhalation: rest in well-ventilated area; administer oxygen if breathing difficult; seek immediate medical attention, evacuate to nearest emergency facility. Ingestion: do NOT induce vomiting; loosen tight clothing (collar, tie, belt); seek immediate medical attention, evacuate to nearest emergency facility.
personal_protective_methods: Radium bromate: engineering controls (process enclosures, local exhaust ventilation) to keep airborne levels below exposure limits. No practical PPE protects against externally penetrating gamma radiation — monitoring devices are the only means to prevent excessive gamma exposure entry. PPE (typical firefighter turnout gear incl. SCBA and radiation detection device/dosimeter) is effective against particulate-borne (alpha/beta) radiation hazards, depending on radiation level; followed by appropriate personnel/equipment decontamination. Large spill: splash goggles, full suit, dust respirator, boots, gloves, SCBA to avoid inhalation. Suggested protective clothing might be insufficient — consult a specialist BEFORE handling radioactive material.
respirator_selection: Full-face air-purifying respirator with P-100/HEPA filter for particulate protection; SCBAs provide highest protection level. NIOSH CBRN-approved respirators preferred; incident commander may allow alternative NIOSH-approved respirators (SCBAs, full-face powered/nonpowered air-purifying with P-100/HEPA) where CBRN-specific units unavailable. These recommendations address only radioactive-particulate inhalation protection, not chemical/biological co-contaminants. Above NIOSH REL, or where no REL at any detectable conc.: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA.
storage: Store in ventilated area to prevent radon (Rn) accumulation.
shipping: Radioactive material, Type A package nonspecial form, nonfissile or fissile-excepted: 'RADIOACTIVE MATERIAL' label; Class 7. A1/A2 values for Ra-226 per 10CFR71 Appendix A: A1 (Special Form) 0.3 TBq (8.11 Ci); A2 (Normal Form) 0.02 TBq (0.541 Ci). Special form materials (per 49CFR173.403/173.469) are high-physical-integrity encapsulated sources posing hazard only via direct external radiation even under severe accident conditions.
spill_handling: Notify authorities. Do not touch spilled material. Cover with absorbent paper or dike with absorbent. Isolate area to prevent spread/personnel exposure. Prevent sewer/basement/confined-area entry; dike if needed. Survey spill site with monitoring equipment; evaluate skin/clothing/lab-equipment contamination. If skin/clothing contamination present, assume a MAJOR spill — do not attempt cleanup; confine potentially contaminated individuals to prevent further spread. Shield source if possible without increasing exposure to self/others. Leave affected room, lock doors to prevent entry. Contact local/state authorities and DOE Radiological Response Team for disposal assistance.
fire_extinguishing: If radioactive material Type A package nonspecial form is fire-involved, first contact DOE Radiological Response Team plus state/local authorities. Do NOT use water; use suitable dry powder, graphite, soda ash, powdered sodium chloride, or sand.
disposal_method: Radioactive material is waste and must be retained in containers for disposition by the authorizing institution. Drain disposal prohibited. Operating institution responsible for proper radioisotope disposal arrangements. Use, storage, transportation, labeling, disposal regulated via NRC 10CFR and 49CFR (transportation).
extraction_notes: References: ATSDR Toxicological Profile for Radium (1990); Bentor, ChemicalElements.com—Radium (2010); OSHA Standard 29CFR1910.1096 (Ionizing Radiation); EPA Manual of Protective Action Guides and Protective Actions for Nuclear Incidents (May 1992); DOE Radiological Emergency Response Health and Safety Manual (May 2001); USAMRICD Field Management of Chemical Casualties, 2nd ed. (Jul 2000). This entry describes radioactive materials with historical/current civilian, medical, and industrial uses; content reproduced is limited to standard published radiation-safety, decontamination, and emergency-response data.

Synonyms: Castor bean toxin; Ricine; Ricinus lectin; Ricinus agglutinin; Ricinus toxin; Lectin isolated from seeds of the castor bean; Ricinus communis protein/polypeptide
un_na_number: UN3462 (toxin, extracted from living sources, n.o.s.)/153
regulatory_authority: Report any WMD release to National Response Center 1-800-424-8802. Hazard Symbol T; R26/27/28;R42/43; S23;S28;S36/37;S45. WGK: no value assigned to these CAS numbers; based on toxicity, Class 3 (severe hazard to waters) may apply.
carcinogenicity_status: Information on carcinogenicity, developmental toxicity, or reproductive toxicity from chronic/repeated exposure is unknown at this time.
description: White powder; lethal, delayed-action cytotoxin, persistent in the environment (CDC). Stable under ambient conditions; destroyed by heat and household bleach solution contact. Detoxified in 10min at 80°C/176°F, or 1h at 50°C/122°F, at pH 7.8. Michaelis constant (KM)=0.1μmol/L for ribosomes; enzymatic constant (Kcat)=1500/min.
potential_exposure: Potentially fatal. Mutagen, teratogen. Protein lectin found in castor beans (Ricinus communis), one of the most potent/lethal substances known — ~500μg can kill an adult within days. Castor plant/beans are important commercial industrial crops (castor oil production); waste mash from castor-oil processing is 3-5% ricin by weight. Castor plant is an attractive ornamental found in yards/gardens; found in 25+ US states and other regions (dies in freezing weather). Ricin poisoning can occur via accidental castor-bean ingestion (including bead-necklace use in some countries). Ricin enters cells and inhibits protein synthesis, causing systemic shutdown within hours once this mechanism is halted. Not contagious, doesn't spread person-to-person. Because it's a chemical made by living things rather than a living organism itself, considered less effective as a mass military weapon than pathogens like anthrax/ebola, but poses an accessible terrorist-weapon risk given ease of production/use. Extremely hazardous when freeze-dried (easily dispersed powder) — lab personnel typically directed to avoid freeze-drying it. No known antidote/vaccine/effective therapy exists; antibody-therapy research is ongoing.
incompatibilities: Stable at ambient temperature. Destroyed by 0.1% sodium hypochlorite (household bleach) solution exposure for 10min. Toxic portion is heat-stable at ambient temps, begins decomposing at 60°C/140°F; most toxicity lost at 80°C/176°F in ~30min. Emits toxic NOx gases when heated to decomposition. Avoid strong oxidizers.
other_national_oels: ChemWatch: 0.00006 mg/m3 Ceiling limit (sensitizer, per CDC).
determination_in_air: No NIOSH or OSHA methods available.
human_health_water: Unknown.
determination_in_water: Multiple EPA/DHS-evaluated water detection technologies (2004-2006 study) with varying sensitivity: test-strip and immunoassay methods (BADD Test Strips, BioVerify Test Kits, RAMP Test, BioThreat Alert Test Strips, ELISA, QTL Biosensor), with lowest detectable concentrations ranging from 0.0005 to 20 mg/L depending on method; Bio-Threat Alert test strips reported as most accurate.
ld50: Oral-ingestion 1-20mg/kg (≈8 castor beans). Human-injection 1-1.75μg/kg. Human-inhalation 21-42μg/kg. Oral-mice ~3μg/kg (injection or aerosol). Human (general) ~1mg/kg; a single seed can be fatal. ~500μg may be enough to kill an adult (about what fits on a pinhead).
routes_of_entry: Can be absorbed by all exposure routes. Normally enters via ingestion; aerosolized ricin enters via inhalation. Attaches to cell surfaces of various tissues, particularly stomach lining (ingestion) or upper respiratory tissues (inhalation).
target_organs: Lungs, eyes, skin (primarily via cuts/bruises); liver, CNS, kidneys, adrenal glands (late-phase cytotoxic effects).
short_term_effects: Symptoms depend on ricin purity, exposure level/route, and dose. Initial symptoms usually appear 6-10h to 3 days post-exposure (as early as 45min if ingested on an empty stomach). Death can occur 36-72h post-exposure depending on route/dose; victims may linger 10-12 days before death or recovery. Surviving >5 days without complications reduces death likelihood. Inhalation: within hours, respiratory distress, labored breathing, SOB, chest tightness, hypoxemia, fever, cough, nausea, sweating, aching muscles; heavy sweating may precede noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (occurring later, 1-3 days post-exposure, unlike phosgene's ~6h), worsening breathing and causing blue skin; may progress to low blood pressure, blue skin, multisystem organ failure, respiratory failure, death. Skin: uncertain absorption through intact skin (believed low-risk); may be absorbed through damaged/irritated skin or via solvent carrier; sufficient absorption produces ingestion-like symptoms; injection causes local muscle/lymph-node death, potentially leading to liver/kidney failure and death. Eyes: tearing, eyelid swelling, pain, redness, corneal injury. Ingestion: within hours — nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain/cramping, diarrhea (possibly bloody), lowered blood pressure, hallucinations, bloody urine, GI bleeding, low/no urinary output, pupil dilation, fever, thirst, sore throat, headache, vascular collapse, shock; severe vomiting/diarrhea may cause severe dehydration and multisystem organ failure; organs (liver, spleen, kidneys) may fail within days. Late-phase: cytotoxic liver/CNS/kidney/adrenal effects typically 2-5 days post-exposure; patient may be asymptomatic during the preceding 1-5 days (CDC).
long_term_effects: Repeated exposure may cause allergic/asthma-like symptoms — nasal/throat congestion, itchy watery eyes, hives, chest tightness, wheezing in acute cases. May affect kidneys, liver, pancreas. Animal studies suggest possible severe human lung damage.
points_of_attack: Lungs, eyes, skin (primarily via cuts/bruises). Unbroken-skin toxicity risk is low but allergic skin reaction risk remains.
medical_surveillance: Symptoms resemble other illnesses, especially flu, complicating diagnosis. Lab testing may show metabolic acidosis, elevated liver/renal function tests, hematuria, leukocytosis (2-5× normal).
first_aid: No antidote exists. Send all exposed persons to nearest hospital emergency department. Have potentially exposed persons shower and change clothes immediately. See a doctor same-day given rapid symptom onset (as little as 1.5 days). Remove ricin from the body as quickly as possible; treatment requires hospital setting; alert medical staff to exposure potential for their own protection and appropriate treatment. If awaiting medical assistance, keep victim comfortable. If ingested: secure airway; gastric lavage may be considered only if performed shortly after ingestion (generally within 1h), weighing GI-tract injury-aggravation risk. Treatment is primarily supportive, tailored to exposure route (inhalation/ingestion/eye/skin). Do NOT induce vomiting. Rinse mouth; flush stomach with activated charcoal if very recently ingested (note: superactivated charcoal may have little value for large molecules like ricin, per USAMRICD); wash eyes with water if red/irritated. Supportive care: IV fluids, circulatory/respiratory support, medications for seizure/low blood pressure; fluid input critical (losses up to 2-2.5L probable). If drowsy/unconscious, give nothing by mouth; if vomiting, lean patient forward or place on left side (head-down if possible) to maintain airway and prevent aspiration. Monitor/restore fluid and electrolyte balance; early aggressive IV fluid/electrolyte replacement. Administer oxygen if breathing is difficult/labored due to pulmonary fluid.
personal_protective_methods: Level A (fully encapsulated suit with SCBA) when entering areas with unknown contaminant/concentration, until monitoring confirms. Recommended materials: Tychem BR or Responder CSM. Decontamination: responders wear Level A when decontaminating a known attack area; otherwise stay away. Move quickly — decontamination delay matters. Only decontaminate aerosolized-ricin scenes with proper equipment/training; do not enter hot zone without them. Even if uncertain of contamination, shower thoroughly and change clothes ASAP post-incident; bag clothing in labeled durable 6-mil polyethylene bags. Decontaminate non-ambulatory victims without touching/entering hot zone if possible; ensure victims are decontaminated before leaving the area to prevent spread; avoid breaking skin, cover open wounds during decon. CDC-recommended decon solution: detergent-water (pH 8-10.5); soft brushes for PPE contamination removal. Household bleach also recommended for people/surface cleanup: fresh daily 0.5% sodium hypochlorite solution (10% household bleach diluted 1:9 with water), 15min contact time; avoid eyes/open wounds (especially abdomen/spine/brain)/mouth; wash off after 15min. Absent pH-adjusted solutions, wash with warm soapy water, using a hose/spray/fog system to avoid touching the victim; begin washing immediately without waiting for soap or clothing removal (down to undergarments). Wash-strip-wash-evacuate protocol: wash first, victim self-removes clothing, wash again (with soap if available), then move upwind/uphill away from hot zone.
respirator_selection: Pressure-demand SCBA (CBRN-rated if available) recommended for nonroutine emergency response situations.
storage: Blue: poison, secure locked location. Cool, dry, well-ventilated area, away from foodstuff containers.
shipping: Toxin, extracted from living sources, n.o.s.: 'POISON (TOXIC)' label; Class 6.1(a), Packing Group III (per NIOSH), though Packing Group I treatment may be advisable.
packing_group: III (NIOSH; Packing Group I treatment may be advisable)
spill_handling: Avoid generating dust. Potential aerosol attack — do not breathe or contact suspected ricin particles; victim clothing/body may carry contamination — avoid contact. Stay out of suspected-contamination areas until equipped with Level A PPE (protective clothing + respiratory protection). Shut off HVAC systems to prevent aerosolized-droplet building-wide spread. Keep public away; call for medical assistance immediately. Do not allow contaminated persons to leave the hot zone — ricin persists in clothing/bedding for extended periods, requiring quarantine and decontamination of people and materials; don't release anyone until medically examined. Do not breathe, touch, or eat anything potentially contaminated. Notify federal authorities and local health/pollution/environmental agencies. See Decontamination.
fire_extinguishing: Foam, dry chemical powder, BCF (bromochlorodifluoromethane/Halon 1211, where permitted), CO2, water spray/fog (large fires only). Emits toxic NOx gases when heated to decomposition.
disposal_method: Do not clean up or dispose of ricin except under specialist supervision.

determination_in_air: M8/M9 detector paper, detector ticket, blue band tube, M256/M256A1 kits, bubbler, DAAMS, ACAMS, RTM, DCAC, M8/M43, M8A1/M43A2, HYPED, CAM-M1, MINICAM, RTAP. Real-time low-level alarmed monitors required for GB operations; absent these, IDLH atmosphere must be presumed.
human_health_water: Dangerous to aquatic life in high concentrations; may be dangerous if it enters water intakes. Breaks down quickly in water and moist soil; small amounts may evaporate or migrate below soil surface into groundwater. Bioconcentration in aquatic organisms not expected to be an important fate process.
determination_in_water: M-272 Chemical Agent Water Testing Kit, detection limit 0.02mg/L for nerve agents. Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow=-1.4 (estimated).
ld50: Human lethal dose ~0.01mg/kg. LCt50=100 mg-min/m3. LD50 (skin) 1.7g/70kg man; (mice) 200μg/kg.
routes_of_entry: Inhalation, ingestion, skin/eye contact. Absorbed through skin.
target_organs: Respiratory system, CNS, skin, eyes, plasma/RBC cholinesterase. Liver and kidney damage.
short_term_effects: Extremely toxic; extremely active cholinesterase inhibitor. Toxic effects similar to parathion but more severe/dangerous. Single skin drop can cause death; death may occur within 15min of fatal-dose absorption. Symptoms occur within minutes to hours depending on dose: miosis (pupil constriction) and visual effects, headache, pressure sensation, runny nose, nasal congestion, salivation, chest tightness, nausea, vomiting, giddiness, anxiety, difficulty thinking, sleep difficulty, nightmares, muscle twitches, tremors, weakness, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, involuntary urination/defecation.
long_term_effects: Cholinesterase inhibitor — cumulative effect possible. May damage nervous system w/ repeated exposure (convulsions, respiratory failure). Limited data suggest chronic/repeated exposure may cause delayed postural sway and/or impaired psychomotor performance (neuropathy).
points_of_attack: Respiratory system, CNS, skin, eyes, plasma/RBC cholinesterase. Liver and kidney damage.
medical_surveillance: Severely exposed patients should be evaluated for persistent CNS effects. Consider points of attack in preplacement/periodic exams. CBC. Thyroid function evaluation. Lung function tests. CNS tests. Liver/kidney function tests.
first_aid: Antidote administration is critical but may be difficult in the immediate hazard zone if antidotes/procedures aren't available there. Do NOT administer antidotes preventatively. Diazepam (or other benzodiazepines) given for evidence of seizures (moderate-severe exposure). Inhalation: hold breath until protective mask donned; for severe signs (chest tightness, pupil constriction, coordination loss), administer all three Nerve Agent Antidote Kit Mark I injectors in rapid succession (or atropine per physician direction); may repeat at 5-20min intervals up to three injection series, no further without medical direction, with injection record maintained; artificial respiration if breathing stopped (mouth-to-mouth only if approved delivery systems unavailable and no facial contamination); administer oxygen if breathing difficult; seek medical attention immediately. Eyes: flush immediately with water 10-15min, then don protective mask; miosis alone (without other signs) doesn't warrant injection — take individual to medical facility for observation instead. Skin: don protective mask, remove contaminated clothing, immediately wash with copious soap/water, 10% sodium carbonate solution, or 5% liquid household bleach, rinse well; administer Mark I Kit intramuscular injection only if local sweating/muscular twitching observed; seek medical attention immediately. Ingestion: do NOT induce vomiting (first symptoms likely GI); immediately administer Mark I kit autoinjector intramuscular injection. Medical treatment: monitor ECG and respiration/ventilation adequacy; supplemental oxygenation, frequent secretion suctioning, endotracheal intubation, assisted ventilation may be required; diazepam (5-10mg adults, 0.2-0.5mg/kg children) for convulsion control (lorazepam/other benzodiazepines usable; barbiturates/phenytoin/other anticonvulsants ineffective); atropine administration (if not already given) should precede benzodiazepines for optimal seizure control; inhalation-exposed patients with chest pain/tightness/cough should be observed/examined periodically for 6-12h to detect delayed bronchitis, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or respiratory failure (NIOSH).
personal_protective_methods: Level A PPE: rubber gloves, protective clothing, goggles, respirators, butyl rubber gloves (M3/M4, Norton chemical protective glove set), Tyvek 'F' decontamination suit for barrier protection against chemical warfare agents. Airtight impermeable clothing (butyl rubber or coated fabric) for personnel entering heavily contaminated areas; may be penetrated after hours of heavy-concentration exposure — liquid contamination must be neutralized/removed ASAP. Published swatch-test breakthrough times (various commercial Level A suits/gloves) generally exceed 225-480min for GB. Call US Soldier and Biological Chemical Command/Edgewood Research Development and Engineering Center if proper equipment/training unavailable. Contact lenses not permitted; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respiratory protection worn; wash immediately if skin wet/contaminated; emergency showers/eyewash provided.
respirator_selection: When used as a weapon: NIOSH CBRN-certified SCBA. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFOvHie/SCBAE. US Army M40-series mask (replaced M17A1) provides complete respiratory protection against known military chemical agents but not in oxygen-deficient environments, nor against industrial toxics (ammonia, CO); not approved for civilian use. Per Riegle Report tiers: <0.0001mg/m3 — full face-piece chemical-canister air-purifying mask for escape (M9/M40-series acceptable); 0.0001-0.2mg/m3 — NIOSH/MSHA/EN149-approved pressure-demand full face-piece SCBA or supplied-air respirator with escape cylinder, or equivalent full face-piece chemical-canister mask (M9/M17/M40-series); >0.2mg/m3 or unknown — NIOSH/MSHA/EN149-approved pressure-demand full face-piece SCBA suitable for high agent concentrations with protective ensemble.
storage: Buddy system required. No smoking/eating/drinking in agent-containing areas. Periodic container leak inspection (visual or detector kit). Stringent personnel-practice controls. Decontamination equipment conveniently located; rapid-evacuation exits; chemical showers/eyewash/personal cleanliness facilities provided. Thorough post-shift showering with attention to hair/face/neck/hands.
shipping: Toxic, liquids, organic, n.o.s. (inhalation hazard, Packing Group I, Zone A): 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label, inhalation hazard; Class 6.1, Packing Group III (per NIOSH source).
spill_handling: Cover spills with vermiculite/diatomaceous earth/clay/fine sand/sponges/paper-cloth towels. Decontaminate with copious ≥10wt% aqueous NaOH solution. Scoop into fully removable-head drum with HDPE liner; cover contents with decon solution before sealing; decontaminate/label drum exterior per IAW/EPA/DOT regs. Overpack leaking containers with vermiculite between interior/exterior containers. Alternative decontaminants (order of preference) if 10% NaOH unavailable: DS2 (2% NaOH, 70% diethylenetriamine, 28% ethylene glycol monomethyl ether), sodium carbonate, Supertropical Bleach Slurry (STB). Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate. Water alone removes the fluorine atom, producing a nontoxic acid; decontaminants include bleach slurry, dilute alkali, hot soapy water, steam, ammonia. Absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid confined spaces (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Isolation (weapon-use scenario, first 30min, may increase w/ time) — small: 200ft/60m, downwind 0.3-0.8mi day/1.3mi night; large: 2500ft/800m, downwind 1.4-2.8mi day/2.3-4.5mi night; tank/rail/truck fire: isolate/evacuate 800m (1/2 mile) all directions.
fire_extinguishing: Highly volatile poison (organophosphate); vapor/skin/eye contact or swallowing can kill, symptoms may be delayed hours. If exposure occurs, remove/isolate gear immediately, thoroughly decontaminate personnel. Storage containers may explode/rocket. Vapors heavier than air, collect in low areas. Combustion products (CO, fluorine, phosphorus oxide) less deadly than the material itself. Reacts with steam/water producing toxic corrosive vapors. Evacuate all non-firefighting personnel; contain fires to prevent uncontrolled-area contamination. Positive-pressure full face-piece NIOSH-approved SCBA required where oxygen deficiency risk exists or per fire chief/CAI officer direction; appropriate protective-clothing levels for rescue/reconnaissance responders. Complete protection required; have decontaminants (bleach, alkali) and atropine available. Dry chemical/CO2/foam extinguishers. Cool exposed containers from secure location with water spray; withdraw if venting sound rises or tank discolors.
disposal_method: Open-pit burning or burying of GB or GB-contaminated items in any quantity is prohibited. Detoxified GB (per decontamination procedures) can be thermally destroyed by incineration in an EPA-approved incinerator per RCRA regulations. Decontamination chemistry: minimum 56g decon solution per gram GB; agitate ≥1h; final pH must exceed 11.5 (add NaOH as needed to sustain pH>11.5 for 60min) using 10% NaOH, or alternatively 10wt% sodium carbonate (agitate 1h, react 3h total, final pH>10), or 5.25% sodium hypochlorite, or 25wt% monoethylamine (MEA, fully dissolved in water before agent addition) at the same 56g:1g ratio with 1h agitation. Scoop material into fully removable-head HDPE-lined drum; cover with decon solution before sealing; decontaminate/label drum exterior per IAW/EPA/DOT regs; overpack leaking containers with vermiculite; dispose of exterior-decontamination material per IAW/federal/state/local regs; conduct general-area monitoring to confirm atmospheric concentrations remain below exposure limits.
extraction_notes: References: EPA CHIP: Sarin (Nov 1987); The Riegle Report, US Senate 103rd Congress (May 1994); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet: Sarin (Apr 2004); Schneider et al., CHRIS 1 CD-ROM v2.0, USCG Chemical Hazard Response Information System (2007); Belmont, TR Tests of Level A Suits Executive Summary, US Army CBRD-EN (Jun 1998). This entry describes the chemical warfare nerve agent Sarin/GB; content reproduced is limited to standard published civilian/military emergency-responder safety, detection, decontamination, PPE, and medical-treatment data — no synthesis or weaponization information is included.
