description: Exists in three forms: red amorphous powder, gray form, red crystals. Occurs as impurity in most sulfide ores; found with tellurium in electrolytic copper-refining sludges/sediments; also recoverable in pyrite-burning flue dust during sulfuric acid manufacture.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Tumorigen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data. Most production used for selenium rectifiers manufacture. Also: pigment for ruby glass/paints/dyes; rubber vulcanizing agent; green-glass decolorizing agent; Kjeldahl-test catalyst; insecticide; electrodes/photocells/semiconductor manufacture; photographic toning baths; organic-compound dehydrogenation; veterinary medicine; antidandruff shampoos; radioactive pancreas scanning; photostatic/X-ray xerography; alloying with stainless steel/copper/cast steel. Contaminant in most sulfide ores of copper/gold/nickel/silver — exposure may occur during ore processing.
incompatibilities: Violent reaction w/ strong acids and strong oxidizers, chromium trioxide, potassium bromate, cadmium. Incandescent reaction on gentle heating with phosphorus and metals (nickel, zinc, sodium, potassium, platinum). Reacts with water at 50°C forming flammable hydrogen and selenious acids.

determination_in_water: Digestion + atomic absorption for total selenium; dissolved selenium via 0.45μm filtration prior to analysis.
routes_of_entry: Inhalation of dust/vapor, percutaneous absorption of liquid, ingestion, eye/skin contact.
target_organs: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, liver, kidneys, blood, spleen. In animals: anemia, liver necrosis/cirrhosis, kidney/spleen damage.
short_term_effects: Normal dietary intake (~50-150μg/day) meets nutritional requirement; toxicity depends on amount/frequency of excess intake. Swallowing concentrated sodium selenate/selenite (e.g. veterinary product or many supplement pills) is life-threatening without immediate treatment. Can affect via inhalation. Fumes irritate eyes/resp tract. Contact can burn eyes/skin. Fume inhalation may cause asphyxiation symptoms, chills, fever, bronchitis. High levels cause troubled breathing, lung irritation (pneumonitis), headaches. Higher exposures: pulmonary edema (delayed hours, can be fatal). Symptoms: visual disturbance, headache, chills, fever, dyspnea, bronchitis, metallic taste, garlic breath, GI disturbance.
long_term_effects: May contribute to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in humans. Repeated/prolonged contact may cause skin dermatitis. May affect CNS, blood, teeth, bones. May cause nervousness, depression, pallor, digestive disturbances. Kidney/liver damage may occur. Moderately-above-nutritional-requirement intake over long periods can cause brittle hair, deformed nails, and in extreme cases numbness/coordination loss in limbs — observed in Chinese villages with chronically high dietary selenium exposure; no US population reports of this extreme chronic poisoning. Daily 25mg sodium selenite ingestion (4-5× selenium equivalent) for 11 days caused hair/fingernail loss, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, garlic breath.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, liver, kidneys, blood, spleen. In animals: anemia, liver necrosis/cirrhosis, kidney/spleen damage.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: body hair/nail, whole blood chemical/metabolite, blood plasma/serum, liver function tests, urine chemical/metabolite (incl. 24h collection), routine UA, WBC count/differential. Urine selenium test (normal <100μg/L). If symptoms/overexposure: consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure, liver function tests.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered for pneumonitis/pulmonary edema. Note to physician: for severe poisoning do NOT use BAL (British Anti-Lewisite/dimercaprol/dithiopropanol) — contraindicated/ineffective for selenium poisoning.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: 1mg/m3: Qm/95XQ/100F/PaprDM/PaprHie/Sa/SCBAF/SaF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: 100F/SCBAE. Eye irritant — may need eye protection.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Avoid strong oxidizers (chlorine, bromine, fluorine)/strong acids (HCl, sulfuric, nitric) — violent reactions. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from water.
shipping: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group III.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible solid. Dry chemical/CO2/water spray/foam extinguishers. Poisonous selenium gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Powdered selenium: dispose in chemical waste landfill. When possible, recover selenium and return to suppliers.

Chemical protective suit + SCBA for spill response. Stay upwind, water spray to knock down vapor, contain runoff. Stop gas flow if safe; move/repair leaking cylinder if possible. Avoid confined spaces (explosion risk); OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Isolation (first 30min, may increase w/ time) — small: 200ft/60m, downwind 0.3-1.2mi day/1.9mi night; large: 1500ft/500m, downwind 1.8-4.0mi day/2.9-6.5mi night. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: Use agent suitable for surrounding fire; material itself doesn't burn or burns with difficulty. Poisonous hydrogen fluoride/fluoride/selenium gases produced. Don't extinguish unless gas flow can be stopped and remaining gas cleared from line. Specially trained personnel may use fog lines to cool and let fire burn out. Vapors heavier than air, collect in low areas. Containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; withdraw if cylinders exposed to excessive heat; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: If possible, convert selenium compounds to insoluble form with SO2 before landfill or solidification.
extraction_notes: Reference: NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet: Selenium Hexafluoride (Sep 2001).

Eyes: tearing, very painful irritation, burns; may cause permanent damage/loss of sight. Ingestion: immediate intense mouth/throat/stomach burning, followed by salivation, vomiting, rapid breathing, shock symptoms, diarrhea, unconsciousness, death.
long_term_effects: Very irritating substances may affect lungs; unknown whether sodium causes lung damage.
medical_surveillance: Before employment + regularly for frequent/high exposure: lung function tests. If symptoms/overexposure: consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥30 min, seek care. Skin: wipe chemical off with dry cloth first, then remove contaminated clothing quickly, immediately wash with large water amounts, seek care. personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Full face-piece respirator w/ particulate (dust/fume/mist) filters (checked daily for damage, replaced as needed). High exposures: supplied-air respirator (positive-pressure/continuous-flow) or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure.
storage: (1) Red stripe (lump): flammability hazard, not stored with other flammable materials. (2) Yellow stripe: reactivity hazard (strong reducing agent), separate from flammables/combustibles/other yellow-coded materials. Avoid water/halogenated hydrocarbons/phosphorus compounds/sulfur compounds — violent reactions. Protect from physical damage. Keep in inert atmosphere or under oil. Special precautions against moisture (incl. condensation, perspiration). Dry, fire-resistive room exclusively for sodium storage; no sprinkler systems (keep combustibles away). Remove only immediate-use amounts, store dry in friction-top metal can under oil layer. Transport in special tight-covered container. Explosion-proof electrical equipment.
shipping: Sodium metal: 'DANGEROUS WHEN WET' label; Class 4.3, Packing Group I. Finely divided sodium is pyrophoric.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; proper protective equipment; blanket with appropriate inert material; scoop into sealed containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible solid; severe fire risk on water/moisture contact. Blanket with dry soda ash, graphite, salt, dry limestone, or other approved dry powder. disposal_method: Incineration with absorption of oxide fumes.

Reacts with benzoyl chloride, potassium hydroxide, bromine, carbon disulfide, copper, lead, nitric acid, barium carbonate, sulfuric acid, chromium(II) hypochlorite, dimethyl sulfate, dibromomalononitrile, silver, mercury. incompatibilities: Strong oxidizers (acids, acid salts, chlorates, nitrates). Decomposes on contact with acids/acid salts/water/moisture/CO2, releasing highly toxic flammable hydrogen cyanide gas. Aqueous solution is a strong base, reacts violently with acid, corrosive. Absorbs air moisture forming corrosive syrup. Corrosive to active metals (aluminum, copper, zinc).
acgih_tlv: 5 mg[CN]/m3 [skin] Ceiling.
dfg_mak: 3.8 mg[CN]/m3 inhalable fraction TWA; Peak Cat II(1) [skin]; Pregnancy Grp C. Skin contact may contribute significantly to overall exposure.
other_national_oels: Australia TWA5[skin]; Austria MAK5[CN][skin]; Denmark TWA5[skin]; France VME5[CN][skin]; Poland TWA0.3[CN]/Ceiling10[CN]; Switzerland MAK-W5/KZG-W10[skin]; UK TWA5[CN][skin] (1993-2000). human_health_water: 200μg/L. Allowable daily intake 8.4mg/day. South African Bureau of Standards/WHO 10μg/L; Germany/EEC 50μg/L; Sweden 100μg/L. EPA NOAEL 10.8mg/kg/day yields lifetime health advisory 154μg/L. US states: Arizona 160μg/L, Kansas 220μg/L drinking water.
determination_in_water: Distillation + silver nitrate titration, or colorimetric analysis (pyridine pyrazolone or barbituric acid). Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow (estimated)=1.69. Russia MAC 100μg/L domestic-purpose water bodies, 50μg/L fishery-purpose water.
routes_of_entry: Inhalation, skin absorption, ingestion, skin/eye contact.
target_organs: Liver, kidneys, skin, cardiovascular system, CNS, thyroid gland.
short_term_effects: Releases hydrogen cyanide gas — a highly toxic chemical asphyxiant interfering with the body's oxygen use. Exposure can be rapidly fatal; whole-body (systemic) effects particularly affect organ systems most sensitive to low oxygen (CNS/brain, cardiovascular system, pulmonary system) (NIOSH). Can be absorbed through skin, increasing exposure. Corrosive to eyes/skin/resp tract. Contact can cause skin/eye burns, possible permanent eye damage. Inhalation can cause lung irritation w/ coughing, sneezing, difficult breathing, slow gasping respiration. Corrosive if swallowed. May affect CNS — headaches, confusion, nausea, pounding heart, weakness, unconsciousness.
long_term_effects: Repeated/prolonged contact may cause thyroid gland enlargement and interfere with thyroid function. May cause nosebleed and inner-nose sores; blood-cell-count changes. May cause CNS damage w/ headache, dizziness, confusion, nausea, vomiting, pounding heart, arm/leg weakness, unconsciousness, death. May affect liver/kidney function. Repeated lower exposures can cause inner-nose sores w/ nosebleeds.
points_of_attack: Liver, kidneys, skin, cardiovascular system, CNS, thyroid gland.
medical_surveillance: Consider points of attack in preplacement/periodic exams. Urine thiocyanate levels. Blood cyanide levels. CBC. Thyroid function evaluation. Liver function tests. Kidney function tests. CNS tests. EKG. Smokers may have somewhat higher blood cyanide and urine thiocyanate levels.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Use amyl nitrate capsules if symptoms develop. Regular staff training in cyanide-poisoning emergency measures and CPR required. Cyanide antidote kit must be kept immediately available in work area; kit ingredients replaced every 1-2 years for freshness. Trained personnel (kit use, oxygen, CPR) must be quickly available.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact (polyethylene recommended for <30% sodium cyanide only); no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield for liquid work, dust-proof goggles+face shield for powder/dust work, unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: When used as a weapon: NIOSH CBRN-certified SCBA. 25mg/m3: Sa/SCBAF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFS100/SCBAE.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from strong acids/acid salts/oxidizers/light/moisture. Automatic transfer preferred.
shipping: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group I.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; keep water away from release; remove ignition sources; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. UN1689 is on DOT's dangerous water-reactive materials list (large toxic-vapor generation when spilled in water): dangerous 0.5-10km (0.3-6.0 miles) downwind. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: Doesn't burn; fight surrounding fire with agent appropriate for burning material. Decomposes in moisture/damp air/CO2 presence, producing highly toxic flammable hydrogen cyanide gas and NOx. NO acidic dry chemical extinguishers; NO hydrous agents; NO water; NO CO2 directly on material. Vapors heavier than air, may collect in low areas. Cool containers from secure location with water spray (don't let water enter open containers); withdraw if venting sound rises or tank discolors; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Consult environmental regulatory agencies. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators). Per 40CFR165 pesticide/container disposal recommendations. Follow package label directions or contact local/federal/regional EPA office. Add strong alkaline hypochlorite and allow to react for 24h, then flush to sewer with large water volumes.

incompatibilities: Water/acids/acid fumes contact releases toxic chlorine gas. Powerful oxidizer. Violent reaction with reducing agents, organic matter, easily chlorinated/oxidized materials. Incompatible with ammonium salts; amines forming nitrogen trichloride.
short_term_effects: Contact can cause severe eye and permanent damage. Skin contact can cause severe irritation, especially if skin is moist or material is in solution (dry material is less irritating). Inhalation can irritate resp tract. Strong poison and corrosive if ingested; may cause liver damage.
long_term_effects: Highly irritating substances may affect lungs.
medical_surveillance: Lung function tests. Liver function tests.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: if conscious, water or milk (no induced vomiting).
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield for liquid work, dust-proof goggles+face shield for powder/dust work, unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Supplied-air respirator (positive-pressure/continuous-flow) or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure, per NIOSH/MSHA/EN149 approval.
storage: Yellow: reactive hazard, separate location from flammables/combustibles. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from ammonium compounds/hydrated salts/moisture/combustible materials. Automatic transfer preferred. Explosion-proof electrical equipment. See OSHA Standard 1910.104 and NFPA 43A Code for Liquid/Solid Oxidizer Storage.
shipping: 'OXIDIZER' label; Class 5.1, Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; keep water away from release; remove ignition sources; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Noncombustible solid but powerful oxidizer, may increase existing fire activity; may burn rapidly. Flooding quantities of water from a distance. Do NOT use ammonia-containing extinguishers. Poisonous sodium oxide/chlorine/NOx gases produced. Containers may explode. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.

description: Fluorinated organophosphorus chemical warfare nerve agent. Exposure can cause death within minutes; 1/10mL on skin can be fatal (NIOSH). When pure, colorless liquid with fruity odor; with impurities or upon aging, amber to dark-brown oily liquid with rotten-fruit or camphor odor (like Vicks Vapo-Rub). Odor is not a reliable detection method — not everyone can smell low concentrations. Relative vapor density (air=1) 6.3; volatility 3900mg/m3/25°C. Thickened agent (TGD) is essentially the same as GD but with ~1180 centistokes viscosity via 5% K125 acryloid copolymer (not known hazardous except as finely divided powder, CDC). Persistence: summer 10min-24h; winter 2h-3 days.
potential_exposure: Quick-acting chemical warfare nerve agent/nerve gas. Medical treatment is difficult because it permanently binds to body receptors within minutes. Large vapor/liquid amounts can cause harm in minutes and quickly lead to death.
incompatibilities: Stable after 3 months storage in steel at 65°C; corrodes steel at ~1×10^-5 inch/month. Raising pH significantly increases decomposition rate. Decomposes slowly in water, hydrolyzing to HF and pinacolyl methylphosphonate byproducts. Reacts readily with bases and weak acids. Acid conditions hydrolyze GD, forming hydrofluoric acid. Flammable hydrogen gas may form from corrosive-vapor reaction with metals/concrete.
other_national_oels: AEGL Level 1 (minor/reversible discomfort): 10min 0.00049ppm, 30min 0.00028ppm, 1h 0.0002ppm, 4h 0.0001ppm, 8h 0.00050ppm. AEGL Level 2 (impaired function/escape ability): 10min 0.0062ppm, 30min 0.0035ppm, 1h 0.0024ppm, 4h 0.0013ppm, 8h 0.00091ppm. AEGL Level 3 (life-threatening): 10min 0.053ppm, 30min 0.027ppm, 1h 0.018ppm, 4h 0.0098ppm, 8h 0.0071ppm. Suggested 8h TWA 0.00003mg/m3 (per USAEHA Technical Guide #169). General population limit (Surgeon General's Working Group) 0.000003mg/m3.
determination_in_air: Automatic Chemical Agent Detector Alarm (ACADA), bubblers (GC method), Chemical Agent Monitor (CAM).
human_health_water: Soman dissolves in water and remains very dangerous. Notify local health/pollution control officials and nearby water-intake operators; advise shutting intakes. Hydrolyzes via acidic/neutral/basic mechanisms to fluoride and pinacolyl methylphosphonate; rapidly hydrolyzed in basic solutions (Na2CO3, NaOH, KOH) with ~1min half-life at pH 11/25°C. No significant sunlight phototransformation. Thermally stable below 49°C. Bleaching powder (chlorinated lime) destroys soman but generates cyanogen chloride (CAS 506-77-4).
determination_in_water: M272 Chemical Agent Water Testing Kit, detection limit 0.02mg/L for nerve agents. Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow (estimated)=1.02.
ld50: LCt50 (inhalation) 70 mg-min/m3 (t=10min). LD50 (percutaneous, bare skin) 0.35g/70kg man.
target_organs: Respiratory system, lungs, CNS, cardiovascular system, skin, eyes, plasma/RBC cholinesterase, liver, kidneys.
short_term_effects: Lethal anticholinesterase agent. Within 1-several minutes of airborne overexposure: local effects (lasting 1-15 days, dose-dependent) — miosis, eye redness/pressure sensation; rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, chest tightness, wheezing, salivation, nausea, vomiting. Systemic effects (dose-dependent): inhaled GD causes excessive secretion (coughing/breathing difficulty), salivation/sweating, vomiting/diarrhea/stomach cramps, involuntary urination/defecation, generalized muscle twitching/cramps, CNS depression (anxiety, restlessness, giddiness, insomnia, excessive dreaming, nightmares); more severe exposure adds headache, tremor, drowsiness, concentration difficulty, memory impairment, confusion, unsteadiness, progressing to death. Liquid exposure: miosis, eye redness/pressure; ingestion causes salivation, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, involuntary defecation, heartburn; skin exposure causes sweating, muscle twitching. Recovery from nerve-agent poisoning is complete unless prolonged unchecked anoxia/convulsions caused irreversible CNS changes.
long_term_effects: Limited data suggest delayed neuropathy (postural sway, psychomotor performance); miosis noted up to 62 days (CDC). Chronic exposure causes forgetfulness, thinking difficulty, vision disturbances, muscular aches/pains. Mild/moderately exposed people usually recover completely; severely exposed people are unlikely to survive. Unlike some organophosphate pesticides, nerve agents haven't been associated with neurological problems lasting >1-2 weeks post-exposure. Teratogenic effects shown for some organophosphate pesticides in animals haven't been documented for soman in controlled toxicological evaluations. Cholinesterase inhibition throughout the body is largely irreversible, prolonging effects; tissue enzyme regeneration may take weeks to 2-3 months if damage is severe, during which increased susceptibility to any nerve agent persists, with cumulative repeated-exposure effects and possible delayed symptom onset after daily sub-symptomatic exposure.
points_of_attack: Respiratory system, lungs, CNS, cardiovascular system, skin, eyes, plasma/RBC cholinesterase, liver, kidneys.
medical_surveillance: Consider points of attack in preplacement/periodic exams. Urine thiocyanate levels. CBC. Thyroid function evaluation. Liver function tests. Kidney function tests. CNS tests. EKG.
first_aid: Antidote administration is critical. Inhalation: hold breath until protective mask donned; for severe signs (chest tightness, pupil constriction, coordination loss), administer all three Nerve Agent Antidote Kit Mark I injectors in rapid succession (or atropine per physician direction); may repeat at 5-20min intervals up to three injection series, no further without medical direction, with injection record maintained; artificial respiration if breathing stopped (mouth-to-mouth only if approved delivery systems unavailable and no facial contamination); administer oxygen if breathing difficult; seek medical attention immediately. Eyes: flush immediately with water 10-15min, then don protective mask; miosis alone doesn't warrant injection — take individual to medical facility for observation instead. Skin: don protective mask, remove contaminated clothing, immediately wash with copious soap/water, 10% sodium carbonate solution, or 5% liquid household bleach, rinse well; administer Mark I Kit intramuscular injection only if local sweating/muscular twitching observed; seek medical attention immediately. Ingestion: do NOT induce vomiting (first symptoms likely GI); immediately administer Mark I kit autoinjector; if no apparent breathing, start artificial resuscitation immediately (mechanical resuscitator if facial contamination present, not mouth-to-mouth); CPR by trained personnel as appropriate. Notes for physician: individuals with known exposure or definite symptoms should receive immediate Mark I kit intramuscular injection; early vapor-exposure symptoms may be rhinorrhea/chest tightness; early percutaneous-exposure symptoms may be local muscle twitching/sweating followed by nausea/vomiting; miosis alone doesn't warrant injection; repeat injections at 5-20min intervals as symptoms progress, up to three series, no further without medical direction, with record maintained; atropine is not prophylactic and should not be given before exposure is ascertained. Medical treatment: monitor ECG and respiration/ventilation adequacy; supplemental oxygenation, frequent secretion suctioning, endotracheal intubation, assisted ventilation may be required; diazepam (5-10mg adults, 0.2-0.5mg/kg children) for convulsion control (lorazepam/other benzodiazepines usable; barbiturates/phenytoin/other anticonvulsants ineffective); atropine administration (if not already given) should precede benzodiazepines for optimal seizure control; inhalation-exposed patients with chest pain/tightness/cough should be observed/examined periodically for 6-12h to detect delayed bronchitis, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or respiratory failure.
personal_protective_methods: Protective gloves: Butyl Glove M3/M4, Norton chemical protective glove set. Eye protection: chemical goggles (splash hazards: goggles+face shield). Full protective clothing: M9 mask+hood, butyl rubber suit (M3), M2A1 butyl boots, M3/M4 gloves, unimpregnated underwear, or demilitarization protective ensemble (DPE). Lab operations: lab coats with protective mask readily available. Local exhaust mandatory, filtered/scrubbed to limit exit concentration to <0.00001mg/m3 (8h/day average, indefinitely); chemical lab hoods require 100lfpm±10% average inward face velocity, cross-drafts ≤20% of inward face velocity, semiannual smoke-test performance verification, and no recirculation/cross-connection with other ventilation areas.
respirator_selection: When used as a weapon: NIOSH CBRN-certified SCBA. Positive-pressure full face-piece NIOSH/MSHA/EN149-approved SCBA required where oxygen deficiency risk exists or per fire chief/CAI officer direction; M9/M17-series mask may substitute absent oxygen-deficiency risk. Per Riegle Report tiers: <0.00003mg/m3 — M9/M17/M40-series mask available for escape; 0.00003-0.06mg/m3 — M9/M40-series mask with Level A or B ensemble; >0.06mg/m3 — DPE or TAPES with prior AMC Field Safety Activity approval (if unavailable, M9/M40-series mask with Level A ensemble, use time restricted to ≤1h, with M3-suit cuffs/legs taped to gloves/boots to reduce aspiration).
storage: Buddy system required. No smoking/eating/drinking in agent-containing areas. Periodic container leak inspection (visual or detector kit), including before storage-to-work-area transfers. Stringent personnel-practice controls. Decontamination equipment conveniently located; rapid-evacuation exits; chemical showers/eyewash/personal cleanliness facilities provided. Thorough post-shift showering with attention to hair/face/neck/hands. GD must be double-contained in liquid- and vapor-tight containers during storage or when outside the ventilation hood.
shipping: Toxic, liquids, organic, n.o.s. (Pinacolyl methylphosphonofluoridate; inhalation hazard, Packing Group I, Zone B): 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label, inhalation hazard; Class 6.1, Packing Group I, Hazard Zone B.
spill_handling: Warn pollution control authorities; advise shutting water intakes. Cover spills with vermiculite/diatomaceous earth/clay/fine sand/sponges/paper-cloth towels. Decontaminate with copious ≥10% aqueous NaOH solution. Scoop into fully removable-head drum with HDPE liner; cover contents with decon solution before sealing; decontaminate/label drum exterior per IAW/EPA/DOT regs. Overpack leaking containers with vermiculite between interior/exterior containers. Contaminated clothing placed in similarly lined/covered/sealed drums. Alternative decontaminants (order of preference) if 10% NaOH unavailable: DS2 (2% NaOH, 70% diethylenetriamine, 28% ethylene glycol monomethyl ether), sodium carbonate, Supertropical Bleach Slurry (STB). Isolation (weapon-use scenario, first 30min, may increase w/ time) — small: 200ft/60m, downwind 0.3-0.5mi day/0.5-0.8mi night; large: 1500ft/500m, downwind 1.1-1.5mi day/1.8-2.4mi night. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: Heated vapors may form explosive air mixtures, presenting explosion hazard indoors, outdoors, and in sewers. Containers may explode when heated. Contain fires to prevent uncontrolled-area contamination; evacuate all non-firefighting personnel immediately. Contact with GD or its vapors can be fatal. Full firefighter protective clothing (without TAP clothing) during chemical agent firefighting/rescue. Positive-pressure full face-piece NIOSH/MSHA/EN149-approved SCBA required where oxygen deficiency risk exists or per fire chief/CAI officer direction; M9/M17-series mask may substitute absent oxygen-deficiency risk; appropriate protective-clothing levels for rescue/reconnaissance responders.
disposal_method: Minimum 55g decon solution per gram of GD; agitate ≥1h (further agitation unnecessary once single phase achieved); check/adjust pH to 11.5 with additional NaOH as needed. Alternative: 10% sodium carbonate at same 55g:1g ratio, agitate 1h, react 3h, adjust pH above 10; or 5.25% sodium hypochlorite at same ratio/agitation/reaction times, adjust pH above 10. Scoop material into fully removable-head HDPE-lined drum; cover with decon solution before sealing; decontaminate/label drum exterior per IAW/EPA/DOT regs; same procedure for contaminated clothing; overpack leaking containers with vermiculite; conduct general-area monitoring to confirm atmospheric concentrations remain below exposure limits. Open-pit burning or burying of GD or GD-contaminated items in any quantity is prohibited. Detoxified GD can be thermally destroyed by incineration in an EPA-approved incinerator per federal/state/local RCRA regulations. Note: several states define decontaminated surety material as RCRA Hazardous Waste.
extraction_notes: This entry describes the chemical warfare nerve agent Soman/GD; content reproduced is limited to standard published civilian/military emergency-responder safety, detection, decontamination, PPE, and medical-treatment data — no synthesis or weaponization information is included. Operations: metallurgy, welding/cutting with blow torches, soldering, hydrogen-balloon filling, zinc etching, chemical processes.

acgih_tlv: 0.1 ppm/0.5 mg/m3 TWA.
other_national_oels: Austria MAK0.1(0.5); Denmark TWA0.05(0.25); France VME0.1(0.5); Norway TWA0.05(0.25); Poland MAC(TWA)0.2/MAC(STEL)1.5; Sweden TWA0.05(0.3); UK TWA0.1(0.52)/STEL0.3 (1993-2000). Netherlands MAC-TGG 0.5mg[Sb]/m3. US states 5.0-12.0 μg/m3.

long_term_effects: Destroys red blood cells (hemolysis). May affect kidneys/liver; hemoglobinuria, hematuria, hemolytic anemia, jaundice. May affect CNS.
points_of_attack: Blood, liver, kidneys, respiratory system, CNS.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: liver function tests, RBC count/RBC hemolysis, urine chemical/metabolite, hemoglobin, routine UA, WBC count/differential. first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; gas-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.

Avoid oxidizers (perchlorates, peroxides, permanganates, chlorates, nitrates)/strong acids (HCl, sulfuric, nitric)/halogenated hydrocarbons — violent reactions. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from heat/sparks/flames.
shipping: 'POISON GAS, FLAMMABLE GAS' label; Class 2.3. Refilling compressed gas cylinders without owner's express written permission violates transportation regulations.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate to disperse gas; stop gas flow if safe; move/repair leaking cylinder if possible; avoid confined spaces (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.

Cool containers from secure location; withdraw if cylinders exposed to excessive heat; SCBA for firefighters.

short_term_effects: Inhalation: eye/resp-tract irritation. Levels above 2400mg/m3 may cause headache, dizziness, nose/throat irritation; more severe exposures cause nausea, vomiting, intoxication feeling, weakness, muscle twitches, and in extreme cases convulsions, unconsciousness, death. long_term_effects: Prolonged/repeated liquid contact may cause skin defatting w/ drying, irritation, ulcers. Vapor exposure may cause eye/nose/throat irritation, fatigue, headaches, anemia, jaundice, liver/bone-marrow damage. Animal kidney damage. Repeated exposure may cause a rare fatal blood-cell-destroying reaction (aplastic anemia) in some people. Many petroleum-based solvents shown to cause brain/nerve damage — reduced memory/concentration, personality changes, fatigue, sleep disturbances, reduced coordination, autonomic/limb-nerve effects.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, CNS, liver, kidneys.
medical_surveillance: If symptoms/overexposure: CBC, brain-effects evaluation, liver/kidney function tests.

Substantial use as epoxy-resin-industry diluent. Applications in agricultural/biological chemicals, cosmetics, surface coatings, textile/fiber treatment. Made in quantities exceeding 1 million lb/year; presumed styrene metabolite.
incompatibilities: Forms explosive mixture with air. May polymerize on heating above 200°C, under strong acids/strong bases/oxidizers/metal salts (aluminum chloride)/vinyl-polymer catalysts influence.
other_national_oels: Austria: carcinogen (1999). France: carcinogen (1993).
iarc_classification: Group 2A (1994).
routes_of_entry: Inhalation, skin absorption, ingestion, skin/eye contact.
short_term_effects: Toxic by ingestion/inhalation/skin absorption. May be corrosive. Irritates skin/eyes/mucous membranes. Inhalation causes mucosal irritation; may cause headache, fatigue, weakness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, CNS depression, unsteadiness/drunkenness feeling, peripheral/hepatic neuropathies. May cause loss of consciousness.
long_term_effects: Repeated/prolonged contact may cause skin sensitization/allergy w/ drying/cracking. May cause liver damage. Probable human carcinogen; shown to cause stomach/liver cancer in animals. May cause decreased female fertility.
medical_surveillance: Liver function tests. Allergist evaluation. Drinking alcohol may increase liver damage caused by styrene oxide.
first_aid: Skin: flood body areas contacted with water; remove contaminated clothing under water stream; use soap; isolate contaminated clothing. Eyes: remove contact lenses, flush with copious water/saline ≥20-30 min, seek care. Inhaled: leave area, breathe fresh air; rescuers need proper respiratory protection; seek care if coughing/breathing difficulty/other symptoms develop, even hours later. Swallowed: if unconscious/convulsing, don't induce vomiting or give anything by mouth, ensure open airway, lay on side w/ head lower than body, transport immediately; if conscious/not convulsing, give water to dilute; if medical advice unavailable, don't induce vomiting, rush to nearest medical facility.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing (polyvinyl alcohol recommended) to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: (as styrene monomer) 500ppm: CcrOv/Sa. 700ppm: Sa:Cf/CcrFOv/GmFOv/PaprOv/SCBAF/SaF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFOv/SCBAE. Eye irritant — may need eye protection.
storage: Green: general storage. Check explosive conc. before confined entry. Cool, dry place; fireproof area separated from strong acids recommended. Automatic pumping preferred. No smoking/open flames; ≥5-gal metal containers grounded/bonded; self-closing valves/pressure-vacuum bungs/flame arresters on drums; nonsparking tools; explosion-proof electrical. Regulated, marked area per OSHA Standard 1910.1045.
shipping: Not on DOT list for label/packaging standards; may be classified as environmentally hazardous substance, liquid, n.o.s.: Class 9, Packing Group III.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; forced ventilation below explosive limit; absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; wash surfaces w/ 60-70% ethanol, then soap, then 60-70% ethanol again; avoid sewers (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Flammable liquid; poisonous styrene oxide gases produced; dry chemical/CO2/alcohol foam/polymer foam. Vapors heavier than air, may travel far to ignition sources, flashback risk; confined-area vapors may explode w/ fire; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
extraction_notes: References: EPA CHIP: Styrene Oxide (Mar 1978); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet (Dec 1999). No Disposal Method Suggested section visible in source.

Super toxic; cholinesterase inhibitor. Symptomatology similar to parathion: nausea followed by vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, excessive salivation, headache, giddiness, dizziness, weakness, chest tightness, blurred vision, tearing, slurred speech, confusion, troubled breathing, convulsions, coma, death.
long_term_effects: Cholinesterase inhibitor — cumulative effect possible. May damage nervous system w/ repeated exposure (convulsions, respiratory failure). Repeated exposure may cause personality changes (depression, anxiety, irritability).
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, CNS, cardiovascular system, blood cholinesterase.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: blood serum, cholinesterase, RBC count. Reassignment away from organophosphate/carbamate work recommended until recovery. If overexposed: repeat tests ASAP, nervous system exam.

storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from oxidizers/moisture. Automatic transfer preferred. No smoking/open flames; metal containers grounded/bonded; explosion-proof electrical.
shipping: Tetraethyl dithiopyrophosphate: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate; stay upwind, avoid low areas; ventilate closed spaces before entry; remove/isolate contaminated clothing at site; don't touch spilled material, stop leak if safe; water spray to reduce vapors. determination_in_water: Violent reaction.
routes_of_entry: Inhalation of vapor, ingestion, skin/eye contact.
short_term_effects: Lacrimator and corrosive. Fumes cause severe eye/skin/upper-resp-tract mucous-membrane irritation. Contact can cause severe irritation, burns, permanent eye damage. Corrosive on ingestion. Higher exposures: pulmonary edema (delayed hours, can be fatal). Exposure can cause headache, nausea, dizziness. Capable of severe pulmonary irritation, but few serious industrial exposure cases reported, likely due to pronounced irritant effects serving as immediate warning at hazardous concentrations.
long_term_effects: May cause lung damage; bronchitis may develop. Repeated exposure can cause skin drying/cracking.
medical_surveillance: Preemployment/periodic exams emphasizing skin/eyes/resp system. Pulmonary function tests may be useful. Lung function tests. Consider chest X-ray following acute overexposure. Exposures may also include sulfur dioxide and hydrochloric acid — see also those compounds.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥30 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: if conscious, water or milk (no induced vomiting). Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: 5ppm: CcrFS/GmFS/PaprS/SCBAF/SaF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFS/SCBAE. Eye irritant — may need eye protection.
storage: White: corrosive/contact hazard, corrosion-resistant location. Containers well closed and upright, away from heat. No water contact — reacts violently in closed vessels. Provisions for washing down spills with large water quantities. Vapor-tight electrical equipment recommended. Separate from oxidizing materials. Automatic pumping preferred. No smoking/open flames; ≥5-gal metal containers grounded/bonded; self-closing valves/pressure-vacuum bungs/flame arresters on drums; nonsparking tools; explosion-proof electrical.
shipping: 'CORROSIVE' label; Class 8, Packing Group I.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; avoid liquid/vapor contact; keep people away; goggles+SCBA+rubber over-clothing (incl. gloves); stop discharge if safe; call fire department; isolate/remove discharged material; notify local health/pollution control agencies; remove ignition sources; ventilate. Aqueous solution is a strong acid, neutralize with lime or soda ash. Absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid sewers (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Isolation (first 30min, may increase w/ time) — land spill small: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.1-0.2mi; land spill large: 200ft/60m, downwind 0.5-0.8mi day/0.8-1.3mi night; water spill small: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.1-0.2mi; water spill large: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.2-0.3mi day/0.8-1.3mi night. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible liquid; poisonous hydrogen chloride/hydrogen sulfide/sulfur oxide gases produced. Do NOT use water — decomposes on water contact producing heat and toxic corrosive fumes. Use chemical extinguishers. Vapors heavier than air, may travel far to ignition sources, flashback risk; confined-area vapors may explode w/ fire; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Wearing protective equipment, spray carefully onto sodium ash/slaked lime mixture; then spray with water, dilute, neutralize, flush to drain.
extraction_notes: References: Sax DPIM Vol5No.6 pp.90-92 (1985); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet: Sulfur Chloride (Oct 1999). This entry notes historical military use of sulfur chloride as a poison; content reproduced is limited to standard published civilian safety, PPE, decontamination, and emergency-response data — no synthesis or weaponization information is included.

description: Noncombustible colorless gas at ambient temperature, strong suffocating odor (threshold 1.1ppm). Shipped as liquefied compressed gas. Relative vapor density (air=1) 2.26.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Agricultural Chemical; Tumorigen, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data; Primary Irritant. Violent reaction with ammonia, acrolein, acetylene, alkali metals (sodium, potassium, magnesium, zinc), chlorine, ethylene oxide, amines, butadiene. routes_of_entry: Inhalation of gas, direct contact of gas/liquid phase on skin and mucous membranes.
short_term_effects: Inhalation: eye/nose/throat irritation. 6-12ppm may cause nose/throat irritation. 10-50ppm for 5-15min: rhinorrhea, difficult breathing, coughing/choking, reflex bronchoconstriction. 50-100ppm tolerable only 30-60min. ≥400ppm may immediately cause throat/lung swelling and fluid accumulation (pulmonary edema, delayed hours, can be fatal), breathing stoppage, pneumonia, death. Skin: 1% (10,000ppm) may irritate moist skin; liquid may cause frostbite/chemical burns. Eyes: irritation at 20ppm+; liquid may cause frostbite and permanent blindness-causing damage. Ingestion: liquid may cause frostbite/chemical burns to mouth.
long_term_effects: Repeated/prolonged inhalation exposure may cause asthma. May cause chronic eye/resp-tract irritation, smell-sense loss, burning/dryness. Stomach problems may occur. May cause permanent lung damage. Repeated 10ppm exposure may cause throat/lung irritation and increased nosebleeds. Limited animal evidence of lung cancer causation. Limited evidence of developing-fetus damage. Persons with asthma, subnormal pulmonary function, or cardiovascular disease at greater risk. Acute-exposure symptoms may be severe: coughing, choking, dyspnea, sneezing, wheezing, chest discomfort. Upper-airway edema/obstruction, bronchoconstriction, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, respiratory paralysis may occur. Fatigue noted. GI effects: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain. Cyanosis may be noted. Can cause death/permanent injury after very short small-quantity exposure; 1000ppm causes death from 10min to several hours via respiratory depression.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: chest X-ray, ECG, pulmonary function tests (FVC, FEV1), sputum cytology, WBC count/differential. Preplacement/periodic exams emphasizing skin/eyes/resp tract. Lung function tests. Eye/nose/throat exam. Consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure. Evaluate pulmonary function, smoking habits, and other pulmonary irritant exposure.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: get medical attention. Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered. Frostbite: seek care immediately, don't rub or flush w/ water, don't remove frozen clothing. No frostbite: wash contaminated skin thoroughly.
personal_protective_methods: Protective clothing to prevent skin freezing from evaporating liquid/vessel contact; no contact lenses; gas-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: 20ppm: CcrS/Sa. 50ppm: Sa:Cf/PaprS. 100ppm: CcrFS/GmFS/PaprTS/SaT:Cf/SCBAF/SaF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFS/SCBAE. Eye irritant — may need eye protection.
storage: White: corrosive/contact hazard, corrosion-resistant location. Keep below 130°F/54°C, protect containers from damage. Outdoor, ventilated, fireproof storage preferred. Per OSHA 1910.101/1910.169 & CGA recommendations.
shipping: 'POISON GAS, CORROSIVE' label; Class 2.3. Sulfurous acid (liquid SO2): 'CORROSIVE' label; Class 8, Packing Group II. Refilling compressed gas cylinders without owner's written permission violates transportation regulations. Cylinders transported secure/upright in well-ventilated truck.
spill_handling: If indoors, evacuate building, confine vapors by closing doors/shutting down HVAC. Restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate to disperse gas. Chemical protective suit + SCBA for spill response. Stay upwind, water spray to knock down vapor, contain runoff. Stop gas flow if safe; move/repair leaking cylinder if possible. Avoid confined spaces (explosion risk); OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Isolation (first 30min, may increase w/ time) — small: 200ft/60m, downwind 0.2-0.7mi day/1.2mi night; large: 1250ft/400m, downwind 1.3-3.6mi day/2.0-5.7mi night. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: Not flammable. Dry chemical/CO2/water spray/fog/foam. SCBA + full protective clothing. Move container from fire area; stay away from tank ends. Cool exposed containers with water from the side until well after fire out. Isolate area until gas disperses; keep unnecessary people away. Containers may explode in fire heat or rupture, releasing irritating toxic sulfur dioxide. Explosive properties on contact with sodium hydride; potassium chlorate at elevated temperatures; ethanol; ether; at very cool temperatures (-15°C); fluorine; chlorine trifluoride; chlorates. Reacts with water/steam producing toxic corrosive fumes. Containers may explode/rocket. Withdraw if cylinders exposed to excessive heat; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Pass into soda ash solution, then add calcium hypochlorite, neutralize, flush to sewer with water.

Synonyms: Sulfur fluoride
regulatory_authority: Air Pollutant Standard Set. Canada WHMIS 1.0%. Not listed Annex 1. WGK: nonwater polluting agent.
international_regulations: Not listed in Annex 1.
description: Colorless, odorless gas. Relative vapor density (air=1) 5.11. Shipped as liquefied compressed gas; condenses directly to solid upon cooling.
potential_exposure: May contain highly toxic sulfur pentafluoride as impurity. Used in electric power applications as gaseous dielectric/insulator, most extensively in high-voltage transformers. Also used in waveguides, linear particle accelerators, Van de Graaff generators, chemically pumped continuous-wave lasers, transmission lines, power distribution substations. Nonelectrical uses: protective atmosphere for magnesium-alloy casting; leak detector; moving-air-mass tracing. Vitreous substitution in owl monkeys shows greater ocular vascular permeability than saline, suggesting potential retinal-surgery application.
incompatibilities: May contain impurities causing hydrolysis on water contact, forming corrosive toxic hydrogen fluoride. Vigorous reaction with disilane.
acgih_tlv: 1000 ppm/5970 mg/m3 TWA.
dfg_mak: 1000 ppm/6100 mg/m3 TWA; Peak Cat II(8); Pregnancy Grp D.

short_term_effects: Liquid contact may cause frostbite. Symptoms: asphyxia, increased breathing/pulse rate, slight muscle incoordination, emotional upset, fatigue, nausea, vomiting. Physiologically inert in pure state; in high concentrations, pure SF6 can act as simple asphyxiant by displacing oxygen. Ordinarily contains variable sulfur fluoride quantities that, in water's presence, hydrolyze to hydrogen fluoride and oxyfluoride compounds (sulfuryl fluoride SO2F2, thionyl fluoride SOF2) with much more toxic health effects. May also be contaminated with more toxic sulfur compounds such as S2F10.
long_term_effects: Repeated high exposures can cause bone fluoride deposits (fluorosis) — pain, disability, tooth mottling. Repeated exposure can cause nausea, vomiting, appetite loss, diarrhea or constipation. Nosebleeds and sinus problems can occur.
medical_surveillance: Urine fluoride level (NIOSH #8308); levels above 4mg/L may indicate overexposure.

personal_protective_methods: Protective clothing to prevent skin freezing from evaporating liquid/vessel contact; no contact lenses; gas-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: (fluorides) 12.5mg/m3: Qm. 25mg/m3: 95XQ/Sa. 62.5mg/m3: Sa:Cf/PAPRDM. 125mg/m3: HieF/SCBAF/SaF. 250mg/m3: Sa:Pd,Pp. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: HieF/SCBAE. Eye irritant — may need eye protection; acid-gas sorbent may be needed.
storage: Green: general storage. Per OSHA 1910.101/1910.169 & CGA recommendations.

Avoid confined spaces (explosion risk); OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Nonflammable gas. Poisonous sulfur oxide/fluorine compound gases produced. Containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; withdraw if cylinders exposed to excessive heat; SCBA for firefighters.

carcinogenicity_status: (strong inorganic acid mists of sulfuric acid) IARC: human sufficient evidence, carcinogenic to humans, Group 1 (1992). NTP 11th Report on Carcinogens (2004): known to be a human carcinogen.
epcra_status: TPQ 1000 lb (454 kg). RQ 1000 lb (454 kg). Section 313 (acid aerosols incl. mists/vapors/gas/fog/other airborne species of any particle size) de minimis 0.1%.
clean_ water_act: §311 Hazardous Substances/RQ (40CFR117.3); §313 Water Priority Chemicals (57FR41331, 9/9/92).
international_regulations: Not listed in Annex 1.
description: Colorless to dark-brown, odorless, oily liquid; commercially sold at 93-98% H2SO4 (remainder water). Fuming sulfuric acid (oleum) gives off free SO2.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Agricultural Chemical; Tumorigen, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data; Primary Irritant. Chemical feedstock for acetic acid, hydrochloric acid, citric acid, phosphoric acid, aluminum sulfate, ammonium sulfate, barium sulfate, copper sulfate, phenol, superphosphates, titanium dioxide manufacture, plus synthetic fertilizers, nitrate explosives, artificial fibers, dyes, pharmaceuticals, detergents, glue, paint, paper. Dehydrating agent for esters/ethers; storage-battery electrolyte; cellulose hydrolysis to glucose; mineral/vegetable oil refining; leather industry. Also fur/food processing, wool-fabric carbonization, gas drying, uranium extraction from pitchblende, laboratory analysis. Among the highest-volume-produced chemicals in the US.
incompatibilities: Strong acid and oxidizer. Violent reaction with water (dangerous spattering, heat evolution). Violent reaction with combustible/reducing materials, bases, organic materials, chlorates, carbides, picrates, fulminates, water, powdered metals. Corrosive to most common metals, forming explosive hydrogen gas.
acgih_tlv: 0.2 mg/m3 (thoracic fraction of aerosol) TWA; suspected human carcinogen (H2SO4 in strong inorganic acid mists).
dfg_mak: 0.1 mg/m3 inhalable fraction TWA; Peak Cat I(1), momentary Ceiling 0.2mg/m3 should not be exceeded; Carcinogen Cat 4; Pregnancy Grp C.
other_national_oels: Egypt/Australia/Denmark/Japan/Norway/Thailand/Turkey/UK TWA1; Austria MAK1; Belgium TWA1/STEL3; Finland TWA1/STEL3[skin]; France VME1/VLE3; Poland MAC(TWA)1/MAC(STEL)3; Russia STEL1[skin]; Sweden NGV1/TKV3; Switzerland MAK-W1/KZG-W2 (1993-2000). ACGIH TLV countries: STEL3mg/m3. Netherlands MAC-TGG 1. US states 2.381-100.0 μg/m3.
human_health_water: EEC and Kansas guideline 250μg/L sulfate drinking water.
iarc_classification: Group 1 (1992, strong inorganic acid mists).
short_term_effects: Inhalation: nose/throat irritation at 5mg/m3; throat/lung swelling and bronchial inflammation at 12-35mg/m3; a few drops in lung air passages may be fatal. Higher exposures: pulmonary edema (delayed hours, can be fatal). Skin: severe irritation, burns, ulceration. Eyes: severe irritation, corneal damage, blindness. Ingestion: teeth damage; mouth/throat/stomach burning; nausea, vomiting of blood/eroded tissue; stomach/intestinal holes; shock; kidney damage. Death may occur from as little as 1oz. Acute ingestion symptoms: salivation, intense thirst, swallowing difficulty, pain, shock; oral/esophageal/stomach burns common; coffee-ground vomitus appearance; high circulatory-collapse potential. Acute inhalation: sneezing, hoarseness, choking, laryngitis, dyspnea, resp-tract irritation, chest pain, nose/gum bleeding, nasal/oral mucosa ulceration, pulmonary edema, chronic bronchitis, pneumonia. Eye contact: irritation, pain, swelling, corneal erosion, blindness. Dermal exposure: severe burns, pain, dermatitis.
long_term_effects: Can cause chronic runny nose, eye tearing, nosebleeds, stomach upset. Repeated/prolonged aerosol exposure risks tooth erosion/pitting. Lungs may be affected by repeated/prolonged aerosol exposure; bronchitis may develop. Exposure above 3.0mg/m3 may cause all above symptoms with greater severity.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: chest X-ray, pulmonary function tests (FVC, FEV1). For frequent/high exposure (≥half TLV): lung function tests before work + periodically, teeth exam. If symptoms/overexposure: consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: if conscious, water or milk (no induced vomiting). Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing (polyethylene, Teflon, Saranex, Neoprene/natural rubber, Viton recommended for >70% solution) to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash. Engineering controls per NIOSH Criteria Document #74-128.
respirator_selection: 15mg/m3: Sa:Cf/PaprAgHie/CcrFAg100/GmFAg100/SCBAF/SaF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFAg100/SCBAE. Eye irritant — eye protection needed.
storage: White: corrosive/contact hazard, corrosion-resistant location. Avoid water/chlorates/chromates/carbides/fulminates/nitrates/picrates/powdered metals — violent reactions. Tightly closed, cool, dry, ventilated, away from sunlight, acid-resistant cement floor. No smoking/open flames. Always add acid to water, never reverse. Extremely corrosive — handle with care. Explosion-proof electrical equipment. Metal-drum contact may release flammable explosive hydrogen gas — storage drums should be acid-resistant-coated.
shipping: Sulfuric acid ≥51%/<51% acid: 'CORROSIVE' label; Class 8, Packing Group II. Fuming, ≥30% free SO3: 'CORROSIVE, POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 8, Packing Group I. Fuming, <30% free SO3: 'CORROSIVE' label; Class 8, Packing Group I. Spent: 'CORROSIVE' label; Class 8, Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Extremely hazardous — enter with extreme care. Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; no exposed skin; keep ignition sources away (explosive hydrogen may form during storage); ventilate. Small spills: cover with sodium bicarbonate/soda ash/slaked lime (or calcinated dolomite, calcium oxide/hydroxide, sodium carbonate), shovel neutralized residue into containers, or cover with sand/earth and shovel; place vermiculite-absorbed acid in sealed containers. Isolate hazard area, deny entry; stay upwind, avoid low areas; ventilate closed spaces before entry. Notify authorities re: water pollution. Don't touch spilled material. Water spray to reduce vapor (don't get water inside container). Dike for later disposal. Avoid confined spaces (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Isolation (fuming/oleum, first 30min, may increase w/ time) — small: 200ft/60m, downwind 0.2-0.6mi day/1.4mi night; large: 1000ft/300m, downwind 1.8-3.6mi day/2.9-5.7mi night. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible liquid; poisonous sulfur oxide gases produced in fire or on water contact. Metal contact releases flammable explosive hydrogen gas. CO2 or dry chemical. Water may be used on nearby combustibles burning near this material, but extreme care needed — direct water application causes heat generation and splattering. Vapors heavier than air, may travel far to ignition sources, flashback risk; confined-area vapors may explode w/ fire; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Add slowly to soda ash/slaked lime solution with stirring; flush to drain with large water volumes. Recovery/reuse of spent sulfuric acid may be a viable disposal alternative; processes available.

description: Odorless, colorless to tan crystalline solid.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Agricultural Chemical; Tumorigen, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector. Herbicide manufacture/formulation/application for woody/herbaceous weed control. EPA issued rebuttable presumption against pesticide registration. The Vietnam-war-era defoliant Agent Orange was a mixture of 2,4,5-T and 2,4-D.
incompatibilities: Aqueous solution is a weak acid. Incompatible with sulfuric acid, bases, ammonia, aliphatic amines, alkanolamines, isocyanates, alkylene oxides, epichlorohydrin, strong oxidizers (chlorine, bromine, fluorine), strong bases.
acgih_tlv: 10 mg/m3; not classifiable as human carcinogen.

human_health_water: EPA lifetime health advisory 21.0μg/L. Mexico limits: 100μg/L estuaries, 10μg/L coastal waters. Kansas guideline 700.0μg/L drinking water.
determination_in_water: Liquid-liquid extraction and gas chromatography. Fish Tox 9154.36150000 ppb (VERY LOW). Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow=3.99.
iarc_classification: Group 2B (1987).
routes_of_entry: Inhalation, ingestion, skin/eye contact. Absorbed through skin.
short_term_effects: Irritates eyes/skin/resp tract. Inhalation: increasingly severe symptoms may include nose/throat irritation, weakness, tiredness, metallic mouth taste, appetite loss, diarrhea, heart problems, heart failure, death. Skin: reddening/itching may develop; slow absorption may contribute significantly to total exposure. Eyes: irritation may develop. Ingestion: 350mg produces only metallic taste lasting ~2h; ~4 teaspoonfuls (150lb man) may cause weakness, tiredness, appetite loss, diarrhea, heart problems, heart failure, death. Note: reported effects often from accidental exposures at unknown levels/duration; 2,4,5-T may be contaminated with small amounts of the more toxic 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD, Dioxin), so some symptoms may be attributable to contaminants.
long_term_effects: Levels above the standard may produce skin irritation, acne-like skin sores, small-patch skin-coloration loss, GI tract ulcer, nerve disorders causing muscle-control difficulty. Animal studies suggest possible increased infection susceptibility. Genetic-material changes and birth defects reported in lab studies, possibly due to 2,4,5-T or its contaminant; human relevance unknown. Animals: ataxia, skin irritation, acne-like rash, liver damage. Human Tox 70.00000 ppb (LOW).
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: blood plasma, urine chemical/metabolite (incl. 24h collection). If symptoms/overexposure: liver or kidney function tests.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Note to physician: if ingested, remove by lavage or emesis; general supportive measures for CNS depression; quinidine for myotonia.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: 50mg/m3: Qm. 100mg/m3: 95XQ/Sa. 250mg/m3: Sa:Cf/100F/PAPRDM/SCBAF/SaF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: 100F/SCBAE.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from strong oxidizers (chlorine, bromine, fluorine)/strong bases. Automatic transfer preferred. Regulated, marked area per OSHA Standard 1910.1045.
shipping: Phenoxy pesticides, solid, toxic, n.o.s.: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group III.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Soil Adsorption Index (Koc) 80.
fire_extinguishing: May burn but doesn't readily ignite. Dry chemical/CO2/water spray/foam extinguishers. Poisonous phosgene/hydrogen chloride/chlorine gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Two procedures discussed: (1) mix with excess sodium carbonate, add water, let stand 24h before flushing to drain with excess water; (2) pour onto vermiculite and incinerate with wood/paper/waste alcohol. Per 40CFR165 pesticide/container disposal recommendations. Follow package label directions or contact local/federal/regional EPA office. Consult environmental regulatory agencies. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators).

Synonyms: GA (military designation); Ethyl dimethylamidocyanophosphate; Ethyl N,N-dimethylphosphoramidocyanidate; Gelan 1
regulatory_authority: DHS Screening Threshold: theft hazard, cumulative 100g. Not IARC/ACGIH/OSHA/NTP-listed carcinogen. TPQ 10 lb. RQ 10 lb. DOT inhalation hazard chemical; Army Regulation AR 50-6 governs chemical-agent shipment, escorted per AR 740-32. DOT regulated marine pollutant (as cyanide mixtures/solutions). Canada NPRI; CEPA Priority Substance List, ocean dumping prohibited. Not listed Annex 1. WGK: none assigned.
carcinogenicity_status: Not listed by IARC, ACGIH, OSHA, or NTP as a carcinogen.
epcra_status: TPQ 10 lb (4.54 kg). RQ 10 lb (4.54 kg).
international_regulations: Not listed in Annex 1.
water_solubility: Soluble; readily hydrolyzed forming hydrogen cyanide; 9.8%/25°C, 7.2%/20°C
description: Organophosphorous nerve agent, among the most toxic known chemical warfare agents. Exposure can cause death in minutes; 1/10mL on skin can be fatal. Clear, colorless to brownish, oily liquid, slight fruity/almond odor (no odor when pure); odor is not a reliable detection indicator; tasteless. Vapor density (air=1) 5.6; volatility 490mg/m3/25°C. Chemically similar to malathion, parathion, and other organophosphates. Persistence: summer 10min-24h; winter 2h-3 days.
potential_exposure: Highly persistent (may remain liquid >24h) chemical warfare agent; military nerve gas. Nerve agents are more toxic/potent than insecticides. Note: if used as a weapon, notify US DoD Army; damage/death may occur before chemical detection. Detection: M8 paper (yellow) or M256-A1 Detector Kit (detection limit 0.005mg/m3).
incompatibilities: Decomposes slowly in water. Acidic conditions hydrolyze GA to hydrofluoric acid. Raising pH significantly increases decomposition rate; rapidly hydrolyzed in basic solutions (Na2CO3, NaOH, KOH) with 1.5min half-life at pH 11/25°C. No significant phototransformation in sunlight. Thermally stable below 49°C. Metal contact may evolve flammable hydrogen gas. Reacts with oxidizing materials. Destroyed by bleaching powder, producing cyanogen chloride. Decomposes within 6 months at 60°C; complete decomposition in 3.5h at 150°C. May produce hydrogen cyanide, NOx, phosphorus oxides, carbon monoxide.
other_national_oels: STEL 0.0001mg/m3. Suggested permissible 8h TWA 0.0001mg/m3 (2×10⁻⁵ppm) per USAEHA Technical Guide 169. WPL (worker population limit) 0.00003mg/m3. GPL (general population limit) 0.000001mg/m3.
determination_in_air: Military chemical agent detection papers/kits (M18A2 liquid; M256A1, M8A1, M18A2, ICAD, CAM vapor). M8/M9 paper quickly detects nerve-agent presence but not agent type. Accuro/Accuro 2000 (Draeger) Air Sampling/Gas System; NIOSH #5600 (Organophosphorus pesticides); #7904 (Cyanides).
human_health_water: Dissolves in water and remains very dangerous. Notify local health/pollution control officials and nearby water-intake operators; advise shutting intakes. Dangerous to aquatic life in high concentrations. Broken down quickly in water, but small amounts may evaporate. Broken down quickly in moist soil; small amounts may evaporate or contaminate groundwater. Persists 1.5-2 days in soil. Bleaching powder destroys tabun but produces cyanogen chloride (CAS 506-77-4).
determination_in_water: M272 Chemical Agent Water Testing Kit, detection limit 0.02mg/L for nerve agents. Cyanides: distillation + silver nitrate titration, or colorimetric analysis (pyridine pyrazolone or barbituric acid). Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow (estimated)=0.29 (also reported as 1.4).
ld50: LD50 (skin, human) 1.0g/70kg (156.8lb). LCt50 (human, inhalation) 400 mg-min/m3; median incapacitating dosage 300 mg-min/m3; respiratory lethal dosages kill in 1-10min. LD50 (monkey, percutaneous, shaved skin) 9.3mg/kg; LCt50 (monkey, inhalation) 187 mg-min/m3 (t=10). LCt50 (man, inhalation) 135 mg-min/m3 (t=0.5-2min) at RMV 15L/min; 200 mg-min/m3 at RMV 10L/min.
target_organs: Respiratory system, lungs, CNS, cardiovascular system, skin, eyes, plasma/RBC cholinesterase, liver, kidneys.
short_term_effects: Nerve agent, cholinesterase inhibitor. Skin absorption sufficient to cause death may occur in 1-2min but may be delayed 1-2h. Symptoms in normal appearance order: runny nose, chest tightness, dimmed vision/pinpoint pupils, breathing difficulty, drooling/excessive sweating, nausea/vomiting/cramps, involuntary defecation/urination, twitching/jerking/staggering, headache, confusion, drowsiness, coma, convulsions, followed by breathing cessation and death. Similar in action to GB (sarin) but only ~half as toxic by inhalation, while more irritating to eyes at low concentrations. Symptom number/severity depend on quantity and entry rate; very small skin doses may cause only local sweating/tremors. Onset slower from skin than respiratory dosage. Not listed as a carcinogen by IARC/ACGIH/OSHA/NTP.
long_term_effects: Cholinesterase inhibitor; cumulative effect possible. May damage nervous system with repeated exposure, resulting in convulsions, respiratory failure.
points_of_attack: Respiratory system, lungs, CNS, cardiovascular system, skin, eyes, plasma/RBC cholinesterase, liver, kidneys.
medical_surveillance: Consider points of attack in preplacement/periodic exams. Urine thiocyanate levels. CBC. Thyroid function evaluation. Liver function tests. Kidney function tests. CNS tests. EKG.
first_aid: Inhalation: hold breath until protective mask donned; for severe signs (chest tightness, pupil constriction, coordination loss), administer all three Nerve Agent Antidote Kit Mark I injectors in rapid succession (or atropine per physician direction); may repeat at 5-20min intervals up to three injection series, no further without medical direction, with injection record maintained; artificial respiration if breathing stopped (mouth-to-mouth only if approved delivery systems unavailable and no facial contamination); administer oxygen if breathing difficult; seek medical attention immediately. Eyes: flush immediately with water 10-15min, then don protective mask; miosis alone doesn't warrant injection — take individual to medical facility for observation instead. Skin: don protective mask, remove contaminated clothing, immediately wash with copious soap/water, 10% sodium carbonate solution, or 5% liquid household bleach, rinse well; M258A1 and/or M291 kit for skin decontamination; speed is of extreme importance; administer Mark I Kit intramuscular injection only if local sweating/muscular twitching observed; seek medical attention immediately. Ingestion: do NOT induce vomiting (first symptoms likely GI); immediately administer 2mg intramuscular injection of Mark I kit autoinjectors; seek medical attention immediately. Medical treatment: monitor ECG and respiration/ventilation adequacy; supplemental oxygenation, frequent secretion suctioning, endotracheal intubation, assisted ventilation may be required; diazepam (5-10mg adults, 0.2-0.5mg/kg children) for convulsion control (lorazepam/other benzodiazepines usable; barbiturates/phenytoin/other anticonvulsants ineffective); atropine administration (if not already given) should precede benzodiazepines for optimal seizure control; inhalation-exposed patients with chest pain/tightness/cough should be observed/examined periodically for 6-12h to detect delayed bronchitis, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or respiratory failure. Decontamination: rapid physical agent removal is essential; untrained/unequipped personnel should not enter hot/warm zones; medical personnel wear proper PPE; nerve agents persist in clothing — avoid bare-skin contact, seal contaminated items in double bags; use clean water (hose/spray/fog to avoid touching victim), begin washing immediately without waiting for soap or warm water; flush eyes ≥15min; caution against hypothermia in children/elderly. Wash-strip-wash-evacuate upwind/uphill protocol: vapor-only exposure — remove clothing in clean air, shampoo/rinse hair; liquid exposure — wash ≥3 times with liquid soap, large water amounts, mild-to-moderate friction (avoid brush scrubbing), final rinse with warm/hot water; diluted household bleach (0.5%) may be used for decontamination avoiding eyes/wounds/mouth, washed off after 15min; rinse eyes/mucous membranes/wounds with sterile saline or water; move upwind/uphill from hot zone.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact. Butyl rubber gloves and Tyvek 'F' decontamination suits provide barrier protection; impermeable protective clothing may be penetrated after a few hours of heavy agent-concentration exposure, so liquid contamination must be neutralized/removed promptly. No contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: When used as a weapon: NIOSH CBRN-certified SCBA. Follow OSHA 29CFR1910.134 or EN149. NIOSH/MSHA/EN149-approved respirator, or supplied-air respirator (positive-pressure/continuous-flow), or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure. M40 Series mask (replacing M17A1) provides respiratory protection against known military toxic chemical agents but cannot be used in oxygen-deficient environments, is not approved for civilian use, and doesn't protect against industrial toxics (ammonia, carbon monoxide).
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from strong oxidizers. Automatic transfer preferred. No smoking/open flames; metal containers grounded/bonded; explosion-proof electrical.
shipping: Toxic, liquids, organic, n.o.s. (inhalation hazard, Packing Group I, Zone A): 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group I.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate. Cover spills with vermiculite/diatomaceous earth/clay/fine sand/sponges/paper-cloth towels; treat with copious ≥10% aqueous NaOH solution. Scoop into fully removable-head drum with HDPE liner; treat decon solution with excess bleach to destroy CN formed during hydrolysis; cover contents with additional bleach before sealing; decontaminate/label drum exterior per IAW/EPA/DOT regs. Overpack leaking containers with vermiculite between interior/exterior containers. Alternative decontaminants (order of preference) if 10% NaOH unavailable: DS2 (2% NaOH, 70% diethylenetriamine, 28% ethylene glycol monomethyl ether), sodium carbonate, Supertropical Bleach Slurry (STB). Isolation (weapon-use scenario, first 30min, may increase w/ time) — small: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.1-0.2mi day/night; large: 300ft/100m, downwind 0.4-0.6mi day/night. Fire involving tank/rail car/tank truck: isolate ≥800m (0.5mi) in all directions, consider initial evacuation to same distance. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible liquid; heated vapors may form explosive air mixtures, presenting explosion hazard indoors, outdoors, and in sewers. Containers may explode when heated. Water/fog/foam/CO2 — avoid splashing or spreading GA. Poisonous hydrogen cyanide/NOx/phosphorus oxides/carbon monoxide gases may be produced. Positive-pressure full face-piece NIOSH-approved SCBA where oxygen-deficiency risk exists or per fire chief/CAI officer direction; M9/M17-series mask may substitute absent oxygen-deficiency risk. Complete protection required; have decontaminants (bleach, alkali) and atropine available. Vapors heavier than air, may collect in low areas, travel far to ignition sources, flashback risk; confined-area vapors may explode; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Minimum 56g decon solution per gram of GA; agitate while adding GA, maintain agitation ≥1h; react 24h; titrate to pH 10-12; treat with excess bleach (2.5 mole OCl⁻/mole GA) to destroy CN formed during hydrolysis. Scoop material into fully removable-head HDPE-lined drum; cover with additional bleach before sealing; same procedure for contaminated clothing; decontaminate/label drum exterior per IAW/state/EPA/DOT regs; overpack leaking containers with vermiculite; conduct general-area monitoring to confirm atmospheric concentrations remain below exposure limits.
extraction_notes: This entry describes the chemical warfare nerve agent Tabun/GA; content reproduced is limited to standard published civilian/military emergency-responder safety, detection, decontamination, PPE, and medical-treatment data — no synthesis or weaponization information is included. References: Sax DPIM Vol1No.2 p.63 (1980); EPA CHIP: Tabun (Nov 1987); The Riegle Report (May 1994); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet (Apr 2004); Schneider (Ed.), CHRIS 1 CD-ROM v2.0, USCG/DHS (2007).

incompatibilities: None reported.

regulatory_authority: Carcinogenicity: IARC human limited/animal sufficient evidence, carcinogenic to humans, Group 1 (1997); NTP 11th Report on Carcinogens (2004): known human carcinogen; NCI clear evidence (gavage, mouse/rat; dermal, mouse); NIOSH potential occupational carcinogen. NCI: clear evidence (gavage, mouse/rat; dermal, mouse). NIOSH: potential occupational carcinogen. EPA Gene-Tox: positive carcinogenicity mouse/rat; negative rodent dominant lethal.
