international_regulations: Not listed in Annex 1. Persistent Organic Pollutant (UN); Stockholm Convention Annex C (unintentional production/release, as polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins).
description: White, needle-shaped, crystalline solid. Decomposition begins at 500°C, virtually complete within 21s at 800°C. Formed in chlorophenol manufacturing processes, with formed amount depending on temperature/pressure control. 2,3,7,8-TCDD specifically forms during 2,4,5-trichlorophenol production via alkaline hydrolysis of 1,2,4,5-tetrachlorobenzene.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Agricultural Chemical; Tumorigen, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data; Primary Irritant. No uses except as research chemical. Inadvertent contaminant in herbicide precursors and thus in herbicides themselves. Formed during combustion processes including chemical-waste incineration (chlorophenols, chlorinated benzenes, biphenyl ethers); may be found in flue gases, fly ash, soot particles. Highly persistent in soil; contamination may last years. Most toxic of all dioxins, with bioaccumulation potential in animals. Applied via herbicide formulations (not used per se) — an estimated 2 million US acres treated for weed control with ~15 million lb of TCDD-contaminated 2,4,5-T, 2,4-D, or combinations.
incompatibilities: Decomposes in UV light.
niosh_rel: Carcinogen; limit exposure to lowest feasible concentration.
dfg_mak: 1.0×10⁻⁸ inhalable fraction; Peak Cat II(8) [skin]; Carcinogen Cat 4; Pregnancy Grp C.
other_national_oels: Austria/Finland/France/Switzerland: carcinogen (1993-1999). US states 0-450.0 μg/m3 (wide range, various units).
human_health_water: Insufficient data for freshwater/saltwater aquatic life criteria. Preferably zero for human health. Additional lifetime cancer risk of 1-in-100,000 posed at 4.55×10⁻⁷μg/L (1979). EPA estimated 0.0039μg/L limits cancer risk to 1-in-a-million (1980). Maine guideline 2×10⁻⁴μg/L, Minnesota 2×10⁻⁶μg/L drinking water.
determination_in_water: Methylene chloride extraction + transfer to benzene + capillary column GC-MS with electron impact ionization (EPA Method #613), or GC-MS (EPA Method #625).
ld50: (oral, rat) 0.05 mg/kg.
routes_of_entry: Inhalation, skin absorption, ingestion, skin/eye contact.
target_organs: Eyes, skin, liver, kidneys, reproductive system. Cancer sites in animals: tumors at many sites (liver, lung, mouth, tongue, skin); causes lymphomas in humans.
short_term_effects: One of the most toxic synthetic chemicals and the most toxic of the 75 dioxins. Exposure can cause headache, weakness, digestive disturbances; most symptoms develop slowly over many days. Inhalation can cause nose/throat burning sensation, headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, joint pain, tiredness, emotional disorders, blurred vision, muscle pain, nervousness, irritability, cold intolerance. Itching, swelling, redness, followed by acne-like eruptions (chloracne) commonly occur; chloracne may appear weeks/months after initial exposure and last a few months up to 15 years. Can cause liver, pancreas, circulatory, and respiratory system abnormalities, and death. Skin contact with very small amounts can cause chloracne. Eye contact can cause burning/irritation. Animal studies suggest daily exposure to amounts smaller than one grain of salt may cause severe symptoms and death within a few weeks.
long_term_effects: Can cause chloracne, numbness/tingling in arms/legs. Can cause allergic dermatitis porphyria, GI disturbance, possible reproductive problems. Blood abnormality may include light-sensitive skin, blisters, dark skin coloration, excessive hair growth, dark red urine. Reproductive problems and increased infection susceptibility may occur. Considered a potential occupational carcinogen because extremely low levels cause cancer/birth defects in animals. May cause liver/kidney damage. May be a teratogen. May decrease male/female fertility.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, liver, kidneys, reproductive system. Cancer site in animals: tumors at many sites (liver, lung, mouth, tongue, skin); causes lymphomas in humans.
medical_surveillance: Contact with TCDD should be avoided; careful preplacement and regular physical exams should be carried out where worker exposure cannot be avoided, with emphasis on liver/kidney function studies. Nervous system exam.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Note to physician: liver and nerve function screening tests should be performed; also monitor serum triglycerides and cholesterol.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: At any detectable concentration: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFOv100/SCBAE.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Regulated, marked area per OSHA Standard 1910.1045. Use in isolated area with adequate ventilation (preferably hooded), segregated glassware/tools, plastic-backed absorbent. Thoroughly wash hands/forearms after each manipulation and before leaving work area. Use same precautions as radioactive work.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; warn other workers of spill; protective clothing; collect powder, seal containers; rinse area with 1,1,1-trichloroethane, then wash with detergent/water; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Dry chemical/CO2/water spray/foam extinguishers. Poisonous gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.

No UN/NA-related Shipping section or Disposal Method Suggested section visible in source.

short_term_effects: Thallium salts may be eye/skin irritants and skin sensitizers. Exposure can cause fatigue, weakness, poor appetite, insomnia, mood changes. Acute poisoning rarely occurs industrially, usually from ingestion. When it occurs: GI symptoms, abdominal colic, kidney function loss, peripheral neuritis, strabismus, disorientation, convulsions, joint pain, alopecia develop rapidly. Symptoms (except GI) don't manifest until 12h-4 days after exposure. Death from CNS damage. May affect peripheral/central nervous system, liver, kidneys, GI tract, skin/hair, cardiovascular system — polyneuritis, optic nerve atrophy, encephalopathy, cardiac disturbances, liver/kidney damage, alopecia; exposure may result in death. Nitrate can irritate/burn skin/eyes and damage nervous system (headache, weakness, irritability, pain, 'pins and needles' in limbs, convulsions, coma, death). Sulfate(I) irritates eyes/skin; may affect nervous/cardiovascular systems, kidneys, GI tract; exposure may result in death or hair loss.
long_term_effects: Extremely toxic, cumulative poison. Nonfatal moderate/long-term occupational exposure: early symptoms usually fatigue, limb pain, metallic mouth taste, hair loss (not always an early symptom). Later: peripheral neuritis, proteinuria, joint pains. Occasionally neurological signs are the presenting factor, especially in severe poisonings. Long-term exposure may produce optic atrophy, paresthesia, papillary/superficial tendon reflex changes (slowed responses). Some thallium compounds are animal teratogens.

medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: whole blood chemical/metabolite, biologic tissue/biopsy, nerve conduction studies, urine chemical/metabolite, routine UA. medical_surveillance: Before employment + regularly: plasma and RBC cholinesterase levels. Cholinesterase reduced ≥25% below preemployment levels indicates increased poisoning risk even within 'normal' range; reassignment away from carbamate/organophosphate pesticide work recommended until enzyme levels recover. If symptoms/overexposure: repeat tests ASAP, nervous system exam, CBC, chest X-ray following acute overexposure. Do not drink alcoholic beverages before or during use.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash immediately with soap/water, shampoo hair promptly if contaminated, speed is of extreme importance, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Supplied-air respirator (positive-pressure/continuous-flow) or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure, per NIOSH/MSHA/EN149 approval.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated. Automatic transfer preferred.

description: Thorium (elemental) is a silvery-white, soft, ductile metal, a natural radioactive element; insoluble in water; occurs in monazite, thorite, thorinite minerals, usually mixed with disintegration products. Thorium chloride is a crystalline solid, soluble in water. Thorium nitrate is a crystalline solid that decomposes at 500°C. Thorium oxide (dioxide) is a white crystalline powder or solid, insoluble in water.
potential_exposure: Metallic thorium used in nuclear reactors for nuclear fuel production; incandescent-mantle manufacture; alloying material (especially with lighter metals like magnesium); metallurgy reducing agent; filament coatings for incandescent lamps/vacuum tubes; organic-synthesis catalyst; ceramics; welding electrodes. Exposure may occur during thorium-material production/use, alloy-part casting/machining, and welding fume with thorium electrodes. Thorium nitrate is an oxidizer — combustible/reducing-agent contact causes violent combustion or ignition.
incompatibilities: Metal: powder may ignite spontaneously in air. Heating may cause violent combustion or explosion. May explosively decompose from shock, friction, concussion. Potentially hazardous reactions with strong oxidizers, chlorine, fluorine, bromine, oxygen, phosphorus, nitryl fluoride, peroxyformic acid, silver, sulfur.
teel: TEEL-0: 0.35 mg/m3 (general); 0.75 mg/m3 (nitrate); 31.4 mg/m3 (perchlorate); 25 mg/m3 (oxide); 42.1 mg/m3 (oxalate); 0.75 mg/m3 (hydroxide)

iarc_classification: Group 1 (2001, generally).
routes_of_entry: Ingestion of liquid, inhalation of dust or gas, percutaneous absorption.
target_organs: Bone marrow, lungs, liver, kidneys. Cancer site in humans (thorium dioxide): liver.
short_term_effects: Irritates eyes/skin/resp tract. Inhalation may damage bone marrow and lungs. May affect blood-forming system, reducing WBC-production ability, resulting in pernicious anemia.
long_term_effects: Gas/aerosols can penetrate the body via resp/digestive systems and skin. Only 0.001% of ingested dose retained. Once deposited, remains in bones, lymph system, lungs, other organs, parenchymatous tissues for long periods. Low repeated exposures may scar lungs, damage liver/kidneys. Characteristic effects: blood-forming/nervous/reticuloendothelial-system changes, functional/morphological lung/bone-tissue damage. Chronic radiation disease symptoms appear much later; after considerable time neoplasms may occur and immunological activity may be reduced. Repeated/prolonged skin contact may cause dermatitis. Potential occupational carcinogen. May cause heritable genetic damage and birth defects.
points_of_attack: Bone marrow, lungs, liver, kidneys. Cancer site in humans (thorium dioxide): liver.
medical_surveillance: Personnel monitoring for early symptoms/changes (e.g., abnormal leukocytes in blood smear) may be valuable. For chronic/acute exposure: urine thorium determination, whole-body radiation counts, and breath radon useful for monitoring exposure dose and excretion rates. WBC count. Lung function test. Consider periodic chest X-ray for potentially high/repeated lower exposure.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: (thorium nitrate) full face-piece respirator w/ HEPA filter (greater protection from PAPR). High exposures: supplied-air respirator (positive-pressure/continuous-flow) or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure.
storage: Radioactive. Yellow stripe: reactivity hazard, separate from flammables/combustibles/other yellow-coded materials. Regulated, marked area per OSHA Standard 1910.1045. Thorium nitrate must avoid contact with combustible/organic/readily oxidizable materials — violent reactions.
shipping: Thorium metal, pyrophoric: 'RADIOACTIVE, SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE' label; Class 7. Thorium nitrate, solid: 'RADIOACTIVE, OXIDIZER' label; Class 7.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Thorium dioxide may burn but doesn't readily ignite. Thorium nitrate can cause violent combustion/ignition with readily combustible substances; use dry chemical/CO2/water spray/foam. Poisonous NOx gases produced (thorium nitrate). Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Recovery and recycling is the preferred route.

target_organs: CNS, eyes, liver, urinary tract, skin, blood.
short_term_effects: Especially tributyl/dibutyl compounds may cause acute skin burns — little pain but may itch, heal without scarring. Vapor/liquid-contaminated clothing may cause subacute lesions and diffuse erythematoid dermatitis on lower abdomen/thighs/groin of handlers; lesions heal rapidly upon contact removal. Eyes rarely involved, but accidental tributyltin splashing has caused lacrimation/conjunctival edema lasting several days without permanent injury. Triphenyltin hydroxide found not carcinogenic in NCI bioassay. Certain organotin compounds (especially alkyltin) highly toxic if ingested; trialkyl/tetraalkyl compounds cause CNS damage w/ headaches, dizziness, photophobia, vomiting, urinary retention, some weakness/flaccid limb paralysis in most severe cases. Percutaneous absorption postulated but deaths/serious injury have resulted only from ill-advised oral therapeutic-use attempts. Mechanism not clearly understood, though triethyltin is an extremely potent oxidative-phosphorylation inhibitor. Occasionally mild organotin intoxication seen in chemical labs w/ headache, nausea, EEG changes. Symptoms also include sore throat, cough, abdominal pain, skin burns/itching.
points_of_attack: CNS, eyes, liver, urinary tract, skin, blood.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: CBC (incl. RBC hemolysis), ECG (especially workers over 40), glaucoma exam, liver function tests, urine chemical/metabolite. For organotins, preplacement/periodic exams should include skin, eyes, blood, CNS, liver/kidney function.

personal_protective_methods: Employee training in correct PPE use is important. Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash- or dust-proof goggles+face shield (depending on physical properties) unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash. For organic tin compounds specifically: clean work clothes supplied daily, shower required following shift before street-clothes change.

description: Silvery metal or dry, dark-gray amorphous, lustrous powder. Brittle when cold, malleable when hot. Dry powder easily ignited, burns with intense flame. Autoignition 1200°C (solid); 480°C (powder in air). Ignition temperature of dust cloud 460°C. Minimum Explosive Concentration 0.45 oz/ft3 (USBM). Relative explosion hazard of dust: severe. Most important titanium-containing minerals: ilmenite, rutile, perovskite, titanite/sphene.

Other titanium compounds used in smoke screens, dyeing mordants, cemented-metal-carbide manufacture, thermal insulators, heat-resistant paint/plastic surface coatings.
incompatibilities: Dust may ignite spontaneously in air. Violent reactions with water, steam, halocarbons, halogens, aluminum. Dry powder is a strong reducing agent; violent reaction with strong oxidizers.

medical_surveillance: Preemployment/periodic exams should give special attention to lung disease, especially if irritant compounds involved. Chest X-ray in both exams; pulmonary function evaluated periodically. Smoking history should be taken. Careful attention to eyes and skin.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.

routes_of_entry: Inhalation, percutaneous absorption, ingestion, skin/eye contact.
target_organs: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, CNS, blood, liver.
short_term_effects: Can affect via inhalation. Irritates eyes/skin/resp tract. Exposure can cause dizziness, lightheadedness, passing out. long_term_effects: Repeated exposures can cause headaches, tiredness, nervous tension feeling. Can affect blood cells and clotting ability; hypochromic anemia. Delayed/chronic hazard possible including asthmatic bronchitis w/ coughing/SOB. Alcohol use enhances the effect. May cause liver damage. Liquid destroys skin's natural oils, causing drying/cracking.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, CNS, blood, liver.
medical_surveillance: Before employment + regularly: lung function tests, CBC and platelet count. If symptoms/overexposure: liver function tests, CBC and platelet count.

Note to physician: for inhalation, bronchodilators/decongestants/oxygen as necessary; corticosteroids useful for pneumonitis.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.

Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Dissolve/mix material with combustible solvent, burn in chemical incinerator w/ afterburner+scrubber; observe all federal/state/local environmental regulations.

medical_surveillance: Lung function tests. Consider chest X-ray following acute overexposure.

potential_exposure: Explosive; vulcanizing agent for natural rubber. May be more powerful than TNT and less impact-sensitive, but difficult to produce and not as widely used.
incompatibilities: Sensitive to shock and heat. Incompatible with initiating explosives, combustible materials, oxidizers.

first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). regulatory_authority: DHS Screening Threshold: release hazard 5000lb (commercial grade); theft hazard 400lb (commercial grade). Carcinogenicity: IARC animal inadequate/human inadequate evidence, not classifiable, Group 3 (1996). EPA Gene-Tox: positive histidine reversion-Ames test. Air Pollutant Standard Set. Canada WHMIS 1.0%. Hazard Symbol E, T, N; R2;R23/24/25;R33;R51/53; S1/2;S35;S45;S61. WGK: none assigned.
carcinogenicity_status: IARC: animal inadequate/human inadequate evidence, not classifiable, Group 3 (1996). EPA Gene-Tox: positive histidine reversion-Ames test.
description: Exists in five isomers; most commonly used is 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene. Colorless to pale yellow odorless solid (pellets, cast blocks, cast slabs) or crushed flakes. Ionization potential 10.59eV. Explodes at 232°C (also reported 240°C and 297°C); burns at 295°C when unconfined. Relatively stable high explosive.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Agricultural Chemical; Tumorigen, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data; Primary Irritant. Explosive (bursting charge in military shells, bombs, grenades, mines); intermediate for dyestuffs and photographic chemicals.
incompatibilities: Strong oxidizers, ammonia, strong alkalis, combustible materials, heat. Violent reaction with reducing agents. Rapid heating results in detonation. Explodes when heated to 232°C. May explosively decompose from shock, friction, concussion. Reacts with heavy metals.
acgih_tlv: 0.1 mg/m3 TWA [skin].
dfg_mak: 0.011 ppm/0.1 mg/m3 TWA; Peak Cat II(2) [skin]; Carcinogen Cat 3B; Pregnancy Grp D.
other_national_oels: Egypt TWA0.5; Australia TWA0.5[skin]; Austria MAK0.01(0.1)[skin] suspected carcinogen; Belgium TWA0.5[skin]; Denmark TWA0.1[skin]; Finland TWA0.5/STEL3[skin]; France VME0.5[skin]; Netherlands MAC-TGG 0.1[skin]; Norway TWA0.1; Philippines TWA1.5[skin]; Poland MAC(TWA)1/MAC(STEL)3; Russia TWA0.1/STEL0.5[skin]; Sweden NGV0.1/KTV0.2[skin]; Switzerland MAK-W0.1[skin]; Turkey TWA1.5[skin]; UK TWA0.3[skin]/TWA0.2ppm(0.89)[skin] carcinogen (1993-2000). ACGIH TLV countries: TWA0.1mg/m3[skin]. US states 5.0-12.0 μg/m3.
human_health_water: Russia MAC 0.5mg/L domestic-purpose water bodies.
determination_in_water: Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow=1.60.
routes_of_entry: Inhalation of dust/fume/vapor, ingestion of dust, percutaneous absorption from dust, skin/eye contact.
target_organs: Blood, liver, eyes, cardiovascular system, CNS, kidneys, skin.
short_term_effects: May cause eye/nose/throat irritation w/ sneezing, cough, sore throat. May cause skin irritation, dermatitis; may give skin/hair/nails yellowish color. Numerous worker fatalities from toxic hepatitis or aplastic anemia. May cause methemoglobinemia with cyanosis, weakness, drowsiness, dyspnea, unconsciousness. Ingestion may cause hallucinations/distorted perceptions, cyanosis, GI changes.
long_term_effects: May affect liver, causing hepatitis and jaundice. May affect blood, causing hemolysis, methemoglobin formation; cyanosis may occur. May affect vision, causing cataracts. May cause muscular pains, heart irregularities, renal irritation, menstrual irregularities, peripheral neuritis.
points_of_attack: Blood, liver, eyes, cardiovascular system, CNS, kidneys, skin.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: CBC, aplastic anemia, liver function tests, urine chemical/metabolite, routine UA. Preplacement/periodic exams should give special consideration to allergic-reaction history, blood dyscrasias, medication reactions, alcohol intake. Skin, eyes, blood, liver/kidney function should be followed. Urine may be examined for TNT via Webster test or urinary metabolite 2,6-dinitro-4-aminotoluene; both may be negative if liver injury present.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Note to physician: treat for methemoglobinemia; spectrophotometry may be required for precise urine methemoglobin determination.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing (PVC recommended) to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash. Webster skin test (colorimetric with alcoholic sodium hydroxide) or indicator soap should verify all TNT washed off skin.
respirator_selection: 5mg/m3: Sa. 12.5mg/m3: Sa:Cf. 25mg/m3: SCBAF/SaF. 500mg/m3: SaF:Pd,Pp. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFOv100/SCBAE.
storage: Explosive. Red stripe: flammability hazard, separate from all other flammable materials. Explosion-proof refrigerator, away from reducing agents. Keep material wet with water or treat as an explosive. Away from heat, ignition sources, metal, nitric acid, reducing materials. Protect containers from shock. Nonsparking tools/equipment. Regulated, marked area per OSHA Standard 1910.1045.
shipping: Wetted with ≥30% water by mass: 'FLAMMABLE SOLID' label; Class 4.1, Packing Group I. Dry or wetted with <30% water by mass: 'EXPLOSIVE' label; Class 1.1D, Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; dampen spilled material with alcohol to avoid dust; collect waste material, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Dangerously explosive solid. If burning and conditions permit, don't extinguish — evacuate area and let burn; cool exposures using unattended monitors. If must be extinguished, use any agent appropriate for the burning material. Poisonous NOx gases produced. Cool exposed containers from unattended equipment or remove intact containers if safe. SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Dissolve in acetone, incinerate in unit equipped with afterburner and caustic soda solution scrubber.
extraction_notes: References: EPA CHIP: 2,4,6-Trinitrotoluene (1979); Sax DPIM Vol2No.5 pp.93-96 (1982) & Vol8No.4 pp.75-80 (1988). No TEEL/PAC values visible in source for this entry.

Swallowed: contact physician/hospital/poison center at once; if unconscious/convulsing, don't induce vomiting or give anything by mouth, ensure open airway, lay on side w/ head lower than body, transport immediately; if conscious/not convulsing, give water to dilute; vomiting should not be induced without physician's advice.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.

storage: Green: general storage. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from aldehydes/ketones/nitrates/oxidizers/oxygen/peroxides. Automatic transfer preferred.

description: Nitrogen mustard blister agent (vesicant). Colorless to pale yellow liquid; pure material is odorless, otherwise faint fish- or soap-like odor. Volatility 0.120 mg/L/25°C.
potential_exposure: Sulfur mustards were formerly used as a gas warfare agent; nitrogen mustards have not previously been used in warfare (per NIOSH). Exposure damages eyes, skin, respiratory tract and suppresses the immune system.
incompatibilities: Not stable; undergoes slow but steady polymerization. Avoid contamination with oxidizing agents (nitrates, oxidizing acids, chlorine bleaches, pool chlorine), which may result in ignition. Unstable in light/heat presence, forms dimers above 50°C. Decomposes before/at boiling point under all conditions — reactions could generate enough heat to cause explosion. Polymerizes slowly (munitions effective for years). Heated to decomposition emits hydrogen chloride and NOx. Note: chlorinating agents destroy nitrogen mustards — dry chlorinated lime and high-active-chlorine chloramines vigorously chlorinate the carbon chain to low-toxicity products (less active in water presence); rapidly oxidized by peracids in weakly alkaline aqueous solution, more slowly in acid solution.
other_national_oels: AEL (US Military) 0.003 mg/m3.

determination_in_water: Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow (estimated)=2.27 (per NIOSH).
ld50: Median lethal dose for inhalation 1500 mg-min/m3; for skin absorption (masked personnel) 10,000 mg-min/m3. Median incapacitating dose for eye injury 200 mg-min/m3; for skin absorption 2500 mg-min/m3.
target_organs: Eyes, skin, respiratory tract, immune system, bone marrow/hematopoietic system, lymph nodes, kidneys, reproductive system.
short_term_effects: Extremely toxic; may damage eyes/skin/resp tract and suppress immune system. Cellular changes occur within minutes of contact, but onset of pain/symptoms is delayed — the sooner symptoms occur after exposure, the more likely they are to progress and become severe (per NIOSH). Most toxic of the nitrogen mustards. Irritates eyes at quantities that don't significantly damage skin/resp tract in single exposures. Mild vapor exposure may leave no skin lesions; severe vapor or liquid exposure may cause erythema, irritation, itching, and later blistering in erythematous areas. Resp-tract effects: nose/throat irritation, hoarseness progressing to voice loss, persistent cough; fever, labored respiration, moist rales develop; bronchial pneumonia may appear after the first 24h. Following ingestion/systemic absorption: cell-mitosis inhibition, depressing blood-forming mechanisms and injuring other tissues; severe (possibly hemorrhagic) diarrhea; lesions most marked in small intestine (degenerative changes, necrosis in mucous membranes). Ingestion of 2-6mg causes nausea and vomiting.
long_term_effects: Chronic/repeated exposure may cause bone marrow suppression, damaging the blood-forming (hematopoietic) system, lymph nodes, immune system, kidneys, and reproductive system (per NIOSH). Early bone-marrow-suppression signs: low WBC count, increased infection risk, easy bruising/bleeding tendency. May cause lymph node damage and weakened immune system. Also causes liver/kidney damage and reproductive-system damage in both sexes, leading to decreased fertility. Mutagenic, toxic to the developing embryo, and carcinogenic.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory tract, immune system, bone marrow/hematopoietic system, lymph nodes, kidneys, reproductive system.
first_aid: No antidote exists for nitrogen mustard toxicity. Because health effects may not occur until several hours after exposure, patients/victims should be observed in a hospital setting for at least 24h. Gastric lavage is contraindicated following ingestion due to esophagus/upper-airway perforation risk. Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash immediately with soap/water, speed is of extreme importance, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Keep victim quiet, maintain normal body temperature; effects may be delayed, keep victim under observation. Decontamination: of all potentially exposed areas within minutes after exposure is the only effective means of decreasing tissue damage (per NIOSH). Remove clothes and place contaminated clothes/personal belongings in a sealed double bag. Decontamination should be performed within the first 2min following exposure to prevent tissue damage; if not accomplished in the first several minutes, decontamination should still be performed to remove residual liquid mustard or trapped mustard vapor from skin/clothes, preventing vapor off-gassing or cross-contamination of responders/facilities. Physical removal of the agent — not detoxification/neutralization — is the most important decontamination principle; mustard is not detoxified by water alone and remains in decontamination effluent (dilute) absent hydrolysis. Vapor-exposed patients: remove all clothing in clean air, shampoo/rinse hair to prevent vapor off-gassing. Liquid-exposed patients: wash in warm/hot water at least 3 times using liquid soap (dispose/replace container after use), large water volumes, mild-to-moderate friction with a single-use sponge/washcloth for the first two washes (avoid brush scrubbing — may enhance absorption via skin damage); third wash rinses with large warm/hot water amounts; shampoo for hair; if warm/hot water unavailable but cold water is, use cold water rather than delaying decontamination; rinse eyes/mucous membranes/open wounds with sterile saline or water. Health-care providers should verify adequate decontamination (repeating the process if inadequate) before facility entry, be prepared to stabilize conventional injuries during decontamination, and wear proper PPE.
personal_protective_methods: Totally Encapsulating Chemical Protective (TECP) suit providing CBRN-agent protection; chemical-resistant inner and outer gloves; chemical-resistant boots with steel toe and shank; coveralls/long underwear/hard hat under the TECP suit optional. Take all precautions to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: When used as a weapon: NIOSH CBRN-certified SCBA. Where potential exposure exists: NIOSH-certified CBRN full-face-piece SCBA operated in pressure-demand mode, or pressure-demand supplied-air-hose respirator with auxiliary escape bottle; or NIOSH/MSHA/EN149-approved supplied-air respirator with full face-piece (positive-pressure mode) or full face-piece/hood/helmet (continuous-flow mode); or NIOSH/MSHA/EN149-approved SCBA with full face-piece operated in pressure-demand or other positive-pressure mode.

spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate; avoid inhalation/skin contact; don't touch spilled material, stop leak if safe; water spray to reduce vapors. Small spills: sand/noncombustible absorbent material. Large spills: dike far ahead for later disposal. Avoid sewers (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Isolation (weapon-use scenario, first 30min, may increase w/ time) — small and large spills: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.1-0.1mi day/night. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.

determination_in_water: Neutron activation analysis.
target_organs: Metal and cemented tungsten carbides: eyes, skin, respiratory system, blood. Soluble compounds: eyes, skin, respiratory system, CNS, GI tract.
short_term_effects: Can affect via inhalation. Irritates eyes/skin/resp system. Some tungsten compounds can cause lung/skin problems. Pure tungsten carbide alone shows no health effects; but tungsten carbide often combined with nickel or cobalt (cemented tungsten carbide/'hard metal') — exposure to that combination can cause skin irritation.
long_term_effects: Long-term exposure to tungsten metal and cemented tungsten carbide may cause diffuse pulmonary fibrosis (lung scarring), appetite loss, nausea, cough. May cause blood changes. Tungsten carbide combined with cobalt or nickel can cause skin sensitization, lung allergy w/ wheezing/coughing/SOB; repeated exposure can cause pulmonary fibrosis. Tungsten-soluble-compound long-term exposure in animals: CNS disturbances, diarrhea, respiratory failure, behavioral/body-weight/blood changes.
points_of_attack: Metal and cemented tungsten carbides: eyes, skin, respiratory system, blood. Soluble compounds: eyes, skin, respiratory system, CNS, GI tract.
medical_surveillance: Tungsten-alone exposure: no medical tests necessary. Cemented tungsten carbide (hard metal) exposure: lung function tests before work + periodically; chest X-ray every 2-3 years after ≥5 years of exposure. If symptoms/overexposure: allergist evaluation for skin allergy diagnosis.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield for powder/dust work, unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.

fire_extinguishing: Tungsten is a flammable powder — use dry chemicals appropriate for metal fires. Tungsten carbide itself doesn't burn — use agent suitable for surrounding fire. Poisonous gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Recovery of tungsten from sintered metal carbides, scrap, and spent catalysts described as an alternative to disposal.

Synonyms: Tungsten fluoride
regulatory_authority: DHS Screening Threshold: theft hazard 45lb (≥7.10% conc.). Air Pollutant Standard Set. Canada WHMIS 1.0%. Not listed Annex 1. WGK: none assigned.
international_regulations: Not listed in Annex 1.
description: Toxic, colorless gas or light yellow liquid.
potential_exposure: Strong halogenating agent. Applies tungsten coatings via vapor deposition; electronics/component manufacture; other-chemical manufacture.
incompatibilities: Decomposes on water/moist-air contact, forming corrosive hydrofluoric acid. Violent reaction with methyl silicate.
human_health_water: EPA fluoride standard 4mg/L. Maine guideline 2.4mg/L; Arizona standard 1.8mg/L drinking water.
target_organs: Eyes, respiratory system, CNS, skeleton, kidneys, skin.
short_term_effects: Corrosive. Irritates eyes/skin/resp tract. Liquid contact may cause frostbite. Can affect via inhalation. Exposure may involve both tungsten and fluoride effects. Very high fluoride-level exposure may cause nausea, vomiting, abnormal pain, convulsions, kidney damage. Higher exposures: pulmonary edema (delayed hours, can be fatal).
long_term_effects: Repeated high exposures may affect kidneys. Can cause bone fluoride deposits (fluorosis), possibly causing pain, disability, teeth mottling. Repeated exposure can cause nausea, vomiting, appetite loss, diarrhea, constipation. Nosebleeds and sinus problems can also occur.
points_of_attack: Eyes, respiratory system, CNS, skeleton, kidneys, skin.
medical_surveillance: For frequent/high exposure (≥half TLV): lung function tests before work + periodically. Fluoride level in urine (NIOSH #8308); levels >4mg/L may indicate overexposure. If symptoms/overexposure: consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure, kidney function tests.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered. If frostbite occurred: seek care immediately, do NOT rub affected areas or flush with water, do NOT attempt removing frozen clothing (prevents further tissue damage). If frostbite did NOT occur: immediately wash contaminated skin thoroughly with soap/water.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield for liquid work, gas-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash. Specific engineering controls recommended in NIOSH Criteria Document #76-103: Inorganic Fluorides.
respirator_selection: (as fluorides) 12.5mg/m3: Qm. 25mg/m3: 95XQ/Sa. 62.5mg/m3: Sa:Cf/PaprHie. 125mg/m3: 100F/SCBAF/SaF. 250mg/m3: Sa:Pd,Pp. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: 100F/SCBAE. (as tungsten metal/insoluble compounds) 50mg/m3: 100XQ/Sa/SCBAF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: 100F/SCBAE.
storage: Poison gas. White stripe: contact hazard, separate from solid-white-category materials. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from water. Cylinder handling per OSHA 1910.101/1910.169 and Compressed Gas Association recommendations.
shipping: 'POISON GAS, CORROSIVE' label; Class 2.3. Cylinders transported secure/upright in well-ventilated truck. Refilling compressed gas cylinders without owner's express written permission violates transportation regulations.
spill_handling: Evacuate building, close doors, shut HVAC; restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate to disperse; chemical protective suit + SCBA for spill response; stay upwind, water spray to knock down vapor, contain runoff; stop gas flow if safe; move/repair leaking cylinder if possible; absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth, seal containers; avoid confined spaces (explosion risk); OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Isolation (first 30min, may increase w/ time) — small: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.1-0.5mi day/0.8mi night; large: 500ft/150m, downwind 0.6-1.8mi day/2.8mi night. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: May burn but doesn't readily ignite. Small fires: dry chemical/CO2. Poisonous fluorine gases produced. Vapors heavier than air, collect in low areas. Containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; withdraw if cylinders exposed to excessive heat; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Nonrefillable cylinders disposed per local/state/federal regulations; allow remaining gas to vent slowly into atmosphere in unconfined area or exhaust hood. Refillable cylinders returned to original supplier with valve caps/outlet plugs secured and valve protection caps in place.
extraction_notes: Reference: NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet: Tungsten Hexafluoride (Nov 2000).

Synonyms: Gum spirits; Gum turpentine; Oil of turpentine; Spirits of turpentine; Wood turpentine
regulatory_authority: FDA over-the-counter drug. FIFRA status: canceled/new AI. Air Pollutant Standard Set. Canada WHMIS 1.0%. Hazard Symbol (8006-64-2) Xn, N; R10;R20/21/22;R36/38;R43;R51/53;R65; S2;S36/37;S46;S61;S62. WGK: 2 (8006-64-2, water polluting).
description: Oleoresin from species of Pinus (Pinaceae) trees. Crude oleoresin (gum turpentine): yellowish, sticky, opaque mass. Distillate (oil of turpentine): colorless, volatile liquid, characteristic odor. Chemically contains alpha-pinene, beta-pinene, camphene (monocyclic terpene), and terpene alcohols. Autoignition 253°C (also listed 220-255°C). LEL 0.8%/UEL 6%.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Tumorigen, Human Data; Natural Product; Primary Irritant. Chemical feedstock for floor/furniture/shoe/automobile polishes, camphor, cleaning materials, inks, putty, mastics, cutting/grinding fluids, paint thinners, resins, degreasing solutions. Extracted alpha- and beta-pinenes have recently found use as volatile bases for various compounds. Components d-α-pinene and 3-carene, or their hydroperoxides, may cause turpentine's eczema and toxic effects.
incompatibilities: Forms explosive mixture with air. Violent reaction with strong oxidizers, especially chlorine, chromic anhydride, stannic chloride, chromyl chloride.
acgih_tlv: (turpentine and selected monoterpenes) 20 ppm/112 mg/m3 TWA, sensitizer; not classifiable as human carcinogen.
dfg_mak: (8006-64-2) 100 ppm/560 mg/m3; danger of skin sensitization.
other_national_oels: Australia TWA100(560); Austria MAK100(560); Belgium TWA100(556); Denmark TWA25(140); Finland TWA100(560)/STEL150[skin]; France VME100(560); Hungary TWA300/STEL600; Netherlands MAC-TGG 560; Philippines TWA100(560); Poland MAC(TWA)300/MAC(STEL)840; Russia STEL300; Sweden NGV25(150)/KTV50(300)[skin]; Turkey TWA100(560); UK TWA100(566)/STEL150 (1993-2000). ACGIH TLV countries (NZ/SG/VN): not classifiable as human carcinogen. Russia ambient 2.0mg/m3 momentary/1.0mg/m3 daily average. US states 5.6-13.333 mg/m3.
human_health_water: Russia MAC 0.2mg/L domestic-purpose water bodies.
routes_of_entry: Inhalation of vapor and percutaneous absorption of liquid are the usual occupational-exposure paths (symptoms have been reported from percutaneous absorption alone). Also ingestion, skin/eye contact.
target_organs: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, CNS, kidneys.
short_term_effects: Can affect via inhalation and skin passage. Irritates eyes/nose/throat. Higher levels can affect CNS, causing headache, vertigo, dizziness, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, confusion, rapid pulse. Swallowing liquid may cause chemical pneumonia. High exposures: pulmonary edema (delayed hours, can be fatal). Still-higher levels can cause hematuria, albuminuria, kidney damage, convulsions, death.
long_term_effects: Repeated/prolonged contact may cause skin sensitization and allergy. Liquid destroys skin's natural oils, causing dryness/cracking. May damage kidneys, bladder, nervous system. Can irritate lungs; bronchitis may develop. Various turpentine-oil products vary considerably in toxicity/eczema tendency (probably from δ-α-pinene and 3-carene content), though systematic comparative investigations are lacking.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, CNS, kidneys.
medical_surveillance: If symptoms/overexposure: kidney function tests, allergist evaluation for skin allergy diagnosis, nervous system exam, consider chest X-ray following acute overexposure.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: give plenty of water, seek care (do not induce vomiting). Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing (Teflon, polyvinyl alcohol recommended) to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: 800ppm: Sa:Cf/PaprOv/CcrFOv/GmFOv/SCBAF/SaF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFOv/SCBAE.
storage: Red: flammability hazard, flammable-liquid area/cabinet away from ignition/corrosive/reactive materials. Check explosive conc. before confined entry. Avoid oxidizers (perchlorates, peroxides, permanganates, chlorates, nitrates). No smoking/open flames; ≥5-gal metal containers grounded/bonded; self-closing valves/pressure-vacuum bungs/flame arresters on drums; nonsparking tools.
shipping: 'FLAMMABLE LIQUID' label; Class 3, Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; forced ventilation below explosive limit; absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid sewers (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Flammable liquid; toxic fumes/gases produced. Dry chemical/CO2/alcohol foam extinguishers. Vapors heavier than air, may travel far to ignition sources, flashback risk; confined-area vapors may explode w/ fire; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Dissolve/mix material with combustible solvent, burn in chemical incinerator w/ afterburner+scrubber; observe all federal/state/local environmental regulations.
extraction_notes: Entry completed from batch 107 split (cut off mid-description at end of PDF page 2697). References: Sax DPIM Vol2No.2 pp.75-76 (1982); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet: Turpentine (Oct 1996).

regulatory_authority: Carcinogenicity: NIOSH (uranium, insoluble and soluble compounds): potential occupational carcinogen. Air Pollutant Standard Set. CWA §311 Hazardous Substances/RQ. RQ 100 lb. Canada WHMIS 1.0%. Hazard Symbol (uranium and compounds) T+; R26/28;R33;R53; S1/2;S20/21;S45;S61. WGK: 3 (uranyl acetate dihydrate, highly water polluting).
carcinogenicity_status: NIOSH (uranium, insoluble and soluble compounds): potential occupational carcinogen.
clean_ water_act: §311 Hazardous Substances/RQ (40CFR117.3).
international_regulations: Hazard Symbol T+; R26/28;R33;R53; S1/2;S20/21;S45;S61.
water_solubility: Insoluble (metal, uranium(IV) oxide); highly soluble but unstable (uranyl chloride); soluble (uranyl sulfate)
nfpa_ratings: Health 2, Flammability 0, Reactivity 0 (metal); MEC 60 g/m3. (uranyl nitrate solid) Health 3, Flammability 0, Reactivity 2 (Oxidizer). (uranyl nitrate hexahydrate) Health 3, Flammability 0, Reactivity 1.
description: Silver-white, malleable, ductile, lustrous solid. Weakly radioactive but must be handled with caution. Combustible solid as powder or turnings. Autoignition 20°C (dust cloud); ignition temperature of dust cloud 20°C; Minimum Explosive Concentration 0.060 oz/ft3 (USBM); relative explosion hazard of dust: severe. Natural uranium comprises three isotopes: 238U (99.28%), 234U (0.006%), 235U (0.714%). Over 100 uranium minerals exist; commercially important ones are oxides and oxygenous salts. Ore processing generally involves extraction then acid or carbonate leaching; metal may be obtained from halides via fused salt electrolysis. Uranium(IV) oxide: black to brown crystalline solid or powder. Uranyl chloride (7791-26-6): bright yellow crystalline solid. Uranyl nitrate, solid: yellow crystalline solid.
potential_exposure: Primary use of natural uranium: nuclear-reactor fuel, plutonium production, gaseous-diffusion-plant feed. Also a radium-salt source. Uranium compounds used in glass staining, ceramic glazing, enameling; photographic processes; steel alloying; chemical-reaction catalyst; radiation shielding; aircraft counterweights. Presents both chemical and radiation hazards; exposures may occur during mining, ore processing, and uranium-metal production.
incompatibilities: Uranium metal powder: radioactive, pyrophoric, strong reducing agent. Keep away from chlorine, fluorine, nitric acid, nitric oxide, selenium, sulfur, carbon dioxide, carbon tetrachloride. Complete oil coverage of uranium metal scrap/turnings essential for fire prevention. Uranium(IV) oxide: may spontaneously ignite on air contact when heated above 700°C. Uranium hydride: keep away from strong oxidizers, water, halogenated hydrocarbons. Uranyl chloride: aqueous solutions are chemically unstable. Uranyl nitrate(s): keep away from combustible materials, reducing agents. Uranium hexafluoride: keep away from water.
osha_pel: (natural & insoluble compounds) 0.25 mg[U]/m3 TWA; (soluble) 0.05 mg[U]/m3 TWA.
niosh_rel: (natural & insoluble compounds) 0.2 mg[U]/m3 TWA; 0.6 mg[U]/m3 STEL; (soluble) 0.05 mg[U]/m3 TWA. Potential occupational carcinogen; limit exposure to lowest feasible concentration.
acgih_tlv: 0.2 mg[U]/m3 TWA; 0.6 mg[U]/m3 STEL; confirmed human carcinogen; BEI issued.
teel: TEEL-0: 0.25 mg/m3 (metal/insoluble compounds); 0.284 mg/m3 (uranium oxide, 1344-57-6); 0.0828 mg/m3 (uranyl nitrate, 36478-76-9); 0.05 mg/m3 (soluble compounds)
dfg_mak: (uranium compounds) 0.25 mg[U]/m3 inhalable fraction.
other_national_oels: Australia TWA0.2[U]/STEL0.6[U]; Belgium TWA0.2[U]/STEL0.5-0.6[U]; Denmark TWA0.2[U]; Finland TWA0.2[U]; Norway TWA0.2[U]; Netherlands MAC-TGG 0.2[U]; Philippines TWA0.25[U]; Poland MAC(TWA)0.015-0.075[U]/MAC(STEL)0.12[U]; Russia STEL0.015-0.075[U]; Switzerland MAK-W0.2[U]; Turkey TWA0.05[U]; UK LTEL0.2[U]/STEL0.6[U] (1993-2003). Russia workplace MAC 0.015mg[U]/m3 (soluble)/0.075mg[U]/m3 (insoluble). US states 2.0-6.0 μg/m3.
human_health_water: No criteria set. EPA suggested permissible ambient goal 3μg/L (health-based). US states: 10μCi/L (Massachusetts) to 35μCi/L (Arizona); 15μg/L (Colorado) drinking water. EPA radiological limits: NRC public dose limit 100mRem(0.01Sv)/year; Air (Radium NESHAP) 10mRem(0.1Sv); Water: combined 226Ra & 228Ra MCL 5pCi/L, 224Ra 5pCi/L (limits target ~2 in 10,000 increased lifetime cancer risk); Indoor air action level 4pCi/L radon. OSHA ionizing-radiation limits (29CFR1910.1096): whole body/head/trunk/blood-forming organs/eye lens/gonads 1.25 Rem(0.0125Sv)/quarter; hands/forearms/feet/ankles 18.75 Rem(0.1875Sv)/quarter; skin of whole body 7.5 Rem(0.075Sv)/quarter; minors (under 18) 10% of above; adults may exceed under specified conditions up to 3 Rem(0.3Sv)/quarter per 1910.1096(b)(2).
routes_of_entry: Inhalation of fume/dust/gas, ingestion, skin/eye contact. Uranium salts reported capable of penetrating intact skin: uranyl nitrate, uranyl fluoride, uranium pentachloride, uranium trioxide (uranyl oxide), sodium diuranate, uranium hexafluoride.
target_organs: Soluble compounds: respiratory system, blood, liver, kidneys, lymphatic system, skin, bone marrow (cancer site: lungs). Metal and insoluble compounds: skin, kidneys, bone marrow, lymphatic system (cancer site: lungs).
short_term_effects: Prolonged skin contact should be avoided to prevent radiation injury. Highly toxic; body-fluid-soluble compounds possess highest toxicity. Poisoning generally results from accidents. Acute chemical toxicity primarily damages kidneys; kidney changes precede liver effects in time and degree. Chronic poisoning with prolonged exposure gives pneumoconiosis chest findings, pronounced blood changes, generalized injury. Difficult to separate toxic chemical effects from radiation effects; chronic radiation effects resemble ionizing-radiation effects. Carcinogenicity confirmed related to dose and exposure time; lung cancer, osteosarcoma, lymphoma all reported. Soluble compounds: lacrimation, conjunctivitis, SOB, coughing, chest rales, nausea, vomiting, skin burns, urine casts, albuminuria, high BUN, lymphatic cancer. Insoluble compounds: dermatitis, lymphatic/blood-forming-tissue cancer.
long_term_effects: Can cause dermatitis, kidney damage, blood changes. Potential occupational carcinogen; cancer potential results from alpha-emitting properties and radioactive decay products (e.g. radon).
points_of_attack: Soluble compounds: respiratory system, blood, liver, kidneys, lymphatic system, skin, bone marrow. Cancer site: lungs. Metal and insoluble compounds: skin, kidneys, bone marrow, lymphatic system. Cancer site: lungs.
medical_surveillance: NIOSH tests: whole blood chemical/metabolite, CBC, chest X-ray, urine chemical/metabolite, routine UA. Preemployment exams should give special attention to blood, lung, kidney, liver. Periodic exams: tests for blood changes, chest X-ray changes, renal/liver injury advisable. Urine uranium excretion used as exposure index; whole-body counting also useful. BUN for soluble compounds.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Soluble compounds (especially UF6): clothing to prevent any skin-contact possibility with UF6; eye protection; wash immediately when skin wet/contaminated with UF6 and daily at end of each shift; change work clothing daily if UF6 contamination possible; remove nonimpervious clothing immediately if wet/contaminated; emergency showers/eyewash for UF6. Insoluble compounds: gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Soluble uranium compounds: above NIOSH REL, or where no REL at any detectable conc.: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape (halides/nonhalides): 100F/SCBAE. Insoluble uranium compounds: above NIOSH REL, or where no REL at any detectable conc.: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: 100F/SCBAE.
storage: Radioactive. Red stripe: flammability hazard, separate from all other flammable materials. Yellow stripe (strong reducing agent): reactivity hazard, separate from flammables/combustibles/other yellow-coded materials. Regulated, marked area per OSHA Standard 1910.1045.
shipping: Uranium metal, pyrophoric: 'RADIOACTIVE, SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE' label; Class 7. Uranyl nitrate, solid: 'RADIOACTIVE, OXIDIZER' label; Class 7. Uranyl nitrate, hexahydrate solution: 'CORROSIVE' label; Class 7.
spill_handling: Dry material: evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; uranium chips/turnings covered with oil to prevent fires, collected in sealed containers for later disposal. Liquid: evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate; absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid sewers (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. Seek professional environmental engineering assistance from EPA's Environmental Response Team (ERT), Edison, NJ, 24h hotline 908-548-8730.
fire_extinguishing: Explosion hazard as dust or solid when exposed to flame. Contact local/state/DOE radiological response team. Do NOT use water. Use graphite, soda ash, powdered sodium chloride, or suitable dry powder. Poisonous gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Follow Nuclear Regulatory Commission guidelines for uranium waste; contact NRC regarding disposal notification. Recovery for reprocessing preferred; recovery processes available from wastewaters and process scrap. Burial at authorized radioactive burial site.
extraction_notes: References: EPA Toxicology of Metals Vol.II: Uranium, Report EPA-600/1-77-022 (May 1977), pp.454-472; Sax DPIM Vol2No.2 pp.78-79 (1982, Uranyl Acetate) & Vol4No.1 pp.99-102 (1984, Uranyl nitrate); ATSDR Toxicological Profile for Radium (1990); Bentor, Chemical Element.com—Radium (Nov 2010); OSHA Standard 29CFR1910.1096; EPA Manual of Protective Action Guides and Protective Actions for Nuclear Incidents (May 1992); DOE Radiological Emergency Response Health and Safety Manual, Report DOE/NV/11718-440 (May 2001); USAMRICD Field Management of Chemical Casualties, 2nd ed. Ceramics, cosmetics, paper processing, resins, adhesives, animal feeds; isocyanurate/resin/plastic manufacture; explosives stabilizer; medicines; other uses.

long_term_effects: Prolonged skin contact may cause dermatitis.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.

fire_extinguishing: Combustible solid. Dry chemical/CO2/water spray/foam extinguishers. Poisonous NOx gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.

extraction_notes: References: NY DOH Fact Sheet (Apr 1986); EPA Rainbow Report (1998). No UN/NA number or Medical Surveillance section (separate from First Aid) visible in source.

description: Colorless, almost odorless crystalline solid or powder.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Agricultural Chemical; Drug, Tumorigen, Mutagen; Reproductive Effector. Chemical intermediate for pharmaceutical/pesticide/fungicide manufacture; amino-resin preparation. May react with formaldehyde to give cross-linking agents imparting wash-and-wear fabric properties. Used as solubilizer/cosolvent in pesticide/fumigant/cosmetic manufacture. Formerly used to treat leukemia. Occurs when diethylpyrocarbonate (a wine/fruit-juice/soft-drink preservative) is added to aqueous solutions.
incompatibilities: Gallium, perchlorate, strong oxidizers.
dfg_mak: [skin]; Carcinogen Cat 2; Germ Cell Mutation Cat 3A (as carbamic acid ethyl ester).
other_national_oels: Austria/Finland/Sweden/Switzerland: carcinogen (1993-1999). US states 0-5000.0 μg/m3 (wide range).
determination_in_water: Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow=-0.15.
iarc_classification: Group 2A.
short_term_effects: Can affect via inhalation and skin passage. High exposures may affect CNS, causing dizziness, lightheadedness, unconsciousness. Very high exposures can damage liver, brain, blood-forming organs.
long_term_effects: Carcinogen, may be a teratogen — handle with extreme caution. Repeated exposures can damage liver, brain, blood-forming organs.
medical_surveillance: Before employment + regularly for frequent/high exposure: liver function tests, CBC. If symptoms/overexposure: nervous system exam.
first_aid: Skin: flood body areas contacted with water; remove contaminated clothing under water stream; use soap; isolate contaminated clothing. Eyes: remove contact lenses, flush with copious water/saline ≥20-30 min, seek care. Inhaled: leave area, breathe fresh air; rescuers need proper respiratory protection; seek care if coughing/breathing difficulty/other symptoms develop, even hours later. Swallowed: contact physician/hospital/poison center at once; if unconscious/convulsing, don't induce vomiting or give anything by mouth, ensure open airway, lay on side w/ head lower than body, transport immediately; if conscious/not convulsing, give water or milk to dilute; vomiting should not be induced without physician's advice.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Supplied-air respirator (positive-pressure/continuous-flow) or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure, per NIOSH/MSHA/EN149 approval.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Avoid strong oxidizers (chlorine, bromine, fluorine)/strong acids (HCl, sulfuric, nitric)/strong bases/camphor/menthol/salol/thymol — violent reactions. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated. Regulated, marked area per OSHA Standard 1910.1045.
shipping: Toxic solids, organic, n.o.s.: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Combustible solid. Dry chemical/CO2/water spray/alcohol foam extinguishers. Poisonous NOx gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Consult environmental regulatory agencies. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators). Controlled incineration (incinerator equipped with scrubber or thermal unit to reduce NOx emissions).
extraction_notes: References: EPA CHIP: Urethane (1979); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet (May 2001).

determination_in_water: Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow=1.31. See also NIOSH #2539 (Aldehydes, screening).
short_term_effects: Can affect via inhalation. Contact can severely irritate eyes/skin/nose/throat. Very high levels can cause dizziness, lightheadedness. Poisonous if swallowed.
long_term_effects: Carcinogenicity testing not completed for n-valeraldehyde. Limited studies indicate chemical reactivity/mutagenicity similar to acetaldehyde and malonaldehyde; NIOSH recommends careful consideration for exposure reduction. See NIOSH Current Intelligence Bulletin 55: Carcinogenicity of Acetaldehyde and Malonaldehyde, and Mutagenicity of Related Low-Molecular-Weight Aldehydes [DHHS (NIOSH) Publication #91-112].
medical_surveillance: See Long Term Exposure.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.

Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.

extraction_notes: Reference: NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet: Valeraldehyde (Nov 2000).

regulatory_authority: Carcinogenicity: DFG MAK Carcinogen Category 2. Air Pollutant Standard Set. Except when contained in an alloy: CWA §313 Water Priority Chemicals. carcinogenicity_status: DFG MAK: Carcinogen Category 2.
rcra_waste_numbers: Universal Treatment Standards: wastewater 4.3mg/L, nonwastewater 0.23mg/L (40CFR268.48; 61FR15654, except when contained in an alloy).
epcra_status: Section 313 de minimis 1.0%.

safe_drinking_water_act: Priority List (55 FR 1470, as vanadium).
international_regulations: Not listed in Annex 1.
description: Light-gray or silver-white ductile solid, lustrous powder, or fused hard lump. Produced by ore roasting, iodide thermal decomposition, or from petroleum residues/ferrovanadium-production slags/oil-burning soot. Vanadium carbide (CV): dark-gray powder, insoluble in water.
potential_exposure: Most vanadium produced is used in ferrovanadium, mainly for high-speed and other alloy steels (small amounts in tool/structural steels); usually combined with chromium, nickel, manganese, boron, tungsten in steel alloys. Vanadium carbide used in cutting-tool bits.
incompatibilities: Violent reaction with strong oxidizers: chlorine, bromine trifluoride, lithium, nitryl fluoride, chlorine trifluoride.
dfg_mak: Inhalable fraction; Carcinogen Cat 2; Germ cell mutagen group 2.
other_national_oels: Dust and fume: see Vanadium pentoxide entry.
human_health_water: No US drinking-water standard. EPA suggested permissible ambient goal 7μg/L (health-based). GI absorption of vanadium is extremely low, explaining the lack of acute/chronic oral-toxicity data; inhaled vanadium can produce adverse health effects. Russia MAC/limit 0.1mg/L water basins.
routes_of_entry: For dust and fume: inhalation, ingestion, skin/eye contact.
short_term_effects: Can affect via inhalation. May irritate eyes/nose/throat/air passages, w/ cough and phlegm. Eye contact may cause irritation (see also Vanadium Pentoxide). Ingestion: animal acute poisoning from vanadium compounds has shown nervous disturbances, leg paralysis, respiratory failure, convulsions, bloody diarrhea, coma, death.
long_term_effects: Can cause greenish-black tongue coloration and metallic taste. May cause eczema. Dust/fume may cause respiratory irritation; bronchitis may develop w/ cough, fine rales, wheezing, dyspnea (see also Vanadium Pentoxide).
medical_surveillance: For frequent/high exposure (≥half TLV): lung function tests before work + periodically. If symptoms/overexposure: urine vanadium test. EEC guideline: every-4-month workplace control at 50μg/L urine level, annual control at 5μg/L; workers should be temporarily removed from risk if levels exceed 50μg/L urine (see also Vanadium Pentoxide).
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: (as V) 0.5mg/m3: 100XQ/Sa. 1.25mg/m3: Sa:Cf/PaprHie. 2.5mg/m3: 100F/PaprHie/SCBAF/SaF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: 100F/SCBAE. Eye irritant — may need eye protection.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Avoid oxidizers (chlorates, nitrates, chlorine, bromine trifluoride) — violent reactions. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from heat/sparks. Nonsparking tools/equipment.
shipping: Vanadium compound, n.o.s.: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group I, II, or III.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Large pieces not combustible; fine powder can burn. Dry chemicals appropriate for metal fires. Do NOT use water. Poisonous vanadium oxide gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
extraction_notes: References: NIOSH Criteria for a Recommended Standard: Occupational Exposure to Vanadium, Document #77-222 (1977); National Academy of Sciences Medical and Biologic Effects of Environmental Pollutants: Vanadium (1974); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet: Vanadium (Jan 2007). No Disposal Method Suggested section visible in source.

regulatory_authority: Carcinogenicity: IARC human inadequate/animal sufficient evidence, possibly carcinogenic, Group 2B; NCI clear evidence (inhalation, dust, mouse/rat); NTP carcinogenesis studies (fume) on test (2-year study, Oct 2000). Hazard Symbol T, Xn; R20/22;R37;R48/23;R51/53;R63;R68; S1/2;S36/37;S38;S45;S61. WGK: 3.

description: Odorless, yellow to red crystal or powder (dust); finely divided particulate dispersed in air when vanadium is heated (fume).
potential_exposure: Compound Description (dust): Mutagen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data; Primary Irritant; (fume): Tumorigen. Industrial catalyst in oxidation reactions; glass/ceramic glazes; steel additive; welding-electrode coatings.
incompatibilities: Strong acids, lithium, chlorine trifluoride, peroxyformic acid, combustible substances.
niosh_rel: 0.05 mg[V]/m3 [15min] Ceiling (except vanadium metal and vanadium carbide).
acgih_tlv: Withdrawn.
dfg_mak: Carcinogen Cat 2; Germ cell mutagen group 2 (DFG 2005).
other_national_oels: (dust) Austria MAK0.05; Denmark TWA0.03[V]; Japan 0.5[V2O5]; Poland MAC(TWA)0.05/MAC(STEL)0.5; Switzerland MAK-W50ppm(175); UK TWA0.5[V] total inhalable/0.04[V] fume+respirable (1993-2000). (fume) Austria MAK0.05; Japan 0.1[V2O5]; Poland MAC(TWA)0.05/MAC(STEL)0.1; Sweden NGV0.2[V]; Switzerland MAK-W50ppm(175); UK TWA0.04[V] fume+respirable/TWA5 (1993-2000). determination_in_air: NIOSH #7300 (Elements by ICP); #7301; #7303; #7504 (Vanadium oxides); #9102; OSHA Method ID-185.
human_health_water: Russia limit 0.1mg/L for vanadium, maximum permissible limit for water basins.
iarc_classification: Group 2B.
ld50: Probable oral lethal dose (human) 5-50 mg/kg, between 7 drops and 1 teaspoon for a 70kg (150lb) person. Toxicity approximately equals pentavalent arsenic.
short_term_effects: Irritating to skin/eyes/mucous membranes. Blindness and epistaxis (bloody nose) further complications. Headache, dry mouth, dizziness, nervousness, insomnia, tremor may occur. Acute exposure may result in pulmonary irritation, bronchospasm, hemoptysis, emphysema, anorexia, black stools, pulmonary edema (delayed hours, can be fatal).
long_term_effects: May cause dermatitis, eczema, skin allergy. Repeated dust/fume inhalation may affect lungs; bronchitis may develop w/ cough, fine rales, wheezing, dyspnea. May cause green staining of tongue and skin.
medical_surveillance: Before employment + regularly: lung function tests. If symptoms/overexposure: allergist evaluation for skin allergy diagnosis, consider chest X-ray after acute overexposure, urine vanadium test. EEC guideline: every-4-month workplace control at 50μg/L urine level, annual control at 5μg/L; workers should be temporarily removed from risk if levels exceed 50μg/L urine. OSHA specifically regulated substance — see NIOSH Publication #2005-110 (Dec 2004).
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Observe 24-48h post-inhalation; corticosteroid spray may be considered.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: (as V) 0.5mg/m3: 100XQ/Sa. 1.25mg/m3: Sa:Cf/PaprHie. 2.5mg/m3: 100F/PaprHie/SCBAF/SaF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: 100F/SCBAE. Eye irritant — may need eye protection.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Avoid chlorine trifluoride/lithium/peroxyformic acid — violent reactions. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from heat.
shipping: Vanadium pentoxide, nonfused form: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; don't touch spilled material, stop leak if safe; water spray to reduce vapors. Small spills: sand/noncombustible absorbent material. Small dry spills: clean shovel into clean dry container, cover, move from spill area. Large spills: dike far ahead for later disposal. Ventilate; hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Not combustible but will increase existing fire intensity, especially in combustible-material contact. Use agent suitable for surrounding fire. Poisonous vanadium oxide gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Consult environmental regulatory agencies. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators). May be salvaged or disposed of in a sanitary landfill.
extraction_notes: References: EPA CHIP: Vanadium Pentoxide (Nov 1987); Sax DPIM Vol2No.2 pp.83-84 (1982) & Vol8No.4 pp.81-92 (1988); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet: Vanadium Pentoxide (Oct 1998).
