description: Sulfinated organophosphorus nerve agent; the most toxic of all known chemical warfare agents, capable of causing death within minutes. Colorless to straw to amber-colored, odorless liquid resembling motor oil. Volatility 8.9-10.5 mg/m3/25°C. Vapor density (air=1) 9.2.
potential_exposure: Quick-acting military chemical nerve agent; the most potent of all chemical warfare agents, attacking the nervous system and causing uncontrollable muscle convulsion. Works similarly to pesticides; originally developed in the early 1950s. Highly persistent — can be dangerous for weeks, remains liquid for over 24h. Poses little vapor hazard; the least volatile nerve agent, evaporating about as slowly as motor oil. Highly efficient at skin penetration, more so than other 'G' agents. Used in the M-23 land mine. Never used in combat by the United States; all US stockpiles (~4400 tons) were destroyed in 2008 by the US Army Chemical Materials Agency (CMA). Persistence: Summer 2 days to a week; Winter 2 days to weeks.
incompatibilities: Contact with metals may evolve flammable hydrogen gas. Relatively stable at room temperature. Unstabilized VX (95% purity) decomposed at 5%/month at 71°C. At pH 12, the toxic by-product has a ~14-day half-life, with ~64-fold reduction over 90 days.
other_national_oels: STEL 0.00001 mg/m3. Worker Population Limit (WPL) 0.000001 mg/m3. Suggested permissible airborne exposure: 8h TWA 0.00001 mg/m3 (9×10⁻⁷ ppm), per USAEHA Technical Guide #169. General Population Limit (GPL) 0.0000006 mg/m3.
determination_in_air: M8/M9 detector paper, ACADA, detector ticket; M256/M256A1 kits; bubbler; Depot Area Air Monitoring System (DAAMS); Automated Continuous Air Monitoring System (ACMS); Real-Time Monitor (RTM); Demilitarization Chemical Agent Concentrator (DCAC); M8/M43, M8A1/M43A1, CAM-M1, Hydrogen Flame Photometric Emission Detector (HYFED); Miniature Chemical Agent Monitor (MINICAM).
human_health_water: No criteria set.
determination_in_water: Octanol-water coefficient: LogKow (estimated)=2.06. Hydrolyzes only slowly; hydrolysis products include EA2192 (nearly as toxic as VX, hydrolyzed >1000× more slowly). Common bleach (NaOCl) or superchlorinated bleach/calcium hypochlorite (HTH) oxidation will decontaminate.
ld50: Lowest toxic oral dose (human, TDLO) 4 mg/kg; lowest lethal skin dose (human, LDLO) 86 mg/kg; death within 15min of fatal-dose absorption. Also reported: median human doses LC50(skin) 0.135 mg/kg; ID LC50(skin) 0.07-0.71 mg/kg; LCt50(inhalation) 30 mg-min/m3 (also reported 24 mg-min/m3).
short_term_effects: Summary: exposure can result in unconsciousness, convulsions, paralysis, respiratory failure, death. Acts as a cholinesterase inhibitor. One to several minutes after airborne overexposure: local effects (lasting 1-15 days, dose-dependent) — eyes: miosis, redness, pressure sensation; inhalation: rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, chest tightness, wheezing, salivation, nausea, vomiting. Systemic effects (dose-dependent): excessive secretion causing coughing/breathing difficulty, salivation/sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, involuntary urination/defecation, generalized muscle twitching/cramps, CNS depression (anxiety, restlessness, giddiness, insomnia, excessive dreaming, nightmares); more severe exposure adds headache, tremor, drowsiness, concentration difficulty, memory impairment, confusion, unsteadiness, and may progress to death. After liquid exposure: local effects — eyes (miosis, redness, pressure); ingestion (salivation, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, involuntary defecation, heartburn); skin (sweating, muscle twitching). Systemic effects similar to airborne-exposure effects.
long_term_effects: Chronic overexposure causes forgetfulness, thinking difficulty, vision disturbances, muscular aches/pains (per US Army). Organophosphate pesticides have shown animal teratogenicity, but this has not been documented in carefully controlled VX toxicological evaluations.
medical_surveillance: Chemical Agent Monitor (CAM) can detect VX at 0.1 mg/m3. US military detectors: M256A1 Chemical Agent Detector Kit, M8A1 Automatic Chemical Agent Alarm.
first_aid: Immediate decontamination of even the smallest drop is essential; use M291 Skin Decontamination Kit. Inhalation: hold breath until respiratory protective mask donned; if severe exposure signs appear (chest tightness, pupil constriction, coordination loss), immediately administer all three Nerve Agent Antidote Kit Mark 1 injectors in rapid succession (or atropine per local physician direction); may repeat at 5-20min intervals if symptoms progress, up to three series; no further injections without medical direction; maintain injection record; give artificial respiration if breathing stopped (avoid mouth-to-mouth with facial contamination); administer oxygen if breathing difficult; seek care immediately. Eyes: flush with water 10-15min, then don respiratory protective mask; miosis alone does not warrant injection — take to medical facility for observation instead. Skin: don respirator/protective mask, remove contaminated clothing, immediately wash with 5% household bleach solution, rinse well with water then soap and water; administer Mark I antidote kit only if local sweating/muscular twitching present; seek care immediately. Ingestion: do not induce vomiting (first symptoms likely GI); immediately administer Mark I antidote kit; seek care immediately. Medical observation recommended. Medical treatment: ECG and respiration/ventilation adequacy monitored; supplemental oxygenation, frequent secretion suctioning, endotracheal intubation, assisted ventilation may be required; diazepam (5-10mg adults, 0.2-0.5mg/kg children) may control convulsions; lorazepam/other benzodiazepines may be used (barbiturates, phenytoin, other anticonvulsants ineffective); atropine (if not already given) should precede benzodiazepines for best seizure control; inhalation-exposed patients with chest pain/tightness/cough should be observed 6-12h for delayed bronchitis, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or respiratory failure. Decontamination: rapid physical agent removal is essential; untrained/unequipped responders should not enter hot/warm zones; medical personnel wear proper PPE; decontaminate immobile victims without touching or entering hot/warm zone; nerve agents persist in clothing — avoid bare-skin contact, seal contaminated clothing/belongings in sealed double bag; use clean water (hose spray/fog to avoid touching victim) immediately without waiting for soap or clothing removal; use cold water rather than delaying for warm water; flush eyes ≥15min; avoid hypothermia in children/elderly. Wash-strip-wash-evacuate upwind/uphill: vapor-only exposure — remove all clothing in clean air, shampoo/rinse hair to prevent off-gassing; liquid exposure — wash in available clean water ≥3 times using liquid soap (dispose/replace container), large water volumes, mild-to-moderate friction with single-use sponge/washcloth for first two washes (avoid brush scrubbing — may worsen absorption via skin damage), third wash with large warm/hot water, shampoo for hair; may decontaminate with diluted household bleach (0.5%, one part bleach to 200 parts water), avoiding eyes/wounds/mouth, washed off after 15min. Decontamination water is itself dangerous — ensure victims are adequately decontaminated before release to avoid spreading agent. Rinse eyes/mucous membranes/open wounds with sterile saline or water, then move upwind/uphill away from hot zone. Additional decontaminants beyond household bleach: bleach solids/powders/solutions (NaOCl or Ca(OCl)2); DS2 (2% NaOH, 70% diethylenetriamine, 28% ethylene glycol monomethyl ether); NaOH-moistened towelettes with phenol/ethanol/ammonia. Use 5% bleach or calcium hypochlorite solution (48oz/5gal water) to decontaminate clothing-removal scissors and other items.
personal_protective_methods: Emergency situations: 'moon suit' — positive-pressure, pressure-demand, full-face-piece SCBA or pressure-demand supplied-air respirator with escape cylinder, combined with fully encapsulating chemical-resistant suit maintaining positive internal air pressure. Protective gloves: butyl M3/M4, Norton chemical protective glove set. Eye protection: chemical goggles; goggles+face shield for splash hazards. Other: full protective clothing consists of M9 mask/hood, M3 butyl rubber suit, M2A1 butyl boots, M3/M4 gloves, unimpregnated underwear, or demilitarization protective ensemble (DPE). Laboratory operations: lab coats with protective mask readily available; daily clean smock, foot/head covers required when handling contaminated lab animals.
respirator_selection: When used as a weapon: NIOSH CBRN-certified SCBA. <0.00001mg/m3: M9/M17/M40 series mask available for escape. 0.00001-0.02mg/m3: M9/M40 series mask with Level A or B ensemble. >0.02mg/m3: DPE or TAPES with prior AMC Field Safety Activity approval (M9/M40 with Level A ensemble usable if DPE/TAPES unavailable, time-restricted to ≤1h, with M3-suit cuffs/legs taped to gloves/boots). Local exhaust mandatory, filtered/scrubbed to <0.00001mg/m3 (8h/day average, indefinitely). Chemical laboratory hoods: average inward face velocity 100lf/m ±10%, no point deviating >20% from average; located to keep cross-drafts ≤20% of inward face velocity; visual smoke-test performance verification required; semiannual testing; operations performed 20cm inside hood face; no exhaust-air recirculation from agent areas; no ventilation-system connection between agent and other areas.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Buddy system for handling. No smoking/eating/drinking in agent areas. Periodic container leak inspection (visual or detector kit). Stringent personnel-practice control. Decontamination equipment conveniently located. Rapid-evacuation exit design. Chemical showers/eyewash/personal-cleanliness facilities provided. Wash hands before meals; thorough end-of-shift shower with attention to hair/face/neck/hands and plenty of soap. Agent double-contained in liquid- and vapor-tight containers during storage or outside ventilation hood. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from heat. No smoking/open flames.
shipping: Toxic, liquids, organic, n.o.s.: 'POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 6.1, Packing Group III. Driver given full shipment/emergency information. AR 50-6 governs chemical-agent shipment; escort per AR 740-32.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate; absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; avoid sewers (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. If decontamination kit unavailable, decontaminants include bleach slurry and hot soapy water. Isolation (weapon-use scenario, first 30min, may increase w/ time) — small: 100ft/30m, downwind 0.1-0.1mi day/night; large: 200ft/60m, downwind 0.2-0.3mi day/0.5mi night. Seek CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or EPA Environmental Response Team (908-548-8730) for larger incidents.
fire_extinguishing: Heated vapors may form explosive air mixtures — explosion hazard indoors/outdoors/in sewers; containers may explode when heated; use moon suit/respirator protection. Poisonous NOx/sulfur oxide gases produced. Extinguishing media: water mist/fog/foam/CO2 — avoid methods causing VX splashing/spreading. All non-firefighting personnel evacuated immediately; fires contained to prevent uncontrolled-area contamination. Full firefighter protective clothing (without TAP clothing) worn during chemical-agent firefighting/rescue; respiratory protection required — positive-pressure full-face-piece NIOSH-approved SCBA worn where oxygen deficiency risk exists or per fire chief/CAI officer direction (M9/M17 series mask acceptable when no oxygen-deficiency danger). Rescue/reconnaissance responders wear appropriate protective-clothing levels; do not breathe fumes; V-agent skin contact must always be avoided. Fire may destroy most agent, but care must prevent further contamination of other areas/sewers. VX/VX-vapor contact can be fatal. Vapors heavier than air, collect in low areas. Containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: This entry describes standard published field/laboratory detoxification and destruction procedures, not synthesis or weaponization information. Field procedures (quantities >50g, requiring qualified-expert/safety-officer approval): prepare alcoholic calcium hypochlorite (HTH) mixture (100mL denatured ethanol + 900mL 10% HTH slurry in water, made just before use); use 14g of this mixture per gram of VX, agitating during VX addition and for ≥1h minimum (reaction is exothermic with substantial off-gassing — route evolved gases through a decontaminant-filled scrubber before filtered release); after agitation, add 10% sodium hydroxide to maintain pH 12.5 for ≥24h, then hold pH 10-12 for ≥90 days to prevent hazardous intermediate formation; decontaminate/label drum exterior per EPA/DOT regulations; overpack leaking containers with vermiculite between interior/exterior containers; conduct area air monitoring to confirm compliance with airborne exposure limits. If HTH mixture unavailable, alternative decontaminants in order of preference: DS2 (2% NaOH, 70% diethylenetriamine, 28% ethylene glycol monomethyl ether), Supertropical Bleach Slurry (STB), sodium hypochlorite. Open-pit burning or burying of VX or VX-contaminated items in any quantity is prohibited. Detoxified VX may be thermally destroyed by incineration in an EPA-approved incinerator per RCRA provisions. Several states classify decontaminated surety material as RCRA Hazardous Waste. Laboratory procedures (quantities <50g): if HTH active chlorine ≥55%, use 80g of 10% slurry per gram VX (proportionally more if chlorine activity <55%); agitate during addition and for ≥1h minimum; if phasing continues past 5min, add denatured ethanol (10wt% of total agent/decon) to assist miscibility (minimize ethanol to avoid hazardous-waste formation); after 1h agitation, adjust mixture to pH 10-11; conduct area air monitoring to confirm compliance.

target_organs: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, CNS, GI tract, blood, liver, kidneys.
short_term_effects: Inhalation: vapor irritates nose/throat. Above 200ppm/3-5min can cause xylene intoxication (headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting); continued exposure adds CNS depression (shallow breathing, weak pulse). 230ppm/15min may cause lightheadedness without equilibrium loss. Reversible liver/kidney damage in humans has followed sudden high-vapor-concentration exposure; such levels may also cause lung congestion. ≥10,000ppm can cause strong narcotic effect: slurred speech, stupor, fatigue, confusion, unconsciousness, coma, possible death. Skin: vapor/liquid contact causes defatting, leading to irritation, drying, cracking. Eyes: vapor/liquid may irritate eye/eyelids at 100ppm/15min. Ingestion: immediate mouth/throat burning; stomach/intestine irritation with sharp pains; symptoms similar to inhalation except lung congestion usually doesn't develop.
long_term_effects: Inhalation of vapor and skin contact with liquid are the most probable long-term exposure routes. Inhalation symptoms: dizziness, headache, nausea. Long-term exposure associated with liver/kidney damage, intestinal-tract disturbances, CNS depression. Prolonged skin contact can lead to irritation, dryness, cracking. Repeated exposure can cause poor memory, concentration difficulty, other brain effects, and eye-surface damage.
points_of_attack: Eyes, skin, respiratory system, CNS, GI tract, blood, liver, kidneys.
medical_surveillance: Whole blood chemical/metabolite (incl. end-of-shift), CBC (incl. hematopoietic depression), expired air, urine chemical/metabolite (incl. end-of-shift, end-of-workweek, last 4h of 8h exposure), routine UA. For frequent/high exposure (≥half TLV or significant skin contact): slit-lamp eye exam before work + periodically. If symptoms/overexposure: liver/kidney function tests, urine m-methylhippuric acid concentration (end-of-shift) as overexposure index.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: if conscious, water or milk (no induced vomiting). Note to physician: may require supportive measures for pulmonary edema.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing (Viton, polyvinyl alcohol, Teflon recommended) to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: 900ppm: CcrOv/PaprOv/Sa/SCBAF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: GmFOv/SCBAE. Eye irritant — may need eye protection.
storage: Red: flammability hazard, flammable-liquid area/cabinet away from ignition/corrosive/reactive materials. Avoid strong oxidizers (chlorine, bromine, fluorine) — violent reactions. No smoking/open flames; nonsparking tools. Protect from physical damage.
shipping: 'FLAMMABLE LIQUID' label; Class 3, Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate/restrict unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; ventilate; absorb liquids in vermiculite/sand/earth/peat/carbon, seal containers; oil-skimming equipment/sorbent foams applicable to slicks if done immediately; avoid sewers (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Flammable liquid; poisonous gases produced. Dry chemical/CO2/alcohol foam extinguishers. Vapors heavier than air, may travel far to ignition sources, flashback risk; confined-area vapors may explode w/ fire; containers may explode/rocket. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
disposal_method: Consult environmental regulatory agencies. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators). Incineration.

Skin: wash with large water/soapy water until odor gone; then wash with alcohol or 20% glycerin solution + more water; keep warm but not hot; cover chemical burns continuously with sodium thiosulfate-saturated compresses; no salves/ointments for 24h after injury. short_term_effects: Can affect via inhalation. Zinc dust particles can irritate eyes. clean_ water_act: §311 Hazardous Substances/RQ (40CFR117.3); §401.15 Toxic Pollutant; §313 Water Priority Chemicals (57FR41331, 9/9/92).
description: Gray crystalline solid.
potential_exposure: Compound Description: Agricultural Chemical; Mutagen; Reproductive Effector; Human Data. Acute single-feeding rodenticide.
incompatibilities: Heat and water contact cause decomposition, producing toxic/flammable phosphorus fumes, zinc oxides, and toxic/flammable phosphine gas. Violent reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid, nitric acid, other oxidizers. Reacts with hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, evolving spontaneously flammable phosphine gas. Incompatible with carbon dioxide, halogenated agents.
other_national_oels: Russia TWA 0.1 mg/m3 (1993).
determination_in_air: #7502 (Zinc and compounds); OSHA Methods ID-121, ID-143.
human_health_water: Global standards: EC 100-500μg/L drinking water; Germany 2000μg/L drinking water; Russia 5000μg/L drinking water/1000μg/L surface water/10μg/L fishery-purpose water; WHO 5000μg/L esthetic quality. EPA 5mg/L (5000μg/L) organoleptic-property prevention. Kansas 5mg/L drinking water limit.
ld50: Probable oral lethal dose 5-50 mg/kg, between 7 drops and 1 teaspoon for a 70kg (150lb) person. Ingestion of 4-5g has produced death in human adults (25-50g doses have been survived). Lowest oral lethal dose reported for women: 80mg/kg.
routes_of_entry: Inhalation, ingestion, eye/skin contact. Absorbed through skin.
target_organs: Lungs, liver, kidneys, heart, blood, nervous system.
short_term_effects: Irritates resp tract. Eye contact can cause severe irritation, burns, permanent damage. Skin contact causes irritation. CNS depressant. Dust inhalation followed in several hours by vomiting, diarrhea, cyanosis, rapid pulse, fever, shock; breath smells of phosphine; very caustic, may cause esophagus closure. Phosphine inhalation (formed on flame/water/acid exposure) can cause pulmonary edema (delayed hours, can be fatal). Very caustic when ingested, forms phosphine; most patients die ~30h post-ingestion from peripheral vascular collapse secondary to compound's direct effects; extensive liver/kidney damage can also occur. Oral symptoms: nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, chest tightness, excitement, agitation, chills, faintness, weakness, dyspnea, blood-pressure drop, pulse-rate change, diarrhea, intense thirst, convulsions, paralysis, coma. Early labored breathing, shock, halted urinary output, metabolic acidosis, muscle cramps, convulsions are grave prognostic signs.
long_term_effects: May affect liver, kidneys, heart, nervous system. Repeated low exposures cause chronic poisoning, anemia, bronchitis, GI/visual/speech/motor disturbances.
points_of_attack: Lungs, liver, kidneys, heart, blood, nervous system.
medical_surveillance: Liver/kidney function tests. EKG. Lung function tests. Consider chest X-ray following acute overexposure. CBC.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: seek care for phosphine, remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: seek care for phosphine poisoning; give 1 tbsp mustard in warm water, repeat until vomit fluid clear, avoid oils (no induced vomiting if unconscious). Observe 24-48h post-inhalation (pulmonary edema may be delayed); corticosteroid spray may be considered. Note to physician: for severe poisoning, do not use BAL (British Anti-Lewisite, dimercaprol) — contraindicated/ineffective for zinc poisoning.
personal_protective_methods: Gloves/clothing to prevent skin contact; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: Respirator w/ particulate (dust/fume/mist) filters (checked daily for damage, replaced as needed). High exposures: supplied-air respirator (positive-pressure/continuous-flow) or SCBA full face-piece positive-pressure.
storage: Blue: poison, secure location. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from moisture and oxidizers.
shipping: 'DANGEROUS WHEN WET, POISONOUS/TOXIC MATERIALS' label; Class 4.3, Packing Group I.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; do NOT use water; keep sparks/flames/ignition sources away; keep out of water sources/sewers; keep dry; avoid breathing dusts/fumes from burning material; stay upwind; avoid bodily contact; don't handle broken packages without PPE; wash contacted skin thoroughly. Land spill: dig pit/pond/lagoon/holding area to contain material. Water spill: neutralize with agricultural lime, crushed limestone, or sodium bicarbonate; use mechanical dredges/lifts to remove immobilized wastes/precipitates. Small dry spills: clean shovel into clean dry container, cover, move from area. Large spills: dike for later disposal, cover powder with plastic sheet/tarp; clean up only under expert supervision. Hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies. UN1714 zinc phosphide is on DOT's dangerous water-reactive materials list (creates large toxic vapor amounts when spilled in water); dangerous from 0.5-10km (0.3-6.0mi) downwind.
fire_extinguishing: Do NOT use water or foam (liberates phosphine). Small fires: dry chemical, soda ash, or lime. Large fires: withdraw and let burn. Do not use any acid-reaction agent (CO2 or halogenated agents). Poisonous phosphine/zinc oxide/phosphorus gases produced. Boots, protective gloves, goggles; SCBA for firefighters. Keep unnecessary people away; isolate hazard area; stay upwind; move containers from fire area if safe.
disposal_method: Consult environmental regulatory agencies. Conform to EPA waste regs (≥100 kg/mo generators).
extraction_notes: References: EPA CHIP: Zinc Phosphide (Nov 1987); EPA Rainbow Report (1998); NJ DOHSS Fact Sheet: Zinc Phosphide (May 2000).

Other compounds: Zirconium boride (12045-64-6); Zirconium carbide (12070-14-3); Zirconium chloride (10026-11-6); Zirconium fluoride (7783-64-4); Zirconium hydride (7704-99-6); Zirconium hydroxide (14475-63-9); Zirconium nitrate (13746-89-9); Zirconium nitride (25658-42-8); Zirconium oxide (1314-23-4); Zirconium phosphide (12037-80-8); Zirconium oxychloride (7699-43-6); Zirconyl chloride (10026-11-6).

description: Grayish-white, lustrous metal as platelets, flakes, or bluish-black amorphous powder. Powdered metal is a fire/explosion hazard — may ignite spontaneously, can continue burning under water. Never found free in nature; most common sources are ores zircon and baddeleyite. Generally produced by chloride or iodide reduction; the metal is very reactive, production carried out under inert-gas atmosphere.
potential_exposure: 'Getter' in vacuum tubes; metallurgy deoxidizer; platinum substitute; explosive-mixture priming; flashlight powders; lamp filaments; flash bulbs; rayon-spinneret construction. Zirconium/alloys (nickel, cobalt, niobium, tantalum) used as pump/pipe lining materials for chemical processes and reaction vessels. Pure zirconium: atomic-reactor structural material; alloyed (particularly with aluminum), a cladding material for water-moderated nuclear reactor fuel rods. Zirconium-columbium alloy: excellent superconductor. Zircon (ZrSiO4): foundry sand, abrasive, refractory (with zirconia), casting-mold coating, alkyl/alkenyl hydrocarbon manufacture catalyst, silicone-rubber stabilizer, gemstone; ceramics glaze/enamel opacifier, fritted glass filters. Zircon and zirconia (zirconium oxide, ZrO2) bricks: glass-furnace linings. Zirconia: metal die extrusion, metal-pouring spout linings, oxyhydrogen-flame lime substitute, pigment, abrasive, incandescent lights, enamel/white-glass/refractory-crucible manufacture. Other zirconium compounds: metal cutting tools, thermocouple jackets, textile waterproofing, ceramics, dermatitis/poison-ivy treatment.
incompatibilities: Violent reactions with oxidizers, air, alkali hydroxides, alkali metal compounds (chromates, dichromates, molybdates, salts, sulfates, tungstates), borax, carbon tetrachloride, lead, lead oxide, phosphorus, potassium compounds. Incompatible with boron, carbon, nitrogen, halogens, lead, platinum, potassium nitrate. Powder may ignite spontaneously, continue burning under water. Explodes if mixed with hydrated borax when heated. Fine powder may be stored completely immersed in water.
niosh_rel: 5 mg[Zr]/m3 TWA; 10 mg/m3 STEL (applies to all zirconium compounds as Zr except zirconium tetrachloride).
acgih_tlv: (elemental & zirconium compounds) 5 mg[Zr]/m3 TWA; 10 mg/m3 STEL; not classifiable as human carcinogen.
dfg_mak: (elemental and insoluble compounds) 1 mg/m3 inhalable fraction TWA; Peak Cat I(1); danger of airway/skin sensitization; Pregnancy Grp. (soluble compounds): danger of airway/skin sensitization.
other_national_oels: Egypt TWA5; Austria MAK5; Denmark TWA5[Zr]; Finland TWA5; Hungary STEL5; Poland MAC(TWA)5/MAC(STEL)10; Russia STEL6; Netherlands MAC-TGG 5 (1993-2003). ACGIH TLV countries: STEL10mg/m3. US states 0.8-119.0 μg/m3.
determination_in_air: NIOSH #7300 (Elements by ICP); #8005 (Elements in blood/tissue); see also OSHA Method ID-121.
human_health_water: No criteria set.
short_term_effects: Can affect via inhalation. Dust can irritate lungs, causing coughing and/or shortness of breath.
long_term_effects: Contact can cause allergic skin reaction with small nodules (granulomas). May cause chest X-ray changes, lung granulomas. Animals: skin/mucous-membrane irritation, X-ray evidence of lung retention.
medical_surveillance: If symptoms/overexposure: allergist evaluation for skin allergy diagnosis. If breathing problems occur, consider lung function tests and chest X-ray.
first_aid: Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious).
personal_protective_methods: Skin protection not generally necessary but probably advisable, especially with a history of zircon granuloma from deodorants. Gloves/clothing recommended per supplier guidance; no contact lenses; dust-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respirator; wash if contaminated; emergency shower/eyewash.
respirator_selection: 25mg/m3: Qm. 50mg/m3: 95XQ/PaprHie/100F/Sa/SCBAF. Unknown/IDLH: SCBAF:Pd,Pp or SaF:Pd,Pp:ASCBA. Escape: 100F/SCBAE.
storage: Red stripe (powder): flammability hazard, separate from all other flammable materials. Avoid oxidizers (perchlorates, peroxides, permanganates, chlorates, nitrates) — violent reactions. Tightly closed, cool, ventilated, away from flammable materials. No smoking/open flames; ≥5-gal metal containers grounded/bonded; self-closing valves/pressure-vacuum bungs/flame arresters on drums; nonsparking tools; explosion-proof electrical.
shipping: Dry zirconium powder: 'SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE' label; Class 4.2, Packing Group II.
spill_handling: Evacuate unprotected persons; remove ignition sources; collect powder, seal containers; ventilate; avoid sewers (explosion risk); hazardous-waste disposal may apply; notify downstream water users; OSHA 1910.120(q) applies.
fire_extinguishing: Flammable powder; fire may restart after extinguishing; containers may explode. Dry chemicals appropriate for metal fires, salt, dry sand. Do NOT use water. Poisonous gases produced. Cool containers from secure location; SCBA for firefighters.
